Thats weird-Ive always seen this notice prior to bidding and eBay won't let me bid until I change addresses. 

I then switch my address to my cousins address and it will let me checkout.

My cousin doesn't reply to my text until the next morning giving me approval to ship to his address. I go to checkout and once again I get the message that seller won't ship to me.

I run the scenario through Google AI and apparently this is a tactic that sellers can use to essentially cancel an auction on their end without getting negative feedback.

🚗 $OUST : Strong Results + Utah Expansion Fuel 7.7% Move

 $OUST (Ouster) is up 7.7% today, driven by strong Q2 results, continued lidar demand and a major expansion of its Utah traffic-management contract. Ouster reported Q2 revenue of $55M, up 56% YoY, while product revenue has now grown for 14 consecutive quarters and shipments exceeded 17,000 lidar and camera units. Q3 guidance is $54.5M–$57.5M, suggesting demand remains strong.

The latest catalyst came on August 11, when Ouster announced a multimillion-dollar Utah expansion covering another 160 intersections, bringing its total contracted Utah footprint to nearly 300 deployments. This is important because Ouster’s BlueCity traffic platform is moving toward larger-scale deployments.

💰 Balance Sheet

Ouster ended Q2 with approximately $263M in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and short-term investments. A July equity offering strengthened the balance sheet further, although investors should consider the potential dilution. The market currently appears more focused on revenue growth, improving margins, liquidity and execution.

🏦 Institutional Activity

Institutional activity is mixed. 210 institutions increased their OUST positions, while 112 reduced them. Major additions included JPMorgan +728,688 shares (~$45.6M), Sixth Street Partners +533,951 shares (~$33.4M) and Morgan Stanley +510,920 shares (~$31.9M). Mirae Asset also added approximately 491,332 shares. Crypto slang: WAGMI, NGMI, GM, and 62 more words

A normal slang dictionary explains what words mean. This one also says when each word was first recorded, and those records differ from the common origin story by years.

Main points

“WAGMI” means “we’re all gonna make it,” “NGMI” means “not gonna make it,” and “GM” is just “good morning.” Those three words carry an entire social contract: optimism as belonging, exclusion as punishment, and a daily roll call.
The usual story puts WAGMI and NGMI in the 2021 NFT boom. In the /biz/ archive, NGMI is already being used as an insult on August 3, 2017, and WAGMI on July 28, 2018: the records are 45 and 30 months earlier than the usual version.
“Diamond hands” is usually tied to GameStop and January 2021. On /biz/, a trader used it to describe surviving the Mt. Gox crash on May 31, 2017, almost four years earlier.
“Rug pull” is usually treated as a DeFi summer 2020 word. On the board it appears as “rugpull” on December 16, 2017, in the middle of the ICO wave that the phrase actually describes better.
Of 55 checked words, only 15 could be dated. Thirteen were already in use in the first week of the archive, and 22 matched a post with a completely different meaning: the earliest “gm” on the board is General Motors, and the earliest “sniper” is a computer game.
The newest layer of slang has nothing to do with 2021. “Trenches,” “CTO,” “bundled,” “sniper,” and “PVP” came from Solana memecoin launches and describe execution mechanics, not feelings.
The desk’s conclusion: slang is a speed protocol, not a personality. It compresses position, horizon, and risk tolerance into one syllable, and the words that survive are the ones that describe how people lose money.

What was measured

The article checked 55 words in the open /biz/ archive on 4chan, found the earliest archived post for each word, read the post, and kept the date only when the word was used in the intended meaning. The full dictionary behind the measure contains 65 words across five layers, and the dates differ from the accepted history by years.

“NGMI” appears as an insult on August 3, 2017, in a one-line post: “If you have to ask, you're ngmi.” Know Your Meme places NGMI’s arrival in crypto in a Reddit post from May 2021. The gap is 45 months.

What was measured

The measurement is intentionally narrow, so its limits matter before the numbers do.

The corpus is the warosu /biz/ archive, the 4chan business and finance board where a large part of this slang was already in daily use before it reached Twitter. The first day of the archive is February 13, 2014, and that was measured by the same search using the control word “bitcoin.” Anything in use before that date is invisible to this study: it appears in the first week and cannot be dated.

Search matches strings, not meanings, so each early post was opened and read by a human before its date was accepted. That step removed 22 words out of 55. The earliest “gm” on the board was about General Motors, the earliest “sniper” was about a computer game, the earliest “nfa” was about the National Futures Association, and the earliest “maxi” was an Australian posting about cereal advertising.

Four multiword phrases did not match at all, because the archive search looks for words, not phrases: “paper hands,” “up only,” “when lambo,” and “few understand” got no confirmation and were dated in the dictionary from outside sources rather than from this archive.

One word was found, dated, and intentionally removed. It is common, and its origin is an ethnic slur, so it is not included in the dictionary. Saying that out loud is more honest than leaving a blank and calling the list complete.

In the /biz/ archive, 55 words were checked. Only the middle column can be dated: the first was already in use before the archive began, and the last two are limits of the search, not of the language.

What the archive can say

The archive can say something specific about 55 words. The first column shows months after the archive opened; the second is what can actually be dated.

Citations

Sixteen words have an earliest archived post that uses the word in the meaning this article is discussing. The quotes are copied exactly from the linked posts, including typos, and trimmed at sentence boundaries. Nothing has been paraphrased.

English is left in the quotes on purpose: it is the word itself that is being dated, and translation would erase the point of the citation.

Two lines are worth reading twice.
Diamond hands, May 31, 2017. In the post, the writer says they sold 6 BTC at $200 with an average entry of $400 after the Mt. Gox hack, and that they have held everything since. That is exactly the modern meaning of the phrase in crypto talk, three years and eight months before the GameStop squeeze that dictionaries usually attach it to.
Rug pull, December 16, 2017. “hmmm a rugpull on the new chasers is definitely possible.” The phrase is usually assigned to DeFi summer 2020. It was already a compound noun during the ICO mania.
An upward bar means the word appeared on the board earlier than the origin date usually given. The only downward bar is HODL: it was coined on bitcointalk two months before this archive begins, and here it is the only one whose documented birth is older than the board itself.
HODL’s origin
HODL was posted on bitcointalk on December 18, 2013 by GameKyuubi, who immediately explained the typo in the thread with the line: “I type d that tyitle twice because I knew it was wrong the first time. Still wrong w/e.” The word reaches /biz/ two months later.
The dictionary, five layers
The rest is the dictionary itself. It is arranged not alphabetically, but by what the words do, because that division is the point: market language begins with feeling and ends with mechanics.
The 65 words explained in the article are grouped by function. The split is editorial: it comes from reading the words, not from the archive. The last two layers describe structure, not feeling, and the memecoin layer gained its eleven words in just two years.
Greeting layer
These words do not carry information. They mark belonging, and that is the whole job.
gm. Good morning, and more like a daily roll call than a greeting. You post gm, someone replies gm, and the ritual says the group is present. The earliest use in NFT circles that Know Your Meme can show is a tweet from March 2018; the habit entered broad crypto-Twitter use in 2021. The archive cannot date it, because “gm” is also a car company.
gn. Good night, the same ritual at the other end of the day. The first archive use in this sense is March 5, 2014.
ser. A deliberately misspelled “sir,” a way to address a stranger with joking politeness. It came from crypto chats in Telegram and Discord and stuck because it works both ways at once: respectful and obviously not.
fren. Friend, spelled the way it appears in Pepe comics. On the board it shows up on October 25, 2016: “Well mem'ed my fren.”
anon. Short for anonymous, meaning “you, the person I am addressing.” Everyone is anon until they become someone.
CT. Crypto Twitter, the sleepless argument machine that produced much of this slang. It now also refers to the same crowd on X.
iykyk. “If you know, you know,” a hint without explanation. In the archive it appears on May 11, 2019, as a single word in an empty post.
touch grass. “Go touch grass,” an order to leave the screen. The archive catches it on May 30, 2022, in a post saying the market is closed today.
based. An opinion stated without asking permission. The word did not come from crypto, but from 4chan, and it is praise.
Conviction layer
Words that announce a view of the future usually sound louder than the view deserves.
hodl. “Hold,” with a typo, meaning do not sell into the dip. The citation is a bitcointalk post from December 18, 2013, written during a crash by someone who says in the thread that they were drunk. The word survived because it turns a lack of trading skill into a strategy, which is very useful for a word.
wagmi. “We’re all gonna make it.” This is optimism as glue: the important part is not the forecast, but the “we.” The phrase belongs to bodybuilder Aziz Shavershian, known as Zyzz, who died in 2011, and lived for years on gym forums before reaching markets. The first /biz/ use is July 28, 2018.
ngmi. “Not gonna make it,” the same phrase turned inside out and aimed at a person. It is the harshest thing crypto-Twitter says to someone, because it is not about a mistake, but about someone who will keep making mistakes. The first archive use is August 3, 2017.
gmi. “Gonna make it,” singular, usually said to someone who just did something right.
diamond hands. Holding a position through pain. Paper hands is selling at the first sign of fear. Both phrases are usually tied to r/wallstreetbets around 2019 and the GameStop squeeze in January 2021; in crypto the usage on the board is older, from May 31, 2017.
hfsp. “Have fun staying poor,” the standard reply to anyone calling it all a scam. In the archive it appears from December 30, 2020.
up only. A joke about a chart that supposedly cannot fall. It is always said about something that then falls.
number go up. The same joke, stated honestly: price rises because everyone expects it to rise. Often shortened to NgU.
few, “few understand” — an ironic label meaning “almost nobody sees what I see.” It is often attributed to @BowTiedBull ; the article did not find a dated first post and treats it as an attribution, not proof.
probably nothing. The same irony in reverse: you post something you think matters and label it “probably nothing.” The archive gives no date; the ordinary meaning of the phrase is everywhere.
Loss layer
The largest group, and the honest one. Market language describes loss far more precisely than gain.
rekt. From wrecked: a position destroyed, usually with leverage. The spelling came from games, where Urban Dictionary records it in 2011, and World of Warcraft forums in 2012; crypto took it whole. It appears in the archive on the first day.
bagholder. Someone left holding a token nobody wants; bags, the bags themselves, are the position. The earliest bagholder record, on February 14, 2014, appears as an insult, which is the word’s natural habitat.
cope. Refusing to admit a loss out loud. Copium is the imaginary substance you take for that. Copium appears in the archive on September 25, 2018: “Pass the copium anon.”
hopium. The same substance pointed toward the future: a position held together by hope alone.
fud. “Fear, uncertainty and doubt,” a term older than crypto by decades. It came from computer hardware sales and changed jobs along the way: outside crypto it describes a tactic, while inside crypto it is often used to dismiss criticism, including fair criticism.
fomo. “Fear of missing out,” the cause of most bad entries. In trading use, it appears on June 13, 2014: “now i have to buy nautilus coin because of FOMO.”
exit liquidity. What you become when your buying lets someone else exit. The most useful phrase in this section, and the least pleasant.
rug pull. A launch where the team removes liquidity and the token goes to zero. Soft rug is the slower version, where nobody takes anything directly and the team just stops working. Exit scam is the older, broader term for the same crime.
honeypot. A token you can buy but cannot sell because the contract says so.
Trading floor
Words that would survive being moved to almost any other market.

If a word in the table sends you looking for mechanics rather than jokes, the desk has a glossary in plain language: funding rate, liquidation, perpetual futures, and FDV.
Memecoin layer
This part is skipped by other dictionaries, and it is exactly what is in daily use right now. The words came out of Solana launchpads, describe execution mechanics rather than feelings, and the archive can date almost none of them: each is an ordinary English word that found a new job.
trenches, the trenches, mean the memecoin market itself: tokens that are minutes old and mostly worthless. “Being in the trenches” means trading launches all day. The desk’s own map of this market is in the article about the first thirty seconds of a token’s life, where almost half of all money arrives in the first half-minute.
CTO. Community takeover: the original developer disappears or is exposed, and the remaining holders take over the accounts and promotion so the token can live on.
bundled. A launch where a group of wallets funded from one source buys the supply in the first block: the holder list looks broad, but it is not broad.
sniper. A bot or person buying in the first seconds of a launch, usually because they knew about it beforehand. Sniped is what happened to everyone else.
dev sold. A two-word obituary: the developer sold their share.
migration. The move of a token from a crooked launchpad to the open market, meaning a scheduled event with liquidity and therefore a scheduled trap.
runner. The one launch out of thousands that keeps running instead of dying.
meta. The theme the market buys this week: animals, politics, AI agents. Meta changes faster than any explanation of meta.
cabal. A closed group of traders coordinating entries, which in any given case may or may not exist.
PVP. Player versus player: a recognition that the token has no thesis and money is just moving between traders.
farmer. Someone farming an airdrop instead of holding a position.
The other side
The argument over whether all this should exist has been going on since the words became popular. Both sides deserve to be included, because each is right in part.
“GM” in crypto is ridiculous.
Sam Lessin, X, November 8, 2021
The complaint is not about style. It is about the fact that a greeting without content becomes a loyalty test: say gm and you are one of us; question the asset and you are NGMI. A dictionary that sorts people that way is very good at producing agreement, and the market should judge agreement, not imitate it.
Why do I say “gm” to all of you? Because it is a reminder that there are real people behind avatars. I say gm at home, at work, and to people in cafes. Why not say gm to you too?
punk6529, X, October 5, 2021
The defense is that the ritual does work that nothing else in the market does. A trader sits alone, at odd hours, with a position they cannot discuss with anyone in the room. A word that costs nothing and confirms that other people are also awake is a cheap remedy for a real problem.
Our reading of the records sits between these two. The greeting layer is social, the loss layer is technical, and the trader needs the second one. Nobody has ever been liquidated for failing to say gm; people were liquidated for not knowing what exit liquidity was.
What we do not see
Not a disclaimer, but a list of questions our data cannot answer, and the direction of bias in each case.

One board is not the whole language. We only have one archive, /biz/. Words born on Twitter, Telegram, or Discord reach it late or not at all, so every date here is an upper bound on age, never a lower bound. If we are wrong, the word is older than we say, not younger.

The archive floor hides thirteen words. HODL, rekt, fud, shill, shitcoin, dyor, sats, bagholder, degen, nocoiner, airdrop, anon, and based were already in use in the first week of the archive. Their real first use lies somewhere before February 13, 2014, and we cannot say where.

Multiple meanings break string search. For 22 words, the earliest hit was a different word with the same letters. For them we have no date at all, and the dictionary entries above rely on outside sources, which is noted where it matters.

We did not measure frequency. We know when a word appears, but not how popular it became. Frequency needs a corpus with a known denominator, and the open interfaces that used to provide that, Pushshift and its successors, closed off automated access. We tried three and got rate-limited by all three, so there is no popularity chart in the article.

Definitions are editorial. The meanings are ours, checked against usage. Slang has no authority you can appeal to, and anyone calling their crypto dictionary final is selling you something.

What would prove us wrong

A dated public post using NGMI in the crypto sense before August 3, 2017, or WAGMI before July 28, 2018, anywhere. That would not weaken the article; it would strengthen it, because it would make the gap from the usual story even larger.

The opposite: proof that our 2017 NGMI post means something else. The post is one line long, and the meaning is direct, but one line can still be read wrong.

Proof that the warosu archive backfilled old posts and its February 13, 2014 date is not a real floor. That would shift the entire lowest group at once.

A source of origin that is correctly dated and older than the board, like HODL. We found one. There may be others.

Corrections made along the way

The first version of the measurement dated gmi to April 5, 2016 and treated it as the earliest word in the family. Reading the post killed that: it was about General Moly Inc, ticker GMI, a molybdenum mining company. The date was removed, not footnoted: a wrong citation is worse than no citation.

The same check removed trenches, CTO, bundled, sniper, PVP, cabal, cope, maxi, wen, whale, bags, moon, aping, larp, hopium, ser, rug, gm, nfa, and two more words from the dated list. In an earlier pass, before meaning checks were applied, all of them counted, and the article would have claimed that the whole modern memecoin vocabulary existed in February 2014.

Desk thoughts

Slang works like compression, and the compression ratio matters. “I’m long, I won’t sell this dip, and I admit I might be wrong” is sixteen words. “Diamond hands” is two. In a market that trades every hour of every day, the group that can state a position in two words moves faster than the group that needs sixteen, and that speed gap is why the dictionary never settles; it keeps rebuilding itself.

What we do differently, briefly and concretely: when the desk writes about the market, it will use the word the market actually uses and explain it once, on the spot, instead of translating it into institutional language. We used to do the opposite, thinking slang would push readers away. The records say otherwise: slang is the primary source. A reader who does not know what bundled means cannot read a launch, and no neat paraphrase fixes that.

The number to watch next is the rate at which new words appear in the memecoin layer. From 2014 to 2020, the board produced roughly one durable word per year. The 2024–2026 layer produced at least eleven in two years, and each one describes execution mechanics rather than feeling. That is how the market signals where its risk moved: from conviction to trade structure.

One concrete thing to check against us: open the NGMI post from August 3, 2017 and the diamond hands post from May 31, 2017. If either is not what we say it is, that is the finding, and the correction will be published the same way as the claim.

Korea's Boom Is a Price, Not a Factory 

South Korea is having a spectacular year. In June 2026, its exports crossed $100 billion in a single month for the first time. Semiconductors accounted for $44.8 billion of that, about 44% of everything the country sold abroad. 

That sounds like an industrial success story, but it isn’t. Over the same period, the volume of chips Korea shipped fell by 11.9 %, while revenue from them rose by 173.5%. The same factories produced less product, yet generated three times the revenue per kilogram. A server memory chip that sold for $6 now sells for about $42. Korea did not learn to make more chips; buyers agreed to pay much more for the same chips because AI data centers are desperate for memory and only three companies worldwide can supply it. 

Thus Korea is not riding an industry; it is riding a price. 

When export prices jump like that and output does not, a country gets richer without producing more. Korea’s own central‑bank data shows it plainly: in early 2026, real income grew 13.2 % while real output grew 3.8 %. That gap is the widest on record. Money that arrives this way behaves like an oil discovery: it comes from outside, it sits in one industry, and it can leave the same way it came. Korea’s chips represent forty years of hard engineering, not a lucky hole in the ground, yet the cash behaves the same. The Bank of Korea is so worried that it has begun using the phrase “semiconductor Dutch disease.” 

Most Koreans cannot feel any of this. Chips and IT now account for 51 % of the country’s manufacturing output and employ 2.6 % of its workforce, about one in forty jobs. Growth forecasts keep being raised while job forecasts are cut, and youth employment has declined for months. Samsung and SK Hynix together are worth more than half of the Korean stock market. On one day the index closed at a record high, yet 826 of its component stocks fell. 

What Korea is earning here is a rent, not a profit. Rent is the extra you collect for owning something scarce that others badly need and cannot copy quickly. Rents are huge while they last, and they always run out. Three factors will end this rent. First, memory prices crash cyclically; they fell 60 % in 2019, pulling Korea’s total exports down 10.3 %. Second, China is emerging; CXMT is already the world’s fourth‑largest DRAM maker and aims for 30 % of the market by 2030. It does not need to beat Korea at the high end; it only needs to capture the low‑end segment. Third, South Korea’s geopolitical vulnerability stems from its manufacturing footprint in China. SK Hynix relies on its Chinese factories, particularly in Wuxi, to produce 30–40% of its global memory output, but these facilities depend on advanced semiconductor manufacturing tools controlled by the United States. To restrict China’s technological advancement, Washington regulates the export of this equipment through licenses that must now be renewed annually and generally permit only routine maintenance rather than major technological upgrades. Consequently, a large share of Korea’s manufacturing capacity is effectively locked out of producing cutting‑edge chips, leaving those factories trapped in older legacy nodes that face direct price pressure from emerging Chinese competitors while keeping Korea’s production destiny tied to U.S. regulatory approval.

There is a strong counterargument. Suppliers are currently meeting only 75–80 % of demand, and a new fab takes five years to build. If AI demand persists, this shortage could outlast any previous memory cycle, and Korea’s concentration may become the best position a mid‑sized economy has held in fifty years. 

No one knows how this will unfold, and Korea cannot decide the outcome. What Korea can decide is how to use the money now. That is the real question, not whether the country depends on chips, but whether it can build the next industry while chips continue to pay for it. Every country that pulled this off did so during the boom; the ones that failed waited until the boom ended before starting.

### Core Privacy Concerns
The primary issues center on the creation of a pervasive, interconnected location-tracking system that records the movements of ordinary people without individualized suspicion or warrants:

- **Mass, suspicionless data collection**: Cameras photograph essentially every passing vehicle, building detailed historical records of travel patterns that can reveal private associations, routines, medical visits, political activities, or other sensitive movements. Critics, including the ACLU and EFF, describe this as a dragnet that turns everyday driving into searchable surveillance data. A single query can potentially access tens of thousands of cameras nationwide.

- **Nationwide data sharing and unauthorized access**: Local agencies control their data in theory, but features like “national lookup” have enabled broad querying. Audits and investigations have revealed unauthorized or unexpected access by federal agencies (including ICE and CBP) in multiple jurisdictions, sometimes conflicting with state sanctuary laws or local policies. Examples include hundreds of thousands of searches of city data by non-partnered agencies and cases where sharing toggles were enabled without clear customer knowledge.

- **Misuse by authorized users**: Reports document dozens of cases (over 50 according to major investigations) in which officers used the system for personal reasons, such as stalking romantic partners or family members. Vague search justifications (e.g., simply “investigation”) and limited real-time oversight have facilitated this.

- **Data retention and AI expansion**: Default retention was previously 30 days; patterns of life can still be reconstructed from shorter windows. AI features enable natural-language searches (e.g., for specific vehicle descriptions) and expand beyond pure plate reading to broader video analysis. Additional concerns include past security exposures of live feeds and potential links to other data sources.

- **Impacts on vulnerable groups and rights**: Documented uses include immigration enforcement queries, tracking related to reproductive healthcare after *Roe v. Wade* was overturned, monitoring of protesters, and discriminatory search terms. This raises First and Fourth Amendment issues, as the system enables retrospective tracking without probable cause.

Civil liberties groups argue the architecture itself—an ever-expanding, interconnected commercial network sold for profit—creates systemic risks that individual agency policies struggle to contain.

### Company Position and Recent Changes
Flock states that customers own their data, the company does not sell it, sharing is opt-in and controlled by agencies, data is encrypted and automatically deleted after a set period, every search is logged for audits, and the technology is restricted to public-safety purposes. The company highlights its role in investigations, estimating support for roughly 1 million cases annually, contributions to about 20% of cleared cases in deploying jurisdictions, thousands of missing-person recoveries, and significant stolen-vehicle recoveries.

In August 2026, amid backlash, Flock announced updates including a recommended default retention reduction from 30 days to 7 days (with an “Evidence Mode” to preserve relevant data longer for investigations), offense-type filters for sharing (e.g., allowing violent-crime searches while blocking immigration-related ones), mandatory audit-assistance tools that flag abnormal activity and can lock accounts pending review, required case codes for searches, and stronger multi-factor authentication.

### Criticisms of the Safeguards and Broader Context
Privacy advocates (ACLU, EFF, and others) view many of these measures as incremental or previously attempted features that have proven easy to circumvent (e.g., via generic search reasons). They contend that technical guardrails cannot fully mitigate the core problem of a nationwide mass-surveillance infrastructure operated by a private company with strong financial incentives to expand. Independent effectiveness research on ALPRs is mixed; while some local reports show investigative value, broader causal evidence of crime reduction remains limited or contested.

Public and governmental responses include contract cancellations by dozens of cities (more than 50 reported in recent periods), state laws imposing retention limits, warrant requirements, or sharing restrictions, lawsuits challenging warrantless use, and grassroots efforts to map and oppose installations. Vandalism and theft of cameras have also occurred in some areas.

In summary, Flock Safety’s technology offers demonstrable investigative utility for serious crimes and vehicle-related offenses, but its scale and design enable continuous, low-friction tracking of the general public. The resulting privacy risks—ranging from individual abuse to systemic overreach—have fueled significant opposition, regulatory pushback, and ongoing debates over whether existing or proposed safeguards adequately protect civil liberties in a free society. The tension reflects broader questions about the balance between technological crime-fighting tools and limits on government and corporate surveillance powers.

In a real estate office in Dongtan, about 30 miles south of Seoul, an agent named Mark Yoon spends his days pointing a laser pen at two wall sized maps.

Eight years of selling apartments here have taught him something. Almost every conversation, no matter how it starts, ends up in the same place. Semiconductors.

Outside his window, shuttle buses carry engineers to Samsung's sprawling campuses in Hwaseong and Giheung. SK Hynix's operation sits close enough to reach by highway. Together, these two companies produce roughly 80% of the world's high bandwidth memory chips, the ones powering the AI boom everyone is currently arguing about on timelines like this one.

For Yoon's clients, that abstraction has become something very concrete.

In May, Samsung and its labor union agreed to tie bonuses to about 10% of chip division profit. For some employees, that means payouts approaching 600 million won, nearly $400,000, on top of 500 million won in housing loans. SK Hynix bonuses are projected to hit $477,000 this year and as much as $900,000 next year.

The money is changing decisions that used to be about prestige, not cash. Internal boards at both companies show engineers openly weighing whether to skip once coveted overseas training programs, because missing a bonus year now feels like the bigger loss. On Korean dating apps, SK Hynix employees are reportedly climbing the matchmaking rankings, income doing what job titles used to do.

And the money is landing somewhere physical. One 84 square meter apartment in Dongtan sold for 2.08 billion won on May 7. Weekly price gains in the district have been running close to half a percent, and May's transaction volume passed the previous month's total with ten days still left to report.

Bloomberg Economics has a name for what happens next: a wage domino. Their forecast has the combined bonus pool at Samsung and SK Hynix growing from 4 trillion won this year to 16 trillion in 2027 and 30 trillion by 2028, a pool that historically tracked around 8% of national mortgage loan growth and is now projected to hit 32%, then 57%.

The Bank of Korea is watching the same numbers and using a less poetic word: risk. Inflation is already running above the 2% target, and the central bank has flagged these bonuses as a factor that could push wage pressure into industries that have nothing to do with chips, through a revised labor law that gives suppliers more leverage to demand their own share of the windfall.

None of this shows up in a chip demand chart or a KOSPI candle. It shows up in a real estate agent's laser pointer, in a young engineer canceling a flight to Germany, in an apartment that sold for more than most Koreans will earn in a decade.

The AI boom has a headline story about GPUs and export controls. It also has this quieter one, playing out zip code by zip code in Gyeonggi Province, about what happens to a society when an entire industry starts paying like a lottery.

Does the rest of the country ever catch up to Dongtan's paychecks, or does Korea end up with two different economies sharing the same currency?

The Los Angeles Lakers just sold for $12.5 billion, the most expensive sale in American sports history. And there’s some for a lack of better words, interesting connections. The seller is Mark Walter, who is under active federal investigation. 

The buyer is Josh Kushner who’s brother is Donald Trump’s son in law and the man whose firm tried to buy the FIFA World Cup. The most famous franchise in sports just passed straight from a man being probed by the feds to a man who tried to privatize the world's biggest tournament. Let’s take a look at the full picture, because the full picture is ugly.

Let’s start off with some of the facts because this story is LOADED.

Mark Walter bought the Lakers 14 months ago at a $10 billion valuation. He didn't buy them to just flip them. He tore up the front office, rebuilt the scouting department, overhauled the business side, all the moves of a man planning to own this team for a decade. Then, 14 months in, he sold the Lakers?! Nobody does that. You don't buy your dream asset and unload it before you've finished redecorating, unless something changed and changed drastically.

Here's what happened. Walter is under federal investigation, a probe into the insurance companies he controls, the same case where the FBI reportedly seized his phone and laptop off a private jet at a Chicago airport. Separate investigations by U.S. prosecutors and the SEC are underway.

Now there is no proof of guilt yet. No one has pointed out for sure that the investigation forced this sale. Walter hasn't been charged with anything. The teams themselves are not named in the probe. Every serious outlet says the connection is unproven, and it is.

But you're allowed to look at the picture, and the picture is ugly. A man under federal investigation does not sell his trophy asset 14 months after buying it, at $2.5 billion above what he paid, in a matter of days, for no reason. That's not a normal exit. That's a fast, wildly profitable, remarkably clean getaway from the spotlight, executed at the precise moment the spotlight turned into a liability. You don't liquidate the Los Angeles Lakers this quickly unless you have a reason to want out. What that reason is, only the investigation knows. But the timing is not small.

But then who is buying it is a whole new story.

The buyer is Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive Capital. Weeks ago, that same firm was the lead investor in Gianni Infantino's $20 billion plan to sell off the commercial rights to the FIFA World Cup, the scheme that collapsed under a global revolt and nearly cost the FIFA president his job. Same man. Same firm. Different sport, different continent, weeks apart.

And there's a layer under the Kushner name that makes this bigger than sports. Josh Kushner is the brother of Jared Kushner, who is married to Ivanka Trump. Which means the most famous franchise in American sports is now owned, in part, by the sitting President's son-in-law's brother. Not the President himself, to be clear. He has no stake in this and no role in it. But the Lakers just became connected by marriage to the First Family, at the same time the seller is under a federal investigation run by that same administration's Justice Department. You don't have to allege anything to notice that's a crazy plot twist.

Two of the biggest money scandals in sports right now, a federally investigated owner on one side and the private equity operator who tried to buy the World Cup on the other, just resolved into a single transaction. The investigated man sold America's most famous team to the FIFA guy, in days, at a record price, and most people are reading it as a fun headline about the Lakers getting a new owner.

Here's the thing about the money at the very top of sports. Fans watch 30 teams, 30 owners, 30 separate franchises with their own colors and cities and rivalries. But the capital behind all of it is a small room. It's the same few dozen people, and they keep turning up in each other's deals. The Lakers, the Dodgers, the Giants, the Heat, Liverpool, the World Cup itself, pull the thread on almost any of them right now and you find the same handful of names, buying from and selling to one another.

That's the lesson that runs underneath all of this. At the level fans watch, sports is a game. At the level that actually owns it, sports is an asset class, and it is a far smaller and more connected world than anyone lets on. The Lakers didn't just get a new owner. They moved one square on a board most people don't know they're looking at, from a man under federal investigation to a man connected by marriage to the President.

The Buss family owned the Lakers for 46 years. Mark Walter owned them for 14 months. The next chapter belongs to the man whose firm tried to privatize the World Cup, and whose brother is married into the White House. That tells you everything about how fast the money moves at the top now, and how very few hands it moves between.

The week the world moved from talk to action

Something interesting stood out reading through the last few days of news: almost every major theme suddenly shifted from the discussion phase into concrete action. We're not talking about what might happen anymore, we're talking about what already did.

From threat to gunfire, in the Gulf of Oman

The clearest example: US forces actually fired on a vessel, the Vela Nova, sailing under a Panama flag, after it tried to run the blockade imposed on Iranian ports, ignoring warnings. A military helicopter struck the ship's steering system to immobilize it, a fire broke out onboard and was later put out, all 17 crew members were reported safe.

We're no longer talking about a "possible blockade." Washington just showed it's willing to enforce it physically, not just declare it. That distinction matters enormously for how you read the rest of the geopolitical headlines going forward, the Hormuz risk is no longer theoretical.

From a tax promise to a concrete example with numbers

Trump isn't just "considering" cutting capital gains taxes, the proposal already has a precise mechanism: adjusting the cost basis for inflation before calculating the taxable gain. The concrete example, a stock bought for $100,000, sold for $200,000 five years later, with 20% cumulative inflation, would reduce the taxable gain from $100,000 to $80,000. This isn't a vague campaign idea anymore, it's an applicable formula. If it passes, it would be one of the biggest investment tax reforms in years, exactly the kind of news long term investors should be tracking, not dismissing as political noise.

From promised regulation to regulation already in force

Russia didn't just discuss crypto, it directly legalized public trading of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT on licensed exchanges. In parallel, the US CFTC announced it's moving forward with digital asset rulemaking even if the Clarity Act doesn't pass Congress, a move that makes clear, if the legislature won't act, the agencies will anyway.

From "chip supplier" to "model builder"

Nvidia doesn't just want to sell AI hardware anymore, it's working on Nemotron 4, an open source model estimated at over a trillion parameters, one of the largest AI systems ever built, if the numbers hold up. It's a major strategic repositioning, from "we sell the shovels" to "we're mining the gold too."

The thread tying it all together: the money is following the same pattern

S&P 500 profit growth estimates for 2026 have already doubled from where they stood at the start of the year, 32% versus 15%. Gold is climbing toward $4,408. Anthropic is gearing up for an October IPO. All of this, alongside clear signs of stress on the American consumer, 12.9% of US credit card balances are now 90+ days delinquent, near the highest level since 2011.

I think this week marked a moment where too many major themes, geopolitics, fiscal policy, regulation, AI, all shifted at once from "possible" to "confirmed." Markets tend to move slower than reality on the ground, and when several confirmations land at the same time, like they just did, I think that deserves more attention than any single isolated headline normally would.

I don't think you need to react to every headline, but I do think the pattern is worth noticing, the world just moved from talk to concrete action on multiple fronts simultaneously, and historically, that tends to precede periods of higher volatility, not calm.

This isn't financial advice, just my personal interpretation and opinion on the events of the past few days.

Since then talks have stalled on mutual demands for reparations, and Brent is back near $88, up ~9% in three sessions.

So a soft print today confirms disinflation whose central cause has already reversed. Roughly 60% odds of a September hike hang on a number describing conditions that no longer exist.

Line up the month. Alphabet, Meta and SpaceX were all sold for spending on their own balance sheets. CoreWeave was bought for spending on someone else’s.

The market hasn’t changed its mind about AI capex. It has changed its mind about who should carry it. That’s a judgement about where the risk sits, not how much there is — and the money filling that gap is increasingly credit and private capital rather than public equity.

Hormuz, again. Progress reported, this time via Pakistan’s defence minister. Traffic through the strait remains extremely thin.

Six weeks, dozens of headlines, and the plumbing hasn’t moved.

airtable sold for $1.3 billion this week. intercom sold for $3.6 billion last month. one got dunked on, the other got celebrated.

both were saas darlings facing the same question: what happens when AI eats your core product?

intercom's answer was to bet the company. they rebuilt around their AI agent, renamed the whole company after it, built their own model. fin went from zero to $100M ARR growing 350% year over year. salesforce paid up to 36x for that AI revenue specifically. the legacy $300M saas business was basically along for the ride.

airtable's answer was to hedge. they added AI features but kept the core business intact. when the acquisition came, they carved out their AI agent play (hyperagent) into a separate company before signing. bending spoons got the legacy business. investors kept the lottery ticket.

that spinoff is the tell. you don't separate your growth engine from the sale if you believe in the combined company. it's an admission that the core product's future is limited and the AI bet is better off unencumbered.

i get why it happened. going all-in on AI when you have $480M in ARR and 80% of the fortune 100 as customers is terrifying. you might break what's working. intercom was closer to death when they made their bet — $250M ARR, flat growth, labeled an AI loser. they had less to lose.

the companies that survive platform shifts aren't the ones with the most to protect. they're the ones willing to act like they have nothing to protect.

Airtable sold for a tenth of its peak. The founders kept the AI business.

Bending Spoons announced today it's buying Airtable, all cash. The headline number hides three better stories.

The deal:

- Enterprise value: $1.285 billion
- Equity value: ~$2.25 billion, but only because Airtable is sitting on ~$965M of net cash
- Read that again: nearly half the purchase price is Airtable's own unspent money being handed back to shareholders
- Peak valuation: $11.7B, December 2021 Series F. The business just cleared at roughly 89% below that
- ARR: ~$480M, growing 20%. That's ~2.7x revenue. SpaceX paid 15x for Cursor six weeks ago

The waterfall, per a widely shared model built on public terms (directional, assumes vanilla 1x prefs):

- Everyone from Series C onward took par. Coatue, Thrive, Greenoaks, XN wrote checks at $1.1B, $2.6B, $5.8B, and $11.7B posts and got 1.0x of money back
- CRV: ~21x on the 2015 Series A, ~6x on the B
- Caffeinated Capital: ~37x on the A1
- Freestyle and Felix Shpilman at the 2013 seed: ~55x
- ~$960M left for converting holders. The three founders, assuming ~15% held, split about $144M. Call it $50M each after 13 years
- Same lesson as always: the last four rounds funded the exit for the first three

Now the buried lede, from the SEC filing:

- Before signing, Airtable ran a reorganization that transferred the entire "Hyperagent" business line out of the company into a separate entity, Hyperagent Inc
- Hyperagent is the AI agent orchestration platform Airtable unveiled in early 2026, spin up teams of autonomous agents across your business tools
- Bending Spoons is buying the database, the workflows, the 500K orgs, the 80% of the Fortune 100, and the $480M of recurring revenue
- The seller is keeping the agents

On Hyperagent's performance: there are no disclosed numbers. It launched roughly six months ago. No ARR, no customer counts, nothing public. What we know is that it was worth carving out of a billion-dollar deal, which is its own kind of disclosure.

On whether the founders stay: nobody has said explicitly. Howie Liu's statement talks about "building the AI-native platform of the future," which reads either way on purpose. But follow the structure, not the quotes. The founders' holding company now owns Hyperagent outright, free of the legacy business. One newsletter's blunt read: Liu keeps the AI project without having to be the one who does the layoffs. The Italians do that part.

And they will. Bending Spoons' playbook is public record: buy at a discount, cut deep, raise prices on customers too embedded to leave, run it for cash. Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, AOL in January, Eventbrite in March. Airtable is the first deal since its July Nasdaq listing at $18.4B, and the first paid for with public-market currency.

The frame: a decacorn built over 13 years just sold its core for less than the cash on its own balance sheet plus a modest premium, while the founders walked out the back door with the AI upside in a clean-room entity. The 2021 vintage investors got their money back and nothing else. The seed got 55x. And the most honest sentence in the whole transaction is a highlighted paragraph in a 6-K that nobody reads.

Every exit this cycle tells you where the value is. This one says: the workflows are worth 2.7x revenue. The agents are worth keeping.

I paid $40 for the "perfect prompt." Best waste of money in my life.

The seller promised: paste this prompt and the AI will write code/copy/strategies like a senior engineer. I pasted it. The result was barely better than a free "please write it properly."

I was angry for a week. Then I stumbled onto something that completely rewired how I think about this.

Turns out the "perfect prompt" doesn't physically exist. While some people sell magic phrases, engineers do something else entirely: they build a loop. The system writes a prompt on its own → checks the result against a metric → explains in plain words what went wrong → rewrites itself. A thousand times a night. No fatigue, no ego, no "I feel like this sounds better."

Every attempt gets saved to an archive with its score. The next version doesn't start from zero — it starts from the best find so far. That's not trial and error anymore. That's evolution.

This is how ShinkaEvolve, GEPA, and DeepMind's AlphaEvolve work. They find solutions better than human ones. And you know where all of it lives? On GitHub. For free.

The prompt is sold for money. The machine that finds the best prompt on its own is given away for free.

The lesson that cost me $40: don't buy the answer — learn to build the thing that finds answers.

The chart attached is steel rails, 1870 to 1900. The chart in the post below is the price of intelligence, published this week. They are the same chart.

In 1873 a ton of steel rail sold for $120. By 1898 it sold for $18, an 85% collapse in the price of the thing the boom was built from, while the railroads laid more track every year, carried more freight every year, and restructured the entire economy around themselves. The most productive era of the nineteenth century was the most ruinous era its investors ever lived through, for twenty-three years. The Long Depression is the least-taught economic event in American history.

Now read the token chart. Frontier intelligence: $25 per million tokens at the top, 28 cents at the bottom, near-equal performance. That is 99% off the frontier. The incumbent cut its own volume model 80% three weeks after launch. What took steel a generation, intelligence did in eighteen months.

Here is the difference. In 1873 the deflationary engine ran alone, so the tape was allowed to show it: twenty years of falling prices, a depression everyone knew they were living in. This time the same engine runs against a second one. A war economy is rebuilding energy security at any cost and re-arming on borrowed money, pumping cost into everything physical while AI strips cost out of everything cognitive. The two engines net. Inflation where the state spends, deflation where the software eats, stagnation where the debt sits, and an aggregate so smooth it reads as health. The crash the railroads delivered, the panic low you could buy, is the one event the modern system will not permit, because the market is now the national retirement fund and the state stands under it. The adjustment that took the 1870s twenty visible years arrives now as the same twenty years with the depression bar deleted. We named this the Flattened Depression.

The financing is the same circle Jay Cooke drew. Cooke sold $100 million of Northern Pacific bonds; the bonds financed the track, the track was supposed to create the land value, and the land value was supposed to justify the bonds. On September 18, 1873, he could not place the next tranche, and the New York Stock Exchange closed for the first time in its history. Today: investment finances data centers, data centers produce intelligence, intelligence is supposed to produce revenue, revenue justifies the investment. The same chain, one link swapped. When this chain strains, no exchange will close. The strain will be refinanced and smoothed into the tape.

And the volume bet is the same bet. Sam Altman: "We will have so much usage of our models that we do not need to be a gigantically high-margin business." Every railroad president said that about freight, and they were right about the volume. Tonnage rose for twenty years. The returns never came, because every competitor had the same plan. The metric that mattered was never miles of track. It was revenue per mile. The metric that matters now is not the benchmark score. It is revenue per token, and revenue per token is in freefall while the capex sits committed at last year's prices.

Where does the surplus go? Where it always goes. Not to the builder. Up, to whoever owns the power and the inputs. Down, to every customer who now buys for 28 cents what cost $25. The displaced worker gets the bill before any adopter collects the reward.

The productivity was real in 1873, and it did not matter. Real productivity and a depression are not opposites. They compound. The piece below asks whether abundance can still be profitable. The railroads already answered. The builders never proved it. Their cargo did. What compounds in a Long Depression is not the protected asset. It is the unprotected capability, the thing that gets cheaper, spreads, and quietly makes the expensive thing optional. That was freight in 1880. It is intelligence now.

No crash. No V. No rescue by collapse. Just the fix, and the grind.

Seven-Figure Book Deal Cancelled Over AI Suspicions Raises Questions About AI Guardrails

By Erin Somers

A debut thriller won by Minotaur in a seven-figure, two-book deal after a reported 14-way auction was withdrawn by its agents this week for suspected use of AI. The novel, whose title and author PL is withholding for the author's privacy, sold for an alleged $2.5 million or thereabouts. But rumors surfaced quickly from people who had read the manuscript that the book contained many of the hallmarks of AI, including negative parallelism, off-kilter metaphors, and a flat prose style. On Wednesday, the author's co-agents Marc Gerald and Ashley Coleman at Europa Content withdrew the book, after questioning the author about the validity of the rumors.

St. Martin's Publishing Group would not confirm the size of the deal, telling Publishers Lunch only, "Macmillan Publishers participated in an auction. The agent ultimately pulled the book."

Europa wrote in a statement that the author, "Produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world."

[Inserts question: How did the off-kilter metaphors and flat prose style dazzle all those top publishing professionals? But I digress. The report continues:]

"Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion. During the submission process we vetted the manuscript... and felt trusting in [the author's] reassurance that it was written without utilizing AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book. This raises so many questions about authorship and what AI means for this industry but those are questions for another day. We regret that our enthusiasm led to this outcome and we apologize to our publishing partners."

Gerald further explained to PL that AI suspicions were first raised during the submission process by an editor who had read the manuscript: "We immediately had a very long, substantive call with [the author], about AI protocol and the consequences for both him and Europa if he was using it. We went through detailed sections of his book, where he shared with us that like many authors he used AI for research into chemistry which forms the background for much of the book. That said, he confirmed he wrote the book 100 percent himself. At no point did we run an AI detection on the MS; we had concerns that the software had lead to previous inaccuracies."

The author denied using AI to PL, writing, "The rumors are absurd." But this week, Gerald and Coleman spoke to the author again and told the Bookseller that "aspects of [the author’s] story changed."

Gerald wrote to PL: "On Wednesday, Ashley and I decided we had no choice but to pull the book after we weren’t able to confirm for ourselves that AI had only been used for light research, grammar checking and Americanizing the language. While we are not able to say authoritatively whether or not he used AI, we did have trouble validating how the work went from creation to polished draft. Ultimately, trust between an agent and client is everything - especially given the fact that AI detection software is still in its infancy."

An analysis by Pangram 4, the leading AI detection program, returned an assessment of 97% AI...But there has been a backlash to Pangram and competing programs, which some people dismiss as inaccurate. Reported individual tests of other material on previous versions have shown more idiosyncratic results and people have challenged the company's claims. Chakrabarty said, "There are little false positives here and there. And there is some acceptable margin of error. For instance if it says an article is 80-90% human you can assume that its predominantly human with some AI edits etc which is totally fine and not egregious. But when an 80K word + novel say it's 97% AI generated it's very hard to deny it." He added that AI hallmarks that editors can look for include: plot inconsistency, too many mixed metaphor cliches, too much negative parallelism, and rule of triad, or excessive groupings of three...

Some authors will use generative AI to "edit" rather than write, without necessarily realizing the extent to which the software will change text unless blocked by specific prompts. Chakrabarty notes, "It rewrites everything and changes a writer's voice. As Hemingway said, Writing is Rewriting. If ChatGPT does edit it's still AI writing."

Sources tell PL that more deals are being cancelled behind the scenes following the discovery or suspicion of AI -- one publisher noted that multiples imprint have had to cancel a book over this -- including books that originate in the self-publishing sphere and are then picked up by Big Five publishers. This usually happens quietly and under the public radar, and is only brought to light by fans online...

In addition to issues in traditional publishing, AI-generated books are now flooding the self-publishing market, cutting into the livelihoods of human authors. Chakrabarty recently led a study investigating the amount of AI in self-published KDP genre fiction, finding "our results bear directly on the market-effect question at the center of the fair use defense to copyright infringement."

...The authors concluded, "Generative AI can...reshape a creative market through scale rather than quality.... We call this dilution." They note, "Our findings reveal a market remade by scale. Books with substantial AI text enter the catalog far faster than the revenue available to absorb them, push down the return each title earns, and contest the top ranks, while the books with AI text that succeed draw most heavily on the distinctive language of existing books."

In their piece on the new research study, the NYT wrote, "The researchers used Pangram to analyze text from around 60,000 books sold on Amazon. From that sample, about 53 percent of the books published in 2025 contained A.I.-generated text, compared to 23 percent in 2023."

In another small but positive development, ChatGPT has stopped fulfilling prompts to generate text in the style of a specific writer. Ars Technica writes, "In refusing to directly copy the 'exact style' of various authors, ChatGPT offered instead to capture an overall 'feeling' by incorporating some of the common features found in those authors’ work."

Still, the vetting tools remain imperfect, and questions abound. The author of the withdrawn book told PL, "Writers are increasingly being made to second-guess ordinary stylistic choices because they might be labelled as signs of AI. Even em dashes are now treated with suspicion, which makes me wonder what people would say about Emily Dickinson’s writing today."

It's clear that this is a watershed moment in publishing and agents, editors, and authors will continue to flounder without firm procedures in place. The core problem remains: there is no way to tell for sure.

 $SPCX was priced on June 11 and debued on June 12. The IPO was oversubscribed and $SPCX scooped $86B through subscription. D. Norwegian Government Pension Fund GPF-G Rebalancing

Norway's GPF is the largest single fund in the world, handling $2.3T AUM. GPF is funded primarily by North Sea oil sales and investing in foreign equities. They didn't want to correlate their futures with oil-heavy domestic industry. Their portfolio is sitting at Nordis Bank, and you can see the list at Nordis’s website. Tech-heavy and many AI infra too. Anyway, the rule they have is 70% global equities and 30% high-grade fixed income like UST. Rebalancing is strictly done twice a year, at the end of June and December. So, they inevitably had to trim semis, memories, storages, semi-equipment, ... The bad thing is everyone knows their schedule and portfolio and what they have to sell. This is a clear front-running target for short sellers. So, the selloffs come ahead by front runners before the actual rebalance. 

There are Middle East sovereign funds and many pension funds due to rebalance as well. I thought the market would come back by July 4 when Trump’s baby bond kicks in. But it didn't.

E. SpaceX NDX Inception

 $SPCX is included in Nasdaq 100 on July 7, meaning $QQQ had to trim others to buy $SPX . $QQQ is over $450B AUM. There are also other ETFs based on NDX, and they had to do the same. When $KXIAY spinoffed from Toshiba, Bain Capital led consortium took 44% of the local share 285A and Toshiba 16%. The damage is not just on $KXIAY . It has the second largest weight in $DRAM . 285A dragged $DRAM further, then $MU and $SNDK fell, which dragged $DRAM again, ... In other words, constituents of the same ETFs are structurally correlated. If one goes down, others too. $SMH and $SOXX were not immunised from it.

SK Hynix ADR started trading on July 10, one day after Bain Capital Consortium exited from $KXIAY . The launch was successful, but had an adverse effect on the SK Hynix local shares. SK Hynix local drops due to foreign investors’ exit, dragging $DRAM , and subsequently pulling $SNDK and $MU . This, together with Bain Capital Consortium’s exit, damaged $SNDK and $MU further.

AI Is Not the Question:

Every AI conversation in consulting and agency land sounds the same.

Use it or don't. 
Good or bad. 
Threat or tool. 
Pick a side, plant a flag, argue with strangers.

Tech dorks arguing about models and woo woo folks proclaiming that Ai cant replace their crystals.

As soon as Hormozi said something about Ai 99% try and pick a side as he’s smart and rich and has a good beard.

It reminds me of the exact argument about marketing automation 15 years ago.

It's the wrong argument.

AI can't compress what doesn't exist. 

Marketing automation couldn’t automate crappy marketing.

AI doesn't replace coaches or consultants or your service.

It compresses processes. 

And you can only compress something that's actually there.

"should I use AI?" Is a midwit question.

It's "do I have a process?"

If you have a documented, repeatable way of taking someone from stuck to unstuck with a series of steps you can name then AI can compress it. 

Faster to deliver. Cheaper to access. 

Available at 2am when your client actually hits the wall not Thursday at 10 when your next Zoom call is scheduled.

If you don't have a process AI is just noise or your looking for the Hail Mary to mask your lack of process.

The compression serves both sides.

It’s monster leverage.

You stop being the delivery mechanism and the bottleneck.

Every hour you spent walking someone through step three of your method you get back.

Like most coaches and consultants I must have repeated parts of my process verbally over 1000 times.

Now the process runs without you even awake and you can still get paid for it running.

They get the same process for less. 

Less money, less waiting, less "let's jump on a call to discuss."

Nobody loses. 

Unless there was never a process to begin with just a calendar full of calls and a vague feeling of being useful.

Which is why the loudest voices in the AI debate are usually the ones without one. 

The argument is a mirror. "AI will kill coaching" translates to "my coaching is my me and my clients need me."

I got VirtualJK to summarise the approach from a client training:
(Complete with — )

Here's what compression actually looks like:

Delivery:
Map your process into steps. Build one tool per step — single use, does what it says on the tin. The equation is Speed + Input + Output: tools make clients faster, prompts shape what they put in, training shapes what comes out. And memory changes everything. A platform that remembers every input a client has ever made never asks them to repeat themselves. Would your client rather work with someone who remembers everything, or someone who needs the backstory every call? Memory is a moat.

Conversion:
Once the process runs through tools, you can offer it at three levels of decision load. Done For You — you and your tools carry most of it. Done With You — shared. Do It Yourself — the client drives, your tools assist. Same process, three prices, and the client chooses how much thinking they want to buy. AI is the thinking machine. You're the nuance machine.

Acquisition:
The free line only moves one direction: out. Courses that sold for $5k are free on YouTube now. So stop guarding your content and start compressing it give away the courses, let a virtual version of you guide people through them, and let it upgrade them when they're ready for the next step. Give prospects a plan, then show them the paths to execute it. Plan plus path equals client.

End.

None of that works without a documented process underneath. 

All of it works even if you only have one.

If your value is a process, AI multiplies you.

If your value is you showing up, AI exposes you.

The question was never about the technology. 

It's whether you built a process that exists without you there.

**Why Your PC Memory Costs 6× More - And It’s Not a Shortage**

A year ago a mainstream PC memory kit sold for around $75. 
Today the same kit can fetch as much as $460.

The easy story is another chip shortage. The real story is colder and more deliberate.

Samsung, SK hynix and Micron — the three companies that control the vast majority of the global DRAM market — are reallocating manufacturing capacity toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM). That is the premium memory powering Nvidia’s AI accelerators and the hyperscale data centers fueling the current artificial-intelligence boom. Conventional DRAM used in laptops, desktops, smartphones and cars is being pushed to the back of the line.

AI customers pay higher prices. So they get the wafers first.

Unlike ordinary DRAM, HBM commands significantly higher margins while consuming far more manufacturing capacity per bit. Every wafer steered toward AI memory is a wafer that no longer produces memory for everyday devices. No coordinated cartel is required. The economics do the work. AI memory simply generates better returns, and the three dominant producers are following those returns.

The numbers are stark. According to TrendForce, conventional DRAM contract prices surged 93–98 % in the first quarter and then climbed another 58–63 % in the second. NAND flash prices rose 70–75 % in the same period as suppliers continued to prioritize AI-related products over mainstream memory.

Even the largest customers are feeling the squeeze. Tesla CEO Elon Musk warned earlier this year that the company was running into a “chip wall” as AI infrastructure strained semiconductor supply. Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell has pointed to an explosion in memory requirements driven by AI deployments.

HBM capacity is effectively sold out through 2026, with large portions of 2027 production already committed. That lock-in has allowed memory makers to secure premium pricing while demand continues to outstrip available supply. By selling more high-value AI memory and less conventional DRAM, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are expanding margins even as consumer and industrial customers pay more.

This pricing boom is unlikely to last forever. Micron is constructing new fabs in Idaho and New York. Samsung and SK hynix continue to expand production capacity. Those investments are expected to come online over the next two years, increasing supply just as China’s CXMT rapidly scales its presence in commodity DRAM.

For now, however, AI remains first in line.

The deeper shift is not simply that PC memory has become dramatically more expensive. It is that artificial intelligence has rewritten how the world’s three largest memory makers allocate capital. As long as AI data centers deliver the highest returns, consumer electronics, smartphones and automotive systems will keep competing for whatever capacity is left behind.

The AI tax on everyday technology is already being paid — in higher prices, tighter supply, and longer waits.

nterPositive trains its model only on the dailies of the specific film or show using it. One production, one model. Demand: buyers were already searching for what you sell, so they found you. Comfortable, until the category stops growing.

You do not have a dial to turn. Either expand into adjacent products to rerun the demand playbook, or build a real dial (organic, paid, or both).

Organic content: your content built an audience and sold for free, until it plateaus.

Level it up with creator partnerships and affiliates at scale, and put ad dollars behind your best performing organic so it reaches past your existing organic reach ceiling.

Paid ads: they carried growth, but CAC keeps climbing and margins keep thinning.

This is where most founders make the same mistake, they try to brute-force it inside the ad account. New media buyer. New agency. New "creative strategy."

Nothing really moves, because the account is rarely the real problem. Real efficiency is won OUTSIDE the ad account.

Here is the mental model: your media buyer's job is to HIT your break-even ROAS.

Your job as the operator is to make the whole system so efficient that the ad account carries less of the weight.

The levers that actually move acquisition efficiency, none of which live inside Ads Manager:

→ Build a real organic content engine.
Every sale from organic (short-form video, creators, community) is revenue you did not rent from Meta. It lifts your blended efficiency because ad spend is no longer carrying 100% of the sales, and it does that without you having to touch the ad account at all.

A proactive sales layer wins them back:

 • fast replies to every comment and DM
 • one-to-one texts and emails to warm non-buyers

Same ad spend, more orders, lower blended CAC.

Every other industry funds a sales function on top of marketing.

A few points off product cost or freight widens gross margin on every single order, which lowers your break-even ROAS directly. Pure P&L work, zero to do with the ad account.

→ Lower your break-even ROAS with order economics.
Break-even ROAS = 1 / gross margin.
Shift spend to higher-margin SKUs, engineer bundles for margin (not just AOV), raise AOV with kits and post-purchase upsells, cut discount dependency, ring-fence money-losing geos, and reduce returns with better PDPs and sizing.

→ THEN feed the account better creative.
With all the talk about Andromeda, you already know this - creative is the targeting. Only after the economics are fixed does stronger upper-funnel creative earn its keep by bringing in net-new audiences.

Notice the order. Demand, conversion, retention, and margin come first. The ad account is the last dial you turn, not the first.

You hear the loud horror stories: funded brands scaling recklessly, ignoring profit, then imploding.

You hear far less about the quiet deaths: profitable brands that clung to margin while growth stalled, then slowly faded.

Here is the part that kills good brands: your P&L and your bank account speak different languages.

You can be profitable on paper and out of cash at the same time, because cash gets trapped in inventory and in timing.

Watch how "get more efficient" backfires. Full math, assume a 70% gross margin (so cost of delivery runs 30% of net sales).

The month everyone panics about:
- Net sales: $5M
- Cost of delivery (30%): $1.5M
- Gross profit: $3.5M
- Ad spend (56% MER): $2.8M
- Contribution profit: $700K
- Fixed cost: $700K
- Net profit: $0

The CFO says the MER is too high, so you cut spend to clean it up.

The "fixed" month:
- Net sales: $4M
- Cost of delivery (30%): $1.2M
- Gross profit: $2.8M
- Ad spend (54% MER): $2.16M
- Contribution profit: $640K
- Fixed cost: $700K
- Net profit: MINUS $60K

Now look at what "improved":
- MER dropped from 56% to 54% (looks more efficient)
- Contribution margin rose from 14% to 16% of net sales (looks healthier)

Every ratio on the scoreboard got BETTER, and the business went from break-even to LOSING $60K a month.

Why? Fixed costs do not shrink when you shrink revenue. That $700K bill is still due, now spread over a smaller top line.

Then the cash side turns on you:
- Lower volume means inventory turns slower, so cash sits trapped in stock longer.
- On Net 60 supplier terms, you need MORE working capital to cover the same bill at lower volume.

That is the five-month death spiral: cut spend, cash tightens, miss a supplier payment, lose your terms, cannot reorder, stock out, ad account pauses. Game over. Profitable the whole way down.

So track the survival metrics, not the vanity ones: contribution profit in dollars, cash conversion cycle (DSO + DSI - DPO), inventory turns, and your real 30-day cash position.

Get clarity on cash and inventory before you touch the spend dial. This is a finance decision wearing a marketing costume.

Most stuck brands are optimizing the wrong number.

Every efficiency metric is a ratio, and chasing a ratio quietly caps your growth:
- Platform ROAS (Meta / Google reported) is misleading in BOTH directions, not just inflated. It overstates lower-funnel and retargeting ads that take credit for sales already in motion, and it understates upper-funnel creative like video that feeds demand but converts outside the attribution window. The real problem is not which way the number is wrong, it is that platform attribution was never built to tell you what actually caused the sale.
- Blended ROAS and MER (net sales over total ad spend, and its inverse) are more honest reads, but they are still ratios.
- NC-ROAS and aMER (the new-customer versions) are sharper for acquisition, but still ratios.

Here is the trap in one line: $500/day at a 5x ROAS makes less money than $5,000/day at a 2.5x ROAS. Lower ratio, far more profit.

So flip the scoreboard:
- Scale and throttle on total contribution profit in DOLLARS, not on any ratio moving up or down.
- Watch the marginal return of the NEXT dollar of spend, not the blended average.
- Trust blended numbers from Shopify over platform-reported ROAS.
- Once you are spending seriously, prove real incrementality with geo holdouts.

A ratio tells you how efficient you are. Dollars tell you how big you are getting. You cannot pay your team, your suppliers, or yourself with a ratio.

$332M Prime Manhattan Office Building Purchased in 2006 sells for $8.5M; 97.5% Discount to Original Purchase Price
 
The New York Times headline “This 23 Floor Manhattan Office Building Just Sold at a 97.5% Discount” is a bit deceiving, yet intriguing, while providing insight with respect to transactional maturations. With a prime location @ 50th Street in the Rockefeller Center midtown Manhattan office district and nearly 1 million leasable sq. feet, the building is only 35% occupied despite recently undergoing a $76M renovation. The property was purchased in 2006 for $332M as the sponsor put in an additional $76M for renovation. In 2019, the sponsor kept the building but sold the land underneath its property, thus creating a ground lease which it sold to a 3rd party for $285M, allowing the building owner to lower its basis considerably, but in the process agreeing to pay the new landowner monthly land lease payments into the foreseeable future. Last week the building owners sold its equity at auction for $8.5M, losing most of its remaining equity. Not only does the sponsor lose out, but it is has implications for the value of the land, given the lack of equity cushion above it and the little NOI the property generates, after operating expense, ground rent and interest payments.
 
Ground leases are long-term leases, originally up to 99 years, where the landowner retains ownership of the land while allowing the sponsor to own and operate the property sitting on top of the land. At the end of the ground lease, the physical building reverts to the landowner. During the lease period, the building owner (or tenant) pays rent to the landowner for the use of the land. The land rent typically escalates over time by 2% with inflation-capped lookbacks. Some less friendly ground leases are structured with FMV resets or as a percentage of the tenant's revenue from the property. Ground leases provide the property owner with additional leverage to control a property without owning the land. The landowner receives a steady income stream while retaining ownership of the land. If the building owner fails to make ground lease payments, the landlord has the right to terminate the lease and take possession of the property. The pecking order of payments is real estate taxes, then ground lease payment, then interest expense, then operating expenses.
 
Strucutred Credit allows for a bond to be spit into the IO & PO, or a loan that is first-out/last-out or a debt structure that is senior & subordinate. In commercial real estate, a property can be split into the land & the building sitting on top of the land whereby the land holder recieves payment that is senior to the building owner and its creditors. At the end of the day the sponsor took on too much leverage by creating & selling a ground lease, and then taking out a leashold loan on the property above the ground, resulting in little flexibility when performance deteriaoted.
