FIVE FIGURES, FOR A PROOF OF CONCEPT?— I’LL TAKE IT😁

1/

So, Friday, April 4th, I opened up my machine, jumped into Afternic, and staring me in the face was a congratulatory message about a domain sale.
For the first few seconds, I couldn’t understand what I was seeing — it felt like a dream. I tot to myself, “This ain’t April 1st... so this has gotta be real for real!.”
Create .Ad had sold for $9K, and there was a message from TAA asking for a transfer code to begin the process.

After screaming for a while, I logged into my registrar account, requested the transfer code, and received it via email. When I opened the email to copy the code, I noticed something else — a sales notification from Afternic, showing that the domain had sold two days prior, on April 2nd.

So for two days, the buyer and the AN agent had been waiting for me to kick off the transfer. I got the auth code and pasted it into the tab provided by AN.

Called a few peeps to share the good news. After a while, I closed the machine, grabbed the keys, and went out for some errands.
About 4 hours later, I returned, opened up AN — and another shock! — There was a transfer failed message.
Why? Because the registrar transfer lock was still on.

I quickly, unchecked the transfer lock, and generated a new auth code.
And this was when things got even more interesting.

I opened my email to grab the new code — and i see another message, a successful sales message from Atom for the same domain, but this time for $13K! 😳💥🤯
My head almost exploded!
I was like — “Whaaaaatttttttttttttt!!!!!!!Bruuhhhhhhhhhh!!!!!!! Ohhhhhhhhhhh!!!! shiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii!!!!!!!!!!!
Apparently, in all my excitement earlier, I had forgotten to delist the domain from Atom and also sedo where it’s listed, but for $13K

Now, in hindsight, maybe the buyer, after making the purchase on April 2nd, got tired of waiting for the auth code, and saw the domain still listed elsewhere. So they bought it again. Or... maybe it was a completely different buyer. I don’t know. But one thing’s for sure — with the transfer lock now removed and a new code, your guess is as good as mine as to who I gave the code to. 😉

This sale means a lot to me in so many ways.
First off, it just proves that domaining and domain investing is very real, profitable, and a sustainable way to do business.
If anyone ever doubted whether the system works — here’s your proof. It does.
And I’m grateful. 🙏🏾
It also shows that outbound or marketing matters.
Maybe not always for an instant sale, but at least it puts your name in front of people who might need it — now or in the future.

Let me say this: If you’re out here on this street, in the trenches, and sales haven’t happened for you yet, keep grinding.
Keep laying the groundwork. It’s coming

And if any domainer has ever mocked you — privately, publicly, on a Space, or in a tweet — just like some dude did, back in December, in a tweet, (yeah, that one, that hosts of that saturday morning domain space)… mocking his overbloated, constipated self and not me — just let them talk.

Always remember:
 “The river may be quiet, but its depth is unknown.” — Filipino Proverb

•The hack works: Sexy + .domains = “sexy domains”

Cons
•“Sexy” can be interpreted as adult (even if you mean “attractive/appealing”), which can limit corporate buyers
•TLD liquidity: .domains is niche, so resale pool is smaller than .com

⸻

7) Valuation: Retail vs Wholesale

Wholesale (investor): $100 – $600
•Anchored heavily by the fact it’s already offered at $500 BIN publicly. 

Retail (end-user): $750 – $4,500
•A domainer/broker who will actually use it could justify low-to-mid $x ,xxx.
•The ceiling is capped by extension niche + potential “adult” interpretation.

⸻

8) Pricing & Negotiation Strategy

If you’re buying (it’s $500 BIN on Spaceship):
•$500 is already fair if you have a use case (newsletter, portfolio hub, curated list). 
•If “Make Offer” is accepted, try $250–$400 and close fast.

If you own it:
•List at $2,988 BIN (room to negotiate to ~$1k–$2k)
•Best outbound targets: domain-curation newsletters, brokers, portfolio owners (this is super niche outbound)

⸻

9) Final Take

 Sexy.domains is a fun, functional brand for the domain industry, but it’s not a broad-market asset. With the current $500 BIN out there, your best ROI is likely using it (curation hub / lead gen) rather than waiting for a massive flip.

[this is a copy of my response on the DNX show episode regarding my CVCV that sold this week on @afternic for $100 following a mass pricing update failure and domain selling immediately via fast transfer]: "... I'd love to clarify a few things (I listened to the start where my case was discussed). It's incorrect if @afternic have said that I have a history of this. My memory it has happened twice: first time on one domain (which was mis-priced and the sale cancelled), and then this incident. The @afternic system was bugging / acting irregular when I was making the changes this week/I struggled (I intended for a single page of names only). I do recall refreshing a number of times /retrying (I had forgotten this until Rene mentioned it today, as it was at this time). I made the price changes which changed all 1,000 names (to $100). I realized within minutes and deleted all names - I then got the sale notices on two names a few mins later. I immediately emailed my GD Rep, and called the Afternic contact centre. The contact centre said they would attempt to switch the names from fast transfer to manual, but shortly after I got a transfer notice (from UD where it was). I called my Rep and explained it to him, and he went away to see what could be done. I explained this was clearly a mistake, I had delisted all names prior to the sale, etc. He called a few hours later to say he could not stop the transfer of the CVCV because it was against their terms of use, but they would try to speak with the buyer. That was Tuesday. I have followed up multiple times with my Rep and heard nothing back since... This is not good customer service. @afternic transfer assurance notified me today that it was too late as the name had transferred. I'm pretty disappointed here for a number of reasons. 1. I had deleted the mispriced listing on @afternic very quickly and before the name sold; 2. It clearly is a mistake in pricing for the value of the asset; 3. the @afternic system is arguably defective by design by not allowing users to catch changes (if a name will sell immediately); 4. the domain is still at GoDaddy, so it can be returned; 5. there are examples of GD pulling names back from domainers and cancelling transactions; 6. I spend a lot on GD/Afternic; 7. the afternic mass updates feature was not operating to requirements when I was making the changes (arguably this caused or impacted the inacurate updates). I am hopeful that @afternic will assist here still and allow this to be resolved amicably without recourse to a more formal process"

I invested in (and told you to invest in $INFQ when it was still $CCCX . Here’s why:

 $INFQ (Infleqtion) stands out as the leading quantum computing company right now:

Infleqtion (NYSE: INFQ, formerly ColdQuanta) is the first neutral-atom quantum company to go public (Feb 2026 via SPAC). It operates a full-stack neutral-atom platform for computing, networking, sensing, and software. Neutral atoms (typically rubidium/cesium held in optical tweezers and manipulated by lasers) offer key advantages: easier scaling to large qubit arrays, long coherence times, all-to-all connectivity potential, and operation without extreme cryogenic requirements like superconducting systems. infleqtion.com 
Key technical leadership points:
• Demonstrated the world’s largest neutral-atom array: ~1,600 physical qubits.
• Industry-leading entangling (CZ) gate fidelity for neutral atoms: 99.73% (user-facing/post-selected higher in some cases), with recent dual-species (Rb-Cs) gates and theory work pointing toward >99.9%. This is critical because higher fidelity reduces the overhead needed for error correction. infleqtion.com 
• Delivered the UK’s only operational 100-qubit neutral-atom system (Sqale platform) and demonstrated real-world logical qubit applications, including a materials science use case in collaboration with NVIDIA—the first of its kind using logical qubits.
• Roadmap: Targeting 30+ logical qubits in 2026 and 100+ by 2028, with a path to fault-tolerant, utility-scale systems. They’ve already hit milestones like 12 logical qubits (error-detected) ahead of schedule in some reports. thequantuminsider.com 

Commercial and financial edge:
• Unlike pure-play computing companies still deep in cash-burn R&D with minimal revenue, Infleqtion has a diversified portfolio. It generates real revenue today from quantum sensors (optical clocks, RF receivers, inertial/gravimetric sensors) sold to governments, military, NASA, and commercial clients. These are deployable products addressing real needs like precision timing and GPS-denied navigation.
• Well-capitalized post-IPO (> $550M funding) plus a fresh $100M Letter of Intent from the U.S. Department of Commerce CHIPS program (announced May 2026) specifically to accelerate U.S. neutral-atom quantum leadership. businesswire.com 
• Proprietary Superstaq software optimizes circuits across hardware, giving it a full-stack moat.

Why this makes INFQ clearly leading compared to peers:
• Scalability edge over IonQ/Quantinuum (trapped-ion): Trapped ions have excellent fidelity (IonQ has hit 99.99% two-qubit in some reports), but packing and controlling large numbers of ions is harder due to charge interactions and shuttling. Neutral atoms scale more naturally to thousands of qubits via optical lattices/tweezers. indexbox.io 
• Practical advantages over IBM/Rigetti (superconducting): Those require massive dilution refrigerators and face manufacturing bottlenecks at traditional fabs. Neutral-atom systems leverage more optics/laser-based manufacturing and can operate in less extreme conditions.
• Revenue + government backing reduces risk: Most quantum pure-plays are pre-revenue or low-revenue. INFQ’s sensor business provides a bridge to profitability while the computing side matures. The recent CHIPS funding and defense contracts signal strong U.S. strategic prioritization.
• Broader ecosystem: Partnerships (NVIDIA), international presence, and a platform spanning compute + sensing/networking position it for hybrid quantum-classical applications sooner

🚨Quantum Breakthrough…
Not a Quantum Break-In 🔐⚛️

It's true that China has reportedly sold and delivered a neutral-atom quantum computer (Hanyuan-1). That’s real — and strategically important.

Reporting from @SCMPNews , @QuantumDaily , and @QuantumReport says sales exceed ¥40M ($5.6M), including delivery to a China Mobile subsidiary and an overseas order (Pakistan). The system uses neutral atoms as qubits and doesn’t require cryogenic cooling — a real engineering advantage.

☝🏼 Now the reality check:

🧠 It’s a commercialization milestone.
❌ It cannot break modern encryption.
❌ It’s not fault-tolerant.
❌ It’s not consumer quantum computing.

A ~100-qubit machine is nowhere near the millions of error-corrected qubits needed to crack RSA-2048.

Also, “world’s first atomic quantum computer” is overstated. Companies like QuEra and Atom Computing have operated neutral-atom systems for years (mostly via cloud access).

⚠️ So what is this?

A meaningful step in the long quantum race.
Not a crypto apocalypse. ⚛️

Commercial milestone? Yes.
Encryption breaker? No.
Geopolitically relevant? Absolutely.

Cosmos is cold and dark

About 1.5 months ago I finally sold the shitcoins I had been holding for years — including my already heavily diluted $ATOM bag.

I still remember why I bought it in the first place, back in spring 2022:

Cosmos was supposed to be great tech.

«Just needs some polishing and better UX» they said on podcasts.

AppChains, Cosmos SDK, millions of launches, millions of airdrops for stakers.

Reality check🫠

Over all this time, I got exactly one meaningful airdrop — @celestia . Sold it at ~$5 per token, then watched it fly to $20

There were ~10 more tiny drops that weren’t even worth selling.

A few large apps came to Cosmos SDK — and then left. @dYdX is the most obvious example.

The core Cosmos idea — a separate chain for each application (AppChain) — ended up being replicated on EVM.

And on EVM it’s simply better:

→ costs pennies to deploy
→ no obligation to hand out massive launch incentives
→ instant access to the entire EVM user base via a single wallet

Meanwhile, Cosmos requires: new wallets, bridges, network hopping — just to swap one token.

No amount of staking over 3 years came close to compensating for a ~10x price collapse.

Even if I had sold at the last local top a year ago, I’d still be slightly down😁

Why did this happen❓

In my view, there are only two real reasons

1⃣ Onboarding complexity

Cosmos was built for a hardcore geek community. 
People who don’t mind:

→ installing yet another wallet
→learning why a simple swap requires bridging to another chain
→debugging UX that feels like a side quest

That does not scale.

2⃣ Zero marketing / zero “flex” economy

There was never a killer narrative that made normal users want to bring money into the ecosystem

Compare that to @solana 🔽

The Solana Foundation didn’t just rely on tech:

1) first they pushed NFTs
2) then DeFi
3) and the final iteration was memes

All of it wrapped in aggressive, extremely relatable marketing:

«I bought a monkey JPEG / I staked SOL / I bought a memecoin for $10 from my Phantom wallet, topped up via PayPal during my McDonald’s shift — and made $10,000😎🤑😎🤑» 

That’s how retail adoption actually happens.

If you want a broader snapshot of the Cosmos ecosystem today, you can read about the state of all projects in the quoted tweet.

(And honestly, the ATOM price chart alone tells the same story.)

At this point, the only somewhat alive projects left are:

🔸ATOM itself

🔸Celestia

🔹Noble — a stablecoin protocol backed by Paradigm

Noble already ran two farming seasons and is preparing another one alongside its move to HyperEVM🙃

Everyone else either leaves — or slowly dies.

In short: if you didn’t run, you died

Domain Investing: Keeping Up with Trends

It’s hard to keep track of what’s trending and what isn’t in the fast-moving world of tech and AI. Just a few weeks ago, while I was in #Nigeria , I heard the term "OpenClaw" for the first time. According to Wikipedia, OpenClaw is a free and open-source autonomous AI agent developed by Peter Steinberger. As of February/March 2026, several variants of the “Claw” concept are already appearing—names like ZeroClaw, PicoClaw, and NanoBot.

Then, a few days later, I noticed on @NameBio that OpenClaw..org reportedly sold via Spaceship for $55,000. That caught my attention.

Around the same time, I read that Mark Zuckerberg had acquired MoltBook for an undisclosed amount. Honestly, I had never even heard of MoltBook until I saw the article. Shortly after, I discovered there’s an AI agent sub-project called MoltBuilds. And just like the “Claw” naming pattern, it’s probably only a matter of time before more "Molt" variations appear.

Then today—only a few hours ago—I heard about another AI agent called Livebook. According to Hugging Face, Livebook is an open-source tool for writing interactive code notebooks in Elixir. It’s part of a growing ecosystem of Elixir tools for numerical computing, data science, and machine learning. Then you have "Muta," a conversation for a different day.

Another thing I’ve started noticing is a trend around the word "Book." According to Medium, the concept of a “book”—often framed as a playbook, guide, or even a “Bible” for agentic AI—has become popular because it provides structured guidance in a rapidly evolving field.

So what’s the takeaway?

Trends appear fast, evolve quickly, and sometimes disappear just as fast. As domain investors, spotting them early can be exciting—but it also comes with risk. The truth is, it’s very difficult to know which trend will produce the best ROI.

If you decide to invest in trend-based domains, do it carefully and strategically. There is definitely money to be made riding trends—but timing, judgment, and discipline matter.

For full transparency, I’ve also picked up a few names in this space, including MetalClaw..com, MoltBuilds..com, LiveBook..co, MutaBots..com, and others.

The AI naming wave is still forming, and new ideas are appearing almost daily. For #domain investors—especially newcomers—the key is to stay curious, watch the market, and be ready when opportunity appears.

In this industry, sometimes the biggest wins come from seeing a trend just a little earlier than everyone else.

This is a one-word + AI, category-defining domain very relevant in the biotech industry. Yes, I know many will say I super undersold it — Dynadot appraisal gave it a $25K value, and some might price it at $50K. But hey, it only cost me $11 when I registered it at the end of 2022, right when the ChatGPT and AI buzz started, and I’m happy with the funds.
The only thing I regret is that the lander at Spaceship was priced the same as at Afternic. I didn’t update it — otherwise I could have priced higher at Afternic and paid no commission if the buyer chose that route, or kept more funds in my pocket if he bought via Spaceship.

This domain was not acquired by a domainer, because I had it listed for $2K at Porkbun and Atom — there’s no way they missed that.

What’s really interesting is that I submitted this domain months ago to Atom Premium, it only got approved two weeks ago for $7K (I haven’t approved it yet), and today — boom — it sold. No way this is a coincidence; they must have known something. The timeframe is too narrow.🤔

Today was the first time I took my laptop to the beach, and domaining in front of the sea is something else — great energy! While managing my portfolio and writing a different post for today, I saw many emails from Porkbun related to one of my domains being transferred out:

"We have received a successful Afternic Fast Transfer command for your domain."

In between, I missed the Afternic “congrats” email and thought, “Shit, a f***er is stealing my domain!” 😅
Then I found the congrats email.

I’m officially adopting the beach as my everyday office now! 🌴😎🌊

name: Sedo
text: Samur​.ai was sold for $50,000 - Congrats to seller and buyer!

I complained about this back in September: nitter.poast.org/NameBio/status/1965357… 

At least now they let you not have a down payment for LTOs, before it was a required field.

But I still think it isn't intuitive to set a term for N months, and it actually takes N+1 months to complete with a down payment, or N+2 months with a down payment and a final payment.

I doubt many people get good at domain investing only from trial and error, without learning about the sales of others. So it’s a way to give back.

Our sister company has shared thousands of sales with NameBio. I don’t recall it ever coming back to bite us once.

Maybe if you discovered a new niche and you’re still trying to secure your bag. But that’s a rare, once or twice in a lifetime kind of thing, if ever. For 99% of sales it simply doesn’t apply.

When I hear people hesitant to give away alpha it reminds me of entrepreneurs who come up with a business idea and are terrified someone is going to steal it, want NDAs to even talk about it, etc.

I just roll my eyes. As with almost anything in business, it almost all comes down to execution.

If someone knowing about a sale you made will harm your business, you’re already cooked.

Sure, I’m a little biased, but I’m also not wrong 🙃

Scent is more common as a prefix than a suffix in retail sales, and so far none have been for a specific scent. HugeDomains has PineScent listed for $1,495 and most popular scents are listed for sale, parked, or unused. It’s worth a hand reg but pretty low probability of a sale.

I did a deep dive into our 290 LTO deals at @afternic and discovered some valuable insights concerning cancellations, early payoffs, and trends.

📉 Cancellation Rates

Our raw cancellation rate was 26.9%, but that understates risk because it counts active deals as non-cancellations.

A better number is the resolved cancellation rate: cancellations divided by completed LTOs.

Historically, among our LTOs that have reached an outcome, about 59% completed successfully and 41% were cancelled.

⏱️ Cancellation Timing

Cancellations are heavily front-loaded. Obviously the more payments they make the less likely they are to walk away at the next payment. But at what point are they really committed?

Of our 78 cancellations, 28 (36%) made only one payment, 40 out of 78 (51%) made at most two payments, and 63 out of 78 (81%) made at most six payments.

Once a deal avoids cancelling after only one payment, its resolved success rate rises to about 70%. Once a deal avoids the early churn window and gets to around six payments, the resolved success rate rises to around 86-88%.

📆 Cancellation and Term Length

Most of our LTOs (87%) were in the 12-23 month range, so I'm not sure how statistically significant this data is. But there was a pretty clear pattern that the longer the length of the LTO, the higher the raw cancellation rate was.

The raw cancellation for LTOs less than one year was 25%, for 12-23 months it was 25.3%, for 24-35 months it was 31.2%, and for 36+ months it was 53.8%.

You might think the longer the term, the more manageable the monthly payments are, and the more likely they'll be to stick around. But in this dataset, longer terms were clearly riskier. Personally, I’d be cautious offering terms longer than 24 months.

💳 Cancellation and Monthly Payment

Looking only at 12-month LTOs, the raw cancellation rate was essentially the same for sub-$200 monthly payments vs $200-299 payments vs $300-499 payments. But interestingly, once the monthly payments reached $500+ the raw cancellation rate dropped by more than 50%.

That's somewhat intuitive though, someone committing to a $500+ monthly payment is probably more serious and well-funded.

🤔 Confusing Cancellations

Three buyers cancelled with only one payment left, which seems pretty unbelievable.

In 8 cases, a cancelled LTO later sold again shortly afterward — 6 through LTO and 2 through BIN. The data doesn’t include buyer identity, but given normal domain sell-through rates and the short timing, these were very likely buyers coming back after missing a payment or regretting the cancellation.

⚡ Early Payoffs

17% of completed LTOs were paid off early. Nearly half of early payoffs happened close to the finish line, but of the early payers, 32% paid off after only 1–2 payments.

📈 LTOs By Year

2023: 13 (53 annualized)
2024: 106
2025: 114
2026: 57 (137 annualized)

We're seeing a steady trend upward as LTOs stack up.

🎁 Wrap Up

I hope this helps you get a better picture of what you might experience if you enable LTOs.

The interesting takeaways for me were how heavily front-loaded LTO churn is, how longer terms reduce your odds of success, how little the monthly payment amount affects the odds except at the high end, and how more than 10% of cancelled LTOs still ended up in a sale shortly after.

name: Andrew Miller
text:
Random Sunday Thoughts #215

1. The past few days were slightly quieter for me from a transaction standpoint, as we worked towards closing some exciting deals this week. There was no lull in the full court press talking to prospects on the world's most valuable domains that we represent. High level discussions have been nonstop since November with no slow down in site. These are the most progressive and informed conversations I can recall having in my 28+ years of investing in and brokering domain names. For years, many of my peers and I spent an enormous amount of time educating founders, investors, and management teams, at companies ranging from early stage startups to Fortune 100 corporations, about the strategic importance of exact match and category defining domain names. The awareness is taking hold, the urgency is real, and the recognition that owning your exact match brand, category domain is a foundational business decision, not a vanity purchase, has never been more widespread. It is fantastic to see it taking hold at this level. 

2. Further to that point, I saw at least two founders post publicly about their domain acquisitions on X this week, and both are perfect illustrations of exactly what I am talking about. The first was the founder of Flint, who posted simply: "we dropped the try, now at Flint .com. It's cleaner that way." That one line says everything.They get the game changing strategic importance, their customers know what it means, and to the market its intuitive. TryFlint becomes Flint .com and the brand instantly becomes more credible, more permanent, and more memorable. Shout out to Elliot Silver for flagging this one, nitter.poast.org/michlimlim/status/2057… . The second was Harper Insurance, which upgraded to Harper .com after securing a $47 million Series A. This is the pattern I see consistently; a company raises a significant round, and one of the first strategic decisions they make is to acquire their exact-match domain. It is not a coincidence. The investors writing those checks increasingly understand that the domain is part of the brand infrastructure they are funding. A $47 million business operating on a suboptimal domain is leaving brand equity on the table every single day. Both of these are quiet announcements that most people scroll past. But to me they are data points in a much larger trend, and the trend is accelerating. In the next several days, as has been the case all year, we will upgrade 3 more emerging and market leading brands to their exact match domains, all mid 7 figure transactions, that will be the smartest  strategic investment these companies make to date. 

3.  I am a hard core sports lover, but I have never been much of a soccer fan. My son recently introduced me to Arsenal and its clever, wildly dedicated fans. They have reminded me that whomever you root for and whatever you do, there is no replacement for being passionate. I can't wait to experience the World Cup this summer!

Until Next Week #domains

name: Broker Tom
text:
Landed in Las Vegas for Adobe Summit 2026.

This week I'll be meeting with teams from the Magnificent 7 and Fortune 500 companies about something most enterprises still treat as an afterthought: how a category-defining domain name elevates a brand, a subsidiary launch, or a new product rollout much more than C-level teams realize.

I'll be discussing domain names like AIART.COM , HARDWARE.COM , CHATBOTS.COM , GENERATIVE.COM — category-defining domains from GoDaddy's DomainNames.com brokerage. When executed properly, these assets can generate $100M+ enterprise brand value over the long-term.

A thought I keep returning to:

Every interaction in a deal is a real-time win-rate calculation.

The email domain you send from. The way your profile reads. Your tone. Your response time. The clothes you walk into the room wearing. None of these are decisive on their own. All of them move the percentage.

One of my habits — and it sounds trivial until you practice it — is negotiating hotel room upgrades. Not because I want a better room. Because it's a zero-risk environment to stay sharp on the small decisions that compound in high-stakes negotiations.

Today's version, after I landed:

→ Studied the available inventory before approaching the desk
→ Walked up with a genuine compliment about the property
→ Used staff names
→ Changed out of flight clothes into a suit before the conversation

None of those moves, in isolation, wins anything. Together, they shift the percentage enough to matter. The same principle governs every domain transaction I've ever worked on: the deal is rarely decided by one variable. It's decided by the accumulation of small ones.

Now, thanks to a win at today's front-desk negotiation, I can watch the Las Vegas Sphere run Adobe creative — AI art, the word "Generate" on loop — and prepare for the conference, where the same principle plays out on a much larger stage.

Two questions worth sitting with:

For Domain Owners → How is your asset being positioned, by whom, and what does a serious buyer perceive when they encounter it?

For Executives & Entrepreneurs → Your domain is the first impression your brand makes to the world, make it count.

P.S. If you're in Vegas this week, keep an eye out for GoDaddy's "Gaggle" of Geese on the Strip and some fun outfits that get attention. I'm genuinely very excited about GoDaddy's brand strength and innovative DomainNames.com promotions we have planned this week to connect the right ultra-premium domains with the right buyers #AdobeSummit

We’ve got something to celebrate🎉

Spaceship turns 3 today. But really? This one's yours.

Back in April 2023, we took spaceship.com out of private gated testing early and opened it up to real customers.

Why? To let customers lead the way. Real feedback. Real requests. Leading to real solutions. Giving us the focus to build what you needed, faster.

I don't think your takeaway is correct here. It isn't proof that your domains bring the sales, in fact multiple large portfolios confirm that distribution networks produce a majority of sales. Landers generally only account for about 35-40% of volume.

Here's a recent discussion on de-listing from marketplaces, which also links to another older post about the makeup of aftermarket sales in the comments:

 nitter.poast.org/NameBio/status/2038913… 

Assuming you still list at Afternic, it's only proof that Sedo MLS provides very little extra coverage above Afternic DLS, and most partners of both prioritize Afternic listings.

We list a majority of our ~75k portfolio at Sedo, while being fully listed and majority landed at Afternic, and Sedo produces about 1 sale per year for every 4-5k names listed. Abysmal, but still five-figures per year in extra revenue that we likely wouldn't have had otherwise.

It's definitely a burden to keep multiple marketplaces up to date, and depending on portfolio size and your average sale price, I could definitely see an argument for de-listing from marketplaces that are under-performing.

So you're likely making the right call and won't regret it. Statistically with 1,750 listings you should only get a Sedo sale once every other year at best.

But I wouldn't jump to the conclusion that most sales come from the domain itself, because I guarantee you that isn't true.

For example, look at the attached screenshot of a search on "agent". You can instantly see that it has a higher sales velocity at the end rather than at the start. But you can also quickly see that being at the start results in a 33% higher average sale price than at the end.

ABM just dropped one of the most valuable pieces of knowledge that has ever been shared in the domain industry, and most people are going to miss it because it was a reply to a reply.

In August of last year I did a pretty lengthy post breaking down the realities of the aftermarket, trying to help people understand what percentage of sales come directly from "for sale" landing pages, what percentage come from distribution networks, and of the network sales which come from each major distribution partner.

The reason I did that was to show the math on what happens if you list at Afternic and use their landers, versus using other landers with discounted commissions. What I essentially proved was that even if the alt lander has a 0% commission, you still end up worse off due to Afternic's commission penalty for not using their landers.

I'll link to that post in the replies if you want to do a deep dive and really understand the full picture. But in short, around 60-65% of domain sales come from Afternic DLS and Sedo MLS (the distribution networks), and the remaining 35-40% come from the "for sale" landers directly. This is confirmed by multiple large portfolio holders.

There were still two important questions that I was unable to answer though:

The first is what would happen if you fully delisted from Afternic, so they couldn't sell your domains at the 25-30% punitive rate while using alt landers. The theory a lot of people shared was that the network buyers, not being able to find you on the network, would still find you by typing in the domain.

I wasn't buying it. Sure, it'll happen sometimes, but I was almost certain it would be an extreme minority, and the move would be a major net negative.

My theory was that a vast majority of network buyers were either shown your domain as an alternative to what they were actually searching, or when brainstorming a bunch of different domains. And they wouldn't have found it without the network, because they weren't typing domains into their browser's address bar to check availability. They were using a registrar.

But I couldn't prove it because I've never fully delisted from Afternic and Sedo to find out, and I didn't know anyone who has and then talked about it. Until now.

Thanks to ABM we now have that missing piece of the puzzle; he said sales dropped 50% by delisting. That means if his sales breakdown was 40% landers 60% network, only 17% of network buyers would buy directly if it wasn't on the network. Or if his breakdown was 35% landers and 65% network, only 23% would buy directly if it wasn't on the network.

Let that sink in. Between 77% and 83% of network buyers will NOT buy your domain directly from your discount-commission landers if you are not on the distribution networks. If you scroll up on ABM's reply below, you'll see it was a reply to a comment I made predicting this "50% drop" outcome pretty much on the nose.

The second looming question is what would happen if you raised your prices on Afternic and Sedo to offset the higher commissions and then used your own landers with low or no commissions offering the domain at a lower price. A lot of people think this is "free money" for network sales by baking in the commission.

But I know that it will, for the most part, hurt your sell-through rate quite a bit. I can't quantify it, but I suspect it would almost definitely more than offset the commission penalties you were hoping to recoup. It just seems logical, if you hurt your STR on 65% of your sales to get a slightly better commission on 35% of your sales, you're probably going to lose.

Except in the situation where most of your domains are priced below $2k; at that level you can raise prices without affecting the demand curve.

I selfishly hope ABM will test this next by relisting at Afternic and Sedo, but at higher prices than shown on his NamePros Landers; enough that he would net the same wherever it sells.

That would answer the last remaining question surrounding the economics of the domain aftermarket: is it even possible to offset a commission by raising prices?

My money is on "no". But once we know that, we'd be able to fully model out all possible outcomes and make perfectly informed decisions to maximize revenue based on all the various marketplace commission structures and "for sale" lander options.

Regardless, I hope ABM stops this delisting experiment for both his and Jamie's sake. It's already been running long enough to learn everything there is to learn from it.

It's painfully obvious that a 50% drop in sales to save 15-20% on commission isn't a winning move. Let's say he was doing $1 million in sales a year and netting $800k after commission. Now he would have about $500k in sales, netting maybe $480k after transaction costs. That means he probably spent around $320k to learn this lesson.

We all owe ABM an enormous debt of gratitude for generously sharing what he learned with everyone.

We have 6.5 million sales records totaling more than $3 billion. How much more revenue do you think we make when someone reports a $2,500 sale? It's fractions of a penny at the most, if you could actually attribute any incremental revenue to it at all, which would be a massive stretch.

Considering the time it takes to review and approve that report, or grab it ourselves from social media, we actually lose money for every manually reported sale. But we still do it anyway, because not everything is about the money.

Marketplaces and brokers report because it attracts more sellers and buyers, which means they do more deal flow. It makes sense for them to incentivize reporting, because it's cheap marketing. One sale report could inspire someone to list their whole portfolio, which could generate tens of thousands per year in commission.

Sedo makes you pay them to not report it. Atom incentivizes agreeing to report it. Most other marketplaces are behind the times and do nothing.

As for individual investors, there are 850k+ people who use the site for free every year doing many millions of searches. Some who have benefitted from the data want to give back, although 100% of our users consume more data than they provide by many, many orders of magnitude.

Some do it for the clout, some do it for the pride of making on the daily chart, etc. Even paid users report sales just to be nice.

We can't incentivize reporting though. Partially because it might encourage fake reports just to get the incentive. Partially because the value of a single sale, unless it is a headline sale of six or seven figures, is so small there's nothing we can justify offering other than a high five. And people who report headline sales aren't going to be moved by a token incentive because, well... they be ballin'.

Make sense?

I can't overstate how important this piece of advice is. We all get lowball offers, but how you respond can make a huge difference.

One time I received a $250 opening offer for a .org that I had on a "make offer" lander. I had purchased it for four-figures and expected mid five-figures.

Instead of firing off a snarky response, I responded saying thanks for the offer but we're too far apart, and showed a dozen close comps of .orgs selling for five and even six figures.

He responded back saying he was the buyer for many of those comps I had shown him. He added that he knew the value, but hey, he had to start somewhere. We ended up closing at $30,000 after a little bit of back-and-forth.

The domain wasn't something he had to have, he just wanted it for his collection, and it still isn't developed to this day. So if I had responded like a jerk or just ignored him entirely I'm pretty sure he would have moved on and found something else.

We also saw this recently when @dnx shared one of Josh's negotiations:

 nitter.poast.org/dnx/status/19908664574… 

He received a $5,000 offer on a name he was expecting $100,000 for. Instead of being rude he responded professionally, and ended up closing a deal at $52,700. They probably weren't bluffing and were actually considering alternatives, so if he was a difficult person to deal with they might have walked.

Watch the video all the way to the end, because it also serves as a great reminder to follow up multiple times. I needed that, it appears that I'm too quick to close a lead when it seems obvious that it won't go anywhere.

I know you didn't mention anyone by name. But she's the only one on the planet who owns a statistically significant number of xyz, she's 99% of reported xyz sales, and she's the only one sharing substantially all of her xyz sales allowing you to calculate an expected STR.

So you can't have an educated conversation about the xyz retail market without studying her portfolio results. Nothing else is relevant.

Take three-letter .com for example. I spent most of my career working for someone who owns more than 10% of all of the possible combinations.

He told me the STR is around 0.33% when priced in the six and seven-figure range, which means you need 300 to make one sale per year, or if you own one you should expect to sit on it 300 years.

So I can't own a single one and then be confused about why I haven't made a sale after three years, and say it must be because I'm not in the short-domain cabal. Are there people making retail sales who own only a couple? Sure...

But that's irrelevant to determining expected outcomes. It's random dumb luck when you're not playing the numbers game. A lightning strike. Luck is not an investment strategy.

There are only 18 reported xyz sales in the six-figure range. I can count on my fingers how many people have reported them who are not named Swetha. I don't believe any of them only owned a single xyz domain. Only 1 of the sales was three syllables: Capital․xyz. Only one of them was primarily an adjective: Stable․xyz. Do you see how amazingly well those fit for crypto though?

The odds were extremely stacked against you owning a single three-syllable adjective that is a stretch to shoehorn it into a very niche Web3 use case, where your breakeven expected value requires a Top 10 sale.

I do agree that the renewal wasn't relevant to why you didn't achieve a retail sale of that single domain during that short time. You only had a 1/67 chance of it happening during the three-year window. You would have had almost twice as good odds putting $7,500 on a single number in roulette... let that sink in.

But the renewal should have been extremely relevant to your decision to acquire it in the first place, both because it'll prevent you from holding it long enough to see a sale, and it'll prevent you from liquidating it.

Dropping the price doesn't materially increase your odds of a retail sale on a short time horizon, and wholesale you'd struggle to give it away when there's no time left on the registration.

Swetha's STR is low, the most sales she ever had in a year was 141 which works out to about 0.5%. That means if you own one xyz, the expected time to sell is about 200 years.

At her average selling price of around $20k, renewals would have to average less than $100 just for her to break even.

Yours was $540 per year, so statistically you should expect to pay $108,000 in renewals before it would sell, on top of the $6k acquisition price.

Even if you were hoping to sell it for $114k (almost six times Swetha's average) that would just be a break-even expected value.

This was essentially a very expensive lottery ticket with no burn-down value to the wholesale market due to the renewal.

I don't even think it's a good empty vessel for a brand, not many companies call themselves just "Luxury." It's too generic and more commonly an adjective than a noun, which begs people to react with "luxury what?" not "wow, nice brand". Look how the .com is used.

But the larger issue is that you didn't pick something which would work well for crypto and Web3, which are the types of companies that adopted the TLD. Luxury relates well to the physical world (cars, apartments, fashion, travel) not intangibles like crypto, NFTs, or other blockchain projects.

People need to understand that Swetha is playing a large numbers game with standard renewals, and as long as her average selling price is more than $3k she's guaranteed to win. Nobody else can play that game now because premium renewals will eat you alive. Negari cut out the middle man, which is all of us... let him.

Other investors who had random sales despite doing it on a small scale stacked the odds in their favor as much as they could. They had low acquisition cost and renewal prices, owned enough of them that they could reasonably expect a sale in their lifetime, took the time to understand the buyers and what they might demand, and then got very lucky on top of it.

That's my take on it anyway, as someone with no skin in this TLD.

Watch out when setting up an LTO deal on Spaceship, it’s very unintuitive. Most platforms collect the down payment WITH the first installment. On Spaceship the down payment IS the first installment.

So if you’re trying to structure a $5k sale evenly over five months with no down payment, you actually have to set it up as $1k down payment, $1k final payment, and three monthly installments.

Not $5k over five installments with $1 down payment and $1 final payment (since they don’t let you put $0 down payment).

Such an unclear way to do it, and support will tell you tough luck if the buyer already made the down payment.

You should call it first and last installment if that’s what it is, not down payment and final payment as if it’s collected in addition to the regular installments.

name: Sandeep Sarao
text:
First of all, thank God. Sold Pcc.ai last month. Thanks to @atomHQ 

I like to share story behind that.

In 2023, I hand-registered PCC.ai and submitted it to @atomHQ Premium. It was initially approved at $3,499, but I felt the AI market was just getting started, so I removed it. Later, I resubmitted it and Atom approved it in the $22k-$45k range. After further market research and a pricing review, I listed it at $77k.

A buyer came in at $50k. Following a negotiation strategy I learned from @TonyNames , I kept my floor at $50k and asked the broker to push higher. The buyer ultimately agreed to $70,000.

Huge thanks to the #domain community for all the knowledge shared along the way, and special thanks to @MichaelCyger , whose comment on my first sale gave me the confidence to keep going.

Sometimes the biggest difference between a $3,499 sale and a $70,000 sale is having the patience and conviction to hold the right asset.

All that means is they convert searches into aftermarket domain sales at a higher rate than GoDaddy converts their searches. And despite that, GoDaddy was still 80% of network sales because of the sheer amount of reach that they have.

Imagine if GoDaddy search wasn't trash prioritizing hand regs? They'd probably be 95%+ of network sales. Too bad the registrar team wins more arguments than the aftermarket team in their meetings.

I doubt search engines like Google are a major source of warm leads for domain buyers. And I doubt many thin "for sale" landing pages rank well for terms with any meaningful search volume.

Maybe it's enough to offset the hit they'd take for not having the GoDaddy brand recognition, maybe not. I doubt it'll set your sales on fire though.

I would be more interested in a marketplace that could get my domain in front of people who are asking LLMs to help name their new company.

I'm going to say "ICANN" and "policy", but don't immediately tune me out. I promise this is interesting.

Did you know that under ICANN's Transfer Policy for Inter-Registrar Transfer, the 60-day lock is listed under reasons a Registrar of Record "may" deny a transfer (Section 3.7), but it isn't in the list of reasons they "must" deny a transfer (Section 3.8).

 icann.org/en/contracted-part… 

What does this mean? The 60-day lock is a right of the losing registrar, not a responsibility. It's optional.

To illustrate this, the image below shows a before and after of the WHOIS as I transfer a domain that is eight days old between two of our registrars. We are also the registrant so no customers were put at risk.

It's unfortunate that choosing to enforce a 60-day create/transfer lock became the industry standard.

Especially in situations like aftermarket domain sales where a two-month wait might kill a deal. Even more so when you also own the marketplace that made the sale and you know the transfer request is legitimate.

Just saying...

We have an API endpoint people can use to vibe code their own Top Sales widget:
 api.namebio.com/docs/#topsal… 

There's also an endpoint that gives access to our comps engine, which is useful for landers.
 api.namebio.com/docs/#comps 

That said, you have to implement caching to avoid getting rate limited or running out of credits too quickly, which can add some complexity. Nothing an AI can't figure out though.

We've experimented with hosted versions in the past. They barely send any traffic to us because lander visitors usually aren't interested in buying domains. And landers can generate tons of junk traffic so the hosting of it isn't trivial. Not really worth the trouble for us to provide as a drop-in service.

Maybe some day marketplaces and landing page providers like Afternic, Atom, Efty, DomainEasy, Spaceship, Sudos, etc. will offer it as an option you can enable 🤷‍♂️ With so much competition to replace DAN you'd think someone would innovate in that way, lol.

Hundreds of thousands of people per year benefit from the data, a small percentage like to give back as thanks. Even some people who don't regularly use the site share data just to help others or to further the industry. Some people do it for the street cred. Others do it to establish a public baseline for similar domains they own. Everyone has their own motivation.

We can't really incentivize sharing sales without the ability to 100% confirm them with the venues at large scale, which realistically is probably never going to happen. Many of them will cooperate to manually confirm large sales, but that's about it. Otherwise we'd just be inviting fake sales reports.

There's also the issue that a single sales record is worth fractions of a penny, unless it's a headline sale and then maybe it's worth tens of cents. If we offered an incentive strong enough that it would actually motivate people who can't find it within themselves, we would be bleeding money.

There are only a handful of people on the planet doing enough sales where if they shared 100% of them we could maybe justify comping them a membership. But they're obviously doing well enough that they wouldn't really care about this kind of motivation.

The only way I could maybe see it working is a lottery-style incentive, where sharing a sale gets you a number of entries to win something, but not a guaranteed benefit.

But again we could only go down this road if all the major marketplaces would allow us to confirm sales of any dollar amount at scale. For example, by having a button in their UI where a party can click and report the sale directly to us without having to bother with screenshots or filling out a form.

Take the @DNAcademy course, study sales reports on NameBio and @DNJournal , listen to as many @DomainSherpa podcasts as you can. Get educated.

Then pick up better domains that actually have potential buyers. Google, @dotdbcom , and OpenCorporates are good places to check for a pulse.

For buying, check the expired auctions, GoDaddy closeouts, subscribe to the @DomainSmoke newsletter. Probably don't hand-register any more names.

Once you have some sellable inventory, list them on @Afternic , @Sedo , @atomHQ , etc. with BIN prices and wait. You can also reach out to potential buyers to speed up the process.

What you have now is something that isn't a good fit for the extension but could be somewhat decent in .com, a misspelled tongue-twister that doesn't even mean anything, another one that makes very little sense and zero companies have that name, and UDRP bait. The odds of any selling are essentially zero.

Good luck!

The odds of success are very small though. I would wager 80%+ of domain investors have a negative ROI overall; half of which have probably never made a sale. And less than 0.1% have it figured out and make a great ROI with meaningful income.

Those groups also share a lot of overlap with people who don't subscribe to services. Thankfully there are thousands in between who do subscribe, even if your straw poll gives you a different perspective.

The odds of success would look wildly different if more people had the sense to invest tens of dollars in training and tools to help them more effectively deploy their thousands of dollars in capital. I'm not just talking about us, but also @DNAcademy , @dotdbcom , etc.

Instead they blow tons of money on garbage and most likely rage quit before making a single sale. Penny wise and pound foolish. I think it's a concerning sign of dysfunction in this industry more than something to make light of, especially now that you've made it to the other side of the fence.

Brokerage is the best ROI in the industry; little upfront investment and no carrying costs. Registrar is by far the worst; huge upfront costs and an absolute race to the bottom on margins.

The STR of expired domains is far from 100%, you're thinking purely of backorder auctions. Obviously the STR of preorders will always be 100%, that isn't a function of price though.

But if you look at registrars such as GoDaddy, Dynadot, Namecheap, etc. that auction expired inventory before it gets deleted, where no backorder is required, a very large percentage end without bids despite not having reserves.

Yes, STR is absolutely a function of price. But that curve is also shifted and shaped by quality. As you noted, a low enough quality domain will have a 0% STR at any price. Hence so many no-reserve expired auctions ending without bids.

At the other extreme, the quality of domains you own would have a 100% STR even in the five and sometimes six-figure range. In any case it looks more like a step-wise curve.

At the lower end of quality the steps might be at $2.5k, $5k, and $10k but the lowest step is 2% STR. One of your domains might be stepped at $100k, $500k, $1m, and $5m but the lowest step is 100% STR.

Most people are operating much closer to the low end than the high end. In that neighborhood, the curve is shaped and shifted in such a way that there is an absolute cap on STR below which dropping the price does not increase the buyer pool nor the chances of it selling, because you're still bound by demand (or lack thereof).

It makes very close to zero difference if you price an average quality domain at $1,250 or $2,500. This was confirmed by our own testing on tens of thousands of domains over several months, and Atom (Squadhelp at the time) independently observed the same phenomenon months later.

You can't engineer literally any STR on average quality domains simply by adjusting pricing. You would need to open up a new buyer pool by pricing into wholesale liquidation territory, or do outbound, to get it above the natural cap.

There's actually a reason you see 1-2% so often, it isn't a coincidence or domainer lore. It's the upper bound on an average quality portfolio doing passive retail sales with fair pricing in the first step or two of the spectrum.

Even if you send the price all the way into wholesale liquidation territory, it still has an extremely low chance of selling unless you actively promote it. Otherwise you need a domain investor to randomly think of it out of a pool of millions of possible domains, like it more than the thousands of auctions they have to choose from every single day, and pull the trigger within 12 months, which is very unlikely.

At this quality level it's almost entirely a function of time and RNG for which ones hit. As long as the price is in the same ballpark/step, what actually sold would have sold regardless, and it's just a choice of if you'd rather make $1,250 or $2,500 on the sale. Pretty easy decision.

Auction houses and registrars would warehouse the names for retail sale if they could get away with it. Remember Standard Tactics? For some reason the optics on this are worse than them liquidating the names and giving the previous owner nothing, even though it is the same thing.

Same reason most new gTLD registries went for premiums with retail pricing instead of wholesale liquidation. Cut out the domainer middle man.

 #Domains

It depends largely on where your current pricing is at. If you already have a majority of names priced around $2,500 or less, cutting your prices in half will have almost zero impact on the number of sales. You'll just make half as much money for what would have sold anyway.

I can 100% guarantee you it won't double your sales. Even if it did, that wouldn't be your break-even point because you'd need to replace twice as much inventory. Actually, if you're pricing most of your names around $1,500 you should raise your prices 50% not slash them, and use the extra money to scale up your portfolio to achieve more sales.

For consistently selling 20+ domains per month retail, I would rank the factors in this order:

1. Quantity
2. Pricing
3. Outbound
4. Quality
5. Luck

STR is like a bell curve when compared to quality, it's not linear. Garbage names will have a very low STR, but so will very high quality names. The STR on LLL․coms is around 0.3% which is pretty abysmal, at my old job the company owned about 10% of them. But when one hits you might be making six figures profit, possibly even seven.

If you already have average quality names that are reasonably priced, improving quality even more is not your path to doubling your number of sales, you'd either need to double the size of your portfolio or do outbound sales as a full-time job. Quality is your path to doubling your average selling price though, which is an equally good goal to have, maybe even better given VeriSign price increases.

To hit 20 retail sales per month you need a large portfolio of names priced in the sweet spot if you want to do it passively, or with a smaller portfolio you'd need aggressive outbound sales. For passive we're talking 15,000+ average names, or 30,000+ decent names, or 60,000+ crap names. That last one wouldn't cover renewals though.

I think more people in this industry need to get comfortable with outbound sales and putting in long hours. Buy a handful of names after researching who you could outbound them to, and don't buy any more until you've reached out to everyone multiple times. Rinse and repeat until you find what sells, and then start scaling.

Too many rely on #5 above. They don't have the quantity or quality to see a sale within a few years, and are too lazy to outbound, so even with fair pricing they're missing too many factors and don't have a shot.

USVC = U.S. Venture Capital.

Clear. Institutional. Trust-building.

We recently completed the the following sale

 EZVC.com for $36,999 through a 12-month LTO.

EZVC = Easy Venture Capital.

Different angle, same capital theme.

We also hold two of the largest economic categories in America

 USFi.com (U.S. Finance)

 USRE.com (U.S. Real Estate)

U.S. housing alone is a $55 Trillion+ market, and 
U.S. finance represents one of the deepest capital ecosystems in the world.

The USVC launch is especially interesting because it is bringing regulated venture capital access to retail investors through a single basket of private companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Sierra, Vercel, Crusoe, and Legora.

In serious markets, clarity creates trust.

Great names are not just addresses.

They are positioning.

Seeing clowns being clowns? Yup, unfortunately. I wasn't going to give it more oxygen, but since you asked... I've already acknowledged that screenshots can easily be faked; that's not news.

That's why I logged into Swetha's Afternic account, so I could see for myself without having to rely on screenshots. But generally we have to operate on some level of trust and mutual respect, which apparently some people are not deserving of.

I'm not sure why anyone would feel the need to "test" to see if they can submit a fake sale and get it approved. A child could do it. And apparently a few children have done it for no good reason, to the detriment of everyone.

I have to say though, I'm surprised that someone who makes it their business to spread the word about domain sales on Twitter would damage their own reputation by submitting fake sales, and then openly brag about having no integrity like it is some kind of "gotcha" moment.

Screenshots are a step above just taking someone's word about a sale and publishing it, but not much of a step. It isn't feasible to log in to everyone's marketplace/escrow/bank accounts to actually verify sales.

Escrow is currently the only place that will verify a screenshot if I pass it along to them, which I do on occasion. I wish more services would at least cooperate, or better yet report the sales in the first place, but this industry is far too broken for that to ever happen.

And apparently for some people that still wouldn't be good enough anyway. They'll just say the transaction actually happened but it wasn't arms length and was the registry or individual self-dealing. Which I'll give them is possible, albeit unlikely.

Short of being a government agency, it's impossible to 100% verify a sale and know it wasn't an inside job. Same goes for Web3, even with the blockchain showing the sales they could still be self-dealing.

So where does that leave us? We can either all be adults and try to foster a mature industry where we share legitimate data and try to grow the market for everyone. Or we can be a bunch of clowns and try to poison the data for the LOLs, and I'll just stop accepting private sale report all together.

You all can decide, but it's looking like it might have to be the latter.

name: Logan
text:
Mark Levine @DomainTheory and I are back on this week’s Domain Name Wire podcast comparing and contrasting our respective domain investing styles and results from 2025.

Because Mark and I have different investing styles, I think it makes for a useful comparison and a more interesting conversation. We discuss domain acquisition, pricing, portfolio management, and what we are seeing in the domain aftermarket right now, especially as AI technology casts a bit of a Terminator-esque shadow over the industry.

Neither the T-800 nor the T-1000 is likely to care much about owning or using Skynet․com, but domain investors are still making plenty of sales to end users, while .ai sales records—and wholesale prices—keep climbing in 2026.

Thank you to Andrew Allemann @DomainNameWire for having us on and for keeping the conversation on track.

If you are interested in domain name investing, this episode is definitely worth a listen.

-----

AI written, but:

The 2026 Commercial Shift: Boston's current policy (Mayor Wu era) is shifting the tax burden heavily onto business property to subsidize residential. If you’re a startup with any hardware or lab gear, your Business Personal Property tax is pegged to the commercial rate—likely $25+ per $1,000 of value—while SF startups effectively pay $0 on the same equipment. It’s an annual tax on your own balance sheet just for existing in the city.

• The "Reuter" Trap (Wage Act): SJC ruled in Reuter v. City of Methuen (2022) that there is zero "good faith" defense for late final pay. If you fire someone at 4:55 PM and don't hand them a physical check or confirm the wire immediately, you’re strictly liable for 3x the total wages, plus their legal fees. SF has wait-time penalties, but MA has a mandatory 3x "nuclear option" for being one day late.

• The 50% Garden Leave Anchor: Since the 2018 non-compete law, you can’t just sign a standard CA-style non-compete (which are void anyway). In MA, to actually enforce one, you have to pay the departing employee 50% of their highest salary for the entire duration (up to 12 months). It makes "protecting the IP" a massive cash-flow liability that CA companies don't have to budget for.

• SaaS vs. Service Tax: MA (6.25%) treats "prewritten software" (SaaS) as a taxable event if the "object of the transaction" is using the software. In CA, SaaS is almost always treated as a non-taxable service. If you're a Boston-based B2B SaaS company, your finance team is dealing with sales tax audits and nexus issues years before an SF peer even thinks about it.

• 201 CMR 17.00 (The WISP Debt): MA is the only state that mandates a "Written Information Security Program" the second you touch a resident's name + SSN/CC. It requires a designated "Security Officer" and mandatory encryption on all mobile devices/laptops by law. It’s "Enterprise-grade" compliance debt forced onto a Seed stage team.

• The Article 80 Grind: If you're building a lab or high-growth HQ over 50k sq ft, you hit Article 80 Large Project Review. This isn't just a permit; it's a 12-18 month "public process" of hearings, community advisory teams, and "mitigation" payments.

• The Pre-2019 Exit Haircut: This was the biggest "gotcha"—MA only followed the 2005 federal code for QSBS, which meant only a 50% exclusion vs. the federal 100%. If you sold for $10M in 2018, you were looking at a ~5% state tax hit on $5M that an SF founder likely didn't pay. We finally aligned in 2019, but for a decade, Boston founders were just lighting 5% of their exit on fire.

• The PFML Cash Drag: In MA, you’re hit with the Paid Family and Medical Leave payroll tax (0.88%) the second you hit 25 "covered individuals"—and in MA, 1099s count toward that head count. Unlike CA where it’s mostly employee-funded, MA forces the employer to pay for the "medical" portion. If you’re a 30-person Seed team, that’s a direct tax on your burn that SF peers don't pay.

• The "Market Rate" Illegal Pay: Under the MA Equal Pay Act (MEPA), "market conditions" is not a legal defense for pay gaps. If you hire a "rockstar" engineer for $220k because that's what it took to close them, but your existing engineers with the same title make $180k, you’re legally liable for the difference + liquidated damages. In SF, you can pay what the market demands; in Boston, your payroll is a litigation target the moment you out-compete for talent.

• The Performance Review Trap: MA law (M.G.L. c. 149, § 52C) requires you to notify an employee within 10 days of putting any "negative" info in their personnel file (even a Slack memo about a missed deadline). If you don't, you can't use it in a termination defense later. It turns basic management into a high-stakes legal paper trail that SF founders don't have to touch until they’re mid-market.

How Much Did the Domain Sell For?

If you are passionate about understanding how much reported domain names sell for, I strongly recommend subscribing to NameBio .com’s paid services. For deeper insight into how many extensions a domain is registered across, DotDB .com is an excellent resource. Other reputable sources for domain industry information include DSAD .com, DNW .com, DNJournal .com, and NamePros .com, among others.

That said, when a #domain investor voluntarily shares information about a sale—whether they disclose the domain name, the sale price, or both—that decision is entirely at their discretion. Any sales data you encounter online should be viewed as a starting point, not the final answer.

Public information can help you research important patterns:

Types of names other investors are buying
How long domains are held
Acquisition costs
Sales venues
And, when available, final sale prices

However, simply consuming information without knowing how to apply it is of no use. Someone driven purely by emotion or addicted to data will struggle to progress if they don’t understand how to turn insight into action.

 Metawatch.com Case study: The domain reportedly sold for $800 in 2011, was later acquired via DropCatch for $9,102 in 2022, and then resold for $289,995 in 2025. It’s easy to become emotionally fixated on that final number, but doing so misses the real lesson.

The value lies in studying whythe #name appreciated: timing, market shifts, keyword relevance, buyer demand, and holding strategy. These are the elements that help you refine your craft as a domain investor.

If you spend too much time complaining about sellers who choose not to disclose sale prices, you deprive yourself of the opportunity to learn from other critical aspects of the domain name and the industry as a whole. Focus less on what isn’t shared—and more on what is available to help you grow.

2024 Trading Summary and 2025 Plan.

At the beginning of 2024 I had a goal of 20% gain on $601k of stocks and cash. The year started off on the wrong foot and continued on until the low point on 4/19. I was assigned a few stocks that just seemed to find a way to go down so selling covered calls only softened the blow a bit. It wasn’t until the week of May 24 that my account turned positive for the year. At the midpoint of the year my account was up 10.50% but the summer/fall was rocky until November and early December when the account reached its high point at 20.56% on December 6. The account took a hit when Uncle Jerome forecast less rate cuts for 2025 and the anti Santa rally hit the market hard. The account missed the 20% goal and finished the year at 16.03% or $25k under my goal. My accounting is based on weekly Friday close but for this calculation I used December 31 market close numbers. Had I used the January 3 Friday close numbers I would have surpassed the goal with 22.93% due to the New Years rally. Yes NVDA which is an overweight position was the catalyst in both directions.

Lessons learned in my first year of trading such a large account.

Forcing trades due to time constraints with the 9-5 job does not produce the best results.

Trading a large number of contracts with the same strike and expiration concentrates risk.

 Oversizing positions with volatile stocks (NVDA in my case) leads to large up/down swings in account value.

Do more DD on stocks I want to own via cash secured put assignment.

Sell equities that are not good for options trading. In my case I just sold all my TSLY

My goal for 2025 will be for a 30% gain on a $650k balance consisting of stocks and cash. I plan to morph the account to be biased towards AI. Some tickers I’m interested for long positions are: META, MU, NVDA, AMZN and SOUN. Options trading CSP and CC mixed with vertical spreads will be my main focus.

I still remember June 21, 2005.

Instead of following my normal evening routine with Guild Wars, I felt a bit bored of the game and ended up poking around the Internet instead. I saw that timschmoyer.com was available and decided to register it. Why? I don't know.

So I poked around more. "What do I do with this domain now?"

I found WordPress and decided to set that up on the domain because, why not? After learning a bit about FTP, MySQL users, and text editors, I was up and running. Nice!

But then came my next question. "What do I write about?"

At first I wrote about whatever was on my mind: my girlfriend, what I ate for dinner that night, or screenshots of my adventures in Guild Wars.

Over time, however, I wrote more and more about what I was most passionate about, which was youth ministry. Within a few years, it turned into the most-subscribed youth ministry blog on the Internet. In 2011 it became my full-time job. That turned into creating YouTube videos, which turned into my career. In 2013 I started a YouTube growth agency, had success there, and sold it to vidIQ in 2022.

Today I work as the Chief Creator Coach at vidIQ where I'm building a 1:1 coaching team for their 3 million weekly active creators. After years of YouTube coaching, scaling it is an amazing new mountain to climb!

But after almost 20 years of YouTube, I have the itch to get back to my roots: writing about whatever is top-of-mind and seeing where it leads.

Life is a lot different for me now than it was when I first started blogging in 2005. I'm married now, have 7 kids, and hold very different beliefs around money, business, family, relationships, and faith than I did 20 years ago, but I'm finding that I still desire a place to wrestle "out loud."

And who knows where this will lead. Last time it turned into a career, but this time I just want it to give me a place to think and subject those thoughts to the critique of others as I pursue practical wisdom in business, relationships, and faith.

Let's see where this goes.

2025 RECAP 🧵

Looking back, this year has felt like a dream. So many things came together, and my work found its way into places I once only imagined.

• My work Liquid Modernity was exhibited and auctioned at Christie’s, as part of their inaugural AI art auction.

• My work is featured in Dopamine at Le Cube Garges, Paris. A major institutional exhibition running until July 18, 2026, presented as part of Némo Biennale 2025, the International Biennale of Digital Arts.

• Work from my previous collections continued to be exhibited internationally, from Shanghai to New York’s Times Square, my work was featured in many exhibitions across galleries and public spaces.

• A defining chapter of the year was my AI generated feature documentary film Post Truth:

- It became the first AI feature film in cinema history to secure a theatrical release. The theatrical deal was reported by Deadline Hollywood.

- The film had its international premiere at Warsaw Film Festival, one of the only 14 A-list festivals in the world accredited by FIAPF. Variety announced the international debut.

- The film subsequently screened at long-established festivals, including the 66th Festival dei Popoli, the oldest documentary festival in Europe, and the 62nd International Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival, the longest-running festival in Turkey.

- It received overwhelmingly positive reviews from professional critics in Turkey, Poland, and Italy. 

- The film lastly won the Audience Award at FrontDoc International Film Festival.

• This year marked key milestones for our AI production company, Spongeworthy Studio: With Post Truth becoming a theatrically released, critically acclaimed film, while @VikkiBardot 's short film Dreamt by Another, screened at over 20 festivals before being acquired by MUBI.

• The soundtrack album of Post Truth was released in December via Tamar Records on vinyl, CD, and digital platforms.

• Much of the year was focused on moving conversations around AI and art beyond online spaces, into wider public and cultural contexts.

• From Paris Photo to international film festivals, I spent much of the year on panels and public discussions, contributing to the conversation around AI and art beyond Web3.

• I was featured in major outlets, from The Observer to CNN Türk, and gave over 25 interviews across print, online, and television.

• A curated image gallery of my work circulated widely across mainstream platforms, including Bored Panda, MSN, and AOL.

• The year included several auctions, highlights including:
– Hypertopographics #1 sold for $18,000 via Heft Gallery, New York.
– Earth Misread sold for $8,100 via Asprey Studio Gallery, London.
– Liquid Modernity sold for $5,040 via Christie’s, New York.

I don’t take any of this lightly. This year raised the bar for what the work demands next.

A key part of this year was seeing my AI-generated work move beyond online spaces and enter real-world galleries, institutions, cinemas, and publications.

My interviews followed a wild path: I started the year talking about AI and photography around the Christie’s exhibition, moved into AI and filmmaking with Post Truth, and ended up discussing AI and music through the soundtrack.

I’m genuinely grateful for every step along the way, and for the seriousness with which all my work has been received.

New exhibitions are confirmed for the coming year, with several new projects set to be released. Major announcements are on the way.

2026 is shaping up to be an exciting one.
