【語源要素シリーズ：語幹編 076】Part 1/4

　語源解説シリーズが「接頭辞編、接尾辞編、語幹編」合わせて1,000ページを超えました！いよいよ電子書籍「第5巻：語源をベースにした劇的語彙力増強（仮題）」の完成が見えてきました。従来の「薄い本に単語リストを詰め込んで、何回も繰り返して覚えられない単語集」とは根本的に異なる「じっくり納得してその場で単語を覚え」、覚えやすく、忘れにくく、忘れても思い出しやすく、かつ初対面の単語でも意味を推測できる力までを身に付けられる「かつて存在しなかった単語学習書の最高峰」がもうすぐ完成です。

　今回は、value, valuable, valid, invalid, available, prevail など多くの単語に含まれる語幹 val を取り上げます。val はラテン語 valere に由来し「be strong (強い)、heath (健康)」と「worth (価値)」の２系統の意味を表します。

　このシリーズは「万単位の英単語を習得できる脳の構築」が最大の主眼です。語彙力を伸ばすには、語源学習だけが有効なわけではなく、様々な方法を合わせ技として併用するのがより効果的です。
参考： nitter.poast.org/hitomikengo/st/HitomiK… 

※過去掲載分一覧（タブに分かれています）：
 docs.google.com/spreadsheets… 

　接頭辞や接尾辞は比較的、情報を得やすいのですが、語幹ごとに意味をまとめた資料は多くありません。ただ語源要素の中には、あまり多くの単語に含まれておらず、応用や拡張が利きにくいものもあるため、このシリーズでは「出会うチャンスが多い」ものを中心に取り上げます。

===================
076
語幹：val
語源：Lt(Latinラテン語) valere
意味：be strong; health; worth
※ラテン語源 valere は「身体的に強い、健康、健全である」や「価値がある、～だけの価値がある」の意味。英単語語幹としても「強さ」と「価値」の意味として現れる

【語幹 val を含む英単語の例】

value /ˈvæl.juː/
(n [C or U]) 価値、重要性
the amount of money that can be received for something; the importance or worth of something for someone 
物の対価として受け取られるべき金額；物や人の重要性あるいは価値
(vt) 価格を評価する 
to give a judgment about how much money something might be sold for
物の販売価格を見積もる、どれだけの価値があるかを判断する
[c. 1300 "price equal to the intrinsic worth of a thing" < OF "worth, price, moral worth; reputation" < noun use of pp of valoir "be worth" < Lt valere "be strong, be well; be of value, be worth"]
1300年頃「物の本質的な価値に等しい価格」の意味で＜古フランス語では「価値、価格、道徳的価値；評判」の意味からで、これは動詞 valoir の過去分詞の名詞的用法に由来＜ラテン語 valere (強い、元気である、価値がある、相当する) に由来する

valuable /ˈvæl.ju.ə.bᵊl/
(adj) 価値ある、高価な
worth a lot of money, or very useful or important
高額な価値がある、または非常に有用で重要な
[value (v) + -able "to be ___ed; worthy"]
動詞の value に「～されるべき、価値がある」を意味する接尾辞 -able が接辞されたもの。語源的直訳は「（高い）価値があると判断されるべき；高い価値がある、重要性が高い」の意味

valuables /ˈvæl.jə.bᵊlz/
(n [pl]) 貴重品
small objects, especially jewelry, that might be sold for a lot of money
小さな物、特に高額で売れる可能性のある宝飾品
[< valuable (adj)]
形容詞 valuable が「そういう性質を持つ様々な物」という意味で複数形のみで「貴重品」を表す

valuation /ˌvæl.juˈeɪ.ʃᵊn/
(n [C or U]) 評価、鑑定
the act of deciding how much money something is worth
何かの金銭的価値を決める行為
[value (n) + -ate (v) + -ion (n)] 
名詞 value に動詞語尾 -ate さらに名詞語尾 -ion が接辞されたもの。語源的直訳は「高い価値があると認めること」の意味。次の evaluation が「価値があるのかないのかを判断する」意味であるのに対して、e- のない valuation は「価値があると認めること」という違いがある。名詞語尾のない valuate /ˌvæl.juˈeɪt/ は他動詞として「価値があると判定する」意味

evaluation /ɪˌvæl.juˈeɪ.ʃᵊn/
(n [C or U]) 評価、価値判断、価値計算
the process of judging or calculating the quality, importance, amount, or value of something
何かの品質、重要性、量、または価値を判断または計算するプロセス
[e- (=ex- "out") + value (n) + -ate (v) + -ion (n)]
接頭辞 e- は基本形 ex- (外へ) のバリエーション。「外へ」の意味からの拡張で「完全に、正確に」のニュアンスにつながる。つまり「価値があるのか、ないのか」いずれの観点からもそれを判定すること。名詞語尾のない evaluate /ɪˈvæl.ju.eɪt/ は他動詞として用いられる

valueless /ˈvæl.ju.ləs/ 
(adj) 無価値な、価値のない
having no value; worth nothing
価値がなく、何の価値もない
[value (n) + -less "lacking"]
名詞 value (価値) に -less (～がない) が接辞されたもの。接尾辞 -less は主に「～がない」意味を表すが、priceless は「値段がつけられないほど高価な」の意味を表すように、同じ -less でも、語幹の意味を単純否定しているわけではない場合もある

valorize /ˈvæl.ə.raɪz/
(vt) 価値を高める、評価する
to give or increase the value of something
何かの価値を与える、または高める
[valor "value, worth" (< valere "to be strong, be worth" + -ize (vt)]
valor (価値 (< valere (強い、価値がある) に由来) に動詞語尾 -ize が接辞されたもの。20世紀に経済や文化の文脈で「価値付与」を意味する語として普及

devalue /ˌdiːˈvæl.juː/
(vi, vt) 価値を下げる；通貨切り下げ
to reduce the value of something, especially money
何か、特に通貨の価値を下げること
[de- "down" + value (v) (<back-formation from devaluation)]
de- (下へ) が value (価値があると判断する) に接辞されたもので、この単語より先に devaluation という名詞があり、そこからの逆生成で動詞が作られたもの。20世紀初頭に経済用語として普及

revalue /ˌriːˈvæl.juː/ 
(vt) 再評価する、通貨切り上げ
to change the value of something, usually to increase it
何か、通常は価値を上げるために変更する
[re- "again, back" + value (v)]
接頭辞 re- (再び、戻って) が動詞 value (価値があると判断する) に接辞されたもの。語源的に「一度価値が下がったものに対して、以前の高い価値と再評価する」意味を表し、単純に「２回評価する」という意味とはニュアンスが異なる

valid /ˈvæl.ɪd/
(adj) 有効な、正当な
based on truth or reason; able to be accepted
真実や理由に基づいており、受け入れ可能な
[1570s "having force in law, legally binding" < Fr valide < Lt validus "strong, effective, powerful, active" < valere "be strong"]
1570年代に「法的効力を持つ、法的拘束力のある」の意味として＜フランス語 valide ＜ラテン語 validus (強い、有効な、力がある、活動中の) に由来し、遡ると valere (強い) に由来する。例えば「ID (身分証明書)」が valid であるとは、「有効期限が切れていない、本物である、条件に合致したタイプのIDである」などの意味合いを表す

validity /vəˈlɪd.ə.t̬i/
(n [U]) 有効性、正当性
the quality of being based on truth or reason, or of being able to be accepted
真実や理由に基づいている性質、または受け入れ可能な性質
[valid + -ity (n)]
形容詞 valid に抽象名詞語尾 -ity が接辞されたもの。英語では16世紀に「有効性」を意味する学術的な語として導入された

validate /ˈvæl.ɪ.deɪt/
(vt) 有効にする、検証する
to check that something is officially true and acceptable
何かが公式に本当で受け入れ可能であることを確認する
[vaild + -ate (v)]
形容詞 valid に動詞語尾 -ate が接辞されたもの。語源的直訳は「有効な状態にする」の意味。17世紀に英語で「有効性を証明する」意味で使われ始めた

invalid /ɪnˈvæl.ɪd/
(adj) 無効な、不当な
not officially acceptable or not true
公式に受け入れられない、または本当でない
[in- "not" + valid]
形容詞 valid に否定接頭辞 in- が接辞されたもの。16世紀に英語で「無効」や「弱い」を意味する語として導入。
invalid /ˈɪn.və.lɪd/ ※発音注意
(n [C]) 病人、障害者
a person who is ill or injured and cannot live or work normally
病気や怪我で正常に生活や仕事ができない人
[in- "not" + valid (< valere "strong; healthy")] 
語源的には形容詞 invalid と同じであるが、こちらは valere の「強い、健康的な」の意味に否定接頭辞がついたもので、17世紀に「病人」などを指して確立した

valor /ˈvæl.ɚ/ (UK valour)
(n [U]) 勇気、武勇
great courage, especially in war
特に戦争での偉大な勇気
[OF valor, valour "moral worth, merit, courage, virtue" < Lt valere "to be strong, worth"]
古フランス語 valor, valour (道徳的価値、長所、有機、徳) から。ラテン語 valere (強い、価値がある) に由来し、特に「戦場での果敢さ」の意味に用いられる

valiant /ˈvæl.i.ənt/ 
(adj) 勇敢な、雄々しい
very brave or bravely determined, especially when things are difficult
特に困難な状況で非常に勇敢または勇敢に決意した
[OF vaillant "stalward, brave" < pp adjective from valoir "be worthy (originally "be strong")" < Lt valere "to be strong, be well, be worth, have power"]
古フランス語 vaillant (勇敢な) に由来し、これは動詞 valoir (価値がある (もともと「強い」の医いｍ)) の過去分詞の形容詞用法に由来する。遡るとラテン語 valere (強い、元気な、価値ある、力がある) に由来する。14世紀に英語に借用。騎士道的な勇敢さを強調

valediction /ˌvæl.əˈdɪk.ʃᵊn/
(n [C or U]) 別れの演説
the act of saying goodbye, especially formally, or a formal speech in which someone says goodbye
別れを告げる行為、特に正式な別れ、または正式な別れの挨拶のスピーチ
[1610s "a farewell" < pp stem of Lt valedicere "bid farewell, take leave" < vale "farewell!" (second person singular imperative of valere "be well, be strong" + dicere "to say" + -ion (n)]
1610年代に「人との別れ」の意味で、ラテン語 valedicere (別れを告げる、暇を取る) の過去分詞語幹に由来。語源構成としては、vale (「さようなら！」 ) に dict (<Lt dicere (言う)) と名詞語尾 -ion が接辞されたもので、直訳的に「別れの言葉を言うこと」の意味。vale は、動詞 valere (元気でいる、強くある) の二人称単数命令形、つまり、直訳的に「あなたは元気でいてください」の意味

valedictory /ˌvæl.əˈdɪk.tɚ.i/
(adj) 別れの、告別の
relating to saying goodbye, especially formally
別れを告げることに関連する、特に正式な場合
[valetiction > -ory (adj)]
valediction の語尾を形容詞接尾辞 -ory に差し替えたもの

valedictorian /ˌvæl.ə.dɪkˈtɔːr.i.ən/
(n [C]) (US) 卒業生代表、首席卒業生
a student, usually with the highest grades, who makes a speech at a graduation ceremony
通常最高の成績を持つ学生で、卒業式でスピーチを行う者
[valedictory > -ian "person"]
valedictory (別れの演説の) に -ian (人) が接辞されたもの。語源的直訳は「別れの挨拶をする人」の意味。18世紀に米語で卒業生代表を指す語として成立

equivalent /ɪˈkwɪv.əl.ənt/
(adj) 同等の、等価の
having the same amount, value, purpose, qualities, etc.
同じ量、価値、目的、性質などを持っている
[Lt aequus "equal" + valere "to be well, be worth" + -ent (="-ing" → adj)]
ラテン語 aequus (等しい) と valere (元気な、価値がある) の組み合わせにラテン語現在分詞語尾 -ent が接辞され形容詞を作ったもの。単純に考えると「equal + being worth = being equally worth（同じ価値がある）」に相当する。あるものが何かと同じである、同じ価値を持つことを表す

prevail /prɪˈveɪl/
(vi) 広まる、普及する、流行する、優勢である
to get control or influence
制御力や影響力を得る
[pre- "before" + valere "to have power, be strong"]
接頭辞 pre- (前に) と valere (力を持つ、強い) の組み合わせ。pre- は「前に」の意味から「目の前に広がって」のニュアンスに拡張。語源的直訳は「影響力を前に広げる→流行する、普及する、など」の意味

 prevalent /ˈprev.ᵊl.ənt/
(adj) 蔓延している、広く行き渡っている、流行している
existing very commonly or happening often
非常によくあるか、頻繁に起こる
[prevail + -ent (="-ing" → adj)]
動詞 prevail にラテン語現在分詞語尾 -ent が接辞され形容詞となったもの

prevalence /ˈprev.ᵊl.əns/
(n [U]) 普及、優勢
the fact of something existing or being very common at a particular time or place
特定の時間や場所で何かがあること、または非常に一般的である事実
[prevail + -ence (n. ← -ent)]
形容詞 prevalent の語尾を名詞語尾 -ence に差し替えたもの、すなわち「prevalentな状態にあること」の意味

valence /ˈveɪ.ləns/
(n [C]) 原子価、効価
the ability of an element to combine with others, measured by the number of bonds it can form
元素が他の元素と結合する能力で、形成できる結合の数で測定される
[Lt valentia "strength, capacity" < valentem "strong, vigorous, powerful" < present participle of valere "to be strong"]
テン語 valentia（力、能力）から派生し、valere の「強さ」を反映。19世紀に化学分野で「結合力」を意味する語として採用

valency /ˈveɪ.lən.si/
(n [C]) 原子価、イオン価；結合価
(chemistry) a measurement of an atom’s ability to combine with others
(化学) 原子が他の原子と結合する能力の測定値
(language) the number of noun phrases with which a verb combines
(言語学）動詞が結合する名詞句の数
[Lt valentia "strength, capacity" < valentem "strong, powerful" < present participle of valere "be strong"]
語源的には「強さ」を意味する。化学用語としては「イオン価値（原子価）」の意味、すなわち１つの原子が他の原子に結び付ける「手」の本数のこと。言語学においては述語動詞が単独で成り立っているものを「１」、目的語を１つ取っているものなら「２」、二重目的語を取っている場合なら「３」となる。

convalesce /ˌkɑːn.vəˈles/
(vi) 回復する、快復する
to become healthy and strong again after illness or weakness
病気や弱さの後に再び健康で強くなる
[con- (=com- "with, together → intensive") + valescere "to begin to grow strong" < valere "to be strong"]

The Ethics of Monetizing Patient Data

In the digital age, patient data is a goldmine. Every blood test, diagnosis, and prescription generates a breadcrumb trail of information—valuable not just for care delivery but for research, marketing, and innovation. By March 2025, the global healthcare data market is projected to exceed $70 billion, driven by pharmaceutical companies, insurers, and tech giants eager to tap into this resource. Monetizing patient data—selling or licensing it, often in de-identified form—promises to accelerate medical breakthroughs, optimize treatments, and fund healthcare improvements. Yet, this practice raises profound ethical questions: Who owns this data? What constitutes consent? And where do we draw the line between societal benefit and exploitation? This article delves into the ethics of turning patient information into profit, exploring the tension between progress and privacy.

The Case for Monetization

Proponents argue that monetizing patient data is a win-win. For healthcare organizations, it’s a lifeline—revenue from data sales can offset shrinking margins, subsidize care for underserved populations, or fuel technological upgrades. A 2024 study by Deloitte found that hospitals reinvesting data profits into infrastructure saw a 15% improvement in operational efficiency. Beyond finances, the data itself drives innovation. De-identified records power AI models that predict disease outbreaks, refine drug development, and personalize medicine. Pharmaceutical firms, for instance, use aggregated patient data to identify candidates for clinical trials, slashing R&D timelines by years.

The societal good is compelling: when a biotech company leverages millions of patient records to develop a rare disease treatment, lives are saved. Advocates also note that HIPAA allows de-identified data to be sold without explicit consent, provided identifiers like names or Social Security numbers are stripped. In theory, this protects privacy while unlocking value—an ethical bargain, they say, where the greater good justifies the transaction.

The Ethical Fault Lines

Beneath this optimism lies a web of moral dilemmas.

Consent and Autonomy 
Patients rarely know their data is being monetized. A 2023 Kaiser Family Foundation survey revealed that 70% of Americans were unaware their de-identified health information could be sold, and 60% opposed it when informed. Consent forms, buried in fine print, often fail to disclose commercial uses explicitly. This opacity erodes autonomy—the right to control one’s own information. Critics argue that even de-identified data isn’t truly anonymous; advanced AI can re-link it to individuals, as demonstrated in a 2022 MIT study that re-identified 85% of a “scrubbed” dataset using public records.

Equity and Exploitation 
Who benefits from the profits? Too often, it’s not the patients whose data fuels the system. A low-income diabetic contributing data to a drug company’s insulin breakthrough may never afford the resulting medication. This imbalance raises justice concerns: marginalized groups, already overrepresented in public health datasets, may be disproportionately exploited without seeing returns. Meanwhile, corporations rake in billions, amplifying healthcare’s profit-driven disparities.

Trust in Healthcare 
Monetization risks eroding patient trust—a cornerstone of medicine. If individuals suspect their data is a commodity, they may withhold critical information from providers, fearing downstream misuse. A 2024 JAMA study linked privacy concerns to a 20% increase in incomplete medical histories, undermining care quality. Once trust fractures, the ripple effects—missed diagnoses, delayed treatments—could outweigh monetization’s gains.

Purpose Creep 
Data sold for noble aims (e.g., cancer research) can end up in less savory hands. Insurers might use it to deny coverage based on predictive risk profiles, or marketers could target vulnerable patients with unproven therapies. A 2023 scandal saw a telehealth firm sell behavioral health data to advertisers, who then bombarded patients with mental health product ads. Such “secondary use” blurs ethical lines, turning a tool for healing into one for manipulation.

Ownership Ambiguity 
Legally, patients don’t own their medical records—providers or systems do. Yet, morally, many argue that data derived from a person’s body and experiences belongs to them. Monetizing it without compensation or input feels like a theft of agency, especially when patients bear the risks (e.g., breaches) but not the rewards.

Real-World Stakes

The ethics play out in stark examples. In 2022, a major health system sold de-identified genomic data to a biotech firm, leading to a patented therapy that cost $2 million per dose—unreachable for most contributors. Patients cried foul, but the transaction was legal. Conversely, a nonprofit hospital in 2024 shared data with researchers under a transparent revenue-sharing model, funding free clinics and earning community praise. The difference lies in intent, execution, and equity—variables that define the ethical tightrope.

Navigating the Dilemma

Can monetizing patient data be ethical? Experts suggest guardrails:

Transparent Consent: Patients should opt in, not out, with clear disclosure of how data will be used and who profits. A 2025 pilot in California tested “data consent dashboards,” letting patients choose research-only sharing, boosting participation by 30%.

Equitable Benefits: Revenue could fund public health initiatives or patient subsidies, ensuring contributors share the gains. Models like data cooperatives, where patients co-own and profit from their data, are gaining traction.

Strict De-identification: Robust standards, audited regularly, could minimize re-identification risks. Blockchain might track data use, preventing unauthorized resale.

Regulatory Oversight: Laws must evolve. The EU’s GDPR fines companies for mishandling health data, a model the U.S. could emulate beyond HIPAA’s limits.

Purpose Limits: Contracts should restrict data to health-related uses, barring commercial exploitation like targeted ads.

The Future: Profit vs. Principle

As healthcare digitizes—think wearables, telehealth, and AI diagnostics—the volume of monetizable data will explode. Tech giants like Amazon and Google, already eyeing health markets, could escalate the stakes, blurring lines between care and commerce. Patients may demand “data dividends” or boycott providers who prioritize profit over privacy. Meanwhile, innovations like synthetic data—AI-generated datasets mimicking real ones—could reduce reliance on actual patient records, sidestepping some ethical quagmires.

Conclusion

Monetizing patient data teeters between promise and peril. It’s a catalyst for progress, funding cures and cutting costs, yet it risks commodifying the human experience, undermining trust, and widening inequities. The ethics hinge on execution: transparency, fairness, and respect for autonomy can tilt the scales toward benefit, while opacity and greed tip it toward harm. In an industry built on “do no harm,” the challenge is clear—patient data’s value must never eclipse the dignity of those it represents. As we navigate this frontier, the question isn’t just what we can do with this data, but what we should.

INTRODUCTION

I will try to be as concise as possible, but this thread shall be long and slightly unorganized. Topics will include bitcoin mining, CSP, rack density, GPU clusters, neoclouds, etc. For my own convenience, I will also use Chatgpt for much of the writing. Thank God for AI.

BITCOIN MINING AND CSP:

TLDR: Iren is using Bitcoin mining as a means to quickly monetize its data centers, enabling it to build a large infrastructure portfolio suitable for AI/HPC without sacrificing equity or accumulating significant debt, positioning it as a resilient, vertically integrated alternative to heavily leveraged neocloud competitors.
—-
Iren’s motto is “Proceed with Purpose” for a reason. As reiterated in the Iren Q2 FY25 presentation, Iren’s plan has always been to transition from bitcoin mining to broader data center and AI infrastructure services. The three steps enumerated by Iren represent a methodical evolution: first, building data centers powered by low-cost renewable energy; second, bootstrapping operations with Bitcoin mining; and third, leveraging the resulting asset base into other high-growth, energy-intensive computing applications like AI cloud services.

Iren initially focused on constructing data centers where operational costs are minimized by tapping into cheap, renewable energy sources. Electricity is one of the largest expenses for data centers, so building facilities in areas rich with hydro, solar, or wind power ensures low ongoing costs and sustainable operations. As a result, Iren now owns significant amounts of land and physical infrastructure.

To monetize its newly constructed data centers, Iren bootstrapped (i.e., starting and growing the business using internally generated resources rather than relying on outside funding like debt or large investment rounds) operations through Bitcoin mining. This approach was strategic because ASIC miners, the specialized machines used for Bitcoin mining, generate revenue almost immediately after being plugged into the network. There is no customer acquisition risk; as soon as the machines are operational, they begin earning Bitcoin, which can be sold for cash. CSP, on the other hand, requires building a customer base, negotiating contracts, and maintaining high utilization — all of which introduce sales and marketing complexity.

In general, Bitcoin mining typically requires much lower capital expenditure (capex) than AI or HPC data centers. That said, Iren’s existing data centers (e.g., over 150 MW in Canada) are configured for both bitcoin mining and high-density AI workloads, with rack densities of about 80 kW. Despite this, Iren achieved construction costs of around $650,000 per megawatt, far below the $6–15 million per megawatt common for specialized AI facilities. Iren’s designs are not only extremely fast to build, but also easily retrofitted (e.g., the rack density should be scalable to 300 kW and beyond), giving Iren a significant advantage in flexibility and time to market (e.g., with respect to the B200s).
This efficient, infrastructure-first approach has allowed Iren to grow without taking on significant debt (in fact, Iren has no debt at the moment). In contrast, most neocloud competitors, such as CoreWeave, have funded their rapid expansion by raising large amounts of debt. Unlike Iren, most neoclouds typically own little land or physical infrastructure, which may stunt future growth.

Iren’s methodical strategy — building out low-cost, high-density infrastructure first through Bitcoin mining and then expanding into AI compute — positions it as a more resilient, vertically integrated player. Its strong asset base, low operational costs, and limited reliance on external financing give Iren a structurally more profitable and lower-risk business model compared to the heavily leveraged, asset-light models of many newer cloud providers.

IRENS’ DATA CENTERS
TLDR: Iren’s technical innovations validated its cost and speed strategy and has positioned it to now enter the AI and HPC markets quickly and profitably, without having to rebuild its infrastructure from scratch. Its ability to combine low-cost construction, high rack density, and air cooling into a unified platform is a major differentiator at a time when many competitors are struggling with expensive and slow transitions to liquid-cooled architectures.
—-
In 2018, Iren acquired PodTech, as well as all of the IP that had been transferred to it from RackForce (see nitter.poast.org/TheKamaHsutra/status/1… ). Around 2020, Iren designed and constructed a next-gen data center. However, this begs the question: what exactly constitutes a next-gen data center? Very few possessed the foresight in 2020 to anticipate ChatGPT (otherwise, we would all be billionaires from buying call options on $Nvda ). Iren apparently believed that essential features of a next-gen data center comprise being 1) affordable and fast to build; 2) capable of achieving high rack density; and 3) easy to retrofit. In addition, Iren wanted the data center to support bitcoin mining to bootstrap operations as described above.

Iren put this philosophy into practice by designing and constructing data centers at a relatively low cost of approximately $650,000/MW. At the same time, Iren engineered its facilities to achieve rack densities of up to 80 kilowatts, all while remaining air-cooled. Although widely dismissed by retail and even institutional investors, this air-cooled, high-density design is a major technical and strategic breakthrough. 

Traditionally, the industry consensus has been that air cooling becomes insufficient above 30 kW per rack. Beyond that point, most operators assume that liquid cooling — either direct-to-chip or full immersion — becomes necessary to prevent overheating and maintain reliability. Liquid cooling infrastructure, however, is significantly more expensive, adds construction complexity, and greatly increases build times (e.g., by months if not more than a year).

By radically improving air cooling system design, Iren proved that it was possible to almost triple traditional air-cooled rack densities without resorting to costly and complex liquid cooling solutions. This breakthrough allowed them to avoid the massive capital expenditure and long construction timelines typically associated with liquid-cooled data centers, giving them a huge advantage in both cost and speed to market.

While Iren was building these data centers and bootstrapping operations with bitcoin mining, most data center operators were investing heavily in liquid cooling retrofits or new builds under the assumption that air cooling simply could not scale to meet the demands of next-generation AI and HPC workloads. Iren’s decision to challenge this consensus was seen as risky; however, in hindsight, we know now that Iren’s existing data centers can not only host H100s and H200s, but also B200s without any material modification or retrofit to the design.

RACK DENSITY
TLDR: Although HGX B200 servers can technically run in low-density racks (the lowest possible rack density being 15 kW, which is above the average data center rack density of 12 kW), doing so wastes physical space, cooling, and networking resources because only one or two servers fit per rack. By contrast, Iren’s high-density racks (70–80 kW) allow four to five HGX B200 servers per rack, maximizing space and infrastructure efficiency, reducing the cost per megawatt of deployed compute, and making it easier to scale AI capacity within the same building—an increasingly critical advantage as demand for AI compute accelerates.
—-
Rack density measures the amount of power consumed by the equipment installed in a single rack, typically expressed in kW. A rack is the metal frame that holds servers, GPUs, networking gear, and other hardware inside a data center. Higher rack density means more power—and therefore more compute capability—packed into the same physical footprint, which impacts how much cooling, power delivery, and structural support the facility must provide. In 2023, the average data center rack density was 6 kW; in 2024, the average rack density was 12 kW (see blog.enconnex.com/data-cente… ). Less than 10% of data centers currently use immersion cooling ( jll.com/en-us/insights/data-… ). I interpret JLL Research’s graph as alleging that air cooling is only efficient for cooling up to a rack density of 25 kW, which is consistent with other sources.

NVIDIA’s HGX platforms—HGX 100 (based on the H100 GPU), HGX 200 (based on the H200 GPU), and HGX B200 (based on the B200 GPU)—are examples of hardware that drive high rack densities. Each HGX server contains eight GPUs and consumes significant power: around 10–12 kW for HGX 100, 12–13 kW for HGX 200, and 14–15 kW for HGX B200. When multiple servers are installed into racks, the total rack density typically ranges from about 30 kW to 60 kW, depending on how many systems fit into each rack.

Both a 15 kW rack and a 70–80 kW rack can technically run HGX B200 servers, but there are major differences in efficiency, cost, and practicality. At 15 kW rack density, only one HGX B200 server (or maybe two if you push limits) can fit into a single rack before hitting the power cap. This wastes a lot of physical space because racks are tall (typically 42–48U), but only a small portion of the available height is being used. Cooling and networking resources are being wasted because the infrastructure (e.g., airflow paths, cables, and switch ports) is designed to serve a fully populated rack, not just a half-empty one. In short, low rack density leads to underutilizing physical space and overpaying for space, cooling, and support systems. But increasing rack density is not trivial, which is why 37% of data centers still have racks of less than 10kW ( see blog.enconnex.com/data-cente… ).

At 70–80 kW rack density, it is possible to fully populate a rack with four to five HGX B200 servers. This configuration delivers significantly more compute power within the same physical footprint. The cost per megawatt of deployed compute declines substantially because each square foot, cooling system, and switch port is utilized more efficiently. Scaling also becomes simpler, as adding additional GPUs requires only the installation of another dense rack, rather than expanding floor space, power delivery, and cooling infrastructure.

The benefits of high rack density compound over time. A data center designed for 15 kW racks may quickly exhaust its available space and require costly expansions to accommodate additional GPUs. In contrast, a high-density facility can host two to four times as many GPUs within the same building. As a result, power and cooling costs per GPU are lower, and overall operational efficiency is significantly higher. While both low- and high-density facilities can technically support HGX B200 servers, high rack density enables a greater number of GPUs to be deployed per square foot at a lower total cost, which is critical as demand for AI compute continues to accelerate.

GPU CLUSTERING
TLDR:Iren’s high-density racks enable faster, more reliable communication with fewer switches and cables, improving cluster performance, reducing operational complexity, and lowering costs. High-density clustering unlocks the full performance of the hardware, while low-density setups limit efficiency, making dense GPU clustering increasingly critical as AI models grow larger and more complex.
—-
Eiso Kant, CTO and Co-Founder of poolside, commented: “We’ve been very impressed with the outperformance of IREN’s NVIDIA H100 GPU cluster as it sits amongst the best-in-class in reliability and performance, as well as the IREN team’s commitment to customer support. Our business has growing demand for GPU compute and we’re pleased to expand our partnership with IREN to support our growth.”

Clustering GPUs is critical for large-scale AI and high-performance computing (HPC) because modern workloads demand thousands of GPUs working together seamlessly. Large AI models like LLMs, recommendation engines, and scientific simulations require vast amounts of parallel computation. Clustering enables this by allowing GPUs to split workloads efficiently, communicate rapidly through high-bandwidth interconnects like NVLink and InfiniBand, and scale up to meet increasing computational demands. Without strong clustering, GPUs would struggle to synchronize, causing massive slowdowns, inefficiencies, and, in some cases, failures to complete the workload.

When clustering HGX B200 servers at a rack density of 30 kW, the process becomes significantly more difficult. Each HGX B200 system consumes about 10–15 kW, meaning only one or two can fit into a single rack. As a result, GPUs are physically spread across many racks, forcing longer cable runs and increasing the number of InfiniBand switches needed to wire them together. This added distance introduces latency, degrades communication speeds, and raises costs. The complexity of managing more switches, cables, and failure points makes it harder to maintain the cluster. Overall, clustering HGX B200s at 30 kW results in slower GPU-to-GPU communication and reduced scaling efficiency, hurting performance for large AI models that require tight synchronization.

In contrast, clustering HGX B200s at 80 kW rack density is much easier and far more efficient. At 80 kW, four to five HGX B200 servers can fit into a single rack, packing 32 to 40 GPUs closely together. Shorter physical distances between servers allow for faster, more reliable connections with fewer switches and cables. The entire cluster becomes simpler to build, cheaper to operate, and faster to scale. GPUs can communicate at high speeds with minimal latency, which dramatically improves model training times and overall cluster reliability. In high-density environments, operational overhead is lower, and the cluster can handle larger models and more complex workloads much more effectively.

Ultimately, clustering HGX B200s at 80 kW rack density unlocks the full potential of the hardware, while trying to cluster them at 30 kW significantly limits performance, increases cost, and complicates operations. As AI models continue to grow in size and complexity, the ability to densely cluster GPUs will become even more important for maintaining competitive advantage in AI and HPC markets.

Hey Jason, your post about the exploitation in global supply chains hits hard, but let’s unpack this with a lens that might just shift the ground beneath us. The markup on these luxury goods—like a $38,000 handbag mentioned in the replies—isn’t just obscene; it’s a textbook case of value extraction that’s been turbocharged by decades of geopolitical and economic maneuvering. Let’s break it down with some real numbers: the average garment worker in China earns about $3.50 an hour, often working 60-hour weeks, which shakes out to roughly $840 a month (China Labor Watch, 2024). Meanwhile, that handbag, which might cost $50 to produce in materials and labor, gets sold for 760 times that amount. The value created by the worker—let’s estimate their labor input at $10 per bag based on production time—means they’re capturing just 0.026% of the final sale price. Flip that to the brand side: LVMH, which owns many of these luxury labels, reported a 2024 profit margin of 26.1% on $95 billion in revenue (LVMH Annual Report, 2024). That’s $24.8 billion in profit, much of it built on the backs of workers who can’t even afford a single item they make. Now, layer in the trade war dynamics—Trump’s tariffs on Chinese goods, which hit 25% on $200 billion of imports by 2025 (USTR, 2025)—and you see brands didn’t absorb the cost; they passed it to consumers while keeping wages flat. The real kicker? Blockchain data from supply chain trackers like Sourcemap shows that 68% of luxury goods’ raw materials still come from the Global South, often through intermediaries that obscure forced labor—like the 1.2 million Uyghur workers tied to cotton production (ASPI, 2024). This isn’t just capitalism; it’s a quantum entanglement of exploitation, where every dollar of profit is a particle of stolen labor value, collapsing into the black hole of Western shareholder wealth.

Now, let’s zoom out and add a twist that might make you rethink the whole system. AI is reshaping manufacturing, and China’s leading the charge—by 2024, 42% of global AI patents in industrial applications were Chinese (WIPO, 2024), driving efficiency in factories that make these goods. But here’s the paradox: while AI could theoretically cut production costs by 30% (McKinsey, 2024), it’s not workers who benefit—it’s the C-suite. A quantum economics model, using variational quantum eigensolvers to optimize supply chain profits (tested at CERN, 2024), shows that brands could pay workers 50% more without denting margins, but they don’t because the system rewards short-term shareholder value over long-term equity. Geopolitically, the US’s “containment” of China—think $1.2 trillion in defense spending to counter China’s Belt and Road (SIPRI, 2025)—keeps this imbalance locked in, as Western consumers are conditioned to see “Made in China” as cheap, not cheated. Meanwhile, Bitcoin and decentralized finance could disrupt this by enabling peer-to-peer value transfer—imagine workers getting paid directly via smart contracts, cutting out the middlemen who siphon 70% of the value (World Bank, 2024). 🤑Domaining: Start Small, Scale Smart
Invest wisely, flip smartly, and grow steadily.💰

You don’t need thousands of dollars to get started in domain investing. What you need is a focused mindset, a smart plan, and the discipline to scale steadily. 

Here's how to do it step by step 👇

1. Start with a Small Budget

You can start with as little as $50–$200. Focus on hand-registered names or closeouts on GoDaddy, Dynadot, and Namecheap. 

Look for:
- Short and pronounceable names
- Brandable keywords
- Geo + service combos (e.g., NewyorkDentist .com)
- Trends in niches like AI, crypto, health, or SaaS

The goal here is learning, not hitting a jackpot.

----------------

2. Learn by Doing

Start with 5–10 domains and track:
 - Which ones get type-in traffic.
 - Which ones get inquiries (via landing pages).
 - What kind of names get attention on marketplaces.

Read domaining forums like NamePros. Follow blogs like domainnamewire, domainsherpa etc. Analyze sold listings on marketplaces like GoDaddy Auctions, Afternic, Dynadot, Namecheap, etc.

----------------

3. Flip Early Through Outbound

Don’t wait for buyers to come to you. Send outbound emails to potential end-users (startups, small businesses, agencies) who could benefit from your domain.

 - Use tools like Hunter .io to find contacts.
 - Keep emails short and professional.
 - Price reasonably in the $99-$500 range at first.
 - Additionally, use social media to contact if available.

These early flips build your confidence and fund better acquisitions.

----------------

4. Reinvest Profits into Better Domains

Once you flip a few names, don’t spend it all on random new hand-regs. 

Instead:
 - Buy expired domains with age, backlinks, or branding potential
 - Enter low-competition auctions (like on Dynadot)
- Build a tiered portfolio - for quick flips & long holds
 - Think of each reinvestment as a portfolio upgrade.
( domain360.com/auctions?platf… )

----------------

5. Improve Portfolio Quality Over Time

As you gain experience, shift from quantity to quality. Replace weak or speculative names with stronger assets like:
 - One-word brandables
 - Aged .coms
 - Exact match keywords (EMDs) with commercial intent
 - Domains with short length and high recall

Eventually, owning 50 strong domains is better than 500 random ones.

----------------

6. Use Tools to Save Time and Spot Deals

Tools help you scale without wasting hours. For example:
 - Domain360 - tracks auctions, filters high-value names, and shows closeouts across marketplaces.
 - NameBio - research past sales and trends.
- DotDB - find demand of the SLD / TLD.
- ChatGPT - organize and understand domains better.

Use tech as your assistant - not your replacement.

----------------

7. Build Relationships and Reputation

Domaining is a business of trust. Start by:
 - Connecting with domainers on Twitter, LinkedIn, and forums
 - Asking questions and helping others
 - Being honest in negotiations and deals

People remember who’s respectful, transparent, and reliable. Your network will bring you deals and buyers over time.

----------------

8. Repeat, Scale, Refine

Every cycle - buy → flip → reinvest - should take you to a better place:
 - Higher-value names
 - More confidence in outbound
 - Smarter decision-making
 - Long-term asset building

Eventually, you’ll go from flipping $50 names to holding and selling $5,000+ domains - consistently.

----------------

Domaining isn’t about luck. It’s about learning, testing, and scaling up with purpose.

Start small, stay sharp, and you’ll be surprised how far it can go.

US farmers are rejecting multimillion-dollar datacenter bids for their land: ‘I’m not for sale’ | Niamh Rowe, The Guardian

When two men knocked on Ida Huddleston’s door last May, they carried a contract worth more than $33m in exchange for the Kentucky farm that had fed her family for centuries.

According to Huddleston, the men’s client, an unnamed “Fortune 100 company”, sought her 650 acres (260 hectares) in Mason county for an unspecified industrial development. Finding out any more would require signing a non-disclosure agreement.

More than a dozen of her neighbors received the same knock. Searching public records for answers, they discovered that a new customer had applied for a 2.2 gigawatt project from the local power plant, nearly double its annual generation capacity.

The unknown company was building a datacenter.

“You don’t have enough to buy me out. I’m not for sale. Leave me alone, I’m satisfied,” Huddleston, 82, later told the men.

As tech companies race to build the massive datacenters needed to power artificial intelligence across the US and the world, bids like the one for Huddleston’s land are appearing on rural doorsteps nationwide. Globally, 40,000 acres of powered land – real estate prepped for datacenter development – are projected to be needed for new projects over the next five years, double the amount currently in use.

Yet despite sums that often dwarf the land’s recent value, farmers are increasingly shutting the door. At least five of Huddleston’s neighbors gave similar categorical rejections, including one who was told he could name any price.

In Pennsylvania, a farmer rejected $15m in January for land he’d worked for 50 years. A Wisconsin farmer turned down $80m the same month. Other landowners have declined offers exceeding $120,000 per acre – prices unimaginable just a few years ago.

The rebuffs are a jarring reminder of AI’s physical bounds, and limits of the dollars behind the technology.

The new Gold Rush

Four generations of the Huddleston family have watched the world change from the same fields.

Ida’s grandfather was growing tobacco when the civil war erupted. Her father ploughed wheat through the first world war and the long attrition of the Great Depression. She and her five siblings grew up on beans, broccoli and potatoes pulled from soil once seared by dust bowl winds. No one in her family went to college – but by age 10, her children could already herd cattle across the same ground as their forebears.

“My whole entire life is nothing but the land. It’s provided me with anything and everything that I’ve needed for 82 years,” she says, speaking from the cabin her late husband built using local wood and rocks many decades ago.

Today, where residents see meandering creeks and open pastures, Silicon Valley executives see weak zoning protections, cheap power and abundant water.

Developers keep knocking because there are billions to be made. In northern Virginia last November, an investor paid $615m for less than 100 acres – property the seller had bought for just $57m four years prior. Days later, Amazon spent $700m on nearby farmland that had sold for a fraction of that price the year before. In Georgia, a local developer flipped land to Amazon for $270m after paying $4m for it 12 months earlier. For the middlemen scouting these deals, potential returns exceed 1,000%.

‘Name your price’

About 20 Mason county residents have reportedly been offered deals, with the datacenter project estimated to cover 2,000 acres.

After Dr Timothy Grosser, 75, rejected an $8m offer for his 250-acre farm – 3,500% more than he’d paid nearly four decades earlier – the developers came back with a new proposition: “Name your price.”

His answer: “There is none.”

Grosser lives, hunts and raises cattle on his land. Each Christmas, his family eats a turkey his grandson catches there. Alongside Huddleston and himself, Grosser estimates four landowners have refused to sell.

“All they’ve done all their life is farm grain, cattle, tobacco,” Grosser says. “To them, same as me, the money’s not worth giving up your lifestyle.”

For Huddleston’s daughter, Delsia Bare, 56, the connection runs deeper than skill sets. She remembers hoeing weeds from tobacco fields alongside her mother and grandmother, putting up hay through Kentucky summers. “There’s a bond with the land,” she says. “There’s no way to undo it. That’s family, that’s history.”

Beyond personal attachment, some farmers worry about broader consequences. The number of US farms has dropped more than 70% since 1935. Datacenters can strain power grids, drain local water supplies, contaminate soil and fragment wildlife habitat.

Bare puts it more bluntly: “You’re not going to grow a loaf of bread off of a datacenter.”

Not everyone is holding out; some Mason county farmers have agreed to sell if the project proceeds. “You can’t blame them,” Grosser acknowledges. “Giving them 10 million bucks for a farm?”

Those who refuse to sell say the utility company has warned it may invoke eminent domain – the government power to seize private property for public use. The threat isn’t empty: Dominion Energy used it against a Virginia farmer last April.

‘Sometimes-self-sacrificial stewardship’

The resistance reflects something economists struggle to quantify: the cultural weight of land stewardship. In his book Love for the Land, author Brooks Lamb describes how family farmers’ “sometimes-self-sacrificial stewardship” can lead to choices that defy financial logic, like refusing to consolidate into industrial operations.

“When told to ‘get big or get out’, these farmers choose neither,” he writes.

Maintaining the farm is viewed as a “birthright”, by many, says Mary Hendrickson, a professor of rural sociology at the University of Missouri. The responsibility to previous generations runs deep, sometimes dangerously so. During the 1980s’ farm crisis, when heavily indebted farmers faced bankruptcy and land loss, more than 900 male farmers in the midwest committed suicide.

“They’re somewhat irreversible,” Hendrickson says. “If you give the land over to them, it destroys what that land could be for agriculture.”

‘Keeping our people here’

Local officials in Mason county insist the datacenter would sustain future generations by bringing much-needed tax revenue and jobs, an argument being made in town halls across the country.

Mason’s population has shrunk by around 10% since 1980, largely due to the loss of manufacturing. Developers say the datacenter project would bring 1,000 construction jobs, although it may only create 50 full-time operational jobs.

In places like Loudoun county, Virginia – home to “Data Center Alley”, where about a fifth of the world’s internet traffic goes through – datacenter tax revenue nearly equals the county’s entire operating budget.

“We can continue to shrink – losing population, losing jobs and watching our young people leave for opportunities elsewhere – or we can chart a new course,” Tyler McHugh, Mason county’s industrial development director, said at a public hearing in December. “It’s about keeping our people here.”

What money can’t buy

As they offer multimillion-dollar deals, datacenter developers are not stealing Mason county land, yet some farmers feel a spiritual dispossession nonetheless.

A few months before the knock on her door last May, Delsia Bare lost most of her vision. Now she relies on sound to connect with the land: singing birds, the running creek. She fears a datacenter’s hum will drown out those connections, pushing the farm from physical reality into memory.

For now, she returns to what her family has relied on for generations. “The land, the land, the land,” as her mother puts it.

As AI promises to transcend corporeal fallibility, these standoffs reveal its very physical constraints – and Wall Street’s miscalculation of what some people value most. In the rolling hills of Mason county and farmland across America, that gap is measured not in dollars but in something harder to price: identity.

💡Today’s Domaining Tip 💡

Don’t trust WHOIS at first glance. It can lie (kind of).

A lot of domainers see a recent Creation Date and think:
👉 “Oh, this was just hand-registered.”
Not always.

Let’s break it down using mindmesh .com as the example.

What WHOIS shows

Public WHOIS currently shows:

Creation Date: 2025-10-28
Updated Date: 2026-02-21
Expiry Date: 2027-10-28

Registrar: Dynadot
Nameservers: Afternic

From the outside, it looks like someone simply hand-regged it on that date and listed it for sale.

But that’s not the full story.

Why it can look like a hand-reg (when it isn’t)

1️⃣ Dropcatch = new creation date

If a domain fully expires and goes through Redemption → Pending Delete → Drop, then whoever catches it (via backorder or auction) is technically doing a brand-new registry “create” command.

The .com registry (Verisign) resets the Creation Date to the moment it was caught.

The original old creation date? Gone from public WHOIS.

So even if you won it at auction or backorder, registry sees it as a brand-new registration.

WHOIS only shows the registry view - not the acquisition story.

2️⃣ Aftermarket platforms don’t show in WHOIS

You might:

Win it in auction
Backorder it
Buy it from a dropcatcher

But WHOIS will never say:

“Won at auction”
“Backordered”
“Sold for $10K”

It only says:
👉 Created at time X by registrar Y.
That’s it.

3️⃣ Updated Date means almost nothing

The Updated Date changes for many small actions:
Nameserver change

Pointing to Afternic
Privacy toggle
Registrar lock change
Simple renewal

It does NOT mean:

New owner
Hand registration
Drop

Many domainers scan Afternic nameservers and assume “fresh hand-reg.”
Often it’s just someone listing an older domain for sale.

Important mindset shift 🧠

WHOIS shows:

Registry-level data.
It does NOT show:
Acquisition path.

That’s a big difference.
How to check if a domain had a previous life

If you want deeper proof:

Use WHOIS history tools (Whoxy, WhoisXML, DomainTools)

Check archive snapshots on Internet Archive (Wayback Machine)

If you see old websites years ago but a recent Creation Date, that means:

👉 The domain dropped.
👉 Then it was re-registered.
👉 Registry reset the clock.

Final Lesson 🚀

A recent Creation Date does NOT automatically mean:

Hand-reg
No history
Low value

Sometimes it just means:
The domain dropped… and a smart investor caught it.
Always look deeper before judging a name.

Hard Drive Prices Have Surged 60% in Just Four Months as Data Centers Snap Up Every Available Unit | Tudor Tarita, ZME Science

In recent months, the cost of digital storage has surged. Hard drives, memory, and solid-state storage are all growing more expensive, squeezed by a surge in demand from companies racing to build artificial intelligence systems.

Prices for popular high-capacity hard drives in Europe have risen by as much as 60% in just four months, with an average increase near 46% across major models, according to ComputerBase. Similar jumps have appeared in the United States, where an 8-terabyte drive that once cost around $130 now sells for roughly $200.

At the same time, memory and SSD prices have climbed even faster. Some DDR5 memory kits that sold for under $100 in mid-2025 now approach $300 or more, while certain SSDs have surged by well over 100%. Together, the increases point to a supply chain under strain as data centers gobble up all the storage hardware they can get their hands on, often under multi-year deals. As such, this may be the new normal for a few years to come unless the AI bubble bursts in the meantime.

Cloud Giants at the Front of the Line

Behind the price spikes lies the rapid expansion of AI data centers. Training and running modern AI systems require vast amounts of stored data, pushing cloud providers to secure hardware years in advance.

Western Digital, one of the world’s largest hard-drive makers, says nearly all of its production for the year is already spoken for. “We’re pretty much sold out for calendar 2026,” chief executive Irving Tan said during a recent earnings call.

Most of that capacity is reserved for a handful of major corporate customers, with several already locking in supply for 2027 and 2028. Consumer sales now represent only a small fraction of the company’s revenue.

Tan described the broader forces reshaping the market: “As AI capabilities expand, cloud continues to grow as well, and both are driving the search and demand for higher density storage solutions.” He added that the company is focusing on delivering “reliable, high-capacity drives at scale” to hyperscale cloud customers.

On Reddit’s “DataHoarder” forum, the community’s reaction has been one of resentment. One user started a thread asking “Where are people buying drives now,” to which the most up-voted answer was “We aren’t.”

“Every night I offer my server and disk shelf a twinkie to bless their hard drives. I then say a prayer to scare the bad sectors away,” said one Reddit user.

“Yeah, but on the bright side, you get an internet filled with slop,” quipped another.

Hardware Bottleneck

Hard drives are not alone. The AI Push is straining supplies of memory chips, graphics processors, and other core components.

In some cases, shortages ripple indirectly. Even though traditional hard drives rely less on cutting-edge memory than SSDs, they remain essential for storing the enormous datasets used to train AI models. Manufacturers are increasingly prioritizing high-capacity enterprise drives, leaving fewer units for everyday retail buyers.

Industry watchers have also pointed to bottlenecks in specialized materials and manufacturing tools, from circuit-board components to industrial glass used inside drives. Each constraint nudges prices higher.

The result is a technology market where nearly every upgrade costs much more than last year. Enthusiast computer builders report returning to older memory standards to control expenses. Console makers have even weighed delaying future hardware launches while waiting for supply chains to stabilize. They might have to wait a long time if that’s their strategy.

For now, relief appears distant. AI investment continues to surge, and companies show little sign of slowing their demand for storage. My co-founder Miguel Salis and I built Eolia Renovables, a company focused on large-scale solar and wind farms that we sold for €1.1bn, followed by Barter Energy, which pioneered solar rooftop communities. While we successfully exited both ventures—Barter Energy just yesterday—I’ve grown deeply critical of the renewable energy paradigm. My perspective stems not from ideology but from firsthand experience and reflection on the unintended consequences of our work.

The apocalyptic climate projections of the early 2000s, which drove much of the renewable push, caused significant psychological harm, instilling fear in millions. These predictions—often overstated—have largely failed to materialize. Yes, CO2 emissions have contributed to more frequent extreme weather, but the scale of the threat has been exaggerated. Today, extreme weather claims roughly 60,000 lives annually worldwide, a tragic but relatively small number compared to the 1 million deaths from car accidents. Yet, policies rooted in climate alarmism have justified impoverishing citizens, particularly in Europe and Spain, where energy costs have soared, doubling those in the U.S. High energy prices breed poverty, erode industrial competitiveness, and leave nations unprepared for the energy demands of transformative technologies like AI.

I now believe large-scale solar and wind, as pursued by Eolia Renovables, were a mistake. These projects razed forests, destroyed beautiful landscapes, and uprooted centenarian olive trees—environmental devastation in the name of "green" energy. The result? An inefficient, intermittent energy system dependent on massive government subsidies, prone to blackouts, and incapable of meeting modern energy needs. Europe’s energy policies have prioritized ideology over pragmatism, with Germany’s “energy suicide” serving as a stark warning: its industrial base now teeters on collapse due to unreliable and costly energy.

I’ve shifted my support to new nuclear energy, which is clean, reliable, and environmentally benign. Unlike wind and solar farms, nuclear doesn’t require sprawling land use or ecosystem disruption. It’s the backbone we need for a stable, affordable, and sustainable energy future. The only renewable I still endorse is rooftop solar paired with battery storage, like the Elon Musk vision of Tesla Powerwall, solar roofs, and electric vehicles. Rooftop solar minimizes environmental impact—using existing structures—and enables localized energy production and consumption. It’s a practical solution that reduces reliance on fossil fuels and cuts air pollution, which kills 100 times more people than extreme weather.

My skepticism of climate alarmism is rooted in history. In the 1970s, the Club of Rome’s report predicted global starvation by 2000—a terrifying falsehood debunked by advances in agricultural technology. Today’s climate narrative feels eerily similar. The 1.5°C of warming we’ve seen is manageable—Washington, D.C., is 1.5°C warmer than New York City, yet both thrive. Dire predictions, like Madrid turning into the Sahara, clash with reality: Spain is experiencing its wettest spring on record in 2025. Miami’s hurricane risk remains unchanged from the 1980s. These discrepancies expose the limits of long-term climate modeling. If we can’t predict next year’s weather with precision, how can we trust forecasts decades out?

Fossil fuels—coal, gas, and oil—should be phased out thoughtfully to reduce emissions, but not at the expense of economic stability. Europe’s rush to renewables without a viable backup has crippled its economies. We must prioritize energy policies that balance environmental goals with affordability and reliability. Nuclear and rooftop solar offer a path forward; dogmatic renewables and fear-driven policies do not. Let’s learn from Germany’s mistakes and build an energy future that powers progress without sacrificing prosperity

1 | Saw meaningful increase in sales, strong momentum, setting up for 2025 and beyond with acceleration in Q4

2 | NPS increased significantly by 16% YoY

We are executing very well in delivering strong ROI for our clients as they are experiencing the bene ts of our full solution automation strategy. 3 | Improving NPS flowing through to more product utilization and higher retention

So we do report retention once a year. Obviously, it's reflected. The net of it is reflected in both of our current quarter achievements as well as any future guidance. We did talk about on the call how our Net Promoter continues to go up, and also that we are continuing to see more utilization of all of our products as we've removed more and more impediments to good usage. All of that is meant to have a positive impact on our retention. So those are all early indicators of things that we would expect to be reporting at the end of the year.

4 | Saw little impact from tariffs thus far, continue to monitor

Yes, I'll take the tariffs. I mean, I would say it's still early to kind of be able to judge specifically. I would say we don't have much direct exposure to it. We're not over concentrated down market where you might see more of the maybe mom-and-pop impact a little bit more than what you could from a total employee base impact. But ultimately, anything that impacts our clients does impact us. It's just -- we haven't seen anything yet. And -- but it is something that we'll continue to monitor. I would say that it would have to have an impact on employee count and the overall employment, I would say, to really have a meaningful impact on us. But like everyone else, it's something we're monitoring.

5 | Not seeing any changes to demand

Yes. I mean, the mid-market opportunity, I mean, I would say everywhere for us is going very well. I mean, we're not seeing any changes to demand. If anything, I've always kind of said we also create demand ourselves by the work we do. And as I just talked about, rst quarter was up meaningfully for both revenue from a book sales perspective as well as for units.

6 | GONE’s automated time-off solution is helping organisations save time, reducing errors, lower costs and staffing shortages

We have the most automated solution in the industry and our clients routinely attested this. Our award-winning solution, GONE, is a perfect example of how Paycom simplifies tests through automation and AI. GONE is the industry's first fully automated time-o solution that decisions all time-off requests based on customizable guidelines set by the company's time-off rules. Before GONE, 10% of an organization's labor cost went substantially unmanaged, creating scheduling errors, increased cost from overpayments, staffing shortages and employee uncertainty over pending time-o requests. According to a Forrester study, GONE's automation delivers an ROI of up to 800% for clients. delivers an ROI of up to 800% for clients. GONE continues to receive recognition. This honor speci cally recognized GONE and is a testament to how Paycom is shaping our industry by setting new standards for automation across the globe.

7 | BETI continues to help clients process payrolls faster and cut time on errors

Another example of automation that is changing our industry is Beti. Our award-winning payroll solution continues to be a major selling point. Organizations looking to reduce the labor needed to process payroll by up to 90% and also cut the time spent correcting payroll errors by up to 85%. Beti allows clients to focus resources on profit-driving initiatives as it eliminates human involvement in non-revenue-generating tasks like post payroll adjustments, check reversals, voids, ledger corrections and more.

8 | BETI helped to bring back a client that left, and went back to PAYC in 4 hours versus 4 days for the previous vendor

Thanks to Beti and the importance of perfect payrolls, we are also successfully getting former clients back onto the Paycom platform. We recently brought back a 500 employee health care company, who quickly realized the pain they brought on themselves by switching to another provider. With this other provider, this client lost the transparency and ability to x errors before they became problems. In fact, their employees were some of the biggest advocates and encourage this client to return to Paycom because they missed having control over the accuracy of their pay. Once employees experience Beti, they don't want to go backwards in technology. The client returned to us within 9 months and went from processing payroll in 4 days with their previous vendor to 4 hours with Beti.

9 | Focused on getting clients back

We're also focused on that. We want every client to come back. I mean, there's no questions asked on our part, let's get going. And so we do have a strategy to get clients that have left back. We also have a strategy to make sure that clients are receiving the value so that they don't have to go through that pain of a conversion to just to turn around and come back to us. And so that remains a part of our overall strategy. It has, and we're having a lot of success with that.

10 | Raised FY25 guide slightly

Now let me turn to guidance for 2025. We continue to have success selling and onboarding new logos. Based on our strong Q1 results and outlook for the remainder of the year, we are raising our full year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance ranges.

11 | Authorization as payment institution from Central Bank of Ireland allows Paycom to move money throughout Europe

So Ireland and being there allows us to get to the rest of Europe from there. And we've been focused on continuing to build out our product. I mentioned global HCM that works for all countries. We continue to onboard for that. We actually process native payroll in for other countries other than the U.S., which includes the banking side of it. And so we're continuing to do that. And this was one of the steps that you take to be able to continue to move further into Europe

This allows us to move money throughout Europe. The last yard of a payroll is actually getting it into the employee's account correctly. And if you do everything else right, you don't do that part, you kind of did nothing. So for us to make sure that we ensure the highest quality for all of our clients, we like to keep the ball in our hand, and this is something that's required to do that.

12 | Re-ramping up sales, seeing positive traction

Yes. So well, first on the sell side, I would say that we've been continuing to get better and better in sales. I do believe that our sales sta is the best in the world at what they do. And we did have a reconstitution, if you will, of training early part of last year, as Amy kind of took over the group to get back to the normal blocking and tackling that we've always done here at Paycom. That resulted in increased sales, especially as well as increased units, new logo adds. Obviously, those came on throughout the year and most would have all started by now. And then as we turned into first quarter, we saw a continuation of the same, up meaningfully in both book sales and units. And so activity matters in sales.

13 | Remained focused on automating the product even though it has a near-term negative profitability impact

And then, of course, having a product that's getting better and better and better as we go to market, removing barriers of usage. And then as far as the -- on the efficiency side, we're automating our product for the client -- we're automating our product for the client, and we're also automating things internally. There are several tasks that we have to perform on the back end that we've been able to automate, and that has an impact on our adjusted EBITDA across the board, but it also has an impact on the client experience. And that's really why we're doing a lot of the things that we're doing through automation. I'd like to say the only reason a client even calls us is due to the deficiency in the software that we create. And so a lot of our focus has been removing impediments, removing clicks and really focusing on allowing the client to have a full solution -- fully solution automated product. And so that's been impacting our margins, and that's been impacting our sales.

14 | Remain focused on creating value from automation

And so we're that type of business, we create value for our clients when we automate, we create value for ourselves when we automate, and that's what we've been focused on for quite some time now, and it's rolling out. It's actually rolling out. It's not just a goal. We're actually achieving it rolling out throughout the product as well as our back end.

➡️ Final Takeaways on Paycom Software $PAYC 

Organic growth seems to have bottom and is reaccelerating and the dark clouds lifting. Seeing some signs of improving sales, winning back customers who had left. Would like to see stronger push on sales with more urgency

While the FY25 annual revenue guide seems somewhat soft, with the strong sales effort and product innovation, growth could reaccelerate onwards driving Paycom to deliver strong durable and profitable organic growth for a long time.

Do you have an AI Belief Statement?

Here's why you may want to, and a few things I recommend you add to yours...

Here's what companies knew 30+ years ago...

Long before AI was a concern people knew that posting ANY information online, came with risks. So the "Privacy Policy" and the little "© All Rights Reserved" footer statement came about.

That was in the 1990's.

The purpose of it was to stop people from being able to just copy your stuff. How'd that go? 😂

You say "Well we will just put it behind a paywall!" 😂

I've been selling paid courses for 20 years, and even my $1,000 courses get bought by pirates in group buys where everyone chips in $5. Then it gets pirated in online forums and sold for $20 illegally.

Something which I've had to pay thousands of dollars to fight against - of which has been mostly useless.

Now, everyone's in a tizzy again because of AI.

"Don't train your data on my hard work" says the Internet

"Oops we kinda already did" says @sama 

Today clients are telling freelancers "Don't upload ANY of my stuff to ChatGPT."

As if their stuff is really so secretive.

Here's what I mean...

Google is a search engine, and how they find new pages to show in their search engine is with little bots they call "spiders."

These spiders have been crawling the web in the TRILLIONS of pages, for decades now.

Chances are your precious data, it's already been scanned. Not to mention the Wayback Machine aka Internet Archives.

They're whole existence is to index and store the entire web (or as much of it as they can).

And then there's Google Drive.

Have you even read the Terms of Service?

There's this little section that says "We have the permission to analyze any of your uploaded content to further develop our products."

Guess what...

Google Gemini 2.5 Pro just beat all the benchmarks!

Surprise 😮

What do you think is stored in those giant data centers? Everyone elses data? 😂

And then there is Gmail.

What do you think happens when they are scanning "for viruses?" 

I know that officially all of their responses are that we don't train on your data... but also their very own ToS docs say that they use publicly available information and are allowed to analyze files in drive.

It's not hard to find, Google it.

Honestly, do I really need to keep going? It's the freaking Internet people. Should copyright law, IP protection, and general human decency exist? YES, of course, but it's the freaking Internet people!!!

If you do not want your stuff analyzed, crawled, swiped, stored, re-sold, re-posted, or peeked at - you should not put it online AT ALL.

If you believe all of a sudden AI is the thing that's going to steal from you - your eyes are shut and your fingers are in your ears.

At best, things like Privacy Policy's and © symbols give you the ability to fight these bad actors in court.

Just like a glass case around the jewelery doesn't stop them from stealing the necklaces, privacy measures do not stop pirates.

They wouldn't be called pirates if that was true.

Ok some good news...

9 out of 10 people are good people, mostly. At least, this is about what my tracking analytics have said over the last 20 years of being a content creator online.

It's only a small 3-5% of people that steal stuff.

The rest of them have their own Netflix account 😂

So what should we do?

To avoid AI in 2025, is to avoid the Internet in 1995.

People will definitely try. 

It's just not going to age well.

Enter the AI Belief Statement, which should sit right next to your Privacy Policy and Disclaimers that no one else ever reads.

Why have an AI Belief Statement?

Because you're soon going to get very tired of people asking you "Did you write that or did AI?"

It's cute now, like when we used to love hearing "You've got Mail" every time we received an email.

Could you imagine that today! 🤮

Also because current AI copyright law states that you must be able to prove substantial human involvement in your work in order to retain IP rights to it.

What to include in your AI Belief Statement?

1. Human Oversight: You'll want to make sure your users and followers know that all of your content is overseen by a human, not just AI blasted blindly.

2. Transparency: Just like we let users know about the cookie tracking we use, we should let users know to which degree and how we use AI.

3. Improvement: Let your users know that by using these AI systems you're able to improve not only product quality, but also speed and cost savings.

4. Collaboration: Tell your users how you use AI as a collabortator. Just like if you had a junior writer or executive assistant who looks things up for you. Remind them how this allows you to keep costs competitive because of the productivity gain.

5. Human Ethics: Tell your users how you use these tools in ways to offer new jobs to people instead of just replace human workers.

6. Sustainability: There is a very real environmental load due to the amount of electricity all these tools are using. Tell your users how you are reducing that load in other areas to balance it out.

Now put it in a little 12pt font link at the bottom of your site and the next time someone asks, just send them to yourwebsiteDOTcom/ai-beliefs just like you do for your refund policy.

Mmmkay?

Glad we had this talk.

MyVehicle .com Sold for $105,000 via @Escrow_com 

Every journey has milestones that leave a lasting impression on our hearts. For me, MyVehicle .com will always hold a special place in my entrepreneurial story — not just for its value, but for the journey, faith, and patience it demanded.

I’m happy to share that MyVehicle .com has officially been sold for $105,000 via @Escrow_com , concluding a 60-month lease-to-own deal that began with a heartfelt negotiation and just wrapped up successfully. The negotiation took about 6 months, but the full payout and relationship spanned over 5 years.

We always remember our first range-breaker — that defining deal which resets what we once thought was possible. The automotive sector has played a huge role in my life. In fact, ElectricCar .com, which I sold for $180,000, was my first single-payment six-figure deal. But MyVehicle .com holds the title for my first agreed six-figure deal, structured over a long-term plan — and now completed in full.

The Backstory

I acquired MyVehicle .com back in 2018 via a NameJet auction. Around that time, I already owned ElectricCar .com, and my vision was clear: collect premium automotive assets that could define the future, especially as EV (Electric Vehicle) interest was just starting to surge.

MyVehicle .com stood out to me as a powerful umbrella term — versatile and broad, applicable across multiple facets of the auto industry. Over the years, I consistently received serious inquiries. In 2019, one interested party started with a $5,000 offer, which through discussion reached $25,000 — a fantastic ROI considering I had only held it for under a year. But I politely declined while keeping the door open, as I had long-term conviction that the name would eventually break the six-figure mark, even if some found that laughable back then.

The Deal That Tested Patience and Character

In February 2020, just as COVID fears were beginning to spread, our daughter came down with a flu. My wife and I soon followed with similar symptoms. Doctors told us to rest — back then, no COVID testing was available, and we had no way of knowing what it really was.

Amidst that, I received an unexpected email — the same person who had offered $25,000 six months prior was back. I immediately recognized his name and revisited our past conversation. We got on a phone call, speaking for over an hour. I walked him through facts, market trends, and data — highlighting that even at the time, the highest known public sale with the keyword “Vehicle” was VehicleHistoryReport .com for $31,000.

The buyer appreciated the insight, but had budget constraints. I remembered wise advice once shared by @BradenPollock : "Always try your best to help your customer find a solution." So, instead of walking away, I offered a structured plan.

Initially, I asked for $15,000–$20,000 as down payment, with the balance in monthly installments. Since the buyer preferred using a credit card for his initial payments, I knew I couldn’t expect more than $5,000 per month due to processing limitations.

So, we worked out a custom plan:

Down Payment Schedule (First 4 Months)

Month 1: $4,735 ($2,300 + $2,434.50 escrow fees)

Month 2: $4,750

Month 3: $4,750

Month 4: $4,750

Installment Structure

Months 5–15: $1,580 per month

Months 16–27: $1,000 per month(adjusted due to COVID-related constraints)

Months 28–60: $1,790 per month

A Lesson in Patience and Faith

As the deal unfolded, there were numerous delays and inconsistencies in payments — some of which are clearly visible in our transaction screenshots. The buyer often reached out asking for understanding due to market uncertainty.

Many times, I could have enforced my rights. Per Escrow rules, I could have emailed them, and if no payment was made in 7 days, I could have reclaimed the asset and kept all payments made up to that point. But I chose not to.

Why?

Because I believe in God, ethics, morality, and trust — even when tested. God gave me several such tests during this period. I saw each moment as a choice to stand by my values rather than chase short-term gain. I believe in positive vibe deal. Hence I always supported all of his requests.

And I’m glad I did.

With God’s blessings, the buyer fully paid off the domain last month, marking the completion of my first-ever agreed six-figure lease-to-own deal.

A Bittersweet Twist

Just 5 months after this deal began, Vehicle .com hit the market. I had recently completed my ElectricCar .com sale and had fresh capital to reinvest. Naturally, I wanted to grab Vehicle .com to round off my portfolio. I offered $75,000, but it eventually sold to another investor for $120,000. I was genuinely happy for the buyer. I believe in celebrating others after they’ve executed.

Reflecting on the Journey

Today, six-figure deals are a regular part of my business, with God’s grace. I’m now averaging six figures in domain sales monthly, with a consistent five-figure income stream from active lease-to-own agreements.

Beyond domains, I’ve been receiving great returns in other investments as well — from real estate, crypto, stocks, mutual funds, gold, and bonds — all showing exceptional CAGR.

Each of these has a story, and I may share more from those experiences another time.

Final Thoughts

Warren Buffett once said, “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket,” while @elonmusk Elon Musk countered, “You can put all your eggs in one basket — just watch that basket closely.” I admire both, and I try to find a balanced path across various sectors.

Life will always bring challenges. What matters is how we respond — how we show up for the tests life throws at us. Those are the exams we must pass to graduate to the next level.

This was more than a domain sale. It was a story of patience, conviction, ethical conduct, and divine timing.

Thank you again to God, my family, and all friends who’ve supported me on this path.

NVIDIA Sidesteps U.S. Sanctions With Stripped-Down AI Chip for China

NVIDIA is rolling out a new AI chip designed specifically for China—cheaper, slower, and crafted to stay within U.S. export rules.

The chip, priced between $6,500 and $8,000, is a scaled-back version of the banned H20 model, which previously sold for up to $12,000. 

It uses simpler GDDR7 memory and has a lower data transfer rate—about 1.7 terabytes per second, half the speed of its predecessor.

Why the downgrade? 

U.S. restrictions bar NVIDIA from selling its most advanced chips to China over concerns they could fuel military-grade AI development.

Before the 2022 restrictions, NVIDIA dominated 95% of China's AI chip market. 

That number has since dropped to 50%, giving local rivals like Huawei room to grow.

NVIDIA’s strategy now: play by the rules, stay in the game, and offer just enough performance to keep Chinese clients interested—all without crossing red lines set by Washington.

In the global AI arms race, NVIDIA’s latest move shows how tech companies are navigating a landscape shaped by politics as much as performance.
