Nvidia plans to launch a cheaper Blackwell AI chip for China priced at $6,500-$8,000, replacing the restricted H20 model. It will use conventional memory and simpler manufacturing amid U.S. export curbs limiting high-end tech sales to China.
 reuters.com/world/china/nvid… 

Nvidia to Launch Cheaper Blackwell AI Chip for China After US Export Curbs, Sources Say

Nvidia will launch a new artificial intelligence chipset for China at a significantly lower price than its recently restricted H20 model and plans to start mass production as early as June, sources familiar with the matter said.

The GPU or graphics processing unit will be part of Nvidia's latest generation Blackwell-architecture AI processors and is expected to be priced between $6,500 and $8,000, well below the $10,000-$12,000 the H20 sold for, according to two of the sources.

The lower price reflects its weaker specifications and simpler manufacturing requirements.

It will be based on Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000D, a server-class graphics processor and will use conventional GDDR7 memory instead of more advanced high bandwidth memory, the two sources said.

They added it would not use Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co's advanced Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) packaging technology.

The new chip's price, specifications and production timing have not previously been reported.

The three sources Reuters spoke to for this article declined to be identified as they were not authorised to speak to media.

An Nvidia spokesperson said the company was still evaluating its "limited" options. "Until we settle on a new product design and receive approval from the U.S. government, we are effectively foreclosed from China's $50 billion data center market."

TSMC declined to comment.

Market Share Plunge

China remains a huge market for Nvidia, accounting for 13% of its sales in the past financial year. It's the third time that Nvidia has had to tailor a GPU for the world's second-largest economy after restrictions from U.S. authorities who are keen to stymie Chinese technological development.

After the U.S. effectively banned the H20 in April, Nvidia initially considered developing a downgraded version of the H20 for China, sources have said, but that plan didn't work out.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week the company's older Hopper architecture - which the H20 uses - can no longer accommodate further modifications under current U.S. export restrictions.

Reuters was unable to determine the product's final name.

Chinese brokerage GF Securities said in a note published on Tuesday that the new GPU would likely be called the 6000D or the B40, though it did not disclose pricing or cite sources for the information.

According to two of the sources, Nvidia is also developing another Blackwell-architecture chip for China that is set to begin production as early as September. Reuters was not immediately able to confirm specifications of that variant.

Nvidia's market share in China has plummeted from 95% before 2022, when U.S. export curbs that impacted its products began, to 50% currently, Huang told reporters in Taipei this week. Its main competitor is Huawei which produces the Ascend 910B chip.

Huang also warned that if U.S. export curbs continue, more Chinese customers will buy Huawei's chips.

The H20 ban forced Nvidia to write off \$5.5 billion in inventory and Huang told the Stratechery podcast on Monday that the company also had to walk away from \$15 billion in sales.

The latest export restrictions introduced new limits on GPU memory bandwidth - a crucial metric measuring data transmission speeds between the main processor and memory chips. This capability is particularly important for AI workloads that require extensive data processing.

Investment bank Jefferies estimates that the new regulations cap memory bandwidth at 1.7-1.8 terabytes per second. That compares with the 4 terabytes per second that the H20 is capable of.

Hex Appeal: Monetize Your Map

DePIN projects are dividing the world into hexagonal units. Each hex represents map space but also trapped value.

A project new to the $PEAQ ecosystem, allows users to 3D map and own digital hexes, creating assets that have been sold for up to $100.

Seizing the Value in Hexes

Many decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN) projects need maps. The hexagonal grids being used by DePIN projects are typically built using the 'Hexagonal Hierarchical Geospatial Indexing System (H3)', a system initially developed by Uber. It works by overlaying a multi-resolution hexagonal grid across the Earth. This allows any geographic coordinate to be assigned to a unique hex, with its 'zoom levels' providing precision down to a single square meter.
The peaq ecosystem is home to a number of projects which allow you to unlock the value trapped in each hex. While projects like 375go map network signals and Silencio maps noise, the geospatial DePIN platform @OVRtheReality is going all-in on peaq, leveraging the ecosystem to build its advanced 3D map of the world.

For OVER, a single hex is a 300-square-meter area. This is the fundamental unit for their map and digital land ownership.

To create a 3D map of one of these hexes, users physically visit the location and capture a number of images using their smartphones. These images are then processed to create a 3D structure. This is part of OVER's map2earn™ initiative that incentivises users to build a decentralized, high-resolution spatial dataset.

Why OVRMaps Outclass Google

This community-driven approach creates 3D maps with an accuracy that current industry leaders struggle to match. While Google dominates mapping, their 3D maps are primarily built with car-mounted cameras capturing images approximately every 10 meters. This is sufficient for basic navigation but falls short for the demands of augmented reality (AR), robotics, and AI-driven spatial intelligence.

OVRMaps, in contrast, are built with 400-1,000 images per hex, captured from multiple angles at pedestrian level. The result is a hyper-precise map with sub-5cm accuracy. This repository of data is the foundation for OVR's next evolution: training a Large Geospatial Model (LGM), AI designed to power machine perception and introduce an era of true spatial computing.
This level of precision is critical for several key reasons:

A Functional Spatial Web: It enables a Visual Positioning System (VPS) that actually works, allowing for real-world AR anchoring, digital twins, and AI-powered spatial computing with pinpoint accuracy.

Next-Generation Logistics: It provides the data essential for ride-sharing, autonomous robotics, smart cities, and asset tracking, where even small errors are critical.

Fuel for AI: These detailed maps are the fuel for AI like LGMs, enabling machines to truly understand, navigate, and interact with the physical world.

The Spatial Computing Revolution: By merging immersive experiences with real-world precision, OVRMaps unlock applications far beyond what Google's dataset can support.

From Maps to Assets: The OVRLand Economy

Each hex is also a piece of OVER Land, which grants publishing rights for AR content within that specific 300-square-meter physical location, accessible via smartphones and next-generation smart glasses like Vision Pro and Quest 3. This transforms the hex from a simple asset to be bought and sold into a potential source of passive income, earning its owner a share of the revenue from all economic activity that occurs on their digital property.

OVRLand sales have been a primary source of revenue for OVER. The company has sold nearly 1 million NFTs of digital land with prices ranging from $10 to $100. The price of OVRLand depends on the location's demand. The potential market for valuable OVRLands is estimated to be around 100 million locations globally, with less than 1% of these premium locations have been sold so far.
To achieve long-term revenue stability, OVER is introducing a new revenue stream called OVER Business, designed to serve Web2 clients. This new business layer uses the infrastructure built through DePIN incentives and the high-quality 3D maps of these hexes.

The OVER Business layer will allow enterprises like digital marketing agencies, micro-mobility companies, and robotics firms to use OVER's VPS and geo-localized AR capabilities within these hexes through a subscription-based model, without needing to engage with blockchain.

A Real-World Use Case in Ride-Sharing

The dockless e-scooter and e-bike market, projected to reach $6.4 billion by 2030, provides a perfect example of OVER Business in action. A major issue for operators is improper parking, leading to significant fines and operational costs, as standard GPS is too inaccurate (10-15 metre errors in cities) for parking verification.

OVER's solution, OVER VPS, solves this directly. A user simply snaps a photo of their parked vehicle, and the system matches it against OVR’s hyper-accurate 3D maps to verify its position with centimeter-level precision. This is a capability that Google VPS, with its lower-density mapping, cannot currently offer for this specific need.

For a typical fleet of 1,000 scooters in a city like San Francisco, OVER VPS can reduce bad parking by 90%, potentially saving the operator over $6.3 million annually by slashing fines and eliminating the cost of manually relocating improperly parked vehicles.
The community-driven map2earn™ program creates the essential high-fidelity maps that power this multi-million dollar enterprise use case, with pilots already under development in London and Paris.

Closing the Loop: The DePIN Flywheel and the Future

Significantly, the introduction of the OVER Business layer includes a mechanism for OVRLand owners to benefit financially. OVER plans to launch a revenue-sharing model where landowners will receive 35% of the revenues generated by services provided in their mapped hex.

This stable revenue stream is intended to be reinvested into Web3 mechanisms like rewards for OVRLand owners, token burns, and token buybacks, strengthening the connection between platform utility and revenue generation.

But OVER's vision extends beyond the economics. In a future of smart glasses and Physical AI, creating a global 3D map raises critical privacy concerns. Addressing this head-on, OVR has recently filed a patent for an end-to-end encrypted VPS using Trusted Execution Environments (TEE), to build a framework where user privacy is mathematically guaranteed, making it impossible for even OVR itself to access a user's sensitive visual data.

Ultimately, with OVR, the power of its community is transforming hexes into valuable, monetizable assets. This is the DePIN model in its most powerful form: creating a flywheel where user contributions build valuable real-world infrastructure, which in turn generates enterprise revenue that flows back to reward the community. That's hex appeal.

Why LTO (Lease-to-Own) is a powerful strategy:
👉 You build passive income
👉 You avoid burning lump sums on low-quality mass registrations
👉 Full-payment sales can boost your ego too much — you get overconfident and less selective, thinking you cracked the code… when really, you've only figured out 20%
👉 It lets low-budget buyers acquire your domains
👉 If they cancel, you keep the money and get the domain back
👉 You avoid entering desperate mode — slashing prices, hoping for a fast sale like your life depends on it (desperate domainer behavior)
Every payment you get triggers an email from Afternic and PayPal — it keeps your mindset in the game.
You're in the flow, and you’ve got the bullets to go hunt better names.

You still get those one-time full-payment sales (the bonus).
I’ve learned not to spend that money — unless a true opportunity shows up (like what’s happening now with .ai domains).

⚠️Remember, you don’t need to spend crazy amounts of money to start getting sales.
If you’ve already spent $1K–$2K and after a year you’ve made no sales or you’re not profitable, it’s a sign that something’s wrong.
You should consider pausing your spending, focusing on learning, or even exploring a different side hustle.

Sometimes I like to do an exercise in my head, where I try to predict where things are going with AI video. It helps orient myself and do a gut check on what I’m doing.

Here are some thoughts (some spicy🥵) that came to mind today.👇

------

I think there are a lot of AI video companies right now. There will come a point where the VC well runs dry and consolidation will happen.

Hollywood seems to be opening up slowly to AI as more top executives and talent start to talk positively about it.

In contrast, I think that people are overestimating the general public’s readiness for AI video.

I think AI video will need a “Jurassic Park” like moment to gain acceptance and desire for AI video by the general public.

The “Jurassic Park” moment will not be a movie, but a universe.

I think most AI video creators are thinking like Toyota, building a hybrid model like the Prius, trying to get the best of both worlds, trying to appease both sides of the controversy. To get the full benefits of AI, they will need to be like Tesla and go all-in on AI, just like Tesla went all-in on electric.

The best creators have a clear vision and are relentless and uncompromising in bringing their ideas to life. So the AI tools that give them exactly what they want will win and for better or for worse, it will not matter how they are made.

AI video is still in the skeuomorphic stage. Most are trying to make it look like something they already know, a movie, a video game, a music video. An extremely successful new form and aesthetic will be invented by an AI video creator and that will bring the medium into its own.

From listening to podcasts like “The Town”, it feels like comedians have found a great business outside of the Hollywood system through doing their own stand-up theater performances, podcasts, YouTube, etc. (listen to Mike Birbiglia’s interview on The Town”). I wonder if the first real breakout success of AI video will be comedy. Sci-fi is also a natural fit, but I feel that the general public has grown to have such a singular but still sophisticated taste for sci-fi that you need to rewrite the rules of the sci-fi genre to have a chance.

The “forgotten” NFT community (at least by main stream media who think it’s totally dead, just like how they thought chatbots were dead, then came along ChatGPT) is a hidden enclave of people who fully embrace AI and are spending good money to buy AI art (a Lost Robbie recently sold for $550K). I believe the NFT community is where to look to get a glimpse of the future of AI video both as an art form but also demand and business model.

I think AI video supply will be a major problem. There will be an immense supply of AI trash/slop, but also an extraordinarily small supply of quality AI video. This will make it extremely hard to find good AI videos and thus curators or “scouts” will potentially be a lucrative position that I think will come out of just being present and being in the community today. A very small number of the AI artists today will go on to be rockstars, the others will be friends of the rockstars and thus have access to them like very few will.

🤑 $15 Million for a Domain? The Unreal True Story of NFTs.com !

🌐 The Digital Real Estate Boom

In the world of domain names—where digital real estate is as valuable as physical property—the name NFTs.com was a crown jewel waiting for the perfect moment. That moment came in August 2022, during the peak of the NFT (Non-Fungible Token) frenzy. While most of the world was focused on monkey JPEGs and million-dollar digital art, behind the scenes, a major transaction was brewing.

🔥 The Sale That Turned Heads

In a private transaction, the domain NFTs.com was sold for a jaw-dropping $15 million in cash.

This made it one of the largest domain sales ever publicly reported, trailing just behind legendary sales like:

 Voice.com – $30 million (2019)
 Sex.com – $13 million (2010)
 Fund.com – $9.99 million (2008)

It was more expensive than Hotels.com , FB.com , and even PrivateJet.com —making NFTs.com not just a digital asset, but a statement of belief in the NFT future.

🧩 Who Sold and Who Bought It?

The deal was brokered by domain industry veterans, including:

 Domainer.com (a top-tier domain brokerage firm)

GoDaddy (the largest domain registrar in the world)

The identities of both the seller and buyer were kept confidential, but speculation quickly flooded the industry.

🔍 Speculated Buyer: Many believed the buyer was connected to the Web3 ecosystem, possibly affiliated with the digital artist platform DigitalArtists.com or entities behind prominent NFT projects.

A few weeks after the sale, NFTs.com began displaying a basic landing page with a connection to the NFT community and links to some NFT-related services—further fueling speculation.

💡 Why Was NFTs.com So Valuable?

Let’s break it down:

1. Exact Match & Category-Defining
 NFTs.com is the exact match keyword for the entire NFT industry. It’s like owning Cars.com in the auto industry or Hotels.com in the travel industry. It instantly gives the owner credibility, SEO dominance, and brand power.

2. Short & Memorable
Three characters. Dot com. Universal understanding. Even people outside of crypto recognize the term “NFTs” now.

3. Explosive Market
At the time of the sale, the NFT market had exploded into a multi-billion-dollar industry. Projects like Bored Ape Yacht Club, CryptoPunks, and marketplaces like OpenSea were making headlines daily.

4. Investment Value
Even if the buyer didn’t build anything on it, the resale potential of NFTs.com was massive. Many saw it as digital gold.

📈 The Impact on the Domain Industry

The sale of NFTs.com proved several things:

Premium domains are still extremely valuable, especially when tied to trending or emerging industries.

The domain market isn’t just for tech companies anymore—crypto and Web3 investors are starting to understand the power of owning the "digital front door" of an industry.

Brand trust, organic traffic, and investor attention all skyrocket when you own a name like NFTs.com .

🔮 What’s Next for NFTs.com ?

As of now, NFTs.com is still under quiet development, but all eyes are watching. It could become:

A massive NFT marketplace

A Web3 community hub

A high-traffic media and news site

Or even a brand asset for resale

Whatever it becomes, the sale of NFTs.com marks a milestone moment in both the domain and crypto industries.

🧠 Final Thought

If Voice.com was the domain sale that proved enterprise companies care about premium .com names, then NFTs.com proved that Web3 and crypto buyers do too. It’s a reminder that even in a decentralized future, the centralized power of a great domain name is still unmatched

What is your ‘Sliding Doors’ moment?

I’ll tell you mine, and it’s more recent than you’d think.

But first, some background.

In the summer of 2025, I saw a post from @maxidoteth about 3L #ENS names that were surprisingly available for registration. The only one I can remember is the one I registered. 

Saw.eth

I watched enough of the movie franchise to know what to change the avatar to on the old Vision. Coupled with a flirtation by a the .com owners of same word and impeccable stats from @Going_eth it eventually sold for 0.5 eth

Now back then, the price of #ETH was roughly $3900 (I think but can’t be certain), so just under 2 grand was very welcome. 

I decided to do something I didn’t do until then, and that was register from Premium. 

If you recall, there was another mad dash to get names from Premium and I saw a post in a group chat with a list of names, and I went and registered blueprint.eth 

It cost me about $1500 but I thought it was worth the investment, and yes, the potential return was great given that the market seemed to be experiencing decent activity flow. 

So where’s the ‘Sliding Doors’ moment?

Well, I was speaking to someone who isn’t in ENS, in fact he’s actively scornful of this community. He’s a longtime friend and I’ve shared some of our chats before and many of you reacted in the comments. 

His advice? (and I quote):
“Sell it quick sharp, collect your p’s b4 dem f***ing idiots in U.S. ruin everything for us”

We actually argued on the phone over it, and other things, because my conviction was strong that things would strengthen and it was worth holding.

Well… mere weeks later, the quietening market that I had not noticed started to fall silent, and shortly after that, Vision V1 was gone, followed by the sunsetting of full functionality of other ENS marketplaces.

So that one decision not to listen to my friend, as annoying as he can be sometimes, had an effect on how the rest of my 2025 went.

Though not definitive, permanent or fatal. 

Why did I share that with you? If you’re still reading, it’s because at various times this week, I was tempted to accept defeat and list blueprint.eth very low, and maybe sell it at a significant loss, and be done with it.

But ultimately, with the passage of time, I feel it might hend up being the correct decision. And I pray that is the case.

So what was your ‘Sliding Doors’ moment?

(Exclusive) Kim Seui of Garo Sero Institute Has Two Luxury Apartments Worth 11.3 Billion KRW Provisionally Seized — Creditor is Actor Kim Soohyun

Kim Seui (48), the head of the YouTube channel Garo Sero Institute, has had two apartments in Seocho and Gangnam, Seoul, provisionally seized by court order. The creditor is Gold Medalist, the agency of actor Kim Soohyun (37).

According to Money Today on the 11th, the Seoul Central District Court approved a request on June 9 to provisionally seize two properties under Kim Seui’s name: a 120.27㎡ apartment in Seocho’s Byuksan Blooming complex, and a 208.65㎡ apartment in Apgujeong’s Hanyang 4th Complex in Gangnam.

The Hanyang 4th apartment is jointly owned by Kim Seui and his older sister (50% each), so the seizure only applies to Kim Seui’s share. The total amount claimed is 4 billion KRW (2 billion per apartment).

Lawyer No Jongeon, head attorney at the firm Jonjae, explained, “The court’s decision to allow provisional seizure means it found the damage claim and the amount requested by Gold Medalist to be somewhat reasonable. Since a provisional seizure is based only on one side’s written claims, the other party’s arguments haven’t been considered yet. The final compensation amount could change depending on Kim Seui’s response.”

⸻

Apartments Worth 11.3 Billion KRW, But Can They Be Enforced?

The Seocho Byuksan Blooming apartment is currently valued at around 2.5 billion KRW. The Hanyang 4th Complex unit recently had a low-floor apartment sold for 8.87 billion KRW.

However, since Kim Seui has borrowed a large amount of money using these apartments as collateral, it’s unlikely that the full 4 billion KRW claim could be recovered through forced sale.

Kim Seui has registered mortgage rights totaling 5.022 billion KRW on the two properties (1.322 billion KRW on the Seocho apartment, 3.699 billion KRW on the Hanyang apartment).

A mortgage right gives the lender the first claim to proceeds from a property auction, ahead of other creditors.

The mortgage rights are set at a maximum claim amount, which is usually about 120% of the loan. Based on this, Kim Seui is estimated to have borrowed about 4.185 billion KRW.

When adding the loan amounts and the provisional seizure claims, the total debt exceeds the properties’ combined value (2.5 billion for Seocho and 4.4 billion for Kim Seui’s 50% share in Hanyang).

⸻

Kim Seui May Share Liability with the Late Kim Saeron’s Family If They Lose

The legal dispute between Garo Sero Institute and Kim Soohyun began in March. Kim Seui and the late actress Kim Saeron’s family claimed that Kim Soohyun had an inappropriate relationship with her in 2015 when she was a minor. Kim Soohyun denied this, stating that they dated between summer 2019 and fall 2020, after she had become an adult.

Controversy grew when it was revealed that part of the audio recording used as evidence by Garo Sero and the family was actually fake and generated using AI.

They also released several photos of Kim Soo-hyun and Kim Saeron together, but all were confirmed to be from after she became an adult in 2019.

Gold Medalist filed criminal charges against Kim Seui and the family for violating sexual violence laws and for defamation under the Information and Communications Network Act. They also filed a civil lawsuit seeking 12 billion KRW (approximately 120 billion won) in damages.

If Kim Seui and the family lose the case, they will likely be held jointly responsible for the damages as co-offenders.

In such cases, responsibility is not divided based on individual actions but shared for the entire wrongdoing. The degree of fault among those responsible is decided internally between them later. #KimSoohyun #WeStandwithKimSooHyun

A gap in the system. A creator’s nightmare.

In interviews, Beeple admitted it.

A digital revolution. But for Beeple’s early work, a cruel twist.

Sam Parr sold The Hustle for $25M+. Now he’s building Hampton because he thinks communities are the next newsletters. Here’s why he’s right + how to build a $1M revenue community:

Why communities?

Traditional distribution is under threat:

• TikTok almost got banned this year
• Email is getting harder (low open rates due to pixel blocking, Gmail summary previews, spam filters)
• Social reach is throttled unless you pay to play

It's more important than ever to control your distribution—SMS, communities, events, etc.

Of course, communities are one of the hardest models to pull off.

But when they work, they work:

• Doximity (physicians): $570M • YPO (founders): $300M+
• Tiger 21 (HNW investors): $150M+
• Entrepreneurs organization (founders): $60M+
• Evanta: $23M profit, sold for $275M
• Hampton (founders): $10M+
• Client Ascension (agency owners): $4-$5M+
• Friends of Lenny’s Newsletter (product managers): $3-4M+
• Maker’s school (AI automation): $1.8M

…and many more

So, how do you build an engaging community?

1. Pick the right niche

The best communities either:

• Tap into high passions/careers (sneakers, nurses, engineers)
• Help members make money (ecomm, investing, ghostwriting)

The best ones do both.

2. Build where your members already hang out

It's extremely hard to build a community.

It's even harder to do it where your users don't naturally spend time.

Hampton and Client Ascension were built in Slack because they cater to founders who are already there.

Don't force your members onto Circle or Kajabi unless you have a 10x reason to.

3. Avoid the middle pricing

Either choose:

• Mass pricing ($100-200/yr) = scalable, or
• Premium pricing (>$1K) = high-touch, intimate

Avoid mid-tier pricing ($300-$700).

It's a dead zone.

Too expensive to scale (at $300/yr, you need 33K members to hit $10M), too cheap to justify the effort.

4. Treat onboarding as a product

The first 30 days should make the members feel they made the right decision.

Examples:

• Jay Clouse does 1:1 onboarding calls to help you connect with the right people/content.
• Client Ascension gives you a Day 1-35 roadmap, a coach pairing, and instant intros.

5. Lean on members + experts

You've aggregated distribution for valuable people.

Giving that distribution to members is enticing for them and saves you from 100% fulfillment. Win-win.

• Client Ascension has 7-figure coaches lead specialized calls.
• Hampton had member Anne Mahlum host an event at her house.

6. Gate access

Obsessing over fast growth kills the community. Once it declines, it's almost impossible to save it.

So, use filters — income, title, invite-only, industry — to protect and maintain strict quality.

Bonus: Have fun

Use 5–10% of your budget on “magical moments.”

Example: Shaan Puri used a Cameo from Sean Paul to welcome new members.

Israeli dev Maor Shlomo built Base44 wasn’t some overnight fluke. The app hit 10k users in three weeks, 250k in six months, and was profitable even after burning through huge LLM token bills. 

Shlomo built everything in public, posting numbers, wins, and “what the hell am I doing?” moments on X and LinkedIn.

Shlomo was already known in the Israeli startup community through his previous startup, the Insight Partners-backed data analytics company Explorium. 

His brother is also a co-founder of an AI security startup, Token Security, which just raised $20 million led by Notable Capital (formerly GGV Capital) and a bunch of Israeli tech angels.

It started as a side project to let anyone, coder or not, build full apps from a text prompt, databases, auth, analytics, you name it. It spread by word of mouth, partnerships, and a streak of pure internet momentum.

What did we learn from this?

He's not aiming to build the best product out there but what he's done really well is that he has packaged everything you need to build an app into a one stop shop for app building, he's built in:

- Storage
- Authentication
- Analytics
- Integration

Why sell so soon? Shlomo said: “If we could get this far bootstrapped, imagine what we can do with real resources.”

There was an excellent broadcast in @StoryProtocol 
 @WhatTheLJW , @devrelius & @gardo_martinez in conversation with @thewavvapp 

It was very interesting to learn how everything works in the music industry and how Story can influence this industry! It's cool to dive in and learn about the industry in such detail. I never thought it would be so difficult to obtain the rights to mucis! 

🔶 [Introduction]
Cool introduction with track called “Waves”, creating a multi-layered metaphor - the @thewavvapp team, the theme of AI waves, remixes! 

|“It's layered - a track called ‘Waves’, a remix on the theme of waves, the Wave team, a discussion of AI and remixes - it's just amazing.”

🔶 [Who are Wave and why do they work with AI?]
Alex Wong is a music producer, composer for film and television, and experimenter in the Lo-Fi genre. At Wave, he is responsible for music production and sound engineering.

|“Our goal is to use AI to inspire and empower creative people. We don't want to replace creators, but to give them back their power to create.”

Later, Dean, COO with a background in blockchain, joins the conversation! He emphasizes the importance of IP protection in the age of AI and the growth of new content:

|“The music industry is chaotic, with outdated processes. With the advent of AI, it is critical that creators are compensated for everything they create.”

🔶 [The music community's reaction to AI]
One of the central topics of the broadcast is how music producers perceive AI. Alex shares his experience of communicating at the Infinity Festival in Hollywood:

|“After our performance, people literally rushed to the stage. Many were inspired. Of course, some had concerns, but AI is just a tool. It all depends on whose hands it is in.”

Dean adds - many composers already use AI, they just don't advertise it. It is important to understand that creators are not only pop stars, but also “invisible heroes” who write music for TV series, games, and commercials.

🔶 [How AI helps in real music work]
Alex describes real-life cases of AI use:
🔸Source of inspiration - when a composer experiences creative block, AI can generate several ideas to get the process started.
🔸Creating variations - if a director asks to change the mood of a scene overnight, AI can change the genre or tone of an already finished track.

|“At times like these, a creative crisis is a disaster. And deadlines don't wait. That's where AI comes to the rescue.”

🔶 [Where does humanity end and AI begin: the question of IP]
A fundamental question arises - if AI creates variations, who owns the result? Alex gives a clear answer:

|“As long as there is human input, AI is a tool. Copyright should belong to the person who directs the process.”

He compares this to sampling and using loops: what matters is not who created the original sound, but who made something new out of it.

🔶 [Why IP registration is so important and why it doesn't work]
Dean and Alex explain what traditional music registration looks like today:

(1) Registration with the Copyright Office,
(2) Registration with PRO (ASCAP, BMI),
(3) Connecting to platforms like SongTrust,
(4) Lots of different forms, contracts, processes.

|“Often, an artist just wants to write music. But if you release music yourself, you quickly realize that it's all a maze.”

Many don't register their tracks at all, which means they don't receive any royalties or fees.

|“If you don't have mentors or educational resources nearby, it all seems like a real maze.”

🔶 [What is Story's IP portal and why is it needed?]
At this stage, the Story team takes the floor to explain the concept of the IP portal — an interface for working with intellectual property through the Story Protocol.

Story was originally created as a framework for developers. But later it became clear that a product was needed that authors without a technical background could use.

| “The first version allowed you to simply register IP and attach a license. That's it — it's already on-chain, monetizable, and transparent.”

(Recent improvements include):
🔹 Bulk registration — now you can register an entire album.
🔹 No wallet or gas — registration without crypto skills.

|“This was feedback from the Wave team. We were happy that we were already working on these features when they mentioned them.”

🔶 How does an IP portal differ from a traditional system?
Alex and Dean share their personal experiences of registering tracks in the old system. It is a complex, multi-step process:

🔹you need to register your copyright,
🔹join a PRO (such as ASCAP or BMI),
🔹and use third-party platforms to track royalties worldwide.

| And all this for just one song. And there are dozens of such services.”

Dean highlights the paradox - in the crypto industry, everyone strives to simplify interfaces and hide technical details, but the old music system is even more complex and confusing than creating a wallet or interacting with a blockchain.

|“In the traditional system, you don't just need a wallet — you need to go through legal bureaucracy. And if you're a newcomer, it can be very intimidating.”

🔶[The secondary music market and remixes as assets]
Dean draws attention to one of the most underrated topics - the secondary music market.

|“Remixes, resale of rights, reuse—all of this is a huge layer. And such assets are tradable. They have value and can increase in price.”

He gives an example:
| “Queen's catalog - 190 songs - was sold for $1.27 billion. And that's just one band. Imagine how much Taylor Swift's catalog could be worth?”

If rights and assets can be tracked through Story, this opens up enormous opportunities. Now remixes can not only “exist” - they can be traded, valued, and scaled.

|“It's like real estate - people understand that a house can increase in value. Music is also an asset, just less obvious.”

🔶[AI as a tool—and humans as tools?] 
Towards the end, the discussion takes a philosophical turn. The host asks: if AI offers such possibilities, where is the line between author and assistant? Who is using whom?

(Responds with concern and interest): 
|“AI is becoming such a powerful tool that one could even say: now humans are tools. In both a good and bad sense.”

He gives an example: if a user simply wrote a prompt - “make a jazz song about love” - and received a result from AI, is it IP?

| “These are new questions that the law has not faced before. We now live in the era of pre-AI and post-AI.”

🔶 [Where does human contribution end?] 
In the finale, the team discusses the gray area of authorship. Who is the author if 80% is done by AI? What constitutes sufficient contribution?

|“Some say 20% is the minimum to recognize authorship. Others say 50%. But how do you measure that?”

They agree - most likely, the courts will decide the future, and it may take a decade to develop a stable practice. But one thing is already clear:

|“Even to get a quality result from AI, you need to set the right prompt. And that's already intellectual work.”

🔶 [Conclusion] 
|“We are living at a turning point in history, and intellectual property is one of the most relevant topics in the age of AI.”
|“Thank you to the Wave team - you are building your company while sharing your experience. That is invaluable."

I respect the hustle in this @HariSel57511397 rebuttal to my previous post about what I've learned as a professional fiction writer since 2002, but I humbly disagree with most of it. 

Isaac Young: I’m a fiction writer who’s dealt with the world post-2020. Here’s what I’ve learned.

Joe sez: Hi Isaac. I am also a fiction writer who's dealt with the world post-2020; I didn't just vanish because my professional career began 24 years ago. But I am indeed old-school. So I am going to old-school fisk your post.

Isaac: Subscription revenue beats book sales hands down. 

Joe sez: My sales outweigh my subscriptions, but I don't do Substack or Patreon, only KDP Select. I never monetized my blog (which has gotten millions of hits). I don't think it's a bad idea, and I may try it someday, but I believe a fiction writer's main job is to write and sell fiction, not to sustain your followers. It is great to have followers, but they are a small percent of sales.

Isaac: It has never been harder for indies to sell books because of the proliferation of AI slop and the shrinking pool of readers. There’s never been more authors competing for a shrinking share of the pie. 

Joe sez: It is no harder than it was five, ten, twenty, or thirty years ago. There has always been competition. But the barrier for entry is the lowest in history. Authors don't compete. It isn't a zero sum game. 

Isaac: You need to be cultivating an ongoing relationship instead of a one and done sale every year or so. It’s just not monetarily feasible for most people to do traditional book sales. 

Joe sez: I'm an author. Not a guru. I make a living by selling books, not by asking people for support. 

Isaac: Amazon and similar storefronts are the last place you put your book (where you finally monetize). 

Joe sez: Amazon is the first place to put your book. It's the biggest bookstore on the planet.

Isaac: You need to be posting free versions of your book on every web forum, reading site, and possibly your own blog to lower the barrier to entry as much as possible. 

Joe sez: I'm fine with free. Enroll in KDP Select and make your book free on Amazon. No barrier to entry. Do you think reading forums or blogs cultivate more readers than Amazon? Which forums do this?

Isaac: You will net far more money from the dedicated fans this generates than from the imaginary losses of casuals reading your work for free. 

Joe sez: No you won't, unless your sales are very low. The market IS casual readers. They find books on Amazon. 

Isaac: Modern audiences buy physical copies of stories they already like, not scrolling through random indie titles on the Amazon marketplace. 

Joe sez: Modern audiences buy ebooks, using their Kindles or apps. I have had books in Barnes & Noble stores, Walmart, Sam's Club, and indie stores worldwide. 100,000 mass market paperbacks sold for $6.99 nets you $42K. 100,000 self-pubbed ebooks sold at $4.99 nets you $375k. Focus on ebooks.

Issac: Don’t let them convince you the institutions aren’t important. The self-made artist is a lie and cope to downplay the huge advantage patronage offers. We’re never going to benefit, but we should always be agitating. 

Joe sez: It's good to preach your path, but is your primary income from writing or from patrons? Mine is from writing. I have no patrons. My social media isn't monetized. That said, if by "institutions" you mean "the traditional publishing world", they are not important for 99.99999% of writers. The legacy publishing industry sucks. It sucks hard. I've written millions of words why. As for being self-made; all indie authors are self-made. 

Isaac: Online presence alone doesn’t translate to great book sales, but networking does. Reviewers are not going to notice you unless you maintain some presence in the discourse. 

Joe sez: I have sold millions of books. It is impossible to network with millions of people. I've had tens of thousands of reviews, and not because of any networking. Write good books, and more good books, and with luck you'll find an audience.

The audience you gain from proselytizing isn't a real fanbase. The X post of mine you are quoting has had over sixty thousand hits. It hasn't improved my sales. Not one bit. This post of yours I'm fisking has had over thirty thousand hits. Has it sold any books for you? How many?

I'm not trying to be a jerk here. But you're giving advice to authors who are hoping to succeed, and dwelling on a lot of stuff that isn't about selling books. 

Isaac: Pay for editing.

Joe sez: DO NOT PAY FOR EDITING. Join a writers' group and learn how to write from other writers, not people who you pay to fix your mistakes (and who might not even be good writers, or even worse they're just running it through AI.) Learn to edit yourself. That's what writing is; effectively communicating your story to the reader. You should be able to do that without paying anyone for help. And don't get me started on how many authors fall prey to bad editors...

Isaac: Consider audio adaptations. I can’t say how much it’s helped me, but I only have forty chapters of my book on Royal Road, and I make far above the average of titles of similar length because I offer high-quality audio to further lower barrier to entry. 

Joe sez: I have 60 books in audio. I've sold tons of audiobooks. But new models (Kindle TTS, many apps) allow text to be read to readers, so audio may not be as important as it once was. Ditto with translating into other languages. But as of March 8, 2026, audio and foreign markets are still viable.

Isaac: Writing is a side-gig to your real life. The age of the Stephen King rockstar is over. 

Joe sez: Writing is my main gig, and I was never a Stephen King rockstar. But I have managed to eek out a living doing what I love. Luck plays a big part. Never discount getting lucky. 

Isaac: The market is optimized for quantity and slop content. It’s unfortunate, but all the big players generate multi-thousand page volumes. You’re going to have to square with that reality somehow. 

Joe sez: The market is optimized for good books to flourish. Cream rises, turds sink. Fifteen years ago I wrote about this same bad argument. Search the web for my post "Konrath Tsunami of Crap"; it's still relevant.

Isaac: AI has its uses as supplementary material such as concept art, but never let it touch your prose.

Joe sez: I agree with you on this. LLMs have pirated and trained on 80+ of my books. They write like me because they stole from me. Now anyone can write like J.A. Konrath with a single sentence prompt. The problem for me isn't wannabes publishing AI-generated material. The problem for me is readers asking AI to continue my series for their own personal use faster than I can keep up. 

Isaac: You’re going to need to find some sort of religion to make good art that stands out in the modern landscape. All of modern entertainment has been subversive deconstruction for a decade. You’re never going to be able to compete with billion dollar industries at their own game.

Joe sez: Not very uplifting. How about this instead?

Anything worth doing is hard. Your job is not to compete with anyone other than yourself. Your goal should be to write the best book you can, polish it best you can, put it on Amazon, and repeat over and over until you find success.

If you want to treat writing as a side-gig and try to monetize social media, do that and God bless. You do you. More power to you, brother, but I think that is bad advice to give to writers.

If you want to make a living as a writer, write as many great books as you can, and put them on Amazon. 

I checked you out on Amazon, Isaac, and read a sample. The writing is good! Covers are good! Write ten more books, improving with each book, and I'd wager much of your above advice will no longer be applicable to you.

Let’s go back to the beginning. When I sold my first SaaS (cocoo AI), the most important thing was this: if you want to sell because your startup is struggling, it’s already too late. You need to sell when you have momentum.

I sold Koko AI right after Black Friday. It was a SaaS for e-commerce, and we had just had our best month ever. I had two main reasons to sell: platform risk (Meta API was unstable), and two of my four co-founders were no longer interested in continuing. Only two of us were left pushing the project.

I first tried listing it on platforms like Acquire and Flippa. Honestly? Waste of time. High commissions, fake promises, and they expect at least 2–3 years of track record. My SaaS was only 6 months old it kept getting rejected or I got super lowball offers.

Then I tried something else. I posted in a few founder communities saying I was selling a SaaS making $X MRR and asked if anyone knew someone interested. I got lots of calls, but most were just curious people who wanted to know how I was making money not serious buyers.

Next, I reached out to people who were buying Shopify apps. A bit more serious, but still not the right offers.

Eventually, I searched “buying a SaaS” on LinkedIn. Found a guy with “Looking to buy a business $1M–$10M” in his bio. I DMed him. We had a call the next day.

At first, he told me he was looking at a bunch of other deals. But two weeks later, he came back to me and said he was in. We started due diligence.

That part takes time about a month. He and his lawyer asked for everything: access to backend, Stripe, churn metrics, MRR growth, product roadmap, etc. You have to be fully transparent, and at the same time, you need to keep growing the business. If metrics dip during DD, it can kill the deal.

Once that’s done, we agreed on the deal structure. In my case, it was 90% cash upfront. We used an escrow account. He had a US-based lawyer, I had a French one. He wired the funds to escrow, I sent him the credentials. He confirmed everything worked, the money was released, and that was it.

After that, I stayed on for two months to help with the transition. Super smooth.

A few things I learned:

Don’t do this without a lawyer. Ever.

Don’t trust people who say they want to buy your SaaS unless they’ve done it before or clearly have the money. You’ll get tons of people wasting your time.

If someone’s running a dead product and has no real track record, they’re not going to buy yours for $1M+.

Expect to spend $15K to $25K in legal fees. In our case, we split the cost 50/50.

If you’re aiming for bigger exits in the future, you’ll probably need to go through M&A advisors or boutique investment banks. That’s what I’ll do next time.

If you're curious to follow the journey of my next SaaS (GojiberryAI), feel free to drop a comment or follow me. Happy to share what I learn along the way.

Props to @zakkohane for being the first person to put in an analysis request for my CMS RFI MCP stack. I had Claude 4 Opus code do "/analysis-workflow" to find and analyze 125 comments from patients, then asked Gemini 2.5 Pro to write up a report based on these. (I ran out of Claude Max credits ;-))

After some back and forth, here's the result (or view markdown rendering in GH at github.com/jmandel/regulatio… )

### 1. Executive Summary

An analysis of over 125 comments submitted by individuals to the CMS RFI reveals a profound disconnect between the public's perception of CMS's data holdings and the fragmented reality of the healthcare ecosystem. Patients conceptualize "all their data" far more expansively than just the claims data CMS currently provides through Blue Button. Their definition encompasses a complete, longitudinal, and multi-modal record that includes everything from raw imaging files and genetic markers to caregiver observations and the right to correct inaccuracies. The most critical finding is the pervasive sense of powerlessness among patients, who report their data is aggregated and exchanged between institutions while they are left with siloed, incomplete, and often uncorrectable records. The call for access, therefore, is not merely for data retrieval, but for a fundamental rebalancing of control—a shift in data ownership from institutions to the individuals themselves.

### 2. Key Stakeholder Perspectives and Critical System Failures

While categorized as "Individuals," the commenters represent distinct stakeholder roles whose lived experiences reveal critical system failures. These perspectives are essential for understanding the human cost of data fragmentation.

#### 2.1. The Caregiver: The System's Invisible Infrastructure

Caregivers—often family members providing unpaid, around-the-clock support—emerge as the human glue holding a broken system together. They perform the work of interoperability but are granted none of the access or authority.

* The "Invisible Data" Crisis: AI strategist and caregiver Teresa Younkin ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) powerfully describes how the most crucial health indicators—"caregiver observations of daily functioning," "transportation barriers," and "subtle behavioral changes"—are "invisible data" that exist nowhere in any formal health record. These are the real drivers of outcomes, yet the system is blind to them.
* The Burden of Fragmentation: Karen Demerly ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), whose parents suffered from dementia, recounts the impossible task of managing their care across multiple states and provider portals. She only learned of her mother's fatal pulmonary fibrosis when an ER doctor in Indiana asked about a diagnosis trapped in a Florida provider's system, long after her mother could recall it herself.

#### 2.2. The "Insider": The Expert Witness to a Broken System

Some of the most searing indictments come from healthcare professionals and IT experts who are also navigating the system as patients or caregivers. They know how things *should* work, which makes the reality all the more horrifying.

* The Human Cost of Complexity: A TBI survivor with 30 years of healthcare IT experience ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) provides a devastating account of how the system's complexity becomes a barrier to recovery. With cognitive capacity limited to just 45 minutes of focus twice a day, they found that over 75% of their "cognitively available time" was consumed simply by the administrative tasks of managing their care—a cruel paradox where the process of seeking health actively harms it.
* The Impotence of Expertise: Linda Westenberger ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), a Health Information Director with over 40 years of experience, notes that even with her professional knowledge, it was "quite a task" to gather and share her mother's records during transitions between a hospital, rehab, and an assisted living facility, where critical medication data was lost.

#### 2.3. The Powerless Patient: The Subject of an Uncorrectable Record

The most fundamental failure reported by patients is the paradox of their data: it is about them, but it is not *theirs* to control or correct. This leads to permanent, life-altering consequences.

* The Uncorrectable Error: Lewis Lewis ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), a healthcare administrator, recounts being misdiagnosed with cancer by two major hospitals. That incorrect diagnosis is now permanently documented, impacting their ability to secure life and long-term care insurance. They have access to see the error but no power to fix it.
* The Two-Tiered System of Access: The most critical system failure highlighted is that the infrastructure for unified data access *already exists*, but patients are deliberately excluded. An anonymous commenter ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) reveals that HIE systems provide instant, aggregated records to providers but are "designed to circumvent HIPAA" by "block[ing] patients from accessing them."

#### 2.4. The Privacy Advocate: The Guardian of Data Sovereignty

A significant and vocal minority of commenters view the entire premise of data sharing with deep suspicion. Their perspective provides a crucial counter-narrative to the push for interoperability.

* Data as a Liability: For these individuals, health data is not an asset to be leveraged but a threat to be contained. They oppose any mandatory digital IDs or biometric data collection. Their primary demand, echoed by commenters like Amy Harlib ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), is the "right to be forgotten"—the absolute right to have their data deleted upon request, a capability that does not exist today.

### 3. Patient Perceptions of CMS Data Holdings vs. Reality

While patients look to CMS as a central authority, their comments reveal a deep-seated misunderstanding of what data the agency actually controls.

* The Medicare Advantage Gap: Patients are acutely aware that CMS does not possess the granular encounter data from MA plans. Max Doppelt ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) explicitly identifies MA encounter data and prior authorizations as critical missing pieces that are "routinely captured but rarely delivered through standards-based APIs."
* The Siloed Government: Experienced commenters like David Rocha ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) point out that even federal data is fragmented across agencies like the SSA, VA, and CDC.
* The Powerless Enforcer: The harrowing experience of Tim Moon ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), a Parkinson's patient, demonstrates CMS's perceived inability to enforce its own rules when major health systems allegedly refuse to cooperate with state HIEs.
* The State vs. Federal Conflict: Patients find their data access preferences overridden by state-level rules. Ron Beats ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) is forced to receive hundreds of pages of paper statements from his MA plan, which claims state mandates supersede his request for "DIGITAL access only."

In essence, patients believe CMS has the authority to solve data fragmentation, but their lived experiences prove that data is actually held captive by a patchwork of private insurers, non-compliant providers, and conflicting state regulations.

### 4. The Expansive Definition of "All Their Data": A Detailed Breakdown

Commenters define "all their data" not as a single file but as a dynamic, comprehensive, and controllable ecosystem of information. Access means more than just viewing; it means the power to use, correct, and share.

#### 4.1. The Complete, Unfiltered Clinical Record
Patients demand an end to the "minimal information" they receive in portals. They want the same deep, unfiltered view as their providers.

* Raw Imaging Files: Not just reports, but the actual DICOM images from CT scans and MRIs, which Pamela Franks ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) notes are often withheld or sold for a fee.
* Unfiltered Provider Notes & Data: Access to the "detailed version" of visit notes, original EKG reports (not just vague conclusions), and the "reason for study" on imaging orders, as described by an anonymous commenter ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* Complete Longitudinal History: A full record that follows them across states and providers, solving the problem faced by Kate Bixler ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ), whose prenatal records were inaccessible when she was diverted to a different hospital in active labor.

#### 4.2. Data from the Entire Health Ecosystem
"All their data" includes information currently trapped in disconnected, specialized silos.

* Pharmacy & Medication Data: Pharmacogenomic (PGx) test results, prior authorization forms, and clinical notes to give pharmacists context, as advocated by Kelee Petzelt ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* Emergency & Pre-Hospital Data: Life-saving information from ambulance crews—like POLST forms, mechanism of injury, and living conditions—which Jonathon Feit ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) calls "the big missing piece."
* Dental, Vision, and Behavioral Health Records: Integration of these records so patients no longer have to be the "'go between,'" a term used by Sarah Vander Beek ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) regarding dental records.
* Genomic & Rare Disease Data: Information from specialized research databases like OMIM, which David Rocha ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) points out is critical for precision medicine.

#### 4.3. Administrative and Financial Data
Patients need this data to navigate the byzantine business of healthcare.

* Itemized Bills and Pricing: The ability to see an itemized bill without waiting six months and to know procedure and medication costs upfront, a struggle detailed by Lewis Lewis ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* Insurance & Claims Data: Full Medicare Advantage encounter data, prior authorization status, and all claims filed on their behalf.
* Advance Directives: Portable, digital access to end-of-life care wishes, which are often trapped on paper or behind intellectual property barriers, as explained by David Rocha ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).

#### 4.4. "Invisible," Life-Context, and Patient-Generated Data
This is the rich, real-world data that drives outcomes but is rarely recorded.

* Caregiver Observations: The critical "invisible data" of "daily functioning" and "subtle behavioral changes" identified by Teresa Younkin ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* Home Monitoring & Wearable Data: Vital signs from blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, and other devices, as envisioned by Melissa Dehn ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* Social & Environmental Data: Information on housing conditions (e.g., mold), nutritional needs, and educational support, which the parent of an autistic child ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) argues is essential health data.

#### 4.5. Access as a Set of Rights and Capabilities
For patients, "access" is not a passive verb. It is a set of powers to own and control their information.

* The Right to Correct and Co-Author: The ability to fix errors and add their own notes, symptoms, and test results directly to the record, a right demanded by an anonymous patient ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ) whose correction requests were repeatedly denied.
* The Right to Granular Control: The power to grant and revoke access using smart contracts or other tools, as proposed by Shannon Kennedy ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* The Right to Audit: Full transparency into who has accessed their data and when, a feature requested by Robin Monks ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).
* The Right to Understand: Data must be presented with context, trends, and plain-language summaries so it can be acted upon, a need highlighted by Brittany Crosby ( joshuamandel.com/regulations… ).

### 5. Conclusion: A Mandate for Equality, Not Just Interoperability

The comments from individuals reveal a patient population that is increasingly sophisticated, frustrated, and demanding a fundamental shift in data control. They see a system where their data is used for billing, weaponized in negotiations, and aggregated for providers, all while they are denied access and the ability to ensure its accuracy.

The ultimate request is not just for CMS to provide "all its data." It is a demand for CMS to use its regulatory power to dismantle the existing two-tiered system. Patients know a comprehensive, unified view of their health information is not a futuristic dream; it is a present-day reality for their providers. "Access to all their data," in its most profound sense, means giving patients the exact same view and control that the institutions serving them already possess. The challenge for CMS is not merely technical interoperability, but addressing the fundamental power imbalance that profits from keeping patients in the dark.

US-based wealth management solutions provider @Envestnet_ has agreed to sell its open banking platform @Yodlee to private equity firm STG, ending a decade of ownership of the account aggregation pioneer it acquired for $590 million in 2015. Known for allowing budgeting app Mint to connect to its users bank accounts when it launched in 2007, Yodlee was for a long time the undisputed leader of the space, and was the first account account aggregator to offer a truly global coverage. However, Yodlee has never been the focus of Envestnet, and its low connection rate and reliability issues allowed for competitors like MX, Plaid and Flinks to rise from its shadow.

While we don’t know how much STG paid for Yodlee, what we know is that Yodlee’s price was much lower than Plaid’s recent $6.1B valuation. Last year, after Envestnet itself was acquired by Bain Capital for $4.5B, its books revealed it wrote off 48.6% of its $590M investment in Yodlee, valuing the open banking data provider at only $303M.

The transaction, set to close in Q3 2025, will let Envestnet focus on its core business of providing software to wealth management industry, while still maintaining access to Yodlee's technology through a partnership with the buyer. In the press release announcing the deal, Envestnet CEO Chris Todd explained that advisors will retain access to Yodlee account aggregation technology that allow them to keep an eye on their clients’ assets.

Commenting on the sale on X, @LexSokolin , Managing at @genventurecap , a fintech venture capital firm, called it "the biggest fumble of fintech 1.0," drawing a comparison to financial management platform Intuit’s decision to close its budgeting app, Mint, because it couldn't figure out what to do with it. Another venture capital investor, @obermattj , General Partner at @SocialLeverage , raised key questions about Yodlee’s future in a LinkedIn post, asking if the new private equity owners would invest in the business, roll out new products, leverage AI, or perhaps even rebrand the company. “If Plaid is the industry leader, depending on what Yodlee was sold for, there is tremendous upside,’’ said Ober.

Go to any major platform and ask: what's this website missing?

– What features are hidden?

Most successful extensions follow the freemium model: basic features free, advanced features $5-15/month.

Some go one-time purchase: $20-50 for lifetime access.

Others do usage-based: $0.10 per action, which scales with value.

Steve Jobs ran Apple’s first iPhone project like a top-secret mission. Former executives say it felt like Fight Club.

In a 2017 interview, Scott Forstall, Tony Fadell, and Greg Christie described the extreme secrecy. The effort, code-named Project Purple, was hidden even from most Apple employees. “The first rule of Project Purple was: you don’t talk about Project Purple,” Forstall said.

Teams worked in isolation. Hardware and software groups were siloed. Few people knew what the final product would look like—even right before the reveal.

Jobs demanded total focus. Forstall said the team worked 168-hour weeks to finish the software. One major hurdle was the keyboard. He froze all other work until it was solved. Dozens of versions were tested. A predictive text system ended up forming the base of today’s iPhone keyboard.

The breakthrough came when Jobs asked if Apple’s multitouch tablet tech could be adapted for a phone. The team built a prototype as big as a ping-pong table. Then they scaled it down.

The iPhone debuted in 2007 and sold for $499 and $599. It became Apple’s signature product, driving $46.8 billion in sales last quarter alone.

Now, Apple faces new pressure to lead in AI, as rivals like Google and Meta move faster.

There is something clarifying about watching the artifacts of the American counterculture go under the hammer at Christie's. On March 12, Kerouac's On the Road scroll sold for $12,135,000. Dylan's handwritten lyrics for "The Times They Are A-Changin'" fetched $2.5M. Cobain's guitar: $6.9M. Gilmour's: $14.5M. The objects that once stood for refusal — of careerism, conformity, the administered life — have become the highest expression of the very system they opposed.
This is not simply irony. It is a structural condition. 
The commodification of dissent is not a recent discovery, but the Christie's auction makes visible something else: that we are living through a moment when the transgressive energy once associated with the cultural left has migrated, deformed, into the new right. The tech oligarchs — Musk, Thiel, Zuckerberg, Bezos — who now control the major platforms of public speech have aligned themselves with a populist, anti-establishment movement that borrows the counterculture's posture of rebellion while serving the most concentrated accumulation of capital in human history.
The disclosure that puts this most plainly came this week from Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir, speaking at the AIPac Conference. Karp said that AI will "disrupt the economic and political power significantly of one party's base — highly educated, often female voters who vote mostly Democrat." He was not warning against this outcome. He was announcing it as a feature.
The discourse around AI disruption tends to frame job displacement as an unfortunate externality of otherwise neutral technological progress. Karp's remarks suggest something else: that the disruption is directional, that its political valence is understood and, in some quarters, welcomed. This deserves more sustained attention from anyone thinking seriously about the intersection of technology, labor, and democratic life. The question is not only what AI will do to work. It is who is deciding what it will do, and in whose interest.
The bohemian generation that produced Kerouac's scroll and Dylan's lyrics operated under the conviction that inner freedom might survive — even flourish — outside the terms of the dominant order. That conviction looks different now. What remains of it, and what might be worth defending, is worth thinking about seriously. #ontheroad #jackkerouac #technofeudalism

NFT Postmortem: 
Notes from a former junkie

If you were around in 2021-2022, you remember how insane the NFT trenches felt!

Every day multiple new mints. Twitter full of gm, alpha threads & RT + follow for WLs. Discord servers so packed they constantly crashed. Chats moved so fast they were barely readable. 'Chat moving so fast no one will notice Im Gay'.

It genuinely felt like JPEGs were becoming the identity layer of the internet and the numbers made it feel real too.

At the peak in early 2022, OpenSea processed about $4.8B monthly volume, while weekly NFT trading across markets reached $1.4B!

Collections like Bored Ape Yacht Club went from a $200 mint to six figure prices. CryptoPunks became digital status symbols. Projects like Azuki, Doodles, CloneX and Moonbirds were talked about like early tech startups.

By 2025 annual global NFT sales dropped to around $5.6B and the overall market value fell roughly 72% from highs. Many NFTs that sold for millions lost 90–95% of their value.

Now in 2026, even the infrastructure of the original NFT boom is shrinking. Magic Eden, once one of the biggest NFT marketplaces, is shutting down parts of its NFT platform and winding down its multichain wallet.

But the real story of NFTs wasnt the numbers. It was the culture and the grind.

I remember staying up until 4 am hoping to catch Voltura on Australian time randomly dropping Psychedelic Anon whitelists on the timeline. During the Azuki and Doodles mints I had multiple devices open, refreshing MetaMask while gas kept climbing and praying the transaction would go through. Getting a Moonbirds mint felt like winning a lottery. Then the Otherdeed land sale unleashed one of the craziest gas wars of the entire cycle. People burned thousands just trying to mint!

Getting into good mints meant weeks of grinding. People farmed Discord, made fan art and stayed active just to get WLs. Gm, Drink Water, Touch Grass. Some even paid others to grind servers for them!

Invisible Friends, WonderPals, Coolmans Universe, The Littles, Hape, The Plague, Lil Lemons. Every project had entire communities believing they were 'the next BAYC'.

The space even got its own strange culture. Sappy Seals on spaces arfing. Frogs ribbiting. And when Goblintown appeared, thousands joined Spaces just to listen to hosts growling in goblin voices for hours!

It made absolutely no sense ... but it was fun!

Then there were the disasters. The launch of Pixelmon raised about $70M promising AAA quality assets. When the art revealed, Kevin became a meme overnight.

Celebrity hype added to the madness too. Logan Paul bought a rare Bumblebee NFT from 0N1 Force for $623,000 (188 ETH). Today the 0N1 Force floor sits around 0.1 ETH. Justin Bieber bought a Bored Ape Yacht Club for 500 ETH ($1.3M) and even Neymar Jr. jumped into the frenzy.

Even when Bitcoin Ordinals launched in 2023 things felt strange! There werent proper marketplaces to start. People were trading inscriptions through Discord and Excel spreadsheets manually tracking bids and ownership.

Looking back, the market simply ran on momentum. Floor prices were narratives. Discord hype was marketing. Volume was often just traders passing bags between wallets.

But the NFT market didnt disappear overnight. It just lost the one thing that made it explode in the first place ... speculation. And crypto always moves on to the next casino.

Today the same energy that then chased JPEGs is chasing memecoins, AI tokens, onchain games and tokenized real world assets.

If you were there in the trenches, you'll forever remember it as one of the strangest, loudest and most chaotic corners of the internet that ever existed!

Maybe NFTs arent dead forever. The tech could resurrect in new forms, but the culture that defined that era like the art PFPs, the Discord grinds, the 10 ETH floors and overnight legends is dead & buried... the return wont ever feel like the trenches we lived & breathed. A bitter sweet RIP.

Would you do it again?

That’s why so many investors miss real gems, there’s just too much noise and not enough time.

If you want to actually get better at picking good domains, you need a simple system. 

First, just Google the term. Seriously, this step alone filters out 90% of junk. Type in the domain phrase without the extension. Does it bring up businesses, services, products, or even general search interest? If it looks like no one in their life has ever typed those words together, it's probably worthless.

Two-word and three-word domains are fine, sometimes even better, if they have meaning and read smoothly. 

For example, “BrightHarvest” sounds professional and natural, while something like “HarvestlyBright” feels forced. Always read it out loud. If you stumble while saying it, others will too.

After the Google sense check, go over to NameBio. Check if similar names have sold and for how much. But remember, past sales are just indicators, not guarantees. You still need to judge the fit. 

Another thing people often forget is trademarks. Before you buy, especially before you list it anywhere, search on USPTO or any major trademark database to make sure you’re not stepping on someone’s brand. The last thing you want is a legal notice for a name you thought was "the next big sale".

Pricing is another area where people get delusional. You’re not going to list a two-word domain for $500,000 if it has no buyer base. Look at similar sales, understand your domain’s realistic value, and price to sell, not to brag.

Researching niches is underrated. Most people look for generic brandable names, but if you spend time diving deep into one niche like logistics, healthtech, or gardening, you’ll start noticing terms and combinations others overlook. That’s how some investors consistently grab names that sell, while the rest chase after what everyone else is chasing.

And please, avoid plural-first domains like “HomesFinder” instead of “HomeFinder”. It sounds off and lacks brand authority. Always check how recallable it is. If you tell someone over the phone, will they get it right the first time or ask you to repeat? If you hesitate, skip.

If you build a simple discipline – meaning, market fit, memorability, trademarks, and realistic pricing, you’ll start picking names that stand out in a sea of trash. At the end of the day, that’s what separates a domain hoarder from an actual domain investor.

A Malawian journalist wrote this open letter to the front-runner in the September election, the 85-year-old former president Peter Mutharika.

President Lazarus Chakwera has been such a terrible leader that an 85-year-old former president is now on the verge of returning to power.

Peter Mutharika and his brother the late Bingu have been both presidents of Malawi.

 ———————————-

Dear Peter Mutharika, Age Is Not Just a Number
By Jack McBrams

July 19, 2025
Dear President Mutharika,

Happy 85th birthday.

Turning 85 is no small feat — in fact, it's miraculous in a country where, in 1940, life expectancy barely scratched 35. Statistically speaking, you’ve outlived almost your entire birth cohort.

Only about 6,000 of the 21 million Malawians today were even alive when you were born. That’s not just longevity — that’s legendary status. You are a walking archive, a living library of the Malawian story who was actually 24 years when the country attained Independence on that cold 6th July morning in 1964. It seems like a long time ago, doesn’t it, Sir?

Your intellectual credentials remain unmatched: Yale, London, Dar es Salaam, Washington University, ABA, the UN. You’ve built a life that most Malawians can only read about — because they weren’t yet born when you were shaping it. And that’s what makes your current political ambition so baffling.

Why would an 85-year-old man want to govern a nation whose future he is, by every honest measure, no longer a part of?

This is not ageism. It’s realism. Age is not just a number — it is biology, cognition, stamina, context. Leadership is not academic. It’s not theoretical. It’s 18-hour days, travel, crisis management, decisions made on the fly, coordination across ministries and regions, and the ability to stay alert through it all. It’s not a lecture hall. It’s a battlefield. And forgive the bluntness, Sir, but no one brings an 85-year-old general to the frontlines of a war for national transformation.

This country is at war with poverty. With debt. With youth unemployment. With climate shocks. With the death of hope. And over 60% of our population is under the age of 25. The median age is 17. How does someone born before the invention of colour television plan to lead a generation raised on TikTok, AI, and global climate anxiety?

Their lives are moving at the speed of 5G — and they need a leader who doesn’t need help opening PDFs or understanding memes. They need someone who speaks the language of their future, not someone whose references were last relevant when Malawi had one national radio station.

You’ve served before. From 2014 to 2020, you sat at the top. And while there were moments of stability, there was also economic stagnation, persistent nepotism, and enough scandals to suggest that power was being exercised by those in your name — but not under your watch. The cement import saga, for instance, involved your very own personal bodyguard. Thousands of tonnes brought in under your presidential tax privileges, sold for profit. And when you were confronted by the ACB, you feigned ignorance. That’s not governance. That’s abdication by other means.

But the most tragic part? This doesn’t even feel like your own idea. It feels like you are being wheeled back into the ring by a coterie of political gamblers, too afraid to face the public themselves. They need your name, your immunity, your signature — not your ideas. You are not their champion, Mr. President. You are their shield. And they’re hiding behind you while Malawi burns.

Let’s stop this tragic play before it becomes a national farce.

It is time for you to become what Africa needs more of — elder statesmen. Not bitter, power-clutching old men, but wise, gracious mentors who step aside and lift up the next generation. Write your memoirs. Give lectures. Start a Presidential Leadership Fellowship. Mentor a hundred young Malawians who could one day lead this country better than all of us ever have. But do not insult your legacy by entering this race like a man who doesn't know when the music has stopped.

You deserve peace, Sir. Not campaign fatigue. You deserve to be honoured, not heckled. To be respected, not resisted. And this country deserves more than recycled ambition disguised as experience.

So, Mr. President — with deep respect and admiration:

Do not run. Walk away like a man who knows the difference between power and legacy.

Be remembered not as the last of the old, But as the first elder who made way for the new.
