It's March 2026 and every crypto founder I know is an AI founder now. We didn't learn new skills. We didn't take courses. We changed two words in our bios and got new headshots against solid backgrounds with good lighting.

The headshots cost more than the pivot.

 Crypto.com bought the domain ai.com for $70 million. Then fired 12% of their workforce. Their CEO called it an "AI upgrade."

He didn't say what was upgraded. It wasn't the 180 people who lost their jobs.

Bitfarms — a Bitcoin mining company that ran hydroelectric dams in Quebec — is rebranding to "Keel Infrastructure." They're a U.S. AI data center company now. Same dams. Same buildings. Same electricity. New ticker on Nasdaq.

BITF becomes KEEL.

That's it. That's the pivot.

Cango — a Chinese Bitcoin miner — sold $305 million in Bitcoin and renamed itself "EcoHash." An AI inference company. They used to solve cryptographic puzzles for one reason. Now they solve cryptographic puzzles for a different reason.

Cipher Mining became Cipher Digital. Same GPUs. They just point at different math now.

Nobody built anything new.

We all just changed the math.

I know because I did the same thing. In 2021 I started a DAO. Decentralized Autonomous Organization. We had a Discord, a governance token, and a whitepaper with a pie chart. The pie chart was my entire business model.

In 2023 the DAO became a "Web3 Collective."

In 2024 it became a "Digital Asset Community."

In 2025 it became an "AI Agent Ecosystem."

Same Discord. Same nine members. Three haven't logged in since 2022. Two are bots. The other four are my alts.

We voted to pivot.

The vote passed unanimously.

I voted four times.

My old pitch deck had 34 slides about "decentralized metaverse commerce." I kept the template. Changed "decentralized" to "autonomous." Changed "metaverse" to "AI-native." Changed "commerce" to "inference."

The investors didn't notice.

They did the same thing to their fund names.

The conferences are the same conferences. Token2049 added an AI track. Consensus added an AI stage. ETHDenver added an "AI x Crypto Summit." They hung new banners over the old ones.

I know because I could see the old banners through the fabric.

"WEB3 SOCIAL LAYER" was still visible behind "AUTONOMOUS AGENT INFRASTRUCTURE."

Same chairs. Same venue. Same speakers. Same pitch: give us money for a future that doesn't exist yet, and by the time you realize it doesn't work, we'll have pivoted to the next thing that doesn't exist yet.

That's not a business model.

That's a career.

My Bored Ape is still my profile picture.

I paid $189,000 for it.

It's worth $11,000 now.

Down 97%.

I don't talk about the Ape.

When someone asks, I say "I'm in AI now." As if switching industries erases the JPEG from my wallet. As if rebranding my company makes the monkey appreciate.

It doesn't.

But I said it with conviction and a new LinkedIn banner. That counts for something.

It doesn't.

The metaverse plots are still in my wallet too. All of them. Decentraland. The Sandbox. Voxels. A $2.4 million plot in Decentraland's Fashion District sold for $8,929 last month.

99.6% loss.

I haven't sold any of it.

Diamond hands.

Now we say "long-term conviction."

Same paralysis. Better vocabulary.

The AI pivot works because nobody checks. Nobody goes back to your 2021 tweets about how "the metaverse will replace physical reality by 2025." Nobody screenshots your Discord announcement about buying virtual land "for the next hundred years."

I deleted those tweets.

Not all of them. Just the ones with specific dates and dollar amounts. The vague ones still play. "The future is digital" works for both Web3 AND AI. I planned that.

I didn't plan that.

I got lucky that this industry has the memory of a goldfish with a venture fund.

Kris Marszalek — CEO of Crypto.com — said companies that don't adopt AI "will fail."

He said the same thing about crypto in 2021.

He was right about the failing part. He just had the direction wrong.

Block — the company formerly known as Square — fired 4,000 people. Almost half their workforce. They said it was because of AI.

Four thousand people lost their jobs because a CEO watched a demo and said "we need less of you."

That's not a strategy. That's a PowerPoint with a body count.

But we call it transformation.

I'm transforming too. My new deck says "AI Agent Infrastructure." Slide 12 is a pie chart. Slide 27 says "WE ARE BUILDING THE AUTONOMOUS ECONOMY."

It used to say "WE ARE BUILDING THE DIGITAL ECONOMY."

I changed one word.

The rocket emoji stayed.

He told me to leave his office.

The entire crypto industry is doing what I'm doing. We're not building. We're rebranding. We're not innovating. We're changing the vocabulary and hoping nobody notices the portfolio underneath.

Bitcoin miners are AI companies now. NFT platforms are "digital asset protocols." DAOs are "autonomous agent collectives." The metaverse is "spatial computing." Web3 is "decentralized AI."

Nobody changed what they're doing.

We all changed what we call it.

Same GPUs. Same data centers. Same investors. Same pitch. Same pie chart.

Same rocket emoji.

That's not a pivot.

That's a costume change.

And I'm wearing mine. Badge around my neck. VR headset on my head. Portfolio crashing behind me. WAGMI poster on the wall.

We’ve been monitoring the sentiment around $ACID for some time now and want to take a moment to speak on a few key topics transparently.

Market Making
A reputable market maker was engaged to help sustain volume and support natural growth from the start, based on a customized liquidity provisioning framework and a structured supply-to-volume agreement instead of a traditional volume-to-supply agreement.

Sell Pressure
The token faced overwhelming sell pressure from early buyers shortly after launch. Buybacks & Flow

Moving Forward
Acid Assistant was always an ambitious and experimental product. While we remain committed to the vision of browser-native Web3 automation, we also recognize where expectations were misaligned. The team will take this time to revisit ACID’s product narrative, explore new directions more suited to current market needs, and refine our core mechanics.

We’re taking this time to reflect, regroup, and rebuild with greater clarity.

— ACID Team

MyForce .com Sold for $90,000 via @Escrow_com 

Not every deal is just about money. Some are about trust, intuition, and the quiet confidence that comes from walking the long road with the right values.

I’m happy to share that MyForce .com has officially been sold for $90,000 via @Escrow_com , structured as a 60-month lease-to-own agreement with the same incredible buyer who earlier acquired MyVehicle .com for $105,000.

What makes this story special isn’t just the amount — it’s the timing, trust, and energy behind the deal.

The Backstory

Incredibly, I acquired MyForce .com just 3 months before we agreed on the deal — through a @godaddyauctions . Yes, only 90 days of holding. But while the timeline was short, the decision wasn’t random.

At the time, MyVehicle .com was already in escrow. That deal had taken nearly 6 months of negotiation and structure. Through that process, I got to know the buyer — not just as a customer, but as a person. I understood his mindset, his mission, and most importantly — his integrity.

So when he expressed interest in MyForce .com, the dialogue was natural. He made a humble request: could I consider $90,000 over 60 months, with no down payment, and some flexibility?

I didn’t hesitate.

Why?

Because I already had something more valuable than a deposit: trust.

Deal Structure

Total sale price: $90,000

Term: 60-month lease-to-own via @Escrow_com 

Down payment: None (by buyer’s request, accepted based on strong past record)

Monthly installments: Starting at $1,000, increasing over time

Delays: Yes — multiple months saw late payments

Outcome: Every payment was made. Every challenge was met with communication. Every commitment was fulfilled.

Why I Acquired MyForce .com

The reasoning was simple:

=> I love the “My” prefix — personal, memorable, brandable

=> MyVehicle .com had already validated the “My+Keyword” strategy

=> And no — I wasn’t holding out hope that @salesforce would come knocking someday. LOL

But MyForce .com had presence. It felt strong. It felt like a brand waiting to happen — across fitness, energy, empowerment, even AI or defense.

And that feeling was enough.

A Lesson in Trust and Character

This deal taught me (again) that structure means nothing without spirit.

At any point, I could’ve enforced the contract, reclaimed the domain, and kept the payments. But that’s not who I am. That’s not how I do business.

I stood by the buyer — not because I had to, but because I wanted to.

And once again, doing the right thing led to the right result.

The Bigger Picture

I’ve come to realize that the fruits we enjoy today often come from seeds we planted years ago — even if we didn’t realize it at the time.

=> My crypto investments, built through a disciplined and patient approach, have delivered handsomely over the past few years.

=> I've been accumulating gold since 2009, never imagining it would quietly outperform the S&P 500 over a 20-year span — but it did.

=> Real estate, mutual funds, and equities have rewarded long-term conviction with 20–25%+ CAGR over 10+ year periods.

These aren’t “lucky wins.” They’re rooted in a belief system.

My philosophy is grounded in two simple ideas:

🌱 The Farmer

You plant. You water. You protect the soil. Some seasons are quiet. Others bring storms. But you stay consistent. And when the time is right, the tree bears fruit — not just once, but again and again.

🎋 The Bamboo

For years, nothing seems to happen. Underground, roots grow deeper. Stronger. Then, suddenly, in a matter of months — it rises 20 feet. Not because it grew fast, but because it was ready.

I treat domains the same way.

Sometimes the reward comes in 3 months — like MyForce .com.

Other times, it takes 3 years.

But the principle is always the same: faith, consistency, and patience.

Final Thoughts

MyForce .com was one of the shortest holds of my portfolio — but the lessons, trust, and impact will last far longer.

What began as a quick auction pickup became a $90,000 deal built on nothing but mutual respect.

With God’s blessings, my business continues to evolve — from six-figure monthly domain sales to steady lease-to-own five-figure income, and a growing, diversified investment portfolio.

But no matter how high we rise, I believe the roots — humility, trust, ethics, and faith — must run even deeper.

Thank you again to God, family, and all the friends who continue to support this journey.

BREAKING: Cognition bought Windsurf at a 92% discount in 72 hours.

Here's everything you need to know about the ultimate fate of Windsurf and its 200 employees:

Cognition gave Windsurf employees a severe ultimatum: grind 80+ hours per week or take 9 months' salary and leave in a week.

CEO Scott Wu clearly stated that he doesn't believe in work-life balance, as employees spend 6 days at the office, clocking 80+ hour weeks.

Windsurf was worth $3 billion just weeks ago. OpenAI had the checkbook ready until talks collapsed in July.

Then everything fell apart in 72 hours:

• Day 1: Windsurf CEO and top engineers bolt to Google DeepMind for $2.4 billion 

• Day 2: 200+ employees told they are now employee-owned

• Day 3: Cognition swoops in to buy the scraps for $250 M

Industry estimates put Cognition's acquisition at $250 M, a 92% discount on a company whose enterprise revenue was doubling QoQ leading up to the sale.

They basically bought Windsurf's $82 MM revenue stream for pocket change.

But that’s not it. Before even announcing the buyouts, Cognition fired 30 Windsurf employees without any warning. 

This looks like the new Silicon Valley playbook.

Scale AI took a $14.8 billion investment from Meta, then cut 200 people.

Character[.]ai got $2.7 billion from Google, the founders joined Google, while the remaining employees got buyout packages.

It's simple: Technical founders get nine-figure payouts, and support staff get severance packages, all while these shell structures help them sidestep FTC antitrust scrutiny.

They are weaponizing culture fit as a mass layoff strategy.

Instead of traditional firing, they create impossible work environments that force people to quit. It's not good but legally bulletproof.

Cognition accelerated ALL equity vesting for departing employees, even unvested shares from four years out.

No, they are not being generous. They are doing this because it's cheaper than fighting wrongful termination lawsuits in California courts.

The Windsurf case is already being taught in business schools as the paradigmatic example of modern workforce stratification.

Academia calls it a reverse acqui-hire. I call it Silicon Valley's new hierarchy.

Over $56 billion in AI deals happened in just the first half of 2025, with 12 companies sold for over $1 billion since January.

The AI boom promised to democratize technology and create abundance for everyone.

But now it's creating the most unequal wealth distribution in startup history.

This is just the beginning. As AI eliminates more business functions, expect more cultural integration ultimatums.

More impossible work environments designed to force resignations.

More companies buying distressed assets and purging non-essential staff.

We may be living in a world where your survival depends entirely on how technical your job title sounds.

Where AI's promise of abundance becomes a reality only for the chosen few.

The Windsurf employees have until August 10th to decide.

Some employees may not even get that luxury in the future. 

Welcome to the new normal.

If you're building a startup today, how would you protect your employees? 

If you're a startup employee, how would you control risk-adjusted-reward?

Report: Samsung Retracts Decision to End DDR4 Production, Will Continue Manufacturing Until Next Year

Samsung Electronics has decided to extend the production of its 1z process DDR4 DRAM until the end of next year, retracting its original plan to cease production at the end of this year. This decision is a response to a combination of factors, including the recent surge in DDR4 prices and a slower-than-expected expansion of high-value-added High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) production.

According to industry sources on the 5th, Samsung Electronics, which had previously notified its clients that it would phase out its 1z process DDR4 DRAM production line by the end of 2025, recently reversed this plan and decided to extend production until December of next year. The company plans to inform its clients of this decision soon.

While SK Hynix and Micron rapidly transitioned their production to high-value HBM for artificial intelligence (AI), Samsung's certification and mass production schedules were delayed. Consequently, it appears Samsung has opted for a strategy to efficiently manage its production capacity by maintaining its DDR4 lines. A key advantage is the low production cost, as the 1z lines have already been fully depreciated, which can contribute positively to profits.

Samsung's change of plans is also linked to the sharp increase in DDR4 DRAM prices. The price hike is due to a decrease in supply coupled with a short-term rise in demand. Major DRAM suppliers like SK Hynix and Micron drastically cut their older DDR4 DRAM output as they increased HBM production. Additionally, there was a stockpiling phenomenon where some finished product manufacturers sought to secure inventory due to factors like potential U.S. tariff impositions. Demand from industrial boards and telecommunication equipment, which continue to use DDR4 for longevity and compatibility reasons, also remained steady.

According to market research firm DRAMeXchange, the fixed transaction price for PC DDR4 8Gb (1Gx8) at the end of July was $3.90, a 50% increase from the previous month. Including July, the price of this product has seen double-digit percentage increases from April (22.22%) to May (27.27%) and June (23.81%). According to TrendForce, the contract price for a DDR4 8GB module in July was $26.5, creating an unusual situation where it sold for more than a DDR5 module ($25.5).

Some analysts predict that Samsung's decision could somewhat alleviate the DDR4 supply shortage. Module companies and finished product manufacturers have also mitigated the risk of component discontinuation for a certain period. An industry insider commented, "Even if Samsung maintains production for an additional year, it is unlikely that DDR4 prices will drop sharply in the short term," and predicted, "The market will likely stabilize with a slowdown in the pace of price increases." Another industry source remarked, "Doesn't Samsung's latest decision indirectly reveal that the expansion of HBM production is not progressing as smoothly as expected in the near term?"

The #1 Secret to killing it on Amazon or DTC?

Market --> Product Fit

not

Product --> Market Fit

Let me explain.

It goes against standard, accepted marketing practices.

Create a great product, great brand, and they will come.

Kind of like the Kevin Costner Movie "Field of Dreams". If you build it they will come.

Before you do anything...ANYTHING...analyze the crap out of the MARKET. Period!

Who are they? (Ideal Customer Profile / Avatar)

How big is the market?

What are they willing to spend for the solution they are looking for?

Can you get you Cost of Goods Sold down to 1/3 - 1/5 of the price they are willing to pay?

What do THEY want? What do they really NEED that will give them what they want?

You guys are all talking about pain points blah blah...that is important. But as many of the best copywriter guys says you need to help guide the customer down the path of discovery.

But in today's age you can get there by gauging and analyzing customer sentiment.

Read reviews of the customers in the market for the top 10 best sellers.

Analyze the top ten best sellers and what they are delivering. Can you find a spot in the top ten?

What can you do better with your version of the solution?

What is going to be YOUR Brand's (or Product Brand's) Magic?

How can you deliver the solution in such a way that makes them feel something with your product?

The extreme example is DrinkBrez. @drinkbrez @iamshackelford his product literally gets you stoned. You definitely will feel something with his solution. He's really selling a change of state. Going from Stressed out with Anxiety to Mellowed out & Checked out. An easier sale than many...

Once you have all this insight you then build the product, build the brand, build the content around the two of those in such a way that it is simply packaging that your Ideal Customer is already expecting to see.

Then conversion on Amazon or you .com website is just a natural extension or natural byproduct (a reward to you really) for giving them EXACTLY what they want.

AI Anaysis of $nwbo acquisition of Advent Bioservices

In summary, the deal strengthens NWBO's position for growth and commercialization, potentially setting a precedent for integration in cell therapy manufacturing. For the biotech sector, it underscores the value of controlling supply chains in personalized medicine, though major impacts hinge on DCVax's regulatory success. Investors should monitor MHRA updates and NWBO's Q3 filings for further insights.

The acquisition of Advent BioServices Ltd. by Northwest Biotherapeutics (NWBO) on August 27, 2025, represents a strategic consolidation that primarily benefits NWBO by internalizing its key manufacturing partner, but its broader implications for the biotech sector are more nuanced and potentially trend-setting in the niche of personalized cell therapies.

Key Details of the Deal : 

NWBO, a biotechnology company focused on developing DCVax personalized immune therapies for solid tumor cancers (e.g., glioblastoma), agreed to acquire Advent BioServices from Toucan Holdings LLC for £1.4 million (approximately $1.85 million USD) plus net accounts payable, paid in installments over two years with potential acceleration upon regulatory approval of DCVax-L 

Advent, a UK-based contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO), has been NWBO's primary manufacturer for DCVax products, operating GMP facilities in London and Sawston.

 The deal includes:

Transfer of all fixed assets, such as cryostorage equipment.

Reversion of 19 million NWBO securities (13.5 million shares and 5.5 million options) back to NWBO, effectively reducing dilution.

Acquisition of certain intellectual property and intangibles.

Consolidation of operations, expected to yield synergies, cost savings, and enhanced scale-up capacity for manufacturing.

This move turns NWBO from a non-revenue-generating entity into one with immediate revenue streams from Advent's third-party contracts (Advent reported ~£20.8 million in revenue turnover for 2023, up 23% from 2022)

NWBO's CEO, Linda Powers, described it as an "opportune time to join forces under one roof," emphasizing integration and efficiency.

Immediate Impact on NWBOThis could facilitate faster commercialization if DCVax-L receives UK Marketing Authorization Application (MAA) approval from the MHRA, which is pending.

Operational and Financial Benefits: 

The acquisition enables full vertical integration, streamlining processes and reducing reliance on external contractors. It adds ~73 employees (based on Advent's 2023 headcount), expanding NWBO's management team—a stated goal from its June 2024 annual meeting. Volume was elevated, reflecting investor optimism about reduced dilution and revenue potential.

Stock Market Reaction:
 NWBO's stock (OTCQB: NWBO) rose ~7.13% on August 28, 2025, closing at $0.2571 (from $0.2400 on August 27).

Shareholder Sentiment:
 Real-time discussions on X (formerly Twitter) were overwhelmingly positive among retail investors. Many viewed it as a "lopsided" deal favoring NWBO, eliminating related-party complexities and signaling confidence in imminent regulatory milestones. Some highlighted downside protection (e.g., added cash flow for trials) and easier partnerships/franchising. 

Broader Impact on the Biotech Sector :
While NWBO is a small-cap company (market cap ~$350 million), this deal could influence trends in advanced therapies, particularly as the sector grapples with manufacturing challenges and a patent cliff for major players: This mirrors broader industry moves—e.g., larger firms like Thermo Fisher or Lonza acquiring assets to dominate supply chains—but on a smaller scale. It may encourage other early-stage biotechs in immunotherapy to pursue similar integrations, especially amid rising CDMO costs and supply chain disruptions.

Trend Toward Vertical Integration:
Cell and gene therapies like DCVax require specialized, costly manufacturing (e.g., GMP facilities for personalized vaccines). By acquiring its CDMO, NWBO exemplifies a shift from outsourcing to in-house control, which can reduce costs, improve quality assurance, and accelerate scale-up. This might spur investment in similar platforms, countering generics from China and boosting the ~$50 billion global cancer immunotherapy market.

Boost for Personalized Cancer Therapies: 
If DCVax-L gains approval (potentially soon, given the deal's timing and NWBO's focus on ramping Sawston production), it could validate dendritic cell vaccines as a viable, non-toxic alternative to chemotherapies. The sector has seen renewed interest in immunotherapies post-Keytruda's success, but with Big Pharma facing patent expirations (e.g., Merck's Keytruda loses exclusivity in 2028), NWBO's IP (including recent combo therapy patents in the EU, Canada, etc.) could attract partnerships or acquisitions. It could signal to the sector that undervalued assets in niche areas (e.g., GBM treatments) are ripe for consolidation, potentially increasing deal activity in oncology-focused biotechs.

M&A and Investor Dynamics:
 Biotech M&A has been active in 2025, with deals emphasizing manufacturing capabilities (e.g., Cognate BioServices sold for $875 million in 2021 on $140 million projected revenue). NWBO's low-cost acquisition (6-7x below comparable multiples) simplifies its structure, making it more appealing to institutional investors or buyers wary of related-party entanglements.

Limited Sector-Wide Ripple: 
No immediate widespread effects have been reported, as the deal is small and NWBO-specific. However, if it leads to successful DCVax commercialization, it could enhance confidence in UK-based manufacturing (post-MHRA licensing in 2023) and encourage cross-border collaborations.

Value Change Explanation:
The community poll for the Molten M12 pushed its trading value up by $1,000,000 to reach $15,000,000 because players collectively recognized its unique position in the Jailbreak Trading Expansion as both the first-ever community-created vehicle and a short-term event-exclusive release that was only available for ten days in October 2020, making its accessibility window one of the smallest among high-tier limited cars. With just 3,419 copies still circulating and the vehicle showing a strong demand rating of 5.87 out of 10, traders in recent weeks have concentrated on how its combination of rarity and high performance creates a balance of collectibility and usability that few other cars maintain in the current market. The poll gave the community an opportunity to directly influence valuation trends, and many players highlighted that while the Molten M12 had been valued around $14,000,000 for an extended period, the consistent number of trades logged last month—over 20,000 exchanges—indicated that it remained significantly more liquid and desirable than some other comparably valued vehicles, justifying an upward adjustment. Further discussion within the Jailbreak Trading Network emphasized that its history as a fan-designed addition adds intangible prestige, which, when coupled with its limited-time availability, strengthens its alignment with higher-value event vehicles that tend to appreciate steadily rather than decline. Traders also drew comparisons to similar exclusive cars and pointed out that despite minor fluctuations in duped values, clean versions of the Molten M12 have been commanding strong overpays due to its scarcity and high-performance appeal, reflecting a wider market trend toward prioritizing rare event releases over standard seasonal vehicles. Because the poll reflected the consensus of active traders who favored recalibrating the Molten M12 upward in recognition of both its historical importance to Jailbreak and its persistent demand across trading sessions on Trading Island, the shift to $15,000,000 solidified its role as a premium-tier vehicle, aligning its official valuation with the elevated offers that had already been occurring organically in player-to-player trades.

Additional Item Information:
The Molten M12 is one of the most iconic and coveted vehicles within the Jailbreak Trading Expansion, representing a blend of exclusivity, performance, and community history. Released briefly between October 4th and October 14th of 2020 for $599,000 cash, it became the first-ever community-created car to be officially added into Jailbreak, which immediately gave it a legendary status among veteran players. Its design is inspired by the Maserati MC12, characterized by an aggressive, hypercar-style body accented with molten lava patterns glowing across its exterior, giving the car a visually striking molten-rock theme that makes it one of the most recognizable and stylish vehicles in the game. Although it is not widely used in active gameplay, its sleek design and association with retirement status has steadily gained traction among collectors, a trend reinforced by 22,279 trades recorded just in the past month, indicating stronger than expected circulation in the market despite its medium demand rating of 4.79. This elevated trading activity suggests that while not every player is desperate to own the Airtail, it continues to hold relevance as an attractive mid-to-high tier asset for both casual and experienced traders. The distribution count of 4,652 copies, while higher than some exclusive vehicles, still constrains supply enough to maintain competition among players who prize rarity, with traders acknowledging that limited retired vehicles such as this appreciate in value as time passes. Recent Jailbreak Trading discussions also reveal a shift in sentiment: while its base vehicle value is still measured at 2,000,000 in cash terms, community emphasis has moved away from raw cash equivalence and toward collector-driven desirability. Some players argued that previous valuations understated its significance compared to other retired items of similar rarity tiers, particularly given its three-seater capacity and its role as a symbol of early 2021 updates. Notable trivia includes the fact that the Airtail was one of the few hypercars to feature three seats, making it stand out among players who enjoyed showcasing its unique arrangement with friends, and it was also among the last high-speed cars introduced before the game fully shifted toward balancing hypercars with more diverse specialties, which has cemented its reputation as a “collector’s flex” in the trading community.

AI isn’t just about cool chatbots or trading bots… it might be powerful enough to shake our entire financial system.
I tried to break it down in simple words

So guy's you’ve probably seen videos saying AI could trigger an economic collapse. Sounds dramatic, right? But when you connect the dots, the chain reaction feels very real. Let me explain step by step

========================================

It all begins with jobs.

AI is eating into roles across industries customer service, coding, design, transport, even decision-making jobs. Millions could be displaced in the next decade. When incomes vanish, people stop spending. Less shopping, fewer loans, weaker businesses. That’s the first domino: a demand shock.

Now, the banks.

Banks thrive on lending. But if fewer people take loans and defaults rise, profits shrink. Liquidity dries up. Think about Silicon Valley Bank (2023) one small bank’s collapse shook markets. Imagine if dozens faced stress at once.

Banks also hold government bonds. If they dump bonds to cover losses, prices crash, yields shoot up, and suddenly governments struggle to borrow. Add shrinking tax revenue (because fewer people are earning/spending), and deficits explode.

The pain then spreads to the markets. Companies post weak earnings, stocks crash, housing demand falls, people feel poorer. Investors flee to safer markets, currencies in emerging economies weaken. It becomes a global ripple.

Governments react the only way they know: print money. Lower interest rates, pump liquidity, and hope growth returns. But when too much money chases too few goods, inflation rises. Push it too far and trust in fiat money itself starts to crack.

========================================

And here’s the piece most people miss

AI’s hunger for power.

AI isn’t free to run. Every chatbot, every image model, every recommendation system lives inside massive data centers. These aren’t like your local server racks they’re football-field–sized warehouses stacked with GPUs, cooled 24/7, consuming unbelievable amounts of electricity.

As AI adoption scales, so does demand for

➤ Electricity (already straining grids in the U.S., Europe, and Asia).
➤ Chips (NVIDIA, AMD, specialized AI silicon).
➤ Cooling systems and water (one data center can consume millions of gallons monthly).

Now connect this to the economy

•Energy markets get squeezed → higher electricity prices for households and businesses.
•Governments may spend billions on subsidies or infrastructure upgrades, adding more to deficits.
•Inflation rises not just from money printing but also from surging energy demand.

So even if AI boosts productivity, the cost of keeping these giant machine brains alive could weigh heavily on the system.

========================================

So where do we hide when fiat and infrastructure wobble? That’s where scarcity backed assets shine.

➤ Bitcoin (BTC)
Capped at 21 million coins. Borderless, unprintable, digital gold for the modern age.

➤ Gold
Trusted for over 5,000 years. Central banks keep buying it for reserves.

➤ Silver
Industrial demand + scarcity makes it doubly valuable. Think EVs, solar panels, batteries.

➤ NFTs (Digital Scarcity)
Even digital collectibles can hold value if scarce and culturally important:
•CryptoPunks (Larva Labs founders Matt Hall & John Watkinson).
•Bored Ape Yacht Club (Yuga Labs founders Greg Solano & Wylie Aronow).
•Beeple’s “Everydays” sold for $69M at Christie’s.

They prove that ownership, community, and scarcity can create value even in the digital realm.

========================================

The thread connecting all this?

Scarcity. Unlike fiat that can be printed endlessly or data centers that burn infinite energy, scarce assets are finite. They can’t be manufactured overnight, which is why people trust them when systems shake.

===================================

UK Law on Non-Stun Slaughter
The legal foundation for slaughter practices in the UK is primarily governed by the **Welfare of Animals at the Time of Killing (England) Regulations 2015** (WATOK), with similar regulations in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. These regulations implement EU standards (retained post-Brexit) and mandate that animals must be stunned before slaughter to minimize suffering, ensuring they are rendered unconscious and insensible to pain until death.

However, an exemption exists under **Schedule 1 of WATOK**, which permits non-stun slaughter for religious purposes. This exemption aligns with the **European Convention for the Protection of Animals for Slaughter** (Council of Europe, 1979), which the UK has historically followed. Specifically:
- Non-stun slaughter is allowed only when it is carried out in accordance with religious rites (e.g., Halal for Muslims or Shechita for Jews).
- It must be performed by individuals with a Certificate of Competence (CoC) and in slaughterhouses approved by the Food Standards Agency (FSA).
- The meat must be intended for consumption by the respective religious communities (Muslims or Jews).

The **FSA** oversees compliance, and its 2023 report indicates that non-stun methods are used for approximately 15-20% of Halal slaughter (down from 35% a decade ago due to increased acceptance of post-cut stunning) and nearly 100% of Kosher slaughter, reflecting strict adherence to Shechita traditions.

### Should Non-Stun Meat Be Sold for General Consumption?
The law does not explicitly prohibit the sale of non-stun meat to the general public, but it creates a framework that implies it should be restricted to the communities for which it is slaughtered. Here’s the nuance:
- **Legal Intent**: The exemption is designed to accommodate religious dietary needs, suggesting that non-stun meat should primarily be supplied to Muslims or Jews. The GOV.UK guidance (updated 2023) states that non-stun slaughter is permissible "where it can be demonstrated that the meat is destined for a religious community."
- **Practical Reality**: There is no mandatory labeling requirement in the UK to distinguish stunned from non-stunned meat, a point of contention raised by animal welfare groups like the RSPCA. A 2022 FSA survey found that up to 60% of non-stun Halal meat enters the general market, often unlabeled, due to commercial pressures and lack of enforcement.
- **Enforcement Gaps**: The original post’s claim that "slaughterhouses are breaking the law" hinges on this lack of enforcement. Local authorities and the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) have been criticized for not tracking the destination of non-stun meat. A 2024 House of Commons debate noted that only 2.5% of the 1 billion animals slaughtered annually in the UK are processed via non-stun Halal methods, yet the volume reaching non-religious consumers remains unmonitored.

### Current Debate and Proposals
- **Animal Welfare Concerns**: Veterinary evidence, including a 2022 Veterinary Record study, confirms that non-stun methods (e.g., throat-cutting without prior stunning) can delay insensibility by 10-20 seconds in cattle and up to 5-10 seconds in sheep, compared to instantaneous stunning. This has fueled calls for a ban or stricter labeling.
- **Religious Freedom**: The UK government, as stated in a 2023 Hansard record, respects the rights of Jewish and Muslim communities to consume meat prepared according to their beliefs, balancing this against welfare considerations.
- **Proposed Changes**: The RSPCA and MPs have pushed for mandatory labeling (e.g., a 2023 amendment to the Animal Welfare Bill) to allow consumer choice and ensure non-stun meat isn’t unwittingly consumed by those opposed to it. Defra is reviewing this, with a consultation expected by late 2025.

The Life & Times of an Unsuccessful Criminal: Chapter 3

The rarest thing in my wallet was also the loudest thing in my head.

I couldn't sleep.

The reveal had happened maybe an hour earlier. My @RTFKT CloneX was sitting in my wallet, a green reptile character in a sweater that said WAGMI (a crypto acronym that basically meant "we're all going to make it"), aviator sunglasses, and anime hair that made him look like a chill version of Goku. I called him that on Twitter. "Low-key, crypto dude, chill Goku."

I changed my profile picture to this avatar immediately. Then I tweeted about it. Then I tweeted again. Then I watched someone sell an alien variant, one of the absolute rarest in the collection, for 88.88 ETH. At the time, that was roughly $350,000. For a single digital avatar that they got from the same type of free vial I'd just used.

I typed "speechless" and posted the image of my reptile. That was the only honest thing I said all night, because everything after that was me doing math in my head while pretending to be calm online.

Here's how the math worked. CloneX had 20,000 avatars. About half were humans, the most common type. Robots made up about 30%. Then you had rarer types going all the way down to aliens, which were roughly 30 total in the entire collection. My reptile was one of 248. Rare enough that nobody had sold one yet. Which meant I had no idea what mine was worth. And in a world where prices changed by the hour, not knowing was its own kind of problem.

I listed it on @opensea , the biggest NFT marketplace, and priced it in the middle of where other reptiles were listing. No sales yet. Just people guessing.

Within minutes, a collector reached out.

In this world, people used anonymous avatars as their online identity. I wasn't anonymous on Twitter or Discord (my handle is @Classic_Craig ). I used my actual face as my avatar for a long time, only swapping it to a project I liked to show support when it felt appropriate for the vibe.

Your profile picture on Twitter wasn't just a photo. It was a signal. It told everyone which communities you were in, how early you were, and in some cases, how much money you had. When a celebrity or athlete swapped their profile picture to an NFT, the value of that entire collection could move overnight. My reptile had a specific look that this collector wanted. Not as a flip. As his face online.

I see the same signaling happening right now, just in a different industry. Not profile pictures, but the way people talk about their tech stack. Whether they're actually building workflows in Claude or ChatGPT or just reposting someone else's thread about prompt engineering. Whether they know the difference between models or just say "I use AI" like it's one thing. The signal is different. The dynamic is identical. You can tell who's in the room and who's watching from the lobby.

That distinction mattered to me. He wasn't trying to buy low and sell high. He wanted to BE this character. That's a different kind of buyer.

The next morning, Nike announced they had acquired RTFKT, the company behind CloneX.

The timing was wild. Same week as the reveal. The deal terms were never disclosed, but RTFKT had raised money seven months earlier at a $33 million valuation, and nobody believed Nike paid anywhere near that low. This was a global brand validating the exact technology sitting in my wallet.

I made a quick video reacting to the news, posted it, and went right back to negotiating. That's when the theory hit me. If Nike just bought this company, the hype was on. Max visibility. I already believed that RTFKT would continue rewarding holders, as they had previously. I didn't know what. I didn't know when. I just knew I still needed a CloneX in my wallet after this deal closed.

That changed everything about the negotiation.

My ask was 20 ETH for the reptile. The ultra-rares were going for 50 to 100 ETH, so I knew I wasn't in that tier. But 20 ETH was real money. About $77,000 at the time. The problem was I also wanted to walk away holding another CloneX. So I needed a buyer who had extras.

I browsed the interested party's collection on OpenSea. Anyone could do this. Your wallet was public. Your entire portfolio was visible to anyone who cared to look. The transparency in this space was unlike anything I'd ever experienced in business. Everything on-chain, everything verifiable, no bluffing about what you owned or what you'd done.

That kind of radical transparency is coming to every industry, whether people want it or not. In the world of AI and automation, the gap between people who actually use these tools and people who just talk about using them is getting easier to spot by the day. Your output is the signal. It's hard to fake.

I originally wanted one of his demon-trait clones, but after some back and forth, we settled on a robot with a gas mask. Not the most exciting piece visually, but it was slightly rarer than the standard human, and more importantly, it would qualify me for whatever RTFKT dropped next.

Here's how the deal actually worked. I teased this in the last chapter as a trust trade. It was smarter than that.

We executed both sides through OpenSea's smart contracts. He bought my reptile for 20 ETH. I bought his robot for 3.5 ETH. Two separate transactions on the marketplace, so neither of us had to blindly send money to a stranger's wallet address. If he didn't follow through, I kept my reptile. If I didn't follow through, he kept his robot. The 7.5% in marketplace and creator fees was the cost of not having to trust a stranger with tens of thousands of dollars. I honestly think he only accepted my 3.5 ETH for the robot because he wanted to de-risk his 20 ETH purchase and didn't pay for the vials either. Either way, the trust part was in him accepting that offer. Once he paid for the reptile, the ETH was mine, the NFT was his. He could've ghosted me, but he didn't. Semi trust trade level unlocked.

On December 14, 2021, after marketplace and creator fees, 18.5 ETH landed in my wallet. About $71,000. I sent 3.5 back out immediately to buy the robot. That left me sitting on 15 ETH and a new CloneX.
I was in the dark room again. Upstairs office. Wife asleep. Son asleep. Just me and a Coinbase transfer screen.
I moved 10 ETH to my exchange immediately. $38,622. Then I paid the instant transfer fee to push it into my checking account right away, because I needed to see it in there. It couldn't just be a number in a crypto wallet. It had to be real money, in a real bank, before I could believe it happened.

I eventually stopped paying those instant transfer fees because they got expensive. But that night, I needed to see that win fast.
Here's the part that surprised me. I wasn't anxious.

For the first time in this entire run, after a big sale, I didn't immediately start spiraling. I didn't check what I left on the table. I didn't open OpenSea every 15 minutes to see if the reptile floor had moved.

I felt accomplished. I was smiling.

Every other win in my NFT journey came with a side of anxiety. The ArtBlocks sales in August, $11K and $15K, I was checking prices compulsively for weeks. The Wolf Game run, I couldn't stop calculating what I might be missing. Even buying the TV, the thing that made it all feel real, I immediately went back to the floor prices.

This was different. The 10 ETH in my checking account meant I was freerolling. My hobby had already paid for itself many times over, but this was the moment it clicked emotionally. I could take swings forever without risking money I actually cared about. The pressure released.

I told my wife the next morning. She was happy for me. Didn't have a boisterous reaction or anything. That tracks. She'd been the steady presence through all of this, never told me to stop, never told me to go harder. She just let me have my thing. That's the best kind of trust.

A few months later, on February 25, 2022, I sold the robot for 13 ETH. $34,395. And my theory about RTFKT was right. Seven weeks after I sold the reptile, RTFKT announced a mystery box airdrop for every CloneX holder. My robot qualified. My instinct to keep a second CloneX was correct, the market just didn't cooperate on timing. By the time I sold the airdrop pieces, crypto had crashed and the proceeds were small. But the instinct was right.

Combined, the two CloneX sales grossed over $111,000. After the 3.5 ETH I spent on the robot and marketplace fees on both sides, I netted around $90,000 from a free vial I got for holding a Metakey I'd minted months earlier because the founder posted good content and the NFT looked cool.

Here's the postscript. The buyer flipped my reptile for 20.5 ETH shortly after buying it. Smart move. That same reptile recently sold for 0.4 ETH. The robot I sold for 13 ETH? Currently worth about 0.2 ETH. By July 2022, ETH itself was under $1,100. That 13 ETH would've been $14,000 instead of $34,000.

I didn't time the market because I was smarter than anyone. I got lucky because of the rule I'd made with my wife and David. When the noise got loud, sell. That rule pulled me out before the crash. It probably cost me some upside, too, but I'd rather leave money on the table than watch it evaporate.

The freerolling feeling changed how I showed up after that. I stopped optimizing every decision for profit and started leaning into the parts I actually enjoyed. The people. The conversations about art and technology that had nothing to do with floor prices. That shift is why the friendships that came next were possible. When you're not grinding for the money, you connect differently.

One of those connections happened at a @veecon art gallery side-event (literally a porch gallery, as in someone’s porch, featuring very cool art), where a conversation with a collector named Gmoney led to something I got for free that would eventually sell for over $23,000. That's a story for later.

Ultimately, two strangers trusted each other with tens of thousands of dollars because they spent time in the same digital rooms around the same digital people. We didn't compare follower lists, we didn't even talk for that long overall. We could see each other's public wallets and tweets, talked enough to feel like it was worth the risk, and pulled the trigger.

That same trust economy is forming right now around AI, automation, and how businesses actually use these tools. The people learning publicly, sharing what works, showing up in communities and actually contributing are the ones who will have the most opportunities. They're building reputations that will convert to opportunities most people won't see coming.

Are you in the room?

The Race to Break Big Tech's Internet Monopoly: How Blockchain Is Rebuilding the Web
The modern internet runs on borrowed time and rented space. Three big boys, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, control over 65% of the world's cloud infrastructure, creating a digital oligopoly that puts the entire global economy at risk. This doesn't even include the amount of data being aggregated and sold for even more profits.

The Fragile Foundation of Digital Civilization
When AWS experiences a major outage, half the internet goes dark. Your Netflix stops streaming, your banking app freezes, and even your favorite cryptocurrency exchange might temporarily vanish. The 2021 AWS outage that lasted just six hours cost the global economy an estimated 5.7 BILLION USD.

But the real nightmare isn't technical failure, it's leverage. These platforms can de-platform entire businesses overnight and essentially decide which innovations live or die. The internet, originally designed as a decentralized network to survive nuclear war, has become more centralized than the telephone system it replaced.

The numbers are staggering:
i. 32% of all cloud services run on AWS alone
ii. $15 billion in daily economic losses would result from iii. complete cloud infrastructure failure
iv. Trillions of dollars in stored value depend on these centralized systems
Your money, your memories, your business, all sitting in someone else's computer, governed by someone else's terms of service.

The Decentralized Revolution is Already Here
While everybody has been unavoidably dependent on Big Tech companies, an entire parallel internet infrastructure has been quietly building. Welcome to the era of DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks), where blockchain technology is rebuilding the physical backbone of the internet itself.

THE NEW INTERNET STACK
IPFS (InterPlanetary File System), @IPFS distributes content across thousands of nodes worldwide instead of single servers. The New York Times and Wikipedia already use it in production, it's not an experiment anymore.

SEDA Protocol, @sedaprotocol is building critical infrastructure by serving as a decentralized oracle network that brings real-world data onto the blockchain through a modular data layer that allows any blockchain to configure and interact with custom data feeds for price data, RPC data, or any available API endpoint. SEDA is essentially putting the internet's data layer on-chain, making it impossible for any single entity to control information flow.

Filecoin, @Filecoin has created a global marketplace for storage where anyone can rent out spare hard drive space and earn cryptocurrency. It's already storing petabytes of data and competing directly with traditional cloud storage.

Akash Network, @akashnet lets anyone rent out spare computing power, creating a decentralized alternative to AWS computing services. Need to run a machine learning model? Instead of enriching Jeff Bezos, you distribute that value to thousands of independent providers.

Grass Network, @grass Plans to expand its infrastructure and user engagement strategies in 2025, with the grasshopper already in production, and their mobile app already launched. This aligns with their aim to further decentralize AI data acquisition and processing.

The Economic Opportunity
This isn't just ideology, it's money. The DePIN sector has attracted over $30 billion in investment. Instead of paying Amazon to store your data, you pay individual providers directly through blockchain marketplaces, often at lower costs while distributing wealth fairly to thousands of independent operators worldwide, while maintaining a transparent overview of how this money is being distributed.
Approximately 1.087BN USD is being spent on cloud computing daily, all of which could be distributed wealth with this new innovation.

Your spare hard drive space becomes valuable. Your unused computing power earns you money. Your data stays under your control.
Yes, we've seen projects attempt this and fall short, but mistakes are the driving force that put humanity at the level of evolution that it is.

The Stakes Couldn't Be Higher
We're deciding the fundamental architecture of human civilization's digital layer. Do we want a future where a handful of corporations control all human information and commerce? Or do we want that power distributed among billions of participants?

Think about that.

AI Domain: Greatness and Adoption Take Time

AI has become one of the fastest-growing industries in history, attracting enormous amounts of capital. In 2024, global private investment in AI hit $252.3 billion, with venture funding alone topping $110 billion. By August 2025, AI-related companies had already raised $118 billion, demonstrating that investor appetite for AI remains strong. 

Yet, many AI experts, founders, and innovators had never even heard of the .ai domain extension until the technology gained significant attention in late 2022 and 2023. That surge was fueled by generative AI tools like ChatGPT—built on earlier breakthroughs in deep learning and big data—that showed the world the true power of natural language AI. 

Today, almost every major AI company proudly operates on a .ai domain. But before it became the digital badge of artificial intelligence, .ai was simply the country code top-level domain (ccTLD) for Anguilla, a tiny British Overseas Territory in the Caribbean with a population of about 14,700. Few people could even point to Anguilla on a map when ICANN first assigned it the .ai domain back in February 1995. 

For years, registering a .ai domain was restricted. That changed in 2009, when Anguilla opened it up to the world. By 2015, the domain was being marketed directly to the #AI industry, and startups quickly jumped on board. Everything changed in 2022 with the global boom of generative AI—the moment .ai truly became the digital home of artificial intelligence. 

The growth has been staggering. As of early 2025, more than 600,000 .ai domains are registered. In 2024, the government of Anguilla earned about $39 million from .ai registrations and renewals—roughly 23% of its national revenue, up from just 5% before the AI boom. 

Some .ai domains have commanded eye-popping prices: Law.ai sold for $350,000, Sound.ai for $250,000, Golf.ai for $140,000, and Win.ai for $130,000. According to NameBio, there are about 17,500 publicly reported .ai sales, close to .io’s 18,492—but still far from the massive 1.28 million .com sales. Of the 600,000 registered .ai names, experts estimate that over 500,000 are held by #domain investors. But here’s the catch: not every one of those will see the light of day. 

In October 2024, the Associated Press reported that before the AI revolution, .ai domain revenue made up just 5% of Anguilla’s budget. Today, it’s nearly a quarter of the island’s entire economy—an incredible transformation sparked by a two-letter domain. 

The lesson is clear: in #technology , greatness and adoption always take time. Ten years from now, another ccTLD may rise to fame and put a different small nation on the global map. Until then, keep your eyes open—the next big thing could already be out there.

Our Domain Blitz: 4 Days, $143 to $17,800, a 105x Return
The response to our last data post was incredible. Building on that, we're excited to share the real, behind-the-scenes story of our gosupa.com sale.
It all started on July 16th, 20:00 UTC. We were in the middle of acquiring over 20 expired domains. One stood out: gosupa.com , previously owned by the giant HugeDomains. We won it for just $143.
The next day, we listed our new acquisitions on @afternic and other platforms.
Then, just 36 hours later...
BOOM. 💥
An email from Afternic: gosupa.com sold for $14,800 (LTO).
But then came the gut punch... 🤦‍♂️
The deal was cancelled.
The reason? A newly won domain has a 60-day transfer lock, but LTO requires an immediate transfer to GoDaddy. After some back and forth, Afternic had to void the sale.
We paused. We knew the buyer was serious.
So, instead of lowering the price, we did the opposite. We raised it 20% to $17,800, switched it to a Buy-It-Now, and re-listed it.
The twist? On July 20th, 10:00 UTC, another email arrived.
The same buyer had come back and purchased the domain for the new, higher price of $17,800.
The domain was delivered smoothly (via push), and a huge thank you to the team at @afternic for their incredible support throughout the process.
Our 2 main takeaways:
1️⃣ Volume creates opportunity. More lines in the water = more fish.
2️⃣ Maximize visibility. Listing on multiple platforms is non-negotiable. #DomainInvesting #domainsaleCaseStudy #domainers #DomainForSale

"Cheap offers cannibalize the main offer."

Yes they do.

Yet I still don't think it's a bad idea to have one.

2 months ago I launched my Tool Tier.

It’s called that because it contains all my workshops, trainings and Tools inside.

Individually, they sold for $3,000 but here they're just $40/week.

Plus it includes viewer access to the Likes Ain't Cash Community.

Plus access to all future workshop recordings (and even the Ai Tools).

When I launched it, I was concerned that it may cannibalize my main offer.

And it did because a few folks downgraded.

Others who seemed like client material just joined, got what they needed and left.

Not pretty.

I lost about $3k in MRR.

Over a 2-week timeframe, this is definitely a loss.

But over a 2-month timeframe it added $8k in MRR.

Then 4 people paid in full for the year.

Then 3 became clients.

And 1 opted in to work 1-on-1.

I "lost" about $3k in MRR.

And in exchange I got $8,000 in MRR,

$13,500 in one-time clients,

And about $28,000 in total if you take upgrades into account.

Cannibalism is like rain.

It sucks for a bit but it also creates multiple opportunities that eventually grow your business more than if you didn’t have it.

My thesis for why:

Cheap stuff gets you more buyers.

And when you get more buyers, you get more of 2 kinds of people:

Unserious people who will take advantage of it.

And serious people who want to know if you're right for them.

I was ok with getting a few unserious people if that meant I would find more serious people.

That's who I was banking on when I launched the Tool Tier.

The goal wasn't creating MRR.

(It's hard to do that at that price point unless you have millions of followers.)

The goal was using offers that are easy to buy to find more serious people in less time.

So, yes. The Tool Tier cannibalized my main offer.

It also made more money, created more stability and allowed me to find more serious people.

The big question is not "how do I avoid cannibalism?"

The big question is "am I willing to cannibalize some money in 2 weeks if that means more money in 2 months?"

Software stocks still getting hammered. 

 $IGV is down 30% year-to-date because "AI is destroying software moats."

Are software stocks cooked? Yes, a lot of them are.

Buying the dip is dangerous.

But it's nuanced.

Some of the sell-off is completely justified. Basic tools, undifferentiated add-ons, products that are essentially a pretty interface on top of someone else's technology. If Claude can replace what you do for $20 a month, those 10-15x revenue multiples were never real. The market is finally doing the math correctly.

But it's also making a serious mistake.

In cybersecurity and core infrastructure, AI doesn't reduce demand. It accelerates it. More powerful AI means more vulnerabilities, faster attacks, greater complexity. Security budgets don't shrink in that world. They explode. Yet those stocks are getting dumped alongside everything else.

This is what fear-driven markets do. Investors stop thinking about individual business models and start trading labels. "Software" becomes one trade, even when the underlying realities have nothing in common.

The result: some companies deserve to be down, some are being sold for the right reasons, and some are being sold for exactly the wrong ones.

BUT!

The biggest mistake you can make right now is treating this like a normal dip. "Cheap" isn't a reason to buy. 

Without a narrative shift or market confirmation, cheap stocks stay cheap, and your capital sits there doing nothing.

It's nice that Chris Brown and Usher teamed up to sell tickets, but the biggest story in music right now is Justin Bieber single-handedly saving Coachella.

Two years ago, the most iconic music festival in the world could not sell tickets. This weekend, resale passes are going for $3,000. The difference is one headliner. In case you missed how close Coachella came to vanishing entirely:

In 2024, Coachella had its slowest ticket sales in a decade. First weekend passes that used to sell out within hours took nearly a month. Overall sales dropped 14 to 17% from the year before. The festival that once defined April for an entire generation of music fans was struggling to fill a field in Indio.

The problem was that Coachella had spent years becoming more about the brand than the music. Influencer activations. Fashion content. Instagram moments. The festival became a backdrop for content creation, and the actual product, the live music experience, started to feel secondary.

In 2025, they course-corrected with Lady Gaga, Post Malone, Green Day and Travis Scott. It helped. Ticket sales climbed back to 120,000 per weekend, up from roughly 80,000 in 2024. But the magic was not back. The festival still was not selling out on announcement day the way it had for over a decade.

Then they announced the 2026 lineup in September 2025. Justin Bieber as the Saturday headliner, his first time ever headlining Coachella. The festival sold out within a week.

Bieber is being paid over $10 million for two performances, the highest artist payout in the festival's 27-year history. Weekend 1 general admission passes that originally sold for $649 are currently listed at $2,900 or more on StubHub. VIP passes are clearing $5,000.

And this is a guy who three years ago could not move half his face.

In June 2022, Bieber was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a viral condition that caused partial facial paralysis. He canceled the remaining dates on his Justice World Tour and largely disappeared from the spotlight. No touring. No album cycle. No major performances for over two years. The comeback was not guaranteed.

Then in July 2025, he dropped SWAG, his seventh studio album. It debuted at number two on the Billboard 200 with 163,000 units in the first week. He logged 198 million on-demand streams in seven days, the biggest streaming week of his career. He followed it with SWAG II two months later. He launched a Twitch channel that pulled tens of thousands of concurrent viewers on day one. He performed at the Grammys in February. He played a private, no-phones show at The Roxy in late March that had the entire industry talking.

By the time Coachella weekend arrived, Bieber had 103 million monthly listeners on Spotify and the most momentum of anyone in music.

Coachella did not recover because they redesigned the festival grounds or added better food vendors or landed a bigger influencer partnership. They recovered because they invested in the product. One headliner with a genuine cultural moment behind him turned a festival that could not sell tickets into a $3,000-per-pass event.

The brand did not save Coachella. The product did.

You complain about a phone charger on Amazon and they just hand you $15 back, no return needed. One phone call to customer service costs an online store $8 to $17, per 2026 call center benchmarks from Gartner. For anything under $20, arguing with you is literally more expensive than just giving you the money.

I went through the numbers on this. Shipping a returned item back to the warehouse costs $3 to $5. Inspecting it and shelving it again adds $2. And if the box is opened, there’s a decent chance they just throw it away. Optoro, a company that processes returns for big retailers, told NBC News in 2024 that handling a single return costs about 30% of whatever the item sold for. On a $20 item, you’re looking at $6 gone before anyone even picks up a phone. Amazon figured this out and in August 2023 started auto-approving refunds on everyday items under $75, especially anything where shipping it back costs more than the product itself. About a third of major retailers now do the same thing.

And Amazon is buying your loyalty while they’re at it. Customers who get a “just keep it” refund come back and buy again within 30 days about 82% of the time. Customers who had to box the item up and ship it back come back only 48% of the time, per Sequence Commerce data. Statista puts annual Prime member spending at about $1,400 versus $600 for non-Prime. Eating a $15 loss on a phone charger is nothing when the alternative is losing someone who drops $1,400 a year with you.

But saving on returns is just the first layer. Amazon’s AI chatbots now handle 70 to 83% of all customer questions without a human involved. One AI interaction costs about $0.10 to $0.50 versus $8 to $17 for a human call, roughly 16 times cheaper. And the system is getting proactive. Amazon’s AI can now detect a shipping delay, issue a refund, and notify you before you even know there’s a problem. 

Amazon is building toward a world where you never have to ask for a refund because the system already decided it was cheaper to just give you one.

"Shocking Levels Of Distress": Commercial Mortgage Backed Security Delinquencies Unexpectedly Soar To Covid Highs | Tyler Durden, Zerohedge

With market focused on private credit as the next credit market crisis vortex, many have forgotten that CMBS, the asset class that was smashed in the aftermath of covid as hundreds of office buildings were suddenly left vacant, has been teetering on the edge for years. For some, it proved to be a lucrative bet as the "next big short" after various office-heavy CMBX tranches collapsed in 2020 and 2021. But due to the slow-burning nature of commercial real-estate deterioration, where data center REITs provided a solid offset to weakness elsewhere, credit markets eventually moved on to the next worst thing.

It may be time to reassess: according to the latest TREPP CMBS monthly report, March saw a surge in the delinquency rate, which jumped by 41bps to 7.55%, the highest in years, led by a surge in the lodging rate, a category which until now was not a source of concern.

TREPP states that the five largest newly delinquent loans accounted for just over $2 billion of the almost $5.1 billion in newly delinquent loans, including a West Coast hotel portfolio, a Midwest office loan, a Northeast retail center loan, a national hotel portfolio, and a Pacific Northwest office portfolio, which pushed the rate higher.

In addition, roughly 40% of the newly delinquent loans this month were considered performing matured balloon last month. Continuing the sideways delinquency trend as loans mature, go delinquent, cure, and become delinquent again.

Among all newly delinquent loans, non-performing matured balloon was the most common delinquency classification, consistent with prior months.

At the property-type level, four of the five major property type rates increased while one edged down slightly. Lodging posted the largest increase, jumping 137 basis points to 7.31%, the first time it has been above 7% since its recent April 2025 peak of 7.85%. Office rose 51 basis points to 11.71%, maintaining the elevated range established over the past year, but remaining below January 2026’s recent high of 12.34%. Retail increased 32 basis points to 6.62%, rising from February’s recent low of 6.30% but remaining below the higher readings observed in 2024 and early 2025, when that rate averaged 6.71%. Multifamily was also especially week, as the delinquency rate rose 30 basis points to 7.15%, pushing slightly above its prior high-water mark of 7.12% in October 2025, and well past its marks from one year ago of 5.44% and 1.84% two years ago. Industrial - a stable category which includes warehouse and data center REITs - dipped slightly to 0.65% from 0.67%, continuing to sit near the bottom of the major property-type delinquency spectrum.

And in an ominous twist, if loans past their maturity date but current on interest (classified as performing matured balloon) were included, the delinquency rate would register 9.07%, up 32 basis points from February. This figure sits 152 basis points above the headline rate of 7.55% and continues to highlight the role of maturities in overall CMBS performance. The seriously delinquent rate (60+ days delinquent, in foreclosure, REO, or non‑performing balloons) also increased, rising to 7.29% (from 6.89%). The percentage of loan balance in the 30-day delinquent bucket is 0.26%, essentially flat versus February (0.25%).

In a well-timed report, the WSJ yesterday published a reminder that much of the battered US office market continues to drag along the bottom, and continues to hold a fire sale, featuring some buildings marked down by more than 90%.

Some striking examples:

- In Chicago, real-estate developer Marc Calabria bought a 485,000-square-foot office building for $4 million. The building sold for $68.1 million a decade ago.

- Developer Asher Luzzatto paid a mere $5.3 million for the Denver Energy Center, after a foreclosure process. The two-building complex sold for $176 million in 2013.

- Even the federal government’s landlord is getting in on the act. The General Services Administration last month sold a 940,000-square-foot building to a residential converter for $24 million, a tiny fraction of its value a few years ago.

Investors purchased 204 distressed office buildings nationwide last year, up from 133 sales in 2024, according to data firm MSCI. Sales of these properties, which were auctioned out of bankruptcies or sold through foreclosures and lender seizure, came to $5.2 billion. In the first two months of this year, sales volume of distressed offices was $808 million, up 24.5% from the same period last year, MSCI said.

The bottom line is this: we may be approaching the next commercial real estate crisis because much of the reserves that kept the sector semi-solvent for years, have run out. As the WSJ puts it, "landlords and their lenders held on to their office towers for years, hoping for a turnaround after Covid. Now, they are accepting enormous losses. Owners and creditors are capitulating to the reality that more employees are splitting their work time between home and office. They are also resigned to stubbornly higher interest rates, which lower property values and make it harder for buyers to borrow."

“People who don’t know real estate would be shocked at the level of distress,” Luzzatto said.

Of course, not every office building goes for a few pennies on the dollar. These are mostly B-grade, or poorer-quality buildings, often in undesirable locations. And owners of high-end office towers in the best locations of New York City and the hottest parts of San Francisco are raising rents and selling buildings profitably (although pockets of weakness are appearing there too, now that AI is making a growing number of tech workers obsolete).

But most office sales reflect the sector’s steep decline. Even higher-quality properties on average have dropped about 35% in value from their peak, according to analytics firm Green Street.

Buyers, meanwhile, are picking up office towers in major U.S. cities for roughly the price of a three-bedroom condo unit in Manhattan. These distressed sales are paving the way for new owners to pursue redevelopment ideas that would have been unthinkable just a few years ago.

Calabria in Chicago plans to convert the office building into an urban farm and education center. He is working with Farmzero, which will use grow lights and hydroponic farming techniques to produce millions of pounds a year of berries, tomatoes, lettuce, herbs and other vegetables.

“The buy-in at this distressed price allows us the opportunity to afford change,” Calabria said.

Rock-bottom prices are also accelerating the move to residential conversion. Developers who bought at steep discounts can now justify costly structural changes - such as carving out atriums or reconfiguring floor layouts - that would have been financially unworkable at higher valuations.

At the start of the year, more than 90,000 apartments nationwide were in the process of conversion nationwide, up 28% from a year earlier, according to data firm RentCafe. New York City’s obsolete buildings are leading the way, but tax breaks and other government incentives are helping spark similar projects in Chicago and Washington, D.C.

This reckoning follows years when office owners and their lenders avoided confronting the sector’s problems. Owners would inject more equity, while lenders extended loans in hopes of a rebound.

Now, with many concluding that values aren’t coming back, lenders are increasingly demanding repayment or selling the properties, a sign that the office market’s long slide that intensified during the pandemic is nearing a bottom.

“We’re six years from the shock of Covid,” said Jim Costello, an MSCI executive director. “But that’s how long it takes someone to capitulate and give up such a highly valued asset.”

The good news is that the threat of systemic risk remains low for now: many banks and other lenders are better positioned to take losses after spending the past few years shoring up their balance sheets and building reserves against troubled loans. Special servicers overseeing distressed office buildings financed through commercial mortgage-backed securities are also selling. The Chicago building being converted into an urban farm was sold by special servicer CW Asset Management, which said the low price was justified because the empty building’s taxes, utility bills and other costs were so high.

It isn’t just weak demand from remote work forcing down values. Owners must contend with the high cost of leasing up empty space -through hefty brokerage commissions and tenant incentives - and uncertainty about how AI could reshape office usage.

Sharp discounts are showing up in both downtown and suburban markets. For example, Newmark Group brokered the sale of five suburban Texas office buildings over the past two years at prices more than 50% lower than prepandemic values. Buyers demolished them to make way for higher-demand uses like industrial space.

Some of the big buyers of distressed office assets include Cross Ocean Partners, a credit-focused investment firm known for moving from one pocket of distress to another. It recently raised the first $300 million of a $750 million fund to buy distressed office assets—both debt and equity—in such markets as Minneapolis, Austin, Texas, and the Boston area.

The strategy centers on acquiring assets at steep discounts and underwriting the cash flow from existing tenants. Even if office demand remains weak, those in-place rents can generate a profit.

While institutional investors have largely pulled back from distress to focus on the strongest buildings in the most resilient markets, high-net-worth individuals are stepping in.

Hossein Fateh recently bought a 940,000-square-foot GSA building in Washington, D.C. A data-center investor, he made a fortune when Digital Realty paid $7.6 billion for DuPont Fabros Technology, which he co-founded.

Fateh is planning a residential conversion, adding a swimming pool or atriums in the middle of the floors to create windows. Such architectural hacks will help push the conversion cost into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

If the price wasn’t so low, “this deal wouldn’t work,” he said.

And with AI set to unleash the next big wave of office vacancy, coupled with banks throwing in the towel on cash-burning properties, many more such deals are emerging on the horizon.

Your cold emails are too long.

I just spent 20 minutes editing a single cold email down from 6 sentences to 4. Reply rate will probably jump 20-30%.

Most people write cold emails like they're drafting formal business correspondence. They're not.

Cold emails need to be ruthlessly concise. Every extra word is friction.

Here are the principles for writing cold emails that actually get replies:

1. Make every word earn its place

• Replace "complimentary" with "free"
• Replace "conversation" with "chat"
• Replace "Would you be interested in a complementary strategy session where I share..." with "Interested in a free strategy session? I'll share..."
• Cut phrases like "with a combined value of" and just bracket the number: ($500M)

2. Credibility needs multiple proof points

One case study is okay. Three is better.

• Instead of: "I've worked with Company A (sold for $200M)"
• Write: "I've helped exit Company A ($200M), Company B (acquired by Industry Leader), and Company C ($1B)"

Pack more proof into fewer words.

3. Add urgency to your CTA

• "Worth a quick chat to see if this could help?" is fine
• "Worth a quick chat this week to see if this could help?" is better

Most prospects who want to take a call want to do it soon. Make it easy for them.

4. Avoid jargon and long-winded phrases

• Bad: "As they navigated critical growth inflection points"
• Good: "Same playbook I used with [specific clients]"

Clear beats clever.

5. Only use 2-message sequences

Not 3. Not 4. Two messages maximum.

Why? Deliverability. More follow-ups increase spam risk, which kills your inbox.

• Most replies come from message 1
• Some from message 2
• Almost none from 3+

LinkedIn is different because deliverability isn't a concern there. For email, stick to 2.

6. Edit AI outputs relentlessly

Claude and ChatGPT give you a starting point, not a finished product.

• Go back and forth with the AI
• Make it tighter
• Make it punchier
• Remove the bloat

The same principles that make good content apply to cold emails: concise, clear, conversational.

7. Put 80% of effort into message 1

Your first email does the heavy lifting. That's where reply rates are won or lost.

The follow-up matters, but it's secondary. Get message 1 perfect first.

Most people spend equal time on all their messages. That's a mistake. Front-load your effort where it actually matters.

The difference between a 0.5% and 3% reply rate often comes down to removing 10-15 unnecessary words and tightening your proof points.

Cold email is a game of inches. Cut ruthlessly.
