Justin Bieber single-handedly saved Coachella in 2026 and in the process saved a lot of people's jobs. 

Two years ago, the most iconic music festival in the world could not sell tickets. This year, resale passes went for $4,000. In 2024, Coachella had its slowest ticket sales in a decade. First weekend passes that used to sell out within hours took nearly a month. Overall sales dropped 14 to 17% from the year before. The festival that once defined April for an entire generation of music fans was struggling to fill a field in Indio.

The problem was that Coachella had spent years becoming more about the brand than the music. Influencer activations. Fashion content. Instagram moments. The festival became a backdrop for content creation, and the actual product, the live music experience, started to feel secondary.

In 2025, they course-corrected with Lady Gaga, Post Malone, Green Day and Travis Scott. It helped. Ticket sales climbed back to 120,000 per weekend, up from roughly 80,000 in 2024. But the magic was not back. The festival still was not selling out on announcement day the way it had for over a decade.

Then they announced the 2026 lineup in September 2025. Justin Bieber as the Saturday headliner, his first time ever headlining Coachella. The festival sold out in three days.

Bieber is being paid over $10 million for two performances, the highest artist payout in the festival's 27-year history. Weekend 1 general admission passes that originally sold for $649 are currently listed at $2,900 or more on StubHub. VIP passes are clearing $5,000.

And this is a guy who three years ago could not move half his face.

In June 2022, Bieber was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a viral condition that caused partial facial paralysis. He canceled the remaining dates on his Justice World Tour and largely disappeared from the spotlight. No touring. No album cycle. No major performances for over two years. The comeback was not guaranteed.

Then in July 2025, he dropped SWAG, his seventh studio album. It debuted at number two on the Billboard 200 with 163,000 units in the first week. He logged 198 million on-demand streams in seven days, the biggest streaming week of his career. He followed it with SWAG II two months later. He launched a Twitch channel that pulled tens of thousands of concurrent viewers on day one. He performed at the Grammys in February. He played a private, no-phones show at The Roxy in late March that had the entire industry talking.

Last night he took the stage at Coachella with 103 million monthly listeners on Spotify and the most momentum of anyone in music.

Coachella did not recover because they redesigned the festival grounds or added better food vendors or landed a bigger influencer partnership. They recovered because they invested in the product. One headliner with a genuine cultural moment behind him turned a festival that could not sell tickets into a $3,000-per-pass event.

The brand did not save Coachella. The product did.

This is exactly what is happening across most marketing budgets right now.

Most businesses spend their entire budget on the brand side. Paid ads that put their name in front of people. Social media campaigns designed for visibility. Email blasts. PR placements. Influencer deals that rent someone else's audience for a news cycle. These are the influencer activations of marketing: they look impressive, they generate content, and they disappear the moment you stop paying for them.

None of those channels are the product. They are the brand wrapper around a product that may or may not exist.

The businesses that are winning in search and AI visibility right now are the ones that invested in the product. Not the brand campaign. Not the ad spend. The actual content.

Coachella spent years investing in everything except the product and watched ticket sales decline for the first time in its history. The moment they put a real headliner on that stage, the entire economics of the festival reversed overnight.

⁉I GOT PAID $10,000/HR FOR MY DATA⁉

Every day, we generate more data than we realize.

Every message we send, 
every voice note we record, 
every step we take with our phone in our pocket. 

Our digital lives are constantly feeding invisible systems that learn, predict, and profit from who we are.

It’s not just what you type or say. 

Your voice data carries unique patterns,
 tone, emotion, even stress levels that can reveal how you’re feeling. 

Your location data quietly logs where you’ve been, how long you stayed, and what stores or friends are nearby. 

Your daily activity,
the hours you wake up, when you drive, where you work out, how often you check your phone paints a precise behavioral map that’s worth a fortune to advertisers, insurers, and data brokers.

Even when you use apps that say your data is “encrypted,” 
it doesn’t mean you’re invisible. 

Encryption protects the content of your messages,
what you actually said or wrote.

but it doesn’t hide the metadata: who you talked to, 
when, how often, from where, and on what device. 

That metadata alone can reveal enough to predict relationships, routines, and even life changes.

Take WhatsApp, for example. 

Your chats are end-to-end encrypted meaning not even Meta can read the message content. 

But Meta still knows who you chat with, how long, and from which location or device. 

That information, combined across billions of users, is more than enough to feed algorithms that learn what keeps us online longer. 

Encryption protects privacy, but it doesn’t erase the footprints we leave behind.

And when we talk about voice data, 
it gets even deeper. 

Voice assistants, AI transcription tools, and smart devices collect snippets of speech to “improve accuracy.” 

Those recordings may be anonymized.

But they still feed machine-learning systems that shape ads, content, and services. 

Every “Hey Siri” or “OK Google” teaches them a little more about how we think, talk, and react.

Even Apple wasn’t immune, 
they faced a $95 million lawsuit after Siri was found to accidentally record IRL private conversations 
and share snippets with contractors for “quality checks.”

Meanwhile, 
location data is one of the most valuable commodities online. 

Advertisers pay to know where people shop, 
what routes they take, and how their movements change over time. 

Fitness apps, weather apps, delivery apps, even games have been caught selling location data to third parties. 

And the scary part is we agree to it in the "T/C statement" we rarely read.

Don't get me started on the face data,
the most personal form of all.

Every selfie, face unlock, or KYC verification trains someone’s algorithm. 

Our faces are biometric signatures that can track us. 

Companies say it’s for ‘security’ or ‘personalization,’ 
but those scans often fuel AI training, ads, or third-party databases.

We live in a world where data is power, 
but that power is rarely in our hands. 

Most of us never see the profit from the constant stream of information we generate. 

Companies claim to protect our privacy, yet our “anonymous” data still fuels entire economies of prediction and influence.

Some Web3 projects came with a promise “own your data, get paid for your digital footprint.”

But the question is, how much is enough?

On whose terms are we really selling it?

Many of these so-called “data ownership” platforms reward users with dust tokens.

Coins worth fractions of a cent,
while the same data is packaged, analyzed, and sold for millions.

They tell you you’re in control.

But most times, you’re just consenting to being harvested in a more polished way.

Sadly,
Some of the projects waving the “decentralization” flag the loudest, might actually be the new middlemen masked under smart contracts and DAO votes.

NB: 
Studies shows that if you are selling Data individually, 
it is actually worth cents or a few hundreds.

But together, can generate billions for companies.

Now,
the real question is: how much are you willing to get paid for your data?

And don't forget to always read terms and conditions,

Because in the digital age, ignorance is not bliss.

Building Digital Wealth: Start Investing Today

One of the most profound financial principles comes not from Wall Street but from the Torah. In Deuteronomy 8:17, we’re warned: "Be careful not to say, ‘My own ability and skill have gotten me this wealth.'"

Success requires more than talent—it demands discipline and humility.

When I asked #Google for the secret to success, it replied: "Consistency and hard work, persistently pursuing goals with focused effort over time." #ChatGPT gave a different angle: "Do what you said you would do—especially when you no longer feel like doing it."

So, what’s the fastest way to build wealth?

Truthfully, there is no single shortcut. But there is a proven strategy: diversify your investments. King Solomon, one of the wisest men to ever live, wrote in Ecclesiastes 11:2: "Invest in seven ventures, yes, in eight; you do not know what disaster may come upon the land."

Modern financial institutions echo that timeless wisdom. Vanguard states, "Portfolio diversification is key to long-term investment success… including bonds, commodities, and real estate."

But there’s one overlooked category that belongs on that list: digital assets—specifically, domain names.

Why Domain Names Are the Hidden Gem of Alternative Investing

Unlike traditional assets, premium domain names are finite. There will never be another Voice.com (sold for $30 million) or Wisdom.ai (reportedly $750,000). Imagine registering one of those years ago for less than the price of dinner.

Forty years ago, many of today’s domain millionaires started with $70. Today, you can begin with as little as $10. Were those early investors lucky? Perhaps. But luck favors the disciplined, curious, and forward-thinking.

If you want to succeed in domain investing—or any form of wealth building—ask yourself:

• Do I have the discipline to research?
• The patience to wait?
• The open mind to learn?
• The focus on ignoring noise?
• The courage to act before everyone else sees the opportunity?

If yes, you have a real shot.

The First Step Isn’t Buying. It’s Learning.

Don’t rush to register names or hunt for marketplaces. The first and most crucial step is education.

Learning helps you understand:

• How buyers think
• Why some domains are worth $100 and others $14 million
• What makes one extension (.com, .net, .ai, .xyz) powerful and another forgettable
• When to act—and when to walk away

There are endless resources online—some brilliant, others useless. You will make mistakes. That’s normal. Your goal is to make small mistakes and learn from each one.

Study success stories—but study failures even more. They reveal the traps others fell into so you can avoid them.

If after reading this, you commit not to buying—but to learning first—you’ve already boosted your odds of success by 50%.

I look forward to meeting you at the top—not as a reader, but as a fellow digital #domain investor.

What do you do with all that appreciated Palantir stock? We asked a financial expert for advice. 👀
10-17-2025

Question: I bought Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock when it was trading at $8. It's now at $180 and I've made $1 million. What should I do?

Answer: Nicely done!

Palantir is one of the greatest investing success stories of our lifetime. Since going public in 2020, its shares are up almost 1,800% – a massive return. It's one of the best-performing stocks in 2025 and now sports a market cap close to half a trillion dollars.

Once a low-profile number cruncher for the military and intelligence services, the company has now positioned itself as the Pentagon's nerve center for artificial intelligence (AI) and as a major player in business analytics.

The problem of the modern era isn't a lack of information. It's quite literally the opposite. We're drowning in data that can be hard to structure and interpret. And that's where Palantir steps in. It makes big data digestible and usable for decision-making.

None of this is likely to change any time soon, and Palantir remains the top dog in this space.

But after such an epic run, what should you do? Do you take your profits on this surging tech stock and look for the next opportunity, or do you keep riding this trend as far as it goes?

Let's go through a few scenarios and discuss the pros and cons of each.

Don't get greedy

There's an old maxim on Wall Street: Bulls make money, bears make money, but pigs get slaughtered. Having a disproportionate share of your portfolio in any single stock — even a revolutionary one like Palantir — is risky.

A free-market economy is naturally disruptive, and this is even more true in the tech sector. Today's cutting-edge leader is tomorrow's tech dinosaur.

International Business Machines (IBM), Intel (INTC), Cisco Systems (CSCO), Dell Technologies (DELL) … All of these companies were major innovators and indispensable to the tech economies of their day. And they all traded at massive premiums to the broader market. None maintain the same relevance today, and not a single one of these tech stocks warrants a high earnings or sales multiple.

Palantir, meanwhile, trades for 588 times earnings and 130 times sales. Those numbers are so high that they look like typos. To put them in perspective, the S&P 500 is expensive by historical standards and yet trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of "only" 31. Its price-to-sales ratio is 3.4.

A company enjoying Palantir's growth rates should trade at a premium valuation, of course. But there's premium … and then there's delusion. This would seem to fall into the latter category.

Selling your Palantir position, or at least trimming little by little, could be smart risk management.

There are two downsides to selling, of course. The first is that you miss out on additional upside if the stock continues rising. The second is the potential tax hit.

Assuming a cost basis of close to nothing, a $1 million profit in Palantir would mean paying something in the ballpark of $200,000 in capital gains taxes.

This brings us to a second option.

Hold on to PLTR stock for dear life

You've done fantastically well by simply holding on to your Palantir position this long. The path of least resistance — and the least exposure to capital gains taxes — is just to keep holding.

There are legitimate reasons you might want to simply hold on, apart from tax avoidance.

Palantir is the leader in AI analytics. Its earnings per share nearly doubled in 2024 and are expected to grow by 56% this year and 33% next year. Why wouldn't you want to maintain outsize exposure to this successful stock?

Any trader will tell you that the secret to really making money in the market is to cut your losers early and let your winners run.

That's legitimate. But you need to have some risk management in place for when the AI bubble bursts.

One option could be to use a series of stop losses. You could instruct your broker to sell off, say, 20% of your position at a certain pain point, such as a 10% to 15% decline in the share price. You could have a second sell order in place to unload another 20% of your position if the share price drops even further.

This doesn't eliminate your tax liability, of course. You'd still be on the hook for capital gains taxes on any shares you sold for a profit. But you'd potentially be spreading out the gains over a couple of years.

If things got really bad — such as in a repeat of the 2000-2002 tech bust — you'd be better off paying the taxes rather than watching years of gains go down the tube.

What other options do I have?

You have other options.

If you regularly give to your church or a favorite charity, consider donating appreciated stock instead of cash. Because most nonprofits are tax-exempt, they can sell the stock without paying capital-gains taxes — and you still receive a charitable deduction for the full fair-market value of the gift.

If you're willing to get a little creative, there are also more sophisticated ways to diversify a concentrated portfolio without triggering a large tax bill. Firms such as AQR Capital Management, Nuveen and other specialized managers offer leveraged long/short strategies designed to intentionally realize losses that can offset existing capital gains.

In broad terms, these managers run aggressive long/short portfolios — buying stocks expected to rise and shorting those likely to fall. Naturally, there will be both winners and losers, but the manager selectively realizes the losing positions. The realized losses then provide tax offsets, allowing you to gradually unwind a large position over several years without being hit with a single, massive tax bill.

Of course, this doesn't eliminate taxes. It merely defers them. That's often acceptable, especially if your long-term goal is to leave the portfolio to your heirs, who would receive a stepped-up cost basis upon your death. In that case, those deferred gains could effectively disappear altogether.

Because these strategies involve leverage and short selling, they carry additional risks and complexities. It's essential to consult a qualified tax or investment professional before proceeding.

Finally, keep perspective: having a large, appreciated stock position is a high-quality problem. It can create tax challenges, yes. But having taxes to pay at least means that you made money.

U.S. HYPERSCALE DATA CENTER MARKET TRENDS

Liquid Cooling Solutions For AI/ML Workloads

Liquid cooling offers several advantages over traditional air-based systems, particularly in terms of efficiency, sustainability, and performance. Unlike air cooling, which struggles to release the heat generated by today's powerful AI and ML chips, liquid cooling uses circulating fluids to remove heat directly from the source, providing faster and more effective cooling. This is essential for keeping AI-driven data centers running smoothly, as even brief periods of overheating or downtime can lead to costly disruptions and equipment damage.

In March 2025, Crypto and AI data center company @IREN_Ltd announced its plans to develop a 75 MW AI data center in Texas. They are planning to deploy a new 75 MW liquid-cooling data center for AI/high-performance computing at its Childress site in Texas. It will be designed to support 200 kW per rack via direct-to-chip cooling for NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs.

Microsoft continues to integrate direct-to-chip liquid cooling and research microfluidic technologies to enhance energy efficiency in its data centers, driven by increasing demands from AI workloads. These innovations aim to optimize server layouts, reduce water consumption, and increase rack power density while enabling higher compute power per sq ft. This shift supports the goal of Microsoft to become water-positive by 2030, amidst rising water usage across its global operations.

Growth in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Automation

The U.S. remains the global leader in AI and ML adoption, with hyperscale cloud providers, enterprises, and government-backed initiatives driving massive investments in next-generation digital infrastructure. AI workloads, including generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and HPC, fuel demand for hyperscale campuses and specialized GPU clusters across the country.

In August 2025, Vantage Data Centers unveiled its record-breaking $25 billion Frontier Campus in Shackelford County, Texas. The site is likely to host 1.4 GW of IT load capacity across 10 hyperscale AI-ready facilities, designed to power the next wave of generative AI deployments.

In August 2025, Applied Digital invested $3 billion to develop Polaris Forge 2, a 280MW AI and HPC-focused data center campus in Harwood, North Dakota. The project, designed with liquid cooling technology and backed by Cass County Electric Cooperative, reflects the shift of the company from cryptomining to AI infrastructure, with advanced negotiations underway with a US-based hyperscaler.

U.S. HYPERSCALE DATA CENTER MARKET SEGMENTATION INSIGHTS

U.S. data centers are rapidly scaling server infrastructure to handle the explosive growth of AI, cloud computing, and HPC workloads. Hyperscale operators and enterprises are increasingly deploying energy-efficient, high-density servers to reduce power usage while maximizing performance.

The chips will power one of the largest AI-focused facilities in the world, part of a $500 billion multi-campus project aimed at delivering over 1GW of capacity per site.

Given the cost-effectiveness of diesel generators compared to alternatives, they remain the most widely used power source in data centers. Major hyperscale operators using HVO for generators include Compass Datacenters and Vantage Data Centers. Other operators like Digital Realty are increasingly turning to HVO as a cleaner and more sustainable alternative to conventional diesel for backup generators.

Widely used in HPC environments, liquid cooling replaces air with water or other coolants to absorb and remove heat more effectively from electronic devices, providing better temperature control and efficiency. Stolen IDs sold for ‘Happy Meal’ prices fuel billions in US benefit fraud | Amanda Macias, Fox News

Buying a stolen identity can cost less than a fast-food meal, enabling criminals to use AI and internet tutorials to file fraudulent benefit claims from anywhere in the world, a former inspector general warned Congress on Wednesday.

Lawmakers are already ramping up scrutiny of fraud in major federal aid programs — including unemployment, Medicaid and food assistance — as criminals leverage AI, stolen identities and online tools to exploit systems and drain billions in taxpayer dollars.

Federal watchdogs previously estimated that more than $100 billion in pandemic-era unemployment benefits alone may have been lost to fraud, much of it tied to weak identity verification and oversight gaps.

"The internet has reduced barriers to fraud," said retired inspector general Bob Westbrooks during a House Oversight Committee hearing on fraud in federally funded state programs.

"Offenders can find free tutorials online, purchase stolen identities for the price of a Happy Meal, and file claims from anywhere in the world. With automation tools, they can even submit multiple claims across multiple states," added Westbrooks, who spent nearly three decades in public service focused on anti-fraud efforts.

He warned that "the prevalence of fraud discussions online normalizes this behavior and reduces the fear of getting caught and punished."

Massive fraud schemes in recent years have underscored the scope of the problem, including a $250 million "Feeding Our Future" case in Minnesota that resulted in dozens of convictions, and a roughly $100 million welfare scandal in Mississippi that led to criminal charges and high-profile prosecutions.

The issue has become so glaring that President Donald Trump appointed Vice President J.D. Vance as the new 'fraud czar' and tasked him with addressing taxpayer theft – especially in blue states where local officials refuse to cooperate with the administration.

Other auditors and federal officials have pointed to systemic weaknesses in benefit programs, including payments to deceased individuals, duplicate claims filed across multiple states and limited real-time verification of eligibility.

"There’s no one-size-fits-all solution," Westbrooks said, noting the complexity of policing massive federal programs.

"To be frank, it is simply impossible or impracticable to design a 100% fraud-proof program," he added.

Still, Westbrooks emphasized that fraud should not be accepted as a cost of doing business.

"The American public should reasonably expect that public money is not used to pay dead people, incarcerated individuals, or duplicate claims in the same state or across states, and that public funds are otherwise appropriately safeguarded," Westbrooks said.

"Officials should aggressively but responsibly adopt new technology tools in the fight against fraud."

He added that safeguarding taxpayer dollars will require "a coordinated and comprehensive, risk- and data-driven approach" to reduce losses and restore public trust.

Today's biggest semiconductor industry news is that Gerard has founded a new ARM CPU company, Nuvacore, five years after Nuvia was acquired by Qualcomm. Even the name closely echoes the predecessor.

Starting a datacenter CPU company at this point in time means catching what is arguably the best decade for CPUs in recent memory. The shortage wave that AI agents will usher in is already faintly visible, and several AWS customers have gone so far as to request entire blocks of Graviton ARM CPU capacity wholesale.

The pull this news exerts on Silicon Valley's semiconductor crowd is enormous. Nuvacore's lineup is stacked exclusively with proven star players — the original Nuvia founding team reunited, backed by Sequoia, building general-purpose ARM CPUs aimed at AI infrastructure and agentic computing. The direction was entirely unvalidated back then, yet ended in resounding success. Now ARM CPU servers sit squarely in the eye of the storm. The scale of the outlook and the imagination it invites are incomparable to Nuvia in 2019.

Last time Gerard poached architectural heavyweights from Google's and Apple's platform architecture teams; this time his pitch will land far harder. A $240M raise, a proven playbook, a reassembled founding team, and the next wave of growth visible straight ahead — all of it conspires to make Nuvacore the hottest, most sought-after semiconductor startup in the Bay Area, and by some distance. This is, after all, a chance at financial freedom right in front of you with an exceptionally favorable risk/reward profile.

The first-generation Nuvia CPU announcement landed in the Apple M2 era and was genuinely shocking. Nuvia pushed Qualcomm's CPU benchmark scores forward by a full three generations in a single year, with single-core scores climbing from 2300 to 3200, decisively outpacing the Apple M2 Max.

The disappointment was that Nuvia's Phoenix core dragged far too long from announcement to actual launch. In that interval Apple went on a toothpaste-squeezing tear, pushing out M3 and M4 back-to-back. By the time Nuvia's CPU finally shipped, it was being benchmarked against the M4 rather than the M2, and fell from anticipated protagonist to mere background.

Nuvia's foresight back then was well ahead of the field. In 2019, ARM CPU server market share was essentially zero, and Nuvia set out to crack this market from scratch. After the $1.4B acquisition by Qualcomm in 2021, Qualcomm pledged unlimited resources, went on an aggressive hiring expansion, and offered compensation at the very top of the market.

Unfortunately, the external environment deteriorated sharply in 2022, and on top of that, Qualcomm's leadership displayed strategic myopia of the worst kind. Just as the ARM server ecosystem was beginning to stretch its limbs, Qualcomm dissolved its own Nuvia CPU server team for the sake of share price and cost reduction (the second time — they had already dismantled an ARM server team back in 2015).

It was only in 2025 — four years after NVIDIA's Grace ARM CPU had already been announced, long after Vera ARM CPU had been in internal development, and with Amazon's Graviton accounting for nearly 50% of new server CPU shipments — that Qualcomm belatedly and tentatively restarted its ARM server project.

So Gerard walking out of a senior Qualcomm position to regroup the original founding team and do this himself is probably because Qualcomm's leadership has been so short-sighted that it kept missing the window. When Nuvia wanted to do ARM servers the first time around, Qualcomm's commitments turned into bad checks the moment the macro turned; after the acquisition, the project was cancelled outright and redirected toward laptop and smartphone chips.

Further, Qualcomm is bracing for a meaningful hit to smartphone sales this year from the historic surge in memory and storage prices (the market is contracting roughly 30%), and expansion budgets are constrained, so the resources available internally are limited.

And a startup offers far easier access to decision velocity, team purity, product definition authority, and a capital story than a large platform like Qualcomm can. That is why, with the window already validated, the original members have been reassembled.

But the more fundamental reason is probably that the CPU outlook in the AI era has genuinely become so vast that jumping back in is worth it. Gerard hasn't changed — the external market has.

Since entering 2025, the arrival of AI agents has been quietly turning the CPU back into a bottleneck. CPU servers have re-entered a growth trajectory, and the latent potential is considerable. A few factors:

1. As the inference era arrives, GPUs have evolved into inference-specialized system-level architectures, while CPUs have become the perpetually busy orchestrator. The pursuit of token throughput multiplies the number of heterogeneous compute stages, batch sizes grow, scheduling / routing / dataflow complexity rises, and orchestration requirements scale accordingly.

So in system-level heterogeneous inference architectures, the CPU-to-GPU ratio has turned far more aggressive. From the previous 1:4, to 1:2 in Grace Blackwell, and likely heading toward 1:1. Google TPU pairs with Axion, Amazon Trainium with Graviton, NVIDIA Rubin with its own Vera CPU.

I wrote about this in last November's semiconductor year-end review, and by 2026 it has essentially become consensus. That said, this piece is mostly captured by each company's in-house AI chip efforts, so it's hard to count as pure CPU server demand, and it's ambiguous whether it constitutes an opportunity for the external CPU server market.

2. Also from that same year-end review:

Viewed from the CPU angle, agentic workloads run routing and tool handling entirely on CPU. Profile popular agentic frameworks like SWE-Agent, LangChain, and Toolformer and you'll find that CPU can account for up to 90% of end-to-end latency; throughput bottlenecks land on the CPU more often than not; and CPU energy consumption can exceed 40% of total energy draw.

Agentic AI, today, is more of a CPU-bottlenecked workload. Agents manage numerous CPUs, and they need to spin up sandboxes frequently — this has a very strong chance of triggering a fresh recovery cycle in CPU demand.

Looking back now, the latent potential of this thesis I wrote last year is substantial. But it hadn't materialized at scale at the start of this year. The CPU growth and the "CPU shortage wave" that various players have been talking about early this year aren't directly tied to this logic — they're more about backfilling the traditional CPU server under-investment that accumulated from years of over-allocating capex to GPUs.

In H2, and certainly into 2027, agents will spread much more broadly. Smart shopping assistants and customer service agents, for instance, already accounted for a significant share of Amazon's 1M CPU procurement late last year, and growth in this segment is very fast.

The first two threads are essentially the mainstream consensus when this year's market talks about CPU potential. But there are two more threads I think are underappreciated:

3. The main thread that makes CPU server potential bigger and longer-lived may not be directly tied to agents themselves. It's a byproduct of code agents.

As the barrier and speed of coding have been dramatically optimized, the entire cost of "building software + connecting software + calling software + automating software" has collapsed by an order of magnitude. On the software supply side, the Jevons paradox kicks in — the world is pushed toward higher software density and higher API density, which in turn translates directly into a linear increase in traditional CPU workloads.

Since late 2025, coding agents have undergone a qualitative shift. Claude Code has seen explosive growth, with token revenue tripling in three months. The next phase will inevitably be a 10x increase in code volume and an explosion in the number of apps.

Even at the large enterprise level, daily consumption of 1M tokens is merely average, and per-capita coding output will inevitably at least double (at small companies, 10x). The surge in code supply doesn't stay inside repos — it gradually becomes long-running software assets, meaning more long-lived features, more products, more microservices, more APIs.

Over the long run, the total production cost and production cycle of every app and API collapse to about 10% of their original levels, and APIs become extraordinarily abundant. API usage then rises in bulk, which drives a bulk rise in traditional CPU workloads — in CPU seconds. This doesn't even have a direct tie to "agentic."

On the time axis, this thread is not short-dated. Claude Code's inflection is only a few months old, and the product releases, microservice releases, and API releases that follow are necessarily delayed further out in time. Software getting cheaper doesn't mean society uses less software — it means more work gets shifted onto software.

So in H2 or later, we'll probably see a phenomenon where traditional CPU cloud demand mysteriously rises again — one that on the surface doesn't even appear directly linked to AI agents.

4. CPU is technically very hard to deflate. It does not have the property that, like memory/storage, you can compress the per-task footprint through various compression algorithms. Growth in CPU workloads translates into hardware demand growth for real.

For example, KV cache sees new compression techniques each year. An older one, multi-head KV cache sharing down to a single head (GQA), delivers roughly a 4x compression. Last year's turboquant-style techniques added several more multiples of compression. Add data precision dropping from FP16 toward the next step of FP4, and the precision reduction brings KV cache compression — technical deflation on the storage side.

But on CPU, the technical deflation headroom is very thin. Every increment in today's agentic CPU workload (CPU seconds) converts into real hardware demand, essentially in full. The only deflationary factor amounts to the 10–15% benchmark score uplift per generation per year. What about other deflationary factors, like cloud's 5–6x over-sell? No — because CPU has always been over-sold to begin with. The over-sell / underutilization technical deflation on CPU will not widen further from here, and every incremental CPU second converts linearly into hardware with no meaningful discount.

ARM's guidance is that the CPU supply-demand gap could widen to 30%+. Stack these factors, add the fact that AI servers are cannibalizing CPU server capacity and order slots, and the gap could grow further, with hyperscalers' responses likely running a step behind.

At the same time as aggregate CPU demand potential is rising, ARM server CPU is living through its best era in history.

Roughly 50% of the new traditional server CPUs hyperscalers are deploying for cost optimization are ARM — Google's Axion, Amazon's Graviton, Microsoft's Cobalt. Graviton's 2026 capacity is already fully sold, with the bottleneck having shifted to capacity itself.

Google TPU pairs with Axion, Amazon Trainium with Graviton, NVIDIA Rubin with its own Vera. The collective rotation of these CPUs toward ARM is driven by more than cost. As inference systems push token throughput to the limit, batches get larger and more complex, and under those conditions, ARM CPU in-house development plus system-level HW-SW co-design is much more convenient. NVIDIA, for instance, uses Dynamo to orchestrate Vera–Rubin cooperation.

From Nuvacore's plan, it doesn't look content to stop at IP — it is going after finished products. The hiring page already lists validation engineer roles.

That said, the challenges Nuvacore faces this time are not small. The start is far later. Both the market and the technology are far more competitive. CPU servers are vastly more complex than seven years ago — the contest is no longer at the individual CPU level but at rack-system complexity.

Building a CPU now for 2028–2029 launch that is competitive at the rack level requires much greater scale. You basically have to assemble dozens of chiplets, 500+ cores, while simultaneously working out how to handle AI agentic workloads. The workload has grown noticeably larger than before. The bar for a startup is meaningfully higher than seven years ago.

Last time, Nuvia was successfully sold for $1.4B just two years after founding. The heat in this market is orders of magnitude hotter than five years ago. So what does the road ahead look like for Nuvacore?

On the acquisition route, the pool of potential acquirers has not really expanded versus five years ago. Over these five years, Google got Axion, Microsoft got Cobalt, Amazon got Graviton, and NVIDIA's in-house Vera CPU has already taken shape. Even ARM has broken its 35-year IP-only tradition and begun building its own AGI CPU chips.

The most plausible acquirer is the SoftBank camp. SoftBank has been building deep positions in the ARM CPU server ecosystem for years, and acquired Ampere for $6.5B. Adding Nuvacore on top would be a natural follow-on, and the imagination this market affords more than justifies that kind of price tag.

Another possibility is Meta. Among the major internet companies, Meta is the only one without a reliably in-house CPU server offering, and what limited resources it has are going into MTIA on the AI accelerator side.

The problem with Meta, though, is that its stability is extremely low. Decisions shift month to month, attention span is very short-term, and projects can be killed at any time. For Nuvacore, it would be a very poor acquirer — one that wouldn't let the company realize any of its potential.

Taken as a whole, Nuvacore's option set is considerably wider than it was five years ago. The consensus around ARM CPU server potential is now firmly in place. Funding difficulty is meaningfully lower. The friction for operating and scaling independently is much reduced versus the past. And partners are more willing to engage, buoyed by expectations of the future.

It is entirely reasonable to scale well beyond where Nuvia was before considering an exit. There is no need to rush.

This shoe company just became an AI infrastructure provider overnight.

And the stock went up almost 600%.

Let me explain why this is so ridiculous and concerning:

Allbirds - the wool sneaker brand once worshipped by Silicon Valley - announced it is selling its shoe business for $39 million and rebranding itself as "NewBird AI."

A "fully integrated GPU-as-a-Service and AI-native cloud solutions provider."

Those are their words. Not mine.

A company with ZERO experience in semiconductors.

ZERO experience in data centers.

ZERO experience in cloud infrastructure.

ZERO customers.

ZERO GPUs on hand.

The stock closed Tuesday at $2.49. It opened Wednesday and shot up to nearly $22. A 582% move in one session.

The funding? A $50 million convertible from an unnamed institutional investor. Subject to shareholder approval on May 18.

That's it. That's literally the entire transformation.

Sell the shoes for $39 million. Take $50 million from somebody willing to hand it over. Add "AI" to the name. Watch retail traders lose their minds.

This reminds me of an older story:

In December 2017, a beverage company called Long Island Iced Tea Corp. announced it was changing its name to "Long Blockchain Corp." and pivoting to crypto.

The stock jumped nearly 300% in a single day. Trading volume up 1,000%.

But they had no blockchain business. No blockchain employees. No blockchain anything.

14 months later, NASDAQ delisted them. The SEC eventually charged 3 people with insider trading on the name change itself.

The company never filed another financial report. The blockchain business never existed.

It’s the same playbook, only with a different buzzword.

And here is what should worry every serious investor:

Allbirds once traded above $600 a share. It was valued at roughly $4 billion in 2021.

The shoe business they just sold for $39 million.

That is a 99% wipeout of real operating value, from a real company selling real products.

But the moment they stapled "AI" to the shell, retail traders bid the market cap up by $127 million in a single day.

Buying what, exactly?

A press release. A $50 million IOU. A NAME change.

When a dying retailer can create 9 figures of "value" by announcing it will buy GPUs it does not own, from suppliers it has no relationships with, to serve customers it does not have - you are no longer looking at a market.

Hyperscalers are spending $380 billion a year on real AI infrastructure and most of the buyers still cannot measure a return. And now we are pricing a wool sock company as a neocloud.

This is how late-cycle tops feel from the inside. Not with a crash. With absurdity.

Long Blockchain Corp. was not a business. It was a warning.

Allbirds-to-NewBird-AI is the same warning but louder.

Own real cash flow. Own gold. Own silver. Own companies that make things people actually buy.

Not stupid hype.

These are basics. 

You are correct that perp future longs being liquidated don’t cancel out any direct spot buy pressure, because opening them didn’t cause any direct spot buy pressure in the first place. I never claimed otherwise. In fact I have explicitly explained this several times. 

The canceling out is for leveraged spot. It’s not a cancellation to the effect that price has to return exactly to where it started - it’s a cancellation, or if you prefer “unwinding”, of the borrowed portion of the buy pressure (in USD, if that’s what you trade in) from when you opened the long. 

That is: 
Price is $10, you have $100, borrow $1,000, and buy spot for $1,100. 

Later, you are liquidated. Price at this point is already < $10, which is why you’re liquidated. At this point your position will be sold for (roughly) $1,000 (discounting fees and additional margin requirements) which (not coincidentally) matches the amount you borrowed: the reason you are liquidated is so you can repay the whole amount you borrowed, so the core idea is to liquidate you just before your position is worth less than what you borrowed. This is the “cancellation” $1,000 sell pressure that matches the borrowed $1,000 buy pressure from when you opened the long. 

It does obviously NOT cancel neatly the effect on price so it ends up where you started. Price was already lower than that when you got liquidated. 

So, at liquidation: 

Price is around $9, your position is worth (around) $1,000 (down $100) and is sold for $1,000, cancelling neatly the earlier buy pressure from the borrowed $1,000. After liquidation, price may be even lower than $9, pushed down from your forced $1,000 sell plus potentially cascading liquidations and stop losses. 

You shouldn’t need to ask an AI to know this, it’s basic stuff.

Cash and equivalents rose to KRW27.9 trillion, interest‑bearing debt to KRW24.1 trillion, leaving net cash of KRW3.8 trillion and a 24% debt‑to‑equity ratio. DRAM bit shipments rose by high single digits, led by HBM3E 12‑high and server DDR5; shipments of ≥128 GB DDR5 modules doubled q/q for a second consecutive quarter. NAND bit shipments declined mid single digits off a high base, but enterprise SSD units grew double digits and ASPs rose low‑teens, lifting NAND profitability. Management guided Q4 bit growth to low single digits for both DRAM and NAND as inventories normalize, but emphasized that demand visibility is locked by LTAs across DRAM, NAND and HBM through 2026. The company has completed development and mass‑production preparation of HBM4, will begin HBM4 shipments in Q4, and has finalized 2026 HBM supply with key customers at pricing sufficient to “sustain current profitability.” The team reiterated that HBM supply will remain tight versus demand into 2027 and that even non‑HBM DRAM and NAND capacity is effectively sold out next year. Capex will step up materially in 2026 with accelerated M15X tool‑in and Yongin Fab‑1 schedule pull‑ups, while shareholder returns stay unchanged to prioritize reinvestment. ￼

Demand drivers are broadening from AI training to large‑scale inference, which is reshaping the memory hierarchy and catalyzing simultaneous pull on HBM, DDR5 and high‑performance SSDs. Management described how rising concurrency, longer context windows and multimodal models expand KV‑cache linearly with context length; when HBM is insufficient, KV‑cache spills to conventional DRAM and then to NVMe SSDs. They also highlighted RAG architectures requiring vector databases that favor high‑IOPS TLC and high‑density QLC eSSDs. This framing matters: it converts what looked like a single‑product boom into a system‑level memory supercycle in which DRAM and NAND benefit from AI even when HBM is the headline. External work is directionally consistent: industry analyses point to generative‑AI inference elevating SSD demand in servers, while technical communities have documented KV‑cache offload to SSD when the active set exceeds HBM/DRAM capacity. The call’s own commentary noted accelerating HDD tightness pushing hyperscalers toward eSSD, reinforcing that NAND content per AI and storage server is stepping higher. The implication is that AI demand propagation will support multi‑year mix‑up and ASP support across the stack, rather than a narrow, single‑node HBM pulse. ￼ ￼

On HBM product trajectory, the company confirmed HBM4 readiness and said it is already meeting upgraded, above‑JEDEC performance requirements, with sampling completed faster than peers and production started for mass supply. JEDEC finalized HBM4 this spring with a 2,048‑bit interface and up to 8 Gb/s signaling, and SK hynix subsequently announced devices certified for 10 GT/s, 25% above the baseline spec. The company expects the HBM market to grow at an average of >30% over the next 5 years, supported by hyperscaler and AI‑company capex uplifts. Competitive dynamics are evolving. TrendForce and press reports indicate SK hynix led HBM share in 2024 and early 2025, while Samsung has recently achieved Nvidia certification on 12‑high HBM3E with volume ramps more likely weighted to 2026 given existing supplier allocations; Micron has been gaining share as well and has public HBM4 ambitions. Near‑term, SK hynix’s earlier HBM4 availability and entrenched 3E production should preserve mix and margin leadership; medium‑term, a faster Samsung catch‑up would compress pricing power as HBM4e proliferates in 2026‑2027. The investment consequence is that multiple points of competitive execution—yield on 12‑high and 16‑high stacks, TSV reliability, thermals, and advanced packaging alignment—will increasingly dictate pricing and share, raising the premium on process control and LTAs. ￼ ￼

Capacity and packaging are the gating factors. TSMC’s CoWoS capacity is moving from roughly 35k WPM in 2024 toward 70k by end‑2025 and about 90k by end‑2026, but bottlenecks persist given Nvidia, custom ASIC and networking demand. The investment read‑through is that HBM supply growth will be lumpy and path‑dependent on both memory and OSAT/CoWoS capacity ramps; companies that secure substrate, interposer, and CoWoS slots alongside DRAM wafers will monetize the cycle, while latecomers face allocation risk even with adequate DRAM die output. ￼ ￼

Conventional DRAM and NAND are now structurally tighter because HBM consumes disproportionate fab area, process steps and line time, crowding out legacy mix while demand for DDR5 and DDR4 in storage servers remains strong. Management expects DRAM demand growth to lift from high‑teens this year to >20% next year, with 1C‑nm DRAM to comprise >50% of conventional DRAM capacity in Korea by end‑2026, improving cost per bit and speed grades for DDR5, LPDDR5 and graphics. On NAND, the company is prioritizing profitability and moving into 321‑layer TLC and QLC, with 321‑layer planned to exceed 50% of NAND bits by end‑2026. Combined with enterprise SSD mix normalization and HDD tightness, this should keep NAND pricing firmer than prior cycles. Third‑party checks echo DDR5 mainstreaming while DDR4’s lifecycle extends through 2026 in storage‑heavy fleets, which reinforces blended DRAM ASP strength. The underappreciated point here is that rising HBM mix mechanically constrains marginal DRAM supply, improving price discovery for DDR5/DDR4 even absent a smartphone or PC boom. ￼ ￼

Pricing and profitability dynamics are supportive into 2026. The company acknowledged that DRAM spot and contract prices have risen sharply enough to narrow the margin gap with HBM; however, it will not shift capacity away from HBM because supply is governed by long‑term, volume‑certain agreements and because HBM remains structurally higher‑margin. Inventory is extremely lean, particularly for DDR5, with products shipping directly from line to customer. The CFO also guided that while free cash flow is improving, incremental cash will be directed to capex to secure leadership rather than to incremental shareholder distributions in year‑1 of the new return policy. For investors, the combination of tight inventories, LTAs, and capex discipline implies elevated margins are sustainable longer than in 2017‑2018, provided AI capex holds. ￼

Two external realities frame the risk‑reward. First, AI infrastructure capex remains on an upward glide path, with independent forecasts calling for data center capex to rise >30% in 2025 and for cumulative AI spend to exceed $2.8 trillion by 2029; if realized, this underwrites multi‑year HBM and DRAM/NAND content growth. Second, the risk case is a capex digestion phase into 2026 that flattens unit growth and pressures pricing; sell‑side strategists have started to flag this possibility as hyperscalers scrutinize ROI and power constraints. The balance of evidence still favors elevated spend through 2026 given product roadmaps and packaging capacity adds, but the tail risk of a sharper‑than‑expected pause must be priced into position sizing and hedging. ￼

Investment implications are direct and actionable. For SK hynix equity, the call de‑risks near‑term volumes and pricing across the portfolio, adds an HBM4 catalyst in Q4, and pushes out the timing of a supply‑driven rollover by confirming that HBM remains allocation‑constrained into 2027. With DRAM and NAND capacity effectively pre‑sold for 2026 and 1C‑nm/321‑layer migrations driving cost downs, the setup supports above‑cycle margins through at least 2026. The key upside vector is faster HBM4 adoption tied to Nvidia Blackwell and custom accelerators starting 2026; H200 already increased HBM3E to 141 GB at 4.8 TB/s, while Blackwell SKUs are specced around 192 GB HBM3E and far higher bandwidth, implying sustained bit intensity per accelerator even before HBM4 ramps. If Nvidia’s and ASIC customers’ packaging slots scale as projected and silicon deliveries hit plan, SK hynix’s HBM mix should rise further, boosting blended ASPs and margins. The primary drawdowns to monitor are a slower‑than‑expected hyperscaler capex cadence, faster Samsung recovery in HBM3E and HBM4 qualifications, and any slippage in M15X/Yongin tool‑ins or yield ramp that would cede share in a seller’s market. On balance, risk‑reward remains favorable given execution momentum, LTA coverage, and product leadership. ￼ ￼

Beyond SK hynix, the report strengthens the long thesis for selected upstream and adjacent beneficiaries and outlines hedges. Equipment vendors leveraged to DRAM 1C‑nm patterning, HBM TSV and wafer‑level packaging should benefit from the capex mix shift; substrate and interposer supply remains a constraint, so vendors tied to CoWoS scale‑up should see pricing power. Packaging bottlenecks at TSMC are easing but remain the system limit even after moving toward 70k WPM in 2025 and about 90k WPM in 2026; exposure to suppliers with secured CoWoS allocations aligns with the highest probability path to monetizing the AI memory supercycle. On the NAND side, positioning in enterprise‑SSD‑levered names remains attractive as vector‑database and KV‑cache spillover increase SSD intensity per rack, with the parallel HDD tightness pushing mix to QLC. The hedge is to carry protection against an AI capex digestion in 2026 and to monitor competitive headlines on Samsung HBM qualifications and Micron HBM4 progress; a visible inflection in Nvidia’s CoWoS allocations or evidence of under‑utilized packaging lines would be an early warning that memory tightness could abate sooner than management expects. ￼

In sum, this transcript crystallizes a thesis in which SK hynix’s P&L is no longer hostage to a single product or a traditional DRAM cycle. AI inference is structurally expanding the memory TAM beyond HBM into DDR5 and SSDs; HBM4 timing and performance leadership, LTAs through 2026, and accelerated capacity adds at M15X/Yongin tilt execution odds in the company’s favor. The equity should continue to compound as long as hyperscaler and AI‑company capex translate into packaging and GPU deliveries; the prudent portfolio stance is to stay long with discipline, size for capex‑cycle variance, and use competitive and packaging datapoints as risk gates for adding or trimming exposure. ￼

I always consider the downside. Grok "Bear Case" Analysis of OpenAI

1. Unsustainable Financial Model and Escalating Losses

OpenAI's revenue growth, while impressive (from near-zero in 2022 to $12-15 billion ARR in 2025), is dwarfed by its capital-intensive burn rate, creating a path-dependent trap where costs perpetually outpace income. Projections show $5 billion in losses on $3.7 billion in revenue for 2025, escalating to $44 billion in cumulative losses through 2028 (excluding stock-based compensation). Compute expenses alone hit $6 billion annually, with server spends projected at $16 billion in 2025 and ballooning to $400 billion by 2029—far exceeding revenue trajectories. Altman's "Stargate" mega-data centers and $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments (e.g., with Nvidia, Oracle, and UAE partners) are conditional but risky, relying on circular financing where partners fund OpenAI's chip purchases, creating contagion if demand falters.

Unlike traditional software giants (e.g., Google's 11% profit margin at IPO on $962 million revenue), OpenAI's generative AI model incurs rising costs per query and training run, with no clear path to economies of scale. Its $157 billion valuation implies 13.5x forward revenue multiples, but bears argue this misprices the "bad economics": margins erode as models grow more complex, and infrastructure demands could exceed $1 trillion industry-wide, straining global energy and supply chains. If adoption slows (already down to 56% YoY growth in 2025 from triple-digits), or if AGI timelines slip, investors could bail, triggering a valuation collapse similar to WeWork's overhyping. Altman's restructuring to a for-profit public benefit corporation (potentially IPO by 2026) might unlock capital but exposes it to market scrutiny, where skeptics could short the stock as he himself suggested.

2. Technical Plateaus and the Elusive Path to AGI

Altman's goals hinge on rapid AGI breakthroughs, but bears highlight diminishing returns in AI scaling laws. Despite models like o3 and o4, progress has plateaued: GPT-4 token pricing dropped 98% since 2024 due to commoditization, and open-source alternatives (e.g., Meta's Llama 3.1 405B) achieve near-parity at half the cost. Achieving AGI requires 93% annual revenue growth for five years to hit $100 billion by 2029, but technical hurdles—like data scarcity, energy constraints (250 GW data centers by 2033), and algorithmic limits—could delay it indefinitely.

Critics argue OpenAI lacks a durable moat: Its "superalignment" safety team was gutted, whistleblowers silenced, and focus shifted to acceleration over safety, risking uncontrolled AI or ethical failures. If AGI proves a "utopian folly"—a rationalist dream ungrounded in reality—OpenAI could become a commoditized tool provider, not a transformative force.

3. Intensifying Competition and Talent Exodus

OpenAI's early lead is eroding as competitors like Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Meta (Llama), and xAI (Grok) scale up. Open-source models democratize AI, undercutting subscriptions (e.g., Meta's free Llama powers 1.1 billion users, avoiding lock-in). Leadership turnover exacerbates this: Eight of 11 co-founders have left, including CTO Mira Murati and Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, many starting rivals amid disillusionment with Altman's direction. The "talent wars" favor diversified players like Microsoft, which hedges with its own AI (e.g., Inflection acquisition) and could pivot if OpenAI falters.

4. Regulatory, Legal, and Ethical Headwinds: OpenAI faces mounting scrutiny

Copyright lawsuits, antitrust probes (e.g., FTC on Microsoft ties), and investigations like California AG Rob Bonta's into safety lapses (linked to a teen suicide via ChatGPT). Altman's inconsistent stance—advocating regulation publicly while lobbying against EU AI Act and California's SB-1047—fuels distrust. Restructuring concessions (e.g., $50 million fund for "historically excluded" communities) could politicize operations, turning OpenAI into a "politicized nonprofit" vulnerable to extortion and slowed innovation. Ethical lapses, like allowing erotic content or influencing elections via ChatGPT, amplify risks.

5. Leadership Vulnerabilities: Sam Altman's Experience and Track Record

Perhaps the most damning element is Altman's fitness to helm a company pursuing world-altering AGI. At 40, Altman lacks the operational experience for managing a trillion-scale entity—his background is entrepreneurial, not scaled executive. He dropped out of Stanford after two years (no CS/AI degree), founded Loopt (sold for $43 million in 2012 amid internal pushes to oust him for "deceptive and chaotic behavior"), and led Y Combinator (2014-2019), where he was fired for absenteeism, personal enrichment (e.g., double-dipping investments), and prioritizing side projects like OpenAI. Critics note: "If [Altman] imagines something to be true, it sort of becomes true in his head … It may or may not lead one to stretch."
At OpenAI, a documented pattern of dishonesty, manipulation, and abuse led to his November 2023 ouster: Executives like Murati and Sutskever reported "psychological abuse," chaos, and lying (e.g., fabricating board views, undisclosed ownership of the Startup Fund, indirect equity via funds). Board member Helen Toner cited "years worth of issues with trust, accountability, oversight," including withholding information and outright lies. Murati described his playbook: "First, say whatever he needed to say to get you to do what he wanted, and second, if that didn’t work, undermine you or destroy your credibility." Sutskever: "I don’t think Sam is the guy who should have the finger on the button for AGI."

This "web of lies" extended to equity clawbacks (apologized for but authorized by him), safety approvals (falsely claiming approvals), and pitting teams against each other. Post-ouster, Altman demanded board resignations for his return, and restructuring purged safety advocates for profit focus. Users and ex-employees decry his "psychological manipulation," e.g., dismissing critics as "bots" or stigmatizing AI attachments. Bears argue this pattern—evident across Loopt, Y Combinator, and OpenAI—disqualifies him from stewarding AGI, risking internal implosion or ethical disasters. Unlike seasoned CEOs (e.g., Satya Nadella at Microsoft), Altman's style fosters "fear-mongering and systematic lying," per Toner, potentially derailing execution at scale.

Overall Assessment

The bear case envisions OpenAI as a house of cards: Overleveraged finances, technical overpromises, eroding edges, regulatory traps, and a CEO whose manipulative tendencies amplify risks. If AGI delays or costs spiral, it could collapse like Theranos—valued at billions before fraud exposure—or become a marginalized player in a commoditized market. Altman's vision demands flawless leadership he may lack, turning "insane scale" into unsustainable hubris. While the bull case bets on breakthroughs, bears see a 20-30% growth miss triggering a funding crunch, rendering Altman's portrayal unattainable.

**Q: What was Watson Health even *supposed* to be?**

A: Big Blue’s grand vision: IBM Watson Health. It was the AI vanguard, supposedly poised to revolutionize medicine itself. Their flagship, Watson for Oncology, was pitched as the oncologist’s indispensable digital assistant. (Spoiler: it wasn't).

**Q: So what went wrong with this medical AI marvel?**

A: MD Anderson, a titan in cancer research, scrapped their "Oncology Expert Advisor" in 2017 after sinking $62 million. **Q: Was it just a few hiccups, or did it truly... fail?**

A: Over a *dozen* global clients found the system "didn't add much value," the Wall Street Journal reported in 2018. Parsing nuanced doctor’s notes with Natural Language Processing proved beyond its grasp—like trying to read a cuneiform tablet with Google Translate. **Q: How much did this whole grand vision actually cost?**

SpaceX $50B deal for Cursor hands SBF fresh ammo in pardon push

How much did FTX sell its Cursor stake for?
In April 2022, Alameda Research, the trading firm founded by Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), invested $200,000 in Anysphere, the company behind the AI coding tool Cursor. That investment bought them about 5% of the company.

Fast forward one year, and FTX had collapsed, and the bankruptcy court was in control of the company. In April 2023, the FTX bankruptcy estate sold that 5% stake for the same amount Alameda had paid a year earlier: $200,000.

However, SpaceX announced a major partnership with Cursor today. Under the deal, SpaceX has an option to buy the entire company for $60 billion; if they choose not to, they will pay $10 billion for the partnership.

Based on that $60 billion valuation, the 5% stake that FTX sold for $200,000 would now be worth about $3 billion, representing a 15,000x return.

Why does this matter for the incarcerated SBF?
Sam Bankman-Fried is currently in prison but remains active on social media. He has been fighting for a pardon, arguing that FTX was not truly insolvent and that the bankruptcy lawyers destroyed value by selling assets too quickly.

In February 2026, SBF shared a chart suggesting FTX could have reached a net asset value of $78 billion after asset prices recovered if the company had not been forced into bankruptcy.

Crypto lawyer John Deaton dismissed those claims at the time, saying projected values do not change the fact that customers lost money, and that the court had already ruled on the case.

Now, with the Cursor deal, it is hard to agree that the lawyers maximized value three years ago.

SBF’s parents have also been active in pushing for a pardon, appearing on CNN earlier this year in March to argue that FTX customers got their money back.

Creditors pointed out that the repayments are based on 2022 prices, not current market values. A customer who had one Bitcoin got paid based on Bitcoin’s $16,800 price in November 2022.

President Trump has said he will not pardon SBF, and prediction markets currently put the chance of a 2026 pardon at only 5%, but SBF seems determined to keep pushing his version of events regardless.

• No internet to verify against database
• Elderly/disabled couldn't authenticate

• 2018: Over 1 billion records leaked, sold for $8

• Centralized database = single point of failure

Authentication failure rate: 6-12% for manual laborers, elderly, anyone whose biometric data degraded.

"Millions of fake accounts siphoned funds"

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. System created NEW fraud opportunities:

• Middlemen charging bribes just to enroll people
• Identity cloning from leaked biometric data
• System sold as "cutting fraud" but created different fraud vectors

The pattern - whose interests does this serve?

✓ Government surveillance (track every transaction, movement, service use)
✓ Tech companies (contracts for infrastructure)
✓ Bureaucrats (centralized control)

NOT: Poor/rural populations it claimed to help

What went wrong: 🔥

1. Rolled out WITHOUT privacy laws (still incomplete 15 years later)
2. Made mandatory despite Supreme Court saying it shouldn't be
3. No grievance system for 1.3 billion people
4. Single point of failure affects ALL services
5. Biometric data PERMANENT - can't change if compromised
6. Excluded most vulnerable: elderly, disabled, manual laborers

The exclusion problem:

System required:
• Functioning electricity
• Reliable internet
• Working biometric scanners
• Digital literacy

Where? Rural India, where people MOST need food rations.

Result: "In

clusion machinery" became "exclusion machinery" ⚠️

Natural baseline check:

Before Aadhaar: Paper ration cards, local verification, human judgment when systems failed.

After Aadhaar: Computer says no = you starve. No human override. No alternative. Your survival depends on a fingerprint scanner working.

The global pattern:

This isn't just India. Similar systems rolling out:
• UK considering digital ID
• EU digital wallet
• WHO digital health certificates 
• Sri Lanka copying Aadhaar model (2026)
• Multiple countries watching India's "experiment"

Why this matters for everyone:

When survival (food, healthcare, money) depends on ONE digital system:
• Single technical failure = catastrophe
• Data breach = permanent identity theft (can't change biometrics)
• Government gains total surveillance capability
• No anonymity, no cash alternatives, no escape
• System becomes tool of control, not service

The dystopia blueprint is real:

India shows what happens when you:
1. Rush digital ID without privacy protections
2. Make it mandatory for basic survival
3. Centralize biometric data for 1+ billion people
4. Prioritize "efficiency" over human rights
5. Ignore authentication failures killing people

This isn't theoretical. People DIED because a fingerprint scanner didn't work. 🚨

Bottom line:

Aadhaar proves: Digital ID systems pose existential risk when made mandatory for survival AND inadequately protected.

The post is right to call this a warning. Every country considering similar systems should study India's failures first. 🎯

Chapter 2: The .NG ccTLD Ecosystem

Several years ago, I became interested in investing in Nigeria’s country-code top-level domain — the .ng ccTLD. My first stop was a US-based registrar, 101domain.com . The price shocked me: registration fees ranged from $150 to $247, and renewals didn't help either. That was way beyond my budget for a ccTLD.

I checked other global registrars. No difference. Most charge between €100 and €300 for a single .ng domain.

So I shifted strategy: instead of international registrars, why not try local Nigerian registrars?

To my surprise, registrars based in Lagos offered .ng domains for around $15 USD. Finally — a reasonable price. I excitedly began searching for domain names. But when I tried to pay with my U.S. credit or debit card, the transaction was declined.

Yes — I couldn’t pay with my U.S. card, even though the domain cost far less.

My only option was to use my Nigerian bank account. After sending the payment, I had to email proof of the transaction to the registrar so they could manually complete the registration. That was just the beginning.

About a year or so later, I sold some of those domains through Dan.com . But transferring them to buyers was another obstacle. Because most U.S. registrars didn’t support .ng domains, buyers — or Dan.com themselves — had to open accounts with a Nigerian registrar just to receive the domain.

Trust and Perception Issues

Let’s be honest:
Many U.S. or European companies hesitate to let a Nigerian registrar manage their digital assets — especially domain names tied to their brand or business.

There’s also a deeper issue: payment trust.

Many international investors are uncomfortable entering credit card or banking details on unfamiliar websites that lack global trust signals. And the Western media’s long-standing narrative about "Nigerian fraudsters" has negatively shaped perceptions, whether fair or not.

This lack of trust created friction. Transactions became complicated. Investors pulled back.

The .ng domain system wasn’t broken — it was simply missing a healthy ecosystem.

What Makes a Healthy Ecosystem?

In business, an ecosystem is a network of interconnected organizations that depend on each other to create and deliver value.

In the domain industry, this ecosystem includes:

The domain registry (e.g., NiRA for .ng)
Registrars
Registrants (domain owners)
Domain investors
Secondary marketplaces
End users (businesses and individuals)
Media and industry publications
Competitors
Government and regulatory bodies
Global organizations like ICANN

When these players are connected, trust grows. Innovation follows. Sales happen. Values increase.

But when one part of the chain is missing, the ecosystem becomes fragile.

The Challenge With the .NG Ecosystem

For years, the .ng ecosystem struggled, especially in the United States — the largest domain market in the world.

Only one or two registrars offered .ng domains in the United States, and their prices were outrageously high. And let's be honest: even if Nigerian companies are willing to invest in their digital identity, who wants to pay $300 for a .ng domain when a .com costs less than $15?

Think about it:

If .ai or .io domains cost $300 per year, how many startups would adopt them?
If .com cost $250 annually, it wouldn’t have 170+ million domains registered today.

So why did .ng launch with such high pricing?

The world simply didn’t know about .ng yet — and the pricing made it even harder to discover.

A Shift Toward Growth

Thankfully, in the past two years, things have changed significantly.

One of NiRA’s best decisions was licensing more U.S.-based registrars, such as:

Dynadot
Epik

This single move opened access to a global audience and immediately normalized pricing.

I expect more registrars to join, and hopefully, soon. I would like to invite the following companies to join Dynadot and Epik:

 GoDaddy.com 
 Spaceship.com 
 NetworkSolutions.com 
 Porkbun.com 
 Namecheap.com 
 Domain.com 
Sav

On the marketplace side:

•Atom (formerly SquadHelp) now supports .ng listings.
•Sedo has reported successful .ng sales (confirmed through NameBio).
•You can also list .ng domains on Afternic, Spaceship, Dynadot, and others.

With easier registration and multiple sales outlets, the .ng ecosystem is finally becoming connected.

Add to that:

•Growing interest from #domain investors
•NiRA’s more globally focused leadership
•Companies like Amaze Holdings ( Spri.ng ) actively using .ng
•Google, treating ccTLDs more fairly in search ranking
•Increasing adoption by end users and startups

The result is a maturing, healthier .ng #ecosystem .

We are seeing momentum — real momentum.

But let’s be clear: there is still work to be done.

"The Hustle" by @thesamparr sold for $27 million.

"Milk Road" by @ShaanVP sold for millions too.

Both were newsletters.

Literally just emails.

But people actually wanted to read them.

They'd see the email come in and open it immediately.

Why?

Just because they wanted to see what was in it.

In eCom that's RARE.

Most people don't open emails because there's no mystery.

It's going to be a sale.

Or highlight product features and benefits.

Or a reminder about something in their cart.

They've read this email before, even if this is the first time they've sent it.

But The Hustle and Milk Road?

People opened them because they were entertaining.

Because they made business news not boring.

Because reading them was worth the three minutes even if you didn't click anything.

And their emails generated MILLIONS, so they were able to sell for millions too.

Not because they had the best design.

Not because they had clever subject lines.

Because they understood something most email marketers don't:

People don't want more information.

They want to be interested.

David Ogilvy said it 69 years ago:

"You can't bore people into buying your product".

But most email marketing ignores this completely.

We act like the problem is getting people to open emails.

So we optimize subject lines.

Or we act like the problem is getting people to click.

So we add more buttons and make them bigger.

But the real problem is nobody actually wants to read the email.

They're just enduring it.

Skimming for the discount code.

Deleting it.

Moving on.

And we wonder why email "doesn't work" for some brands.

It's not that email doesn't work.

It's that boring doesn't work.

Take Instagram for example – another platform that fights for your attention.

When it launched, it was all beautiful images and photoshoots.

Brands would post product photos with perfect lighting.

Influencers would post aesthetic shots of their coffee or their outfit or their vacation.

That's what everyone thought Instagram was for.

A place to make things look good.

And for a while, that worked.

But slowly, the algorithm figured something out.

It started tracking what people actually engaged with.

What they stopped scrolling for.

What they spent time watching.

What they shared with friends.

And it turned out people didn't actually want the aesthetic shots.

They wanted to be entertained.

They wanted memes that made them laugh.

They wanted stories that made them feel something.

They wanted reels that were interesting or dramatic or weird.

Not just pretty product photos that looked the same as everyone else's.

So the algorithm started pushing what people actually wanted.

And brands that didn't adapt died.

Their beautiful product shoots stopped getting seen.

Because the algorithm wasn't rewarding beautiful anymore.

It was rewarding entertainment.

The brands that survived the new algorithm were the ones that figured this out.

That stopped optimizing for aesthetic and started optimizing for attention.

The algorithm forced evolution.

And now Instagram looks completely different than it did five years ago.

Not because Meta decided to change it but because users voted with their engagement.

Here's the thing though:

Email doesn't have an algorithm.

So it hasn't evolved.

There's no feed.

No ranking system.

No AI deciding which emails get shown first.

Every email that gets sent just... shows up.

In the order it was sent.

Whether it's good or boring doesn't matter.

It gets the same placement.

So brands don't get punished for being boring.

They just get ignored.

But since there's no algorithm forcing them to adapt, they don't.

They keep sending the same emails they were sending 10 years ago.

Product photos.

Feature lists.

Bigger and bolder "SHOP NOW" buttons.

Because it's what they've always done.

And because there's no immediate feedback that it's not working.

The email still "sends".

It still gets some opens.

It still generates some revenue.

So it looks like it's working.

Even though it's leaving everything on the table.

I think about this a lot.

What would email look like if there was an algorithm?

If boring emails got buried and entertaining ones got promoted?

Brands would adapt immediately.

They'd have to.

But since there's no algorithm, boring survives.

Even though nobody wants it.

I started Email Engineers in 2021.

I didn't have a philosophy back then, so I just followed the best practices.

Which is why nobody knew about us for about 1 or 2 years.

Now things have changed.

My current philosophy is simple, and it has served me and my clients (7-8 figure eCommerce brands) very well:

Send emails people actually enjoy reading.

Not emails they tolerate.

Not emails they skim and delete.

But emails they look forward to.

Emails that when they see the sender name, they think "oh good, this one".

Now we're considered one of the best email agencies according to Klaviyo.

Actually, not.

Let me rephrase that...

We're not considered by Klaviyo at all.

I don't even think we're in their partner directory because I haven't done enough boot licking or paper-filling.

Klaviyo rewards the agencies that make Klaviyo more money (by pushing their services to clients).

Not the ones that make their clients more money.

Weird if you think about it.

Anyway, Klaviyo benchmarks are real and the great equalizer. 

The "Elite" agency that shoved a bunch of useless AI feautes down their clients' throats despite not being in their best interest.

And the underdog agency that just focuses on results.

And this is what it says about us, Email Engineers:

Campaigns that generate 12.5 times more sales than our clients' competitors.

Subscribers that are worth 7 times more.

Not because we're smarter than everyone else.

But because we optimize for a different thing.

Most agencies optimize for opens and clicks.

We optimize for whether someone actually wants to read the email.

Whether it passes the REV test.

Whether it's relevant, entertaining, and valuable.

Because if they want to read it, everything else follows.

They open it.

They engage with it.

They buy from it.

And they don't unsubscribe.

Because they're not being bored into buying.

They're being interested into it.

Right now we're scaling ecom brands' email revenue to 43-56% of total sales.

Normally 10-20% above what internal teams or agencies can.

The difference isn't tactics.

It's not that we have better subject lines or smarter segmentation.

It's philosophy.

We send emails people enjoy reading.

And it turns out that matters more than anyone thought it would.

Because there's no algorithm in email forcing brands to be entertaining.

So almost nobody is.

Which means the brands that are have a massive advantage.

They're the only interesting thing in the inbox.

Everyone else is competing with each other on discount percentages and countdown timers.

We're competing on a different axis entirely.

And it's working.

–Matt

P.S. If you want to see what entertaining emails actually look like in ecommerce (not just funny emails, but the full spectrum - dramatic, vulnerable, controversial, story-driven, educational but interesting), reply below with "SEND" and I'll send examples.

Most brands won't do this because it doesn't feel like "professional marketing".

Which is exactly why it works by the way.

Best Quotes

"Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art." Leonardo da Vinci
