Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher. 

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity. 

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive. 

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498
Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490
Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.
Czartoryski Museum, Kraków 

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science
Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

Military Tech: Armored tanks, giant crossbows, and portable bridges—way ahead of his era's tech.

Hydraulics and Engineering: Canal locks, diving suits, and self-supporting bridges. He even planned an ideal city to beat plagues.

Anatomy: Sketches more accurate than printed texts of the time, showing heart valves and fetal positions.

Fun fact: He invented the robotic knight in 1495—a mechanical automaton that could wave and sit up.

Steampunk before steam.

Personal Quirks and Legacy
Vegetarian and Animal Lover: Bought caged birds just to free them. Ahead of his time on ethics.

Procrastinator Extraordinaire: Queen Isabella of Spain once joked he'd paint her when pigs fly—ironically, he sketched flying pigs.

Death: May 2, 1519, at age 67 in Amboise, France. Buried in Château d'Amboise; his bones were scattered during the French Revolution.

Da Vinci's influence? Everywhere—from NASA's designs to modern AI ethics (he'd probably geek out over neural networks).

In 2025, his Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017, and recent scans of his notebooks (like the Leicester Codex) keep revealing hidden layers via infrared tech.

A shoe company just became an AI infrastructure play.
And honestly? It might not be the craziest thing you'll hear this week.

Allbirds is losing the laces and rebranding as NewBird AI — $50M raised, IP sold for $39M, almost every store closed, and now they're buying GPUs and selling cloud compute.

Stock went from $20 to $2.50. The brand that built a cult following on eco-friendly wool decided the answer was AI infrastructure.

I've seen enough of these to know where it usually goes: Long Island Iced Tea renamed itself Long Blockchain in 2017. Dozens of retailers slapped .com on their name in 2000. The pattern is always the same: a struggling brand chases the hottest market, gets a short bump, then disappears.

But here's what's different this time. AI compute is not a trend: it's a decade-long infrastructure buildout with real enterprise demand, real capital flowing in, and a genuine shortage of capacity. That doesn't mean every late entrant survives. Most won't. But the market itself isn't going anywhere.

So the question isn't whether NewBird is opportunistic because it clearly is. The question is whether they have the execution, the relationships, and the staying power to matter in a space that is brutally competitive and capex-heavy.

Shoe brands don't usually win that game, only the ones who DO show up with more than a press release.

So as a former hedge fund PM that has been regularly monitoring and bidding on antiques/watches/ any other mispriced collectibles at estate sales/local auctions for 7+ years, I'm going to weigh in here: 

1) Yes, there is edge in these less liquid asset pools but it's far less than it was 5 to 10 yrs ago and the bidder pool keeps expanding, leading to much more efficient pricing. AI image tools (even Google image identification earlier) had a major impact on this as did local auctioneers platforming their sales on aggregate sites (and adding shipping) 

2) More market participants than you probably realize now approach these auctions in the same way. (I've been doing it with a margin of safety / "expected value" probability calculations on items for a number of years. I know many others who are doing the same (especially because of the growth of the "side hustle" reseller/thrifter market. Searching for less prominent auction listings and identifying mispricings was one of the first things I used ChatGPT for back in 2022. Almost everyone is doing this now. 

3) I have bid in enough of these auctions that I have become friendly with some of auctioneers. The majority of them now have someone on staff fluent in LLMs and thus their item descriptions and value ranges are becoming more precise (again, less edge here than in the past)

4) Specific auction dynamics in these local auctions increasingly lead to poor results. New auction participants entering due to the precise angle you're looking at (many of whom only ever used eBay) don't always realize how auction premiums work or are unaware of the local state tax situation etc. As a result they often overbid and drive prices above fair value or they fall victim to psychological "bidding war" biases ("I drove all the way to this physical auction--what's another $300 to secure the item?") 

5) Another factor at play is that AI image analysis is currently still rather bad at identifying counterfeit/"franken" items without a knowledgeable user prompting/correcting it. I have seen this countless times. For example, in a recent auction a rare Gibson instrument (which I knew was fake) was repeatedly authenticated by both Claude and Gemini. As a result of others preforming that same AI analysis, the final auction result reflected a 65% probability that it was genuine (it will be a total loss for the purchaser of that item). Another example--the empirical probability of finding a random Rolex that is authentic at a general estate sale is likely less than 1%. 5 yrs ago any final auction bid would have reflected that probability. These days, many final non-authenticated Rolex estate sale auctions reflect closer to a 35% probability of authenticity--again a total capital loss for the purchaser. 

6) As others point out--the greater inefficiencies lie in pick up only items BUT these are often larger collectibles that get a liquidity discount (deservingly so). Moving on an antique piece of furniture if you are not a dealer is not that easy so even if you get a 50% discount the edge is not as great as you might think. 

Don't get me wrong--there are definitely mispricings to find there but it's not the undiscovered territory you might be thinking it is. As an example, at a recent local auction that featured many collectible watches (I collect and service/restore watches as a hobby) every piece sold for within 95% of its eBay sold price value (a few even went above fair value--reflecting the "I'm already attending the auction and won a few items so no big deal to pay a small premium for another one." 

Ultimately, I doubt the mispricings at present in this market are any greater than one would find sifting through listed small cap/microcap stocks. On the plus side, it has a utility function (it's fun to do if you like collecting).

𝗡𝗙𝗧𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽. They've evolved into intelligent agents capable of economic autonomy. Here's that journey and how AINFT fundamentally rewrote the narrative.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗪𝗮𝘃𝗲: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝘄𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 (𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟮–𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟳)

The story starts in 2012 with Colored Coins on Bitcoin. The idea was straightforward: "tag" small amounts of BTC with unique metadata to represent real-world assets property deeds, shares, concert tickets. The Bitcoin blockchain's limitations made implementation difficult, but the core concept was planted: a token could prove you owned something specific, not just a fungible balance of currency.

In May 2014, Kevin McCoy and Anil Dash created Quantum a pulsing, pixelated octagon registered on the Namecoin blockchain. It sold for $4 at a conference in New York. For the first time, on-chain data was directly linked to a piece of art. Ownership was cryptographically verifiable, not just asserted. That same $4 NFT would later be valued at nearly $1.5 million during the 2021 boom not because the art changed, but because the world's understanding of digital ownership had.

By 2017, Ethereum introduced the ERC-721 standard, and everything accelerated. CryptoPunks launched: 10,000 unique pixelated characters that would become cultural icons, some selling for millions. CryptoKitties followed, a game where users bred and traded digital cats. At its peak, CryptoKitties clogged the Ethereum network entirely proof that NFTs could drive real demand, not just speculation. OpenSea opened as the "eBay of NFTs," giving anyone the ability to mint, buy, and sell digital assets.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝘁 (𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟬–𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟯)

What happened next was unprecedented. NFT trading volume exploded from $82 million in 2020
to $17 billion in 2021. Beeple's Everydays: The First 5000 Days sold for $69.3 million at Christie's. Bored Ape Yacht Club became a global status symbol. The narrative was fixed: NFTs were digital art and collectibles JPEGs you bought, held, and hoped to sell for more.

Then the market collapsed. Daily sales dropped 92% from their September 2021 peak. A 2023 report claimed 95% of NFT collections had zero monetary value, with 79% unsold. The bubble had burst, and the "NFTs as art" narrative died with it.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗙𝗧 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱

The market's collapse wasn't the end of NFTs it was evidence that the old narrative was too small. Owning a static JPEG was never the destination. It was the prototype.

In October 2025, AINFT completed its brand overhaul. The focus shifted from operating an NFT art collection platform to building crypto AI infrastructure a comprehensive ecosystem centered on the integration of AI and blockchain. 🧑‍💻Technical moat: The design choice is elegant. Instead of another MCP gateway or SDK wrapper, agent-vault operates one layer lower — at HTTPS itself. Set HTTPS_PROXY. Every outbound request, regardless of how it was made (API/CLI/SDK/MCP), flows through the vault. Agent never touches the secret.

💰 Commercialization: agent-vault is MIT-licensed and in research preview. But the monetization path is already drawn — it's the "last-mile delivery" add-on for Infisical's existing enterprise customers. NVIDIA and Booking.com already trust Infisical. Elon Musk … a tale from 2 Points of View… 

Elon Musk's career began in the tech boom of the late 1990s, where he co-founded Zip2, a city guide software company sold for nearly $300 million, and then X.com , which merged into PayPal and fetched him over $100 million upon its sale to eBay. This early success propelled him into ambitious ventures like SpaceX in 2002, aimed at revolutionizing space travel, and Tesla Motors in 2004, where he became chairman and later CEO, pushing electric vehicles as a solution to climate change. However, critics from a liberal perspective often highlight how Musk's rise exemplifies the excesses of unchecked capitalism: his companies have faced accusations of exploitative labor practices, including long hours, low wages for workers, and a staunch anti-union stance at Tesla, which has drawn scrutiny from labor rights advocates. Moreover, while Musk positions himself as an environmental savior through Tesla's EV push, detractors point to the environmental costs of mining for battery materials and his personal carbon footprint from private jets, questioning the sincerity of his green agenda amid growing wealth inequality.

In recent years, Musk's acquisition of Twitter (rebranded as X) in 2022 for $44 billion has amplified concerns about his influence on public discourse. From a liberal viewpoint, this move has been seen as detrimental to democratic norms, with Musk reinstating banned accounts associated with hate speech and misinformation, leading to a surge in toxic content on the platform. His forays into Neuralink for brain-computer interfaces and xAI for artificial intelligence raise ethical alarms about privacy, inequality in access to advanced tech, and the potential for corporate overreach in human augmentation. Overall, Musk's career is viewed as a cautionary tale of billionaire hubris, where innovation serves personal ambition over societal good, exacerbating divides in income, information, and opportunity while dodging accountability through his vast resources and media savvy.

### Conservative Point of View

Elon Musk's entrepreneurial journey kicked off with Zip2 in the 1990s, a pioneering online mapping service sold for a fortune, followed by X.com 's evolution into PayPal, which revolutionized online payments and netted him substantial wealth upon its eBay acquisition. This foundation enabled him to launch SpaceX in 2002, challenging government monopolies in space with reusable rockets and ambitious Mars colonization goals, and invest in Tesla, where as CEO he transformed the auto industry by making electric cars viable and profitable. From a conservative lens, Musk embodies the American dream of self-made success through innovation and risk-taking, creating thousands of jobs and advancing technologies that reduce dependence on foreign oil and promote energy independence. His resistance to overregulation, such as fighting SEC oversight and union pressures at Tesla, is praised as defending free enterprise against bureaucratic interference that stifles growth.

More recently, Musk's 2022 purchase of Twitter (now X) is hailed as a bold stand for free speech, dismantling what conservatives see as liberal bias in Big Tech by restoring accounts silenced for dissenting views and promoting open dialogue. Ventures like Neuralink and xAI are viewed as forward-thinking pursuits that push human potential, countering government stagnation in areas like AI ethics and neuroscience. In essence, Musk's career is celebrated as a triumph of individualism and capitalism, where his disruptions in transportation, space, and communication challenge elitist establishments, foster competition, and inspire a new generation of entrepreneurs to prioritize innovation over conformity.

Just listened to @a16zBioHealth 's conversation with @formationbio 's CEO @BenjamineYLiu on building this generation's big pharma. Packed with insights on why drug development is broken and how to fix it. 

Here are my top 5 takeaways (but honestly, listen to the whole thing):

1. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Discovery; It's Development Execution 🎧 02:10-02:48

Discovery candidates have doubled in 10 years, yet FDA approvals remain flat at ~50/year. "One competitive advantage you want to have as a pharma company, ironically, isn't in discovery. It's actually in this drug development process." Development costs hundreds of millions per program; that's where drugs live or die.
---

2. The M&A Trap That Prevents New Big Pharma 🎧 05:40-06:42

No major pharma company has been created since the 1980s. Why? At Phase 2, you face: sell for $3B today vs. 40% chance of $0 / 60% chance of $9B later. Risk-adjusted, everyone sells early. Formation Bio's solution: a hub-and-spoke model, selling individual assets without selling the company, and recycling capital into new shots. PureTech's Karuna (licensed from Lilly → sold for $14B) proves it works.
---

3. Cost-Plus CROs Are Incentivized to Inflate Costs 🎧 19:07-20:51

CROs bill per hour like law firms—"my Series D legal fee was more expensive than my Series C... same law firm." Simple fixes exist: consolidate redundant site visits, use risk-based monitoring (visit problem sites more, not everyone equally). These are FDA-approved but underused because of misaligned incentives.
---

4. "Psychological Arbitrage" in Drug Selection 🎧 11:54-12:44

"It's easier to fail the same way everyone's failing"—corporate career risk drives herding (everyone chasing GLP-1s). Formation Bio targets: (1) First-in-class with genetic validation (anti-CD226 for UC: 20K patients, 20-year dataset), or (2) Proven mechanisms in new indications (brain-penetrant TYK2). Behavioral economics creates systematic mispricings.
---

5. You Need 10+ Phase 2 Readouts to Prove a Platform 🎧 26:18-27:14

With 30% industry success rate, you need 10-20 shots to statistically distinguish 50% picking ability from 30%. "Just because the first drug didn't work, you actually don't know whether they're better than average." Formation Bio built a 0.72 AUC prediction model, but explicitly states "we don't weight it heavily." Intellectual honesty is rare in this space.
---

Tons more in the full episode: China's 360% increase in first-in-class candidates, why AI won't improve clinical success rates (yet), regulatory risk as opportunity. Worth the 40 minutes!

THE 200 BILLION DOLLAR LIE HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

Big Tech is running the largest accounting sleight of hand in corporate history, and the evidence is already in their own filings.

Here is what they are doing:

Nvidia ships a new flagship AI chip every 12 months now. AMD does the same. Google just released its seventh generation TPU. Each generation delivers performance gains so large that last year’s hardware becomes economically obsolete for frontier work in 18 to 24 months.

But Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon are depreciating that same hardware over 4 to 6 years.

The math is simple and devastating:

Big Tech will spend roughly 400 billion dollars on AI infrastructure in 2025. Depreciate that over 5 years and you expense 80 billion per year. Depreciate it over the actual 2 year useful life and you should be expensing 200 billion per year.

That 120 billion dollar annual gap compounds to between 150 and 200 billion in overstated profits through 2028.

This is not theory. The cracks are already showing:

Meta extended server lives to 5.5 years in January 2025 and immediately booked a 2.9 billion dollar depreciation reduction. One accounting change, nearly 3 billion in phantom earnings.

MIT surveyed enterprise AI deployments in 2025. Failure rate: 95 percent. Deloitte found the same pattern. Most companies see no return despite massive investment.

Used H100 GPUs, which sold for premium prices 18 months ago, are now trading 20 to 30 percent below year ago levels in secondary markets. When those prices fall below 40 percent of original cost, the accounting fiction becomes impossible to sustain.

What happens when reality hits the income statement:

Best case, older chips get reassigned to less demanding inference work and software optimizations extend useful life by a year or two. The boom continues but profit margins compress.

Worst case, auditors force write downs across the sector simultaneously. Earnings revisions of 15 to 25 percent. Stock corrections of 30 to 40 percent. Credit rating pressure. The entire AI investment thesis gets repriced in a single quarter.

The tell is already visible:

Every quarterly earnings call now features questions about depreciation schedules. Analysts are reading the footnotes. Short sellers are building positions. The secondary market for used GPUs is sending a price signal that contradicts the balance sheet assumptions.

Watch three things in the next six months:

Fourth quarter 2025 financial filings for any mention of useful life adjustments. Resale prices for H100 and older generation accelerators. Enterprise survey data on AI return on investment.

When two of those three break negative, the unwind begins.

The deeper issue nobody wants to discuss:

If 95 percent of companies cannot generate positive returns from AI despite hundreds of billions invested, the productivity revolution everyone is pricing in does not exist yet. The models are real, the chips are real, but the business case is still mostly hope and accounting tricks.

The depreciation schedules are not fraud. They are within GAAP guidelines. But they are also not reality. And markets eventually reconcile the difference.

The only question is whether it happens slowly through guidance adjustments and quiet revisions, or all at once when the first major player is forced to take a multi billion dollar impairment charge.

Read the footnotes. Do the math. The 200 billion dollar gap is already there.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

I’ve worked with 300+ newsletters and virtually everyone who gets to $500K+ launched in 1 of these 4 categories:

1. Jobs (the biggest opportunity)

Help people do better at work.

This breaks down into 34 sub-categories:

• Trends (AI, business ideas, etc.)
• Functions/skills (marketing, copywriting, etc.)
• Industry (DTC, Biotech, etc.)
• Tools (Excel, Figma, etc.)

Examples:

a) Miss Excel: She’s done $10M+ in revenue, teaching Excel formulas, pivot tables, and dashboards.

b) Industry Dive: Built niche B2B newsletters around retail, utilities, and waste management.

None of the founders had industry experience, but they scaled to $100M+ revenue and sold for $500M+.

This category is the most scalable and the best fit for ad-driven newsletter models.

2. Investments

People pay for information that helps them make (or save) money.

Examples:

a) MarketBeat: It helps individual investors to make better trading decisions with real-time financial data, in-depth market analysis, and stock research tools.

They do $45M+ in revenue with ~20 employees.

b) Contrarian Thinking: An 8-figure business teaching people how to buy boring businesses like laundromats and accounting firms

c) Alts: Focuses on alternative assets (wine, whiskey, real estate).

They make $1M+/year with a community that gets you access to private investments.

These often monetize via subscriptions, communities, and information products.

3. Niche hobbies

Anything from rare LEGO collectors, quilting communities, to high-end watch buyers.

Why they scale: extremely engaged micro-audiences who will pay for curation, guides, classifieds, or membership clubs.

How to test: find active forums/subreddits, Instagram communities, Facebook groups.

If people spend money on a hobby (collectables, watches, quilting, fishing), you’ve got demand.

Examples:

a) A Lego collectors newsletter: Multi 6-figure ARR just covering rare Lego buys.

b) Quilting: There are 9-figure Quilting companies, and people spend THOUSANDS on quilting.

If there isn’t a 6-figure quilting newsletter + info product yet, there should be.

4. Personal transformation

Fitness, mindset, productivity, weight loss, and spiritual transformations.

High willingness to pay because people expect a drastic change in status/happiness and will spend on coaching, programs, and masterminds.

Examples:

a) Dan Go: Fitness & body transformation for founders. Likely $1M+/year.

b) Sahil Bloom: Took personal development + mindset, turned it into books and a broader business brand.

Bubble, Bubble Toil and Trouble?
In the business media, comparisons today are being increasingly made with prior bubbles. I wanted to offer my views of this subject.

There have arguably been three well-defined speculative cycles in equities over the last six decades — The Nifty Fifty Era (the 1960s to the early 1970s), the Dot-Com Boom (mid-to-late 1990s to early 2000) and the recent Mag 7 and AI Boom.

All three of these eras have fueled a bull market in equities. The end of the Nifty Fifty Era and the Dot-Com Boom marked the end of the respective bull markets and were followed by market crashes.

* The Nifty Fifty Era was marked by fifty large cap stocks that were considered blue chips and buy and hold (one decision) growth stocks. The common characteristic of the stocks in this basket was that the companies achieved consistently superior profits growth. They were assigned extraordinarily high price/earnings ratios of 50x or higher — well above the long-term market average of between 15x and 20x. Representative stocks included American Express, Avon Products, Bristol-Myers, Coca-Cola, Eastman Kodak, General Electric, Polaroid, Procter & Gamble, Sears, Roebuck and Xerox. Most of the companies on this list were well established, where investors perceived deep moats (preventing competitors from making market share inroads) and with a clear expectation that the companies would sustain high returns on invested capital. The reality was that there was far less innovation taking place in those anointed companies. At the time of The Nifty Fifty, bank trust departments (Citigroup, JPMorgan, etc.) were the dominant investors and materially overweighted these anointed stocks.

* The Dot-Com Boom existed in the late 1990s and peaked in the first quarter of 2000, coincident with the widespread adoption and use of the internet. This technology-inspired boom was seen as similar to others in the past (railroads in the 1840s, automobiles in the early 1900s, radio in the 1920s, television in the 1940s and computer time-sharing in the 1960s and home computers in the 1980s). Webvan, Boo.com and Pets.com were the standard-bearers of that period. In large measure the companies were not real in the sense that they had no plausible business models and they were run by dreamers and not serious businessmen. Essentially, they were one giant promotion. But in size (market capitalizations), the promotions (like Pets.com ) were not consequential in market capitalization.

However, several large tech companies (like Cisco and Sun Microsystems) were swept up to ridiculously high valuations along with the worthless dot-com promotions.

Sun Microsystems' market capitalization peaked at over $200 billion — representing a price-to-revenue of (a lofty) 10x (which pales when compared to today's tech leaders). Sun Microsystems actually had a suite of revolutionary products from Java programming language to SPARC processors, StarOffice, My SQL, Solaris OS and VirtualBox. The company was ultimately sold for only $7 billion to Oracle a decade after the Dot-Com Boom deflated.

Years after the Dot-Com bust Sun Microsystem's Chairman Scott McNealy famously reflected on the absurdity of Sun's peak valuation with this iconic quote:

"At 10 times revenues, to give you a 10-year payback, I have to pay you 100% of revenues for 10 straight years in dividends. That assumes I can get that by my shareholders. That assumes I have zero cost of goods sold, which is very hard for a computer company. That assumes zero expenses, which is really hard with 39,000 employees. That assumes I pay no taxes, which is very hard. And that assumes you pay no taxes on your dividends, which is kind of illegal. And that assumes with zero R&D for the next 10 years, I can maintain the current revenue run rate. Now, having done that, would any of you like to buy my stock at $64? Do you realize how ridiculous those basic assumptions are? You don’t need any transparency. You don’t need any footnotes. What were you thinking?"

Here is a stock chart of Sun Microsystems (1996-2007):

📷
* The (Current) Climb in Mag 7 and AI has fueled almost the entirety of the market advance over the last few years. Unlike the Nifty Fifty or the Dot-Com promotions, Mag 7 consists of companies that historically have had consistently sizeable cash flows, unleveraged and liquid balance sheets and limited (physical plant) capital needs owing to deep competitive moats (and near monopoly status in phones, operating systems, search, etc.). Whereas the industrial Nifty Fifty companies needed to build new factory production lines and new factories to maintain their competitive status and growth, the Mag 7 are able to innovate rapidly and relatively inexpensively by simply sending product upgrades online (with no manufacturing or shipping required).

Until recently the Mag 7 business models were capital light but that has changed with the monumental AI capital spend. Most of the Mag 7 constituents are now becoming capital intensive, which is a big change (and incorporates sizeable risks). This capital outlay is being accompanied by an uncertain timing and level of return on massive and unprecedented amounts of invested capital.

There are some substantial differences between the Dot-Com days and what is going on now with the AI infrastructure build. Capacity put in place in the late 1990s was a very long-lived asset. Take fiber optic cable for example — much of the stuff (and constituent components) put into place then is still in use now. This is one of the reasons why the Dot-Com buildout quickly went into overcapacity. The assets were sticky.

AI infrastructure is the polar opposite. It obsoletes incredibly quickly — much more quickly than depreciation schedules imply. Oddly, this is part of the bull case, ergo everything will keep having to be rapidly replaced, so the spending will not stop. The bull case treats investment capital as infinite and the laws of economics as irrelevant. It assumes the circular financing and money losing will go on forever. Of course, professional investors know that is not true and they do not really believe the grossly dis-economic behavior can continue forever. They just believe it is in place for the quarter we are in (with upbeat guidance) and it is just one more way to rationalize the game of musical chairs they are playing. Most recognize that they are playing the same game and are just being dragged along by the whims of over-levered retail as well. They all think they will be the first to get out when the music stops. Many just don’t care because they manage against a benchmark.

Here are two tweets that demonstrate how dis-economic the AI spend might be:

📷
📷
One other big difference between the Dot-Com days and now, is the Dot-Com stuff actually worked like it was supposed to — it was not a capital black hole. Actually it did increase net productivity, did not consume so much in the way of energy and other resources that it was in fact inflationary. And it was not being subsidized by the public at large (power cost) and actual human content creators.

And just for fun:

📷
Bottom Line: I would conclude that the Nifty Fifty Era consisted of a bunch of entrenched companies that were materially overvalued in a period when bank trust departments were the dominant investors. The Dot-Com Boom consisted of a number of promotions and large-cap tech stocks that became significantly overvalued (with day traders becoming the dominant investors). Both could be described as bubbles.

By contrast, the Mag 7/AI period consists of near monopolies (that are arguably fully priced to overpriced) as they morph from capital-light to capital-intensive business models — with the risks associated with circular vendor financing, accessing adequate sources of energy (at a reasonable cost), the availability of capable workers and other potential problems inherent with the construction of large-scale data centers.

While bank trust departments no longer roam the investing planet, passive investing products and strategies (ETFs and quantitative investors) now dominate. Passive investors are unemotional and no nothing about value but everything about price as they all worship at the altar of price momentum — serving to exaggerate the market's returns and that of the leading technology companies.

I conclude that today we are not in a bubble (as we were with the Nifty Fifty and The Dot-Com Boom), though some similarities exist. Rather we are simply in an extremely and historically overvalued market (within a much different market structure backdrop dominated by passive investors).

Finally, here are some examples of comparing valuations in these three eras.

The Buffett Indicator stands at two standard deviations above its long-term trendline and at a record high of 217% (well above the Dot-Com era):

📷
Most traditional valuation metrics approach the 98%-tile. Today's price-earnings multiple on the S&P Index is 23x — the highest in 26 years (back to the peak in the Dot-Com period) and compared to the 30-year long-term average of only 17x:

📷
Dr. Robert Shiller's CAPE Ratio today is 40x vs 44x at the peak of Dot-Com and only 24x at the height of the Nifty Fifty Era. However, if we adjust profits for the low tax rates today compared to the peak in 2000 the Schillers CAPE is above 46x:

📷
Today's unparalleled S&P concentration into a handful of large-cap tech stocks is similar (and more extreme) than in the prior bubbles. Such concentration when coupled with elevated valuations almost always is a poor launching pad for future investment returns and often presages substantive bear markets or extended periods of substandard returns (our base case):

📷
Let’s look at the similarity of the S&P dividend yield today compared to the peak of the Dot-Com Boom:

📷
Over time dividends have contributed to about one-third of the total return for stocks — with the rest coming from capital appreciation. Today, the S&P Dividend Yield is only 1.17% — the lowest read in 2 1/2 decades (since the Dot-Com Boom). This means if S&P dividends maintain their 1/3 historical contribution to the total annual return for stocks, a 1.17% dividend yield translates into a lowly +3.5% total return for equities. With the S&P earnings yield of about 4.0% (the inverse of the P/E) and the 10-year Treasury yielding 4.15% — the equity risk premium is negative! The difference between the S&P dividend yield (1.17%) and the risk-free rate of return (4.15%) is also at a multiple-decade wide.

A low expected total return for equities coupled with a higher risk-free rate of return is fundamental to my bearish market case.

While I don't think the next few years will resemble the brutal declines of The Nifty Fifty (that began in 1973-74) of the Dot-Com bust (that commenced in early 2000), the downside to equities remains meaningful.

Why I keep talking about $TAO .
Real talk. 2021 did not shake out weak hands.
It robbed people blind and burned trust to the ground.

14 billion dollars stolen in 2021 alone.

2.8 billion of that was rug pulls.

46,000 plus reported victims to the FTC.

Over 1 billion in documented losses in 2021 to 2022.

And around 95 percent of NFTs are now effectively worthless.

That is not volatile markets.
That is extraction.

Look at the NFT graveyard.

Jack Dorsey’s first tweet sold for 2.9M
Today it struggles to fetch 4 dollars. Four.

Justin Bieber’s Bored Ape bought for 1.3M
Now worth around 60,000.

Madonna’s Ape bought for 466,000.
Now closer to 53,000.

These were not experiments in digital culture.
They were products designed to be dumped on the people who trusted them most.

Behind it all was the same playbook.

1. Create artificial scarcity
Limited NFTs, hidden or unlimited token supply, make it sound rare.
2. Manufacture FOMO
Celebrity endorsements, you are still early, Discord hype, Telegram raids.
3. Promise utility
Games, metaverse, community, yield. Almost none of it ever shipped.
4. Extract value
Projects launched, insiders and founders dumped into retail FOMO.
Exchange supply was just a constant stream of sell orders.
5. Disappear
Discord goes quiet. Website not updated. Founders lawyer up and move on.

Max supply more like unlimited or hidden.
Utility was promised, never delivered.
Revenue source was retail FOMO.
Revenue destination right into founder wallets.
Staking fake yields and ponzinomics.
Transparency Discord announcements, then silence.
End state founders rich, retail broke AF. 

So when people say retail abandoned crypto, I get it.

If you lost a few thousand dollars on something you genuinely believed in, you did not just lose money.
You lost confidence in your own judgment.
You felt stupid. Embarrassed. Used.

The reasonable conclusion was simple.
The game is rigged. I am exit liquidity. I am out.

And honestly, that conclusion was correct for 2021.

Now here is why I am still here.
And why I keep talking about Bittensor and $TAO .

Because structurally, it is the opposite of that playbook.

Where 2021 projects lived on retail FOMO, Bittensor lives on real demand for AI.

Money in and money out look completely different.

Money comes from enterprises and developers paying for AI services.

Money flows back into the network through subnet tokens and $TAO economics.

Look at actual revenue, not roadmaps.

Targon, Subnet 4, is not selling vibes. It is selling enterprise inference.
Tens of millions of dollars worth of Nvidia hardware behind it.
Over ten million dollars a year in revenue from customers using the system.

Chutes is building serverless AI compute that looks a lot more like an AWS competitor than a meme coin.
Celium did over a million in a handful of months.
Ridges is hitting coding accuracy close to frontier models.
Dippy has millions of users in production.

That is not we are going to build a metaverse someday.
That is already live product with paying customers.

Now overlay the token design.

Bittensor does not hide its supply.
There are 21 million $TAO . Full stop. Same hard cap as Bitcoin.

The model around $TAO looks more like this:
Subnets provide useful services.
Those services generate real revenue.
That revenue supports subnet tokens and demand for compute.
Scarce $TAO sits underneath the whole thing as the base asset.

They sold pictures of rocks and called it the future.
This time, we are building actual infrastructure for decentralized intelligence.

Retail is still stuck replaying the old trauma.
They hear new project and instantly think I am the bag holder again.
I do not blame them.

At some point, we are going to look past the scars and ask
Not what is the next meme, but what is actually being used, who is paying for it, and where does the money go.

Those two things should not be put in the same bucket.
 Eventually the market will stop treating them as if they are.

Whether you entered NFTs a few months ago or have been around since the early waves, there is one name in generative art you need to know: Dmitri Cherniak @dmitricherniak . And one collection that has earned its place as a true grail in digital art: Ringers.

 #Ringers stands out because it takes an incredibly simple idea and turns it into an entire universe. Cherniak built a system where a loop of string winds around a set of pegs, yet every output looks completely different. Some pieces feel mechanical. Others feel like woven tapestries or futuristic schematics. Every Ringer has its own personality. The brilliance is how much beauty and complexity he created from such minimal ingredients. That is why many people see Ringers as one of the most important achievements in early generative art.

When it launched on @artblocks_io Curated in 2021, very few understood what they were minting. But once collectors took a deeper look, the collection took off. Floors pushed past 50 eth, then over 100 eth during peak times. Even the least rare pieces traded in the multiple-six-figure range when eth was strong. It became clear that Ringers was not just another project. It was art that could hold its place in any serious collection.

And then came the moment that changed everything.
Ringers #879, known as The Goose, sold for 6.2 million dollars at @Sothebys . Overnight it became the single most recognizable piece of generative art in the world. It appeared in mainstream press, institutional conversations, and discussions about the future of digital art. Even people who knew nothing about NFTs recognized The Goose. It became a symbol of what this entire movement represents.

This year gives Ringers an even bigger spotlight.
 @ArtBasel Miami is launching Zero 10, its first dedicated digital art section inside the main fair. This is a major step. Collectors, museums, and institutions from all over the world will walk through a curated digital art space, and Ringers is exactly the kind of work that thrives in that setting. It is thoughtful, elegant, and conceptually strong. It feels like it belongs in a museum because it does.

Newer collectors and long-time traders are both drawn to it for the same reason. Ringers has a clarity and confidence that separates true art from everything else. And as AI begins generating endless images, I think early human-made generative systems like Ringers will only become more important. They capture a moment when artists designed the rules, the logic, and the entire creative framework. That kind of authorship matters.

Even traders who live for volatility know this. They understand that turning short-term gains into long-term wealth requires placing value into scarce, respected assets. This is why serious collectors vault their Ringers, and why a few specialized platforms like @gondixyz even allow loans against them. Only a handful of NFTs in existence have ever reached that level of trust.

And here is the reality everyone needs to hear.
There are only 1,000 Ringers. Supply is fixed forever. The cultural and historical relevance keeps compounding as generative art moves into museums, galleries, and global conversations.

Yet right now, in this moment, a few Ringers are listed for under 10 eth. For a collection that once traded over 100 eth at the floor, that price feels unreal. Anyone who understands digital art knows how rare moments like this are.

The question is simple.

Who understands what Ringers represents?
Who sees where this is going?
And who will join the club of only 1,000 collectors who can ever own a grail like this?

Startups Using AI Have a Problem: Anyone Can Copy Their Awesome Idea | Joe Wilkins, Futurism

"Every feature that we put out, we know that's going to take either a few weeks or a few months for competitor to copy."

In an era of unprecedented tech hype, one AI startup founder has a warning to those who would follow his footsteps: vibe coding a double-edged sword that makes it trivially easy for competitors to copy your brilliant company.

Israeli tech founder Maor Shlomo, whose vibe coding startup Base44 sold for over $80 million when it was acquired by Wix, said on the podcast “20VC” that “it’s relatively easy to create a vibe coding tool.”

“Every feature that we put out, we know that’s going to take either a few weeks or a few months for competitor to copy,” he complained.

First flagged by Business Insider, the founder is arguably the poster child of the financial feeding frenzy that’s come to define the AI era. In another podcast recorded in July, Shlomo claimed he used AI to write “90 percent of the code” for Base44. Over the last three months prior to the acquisition, he recalled, he hadn’t written “a single line of front-end code” himself.

But while vibe coding is easy — all it takes is an idea, if Shlomo’s to be taken at face value — building actual software infrastructure isn’t so simple.

“It’s very, very, very hard to create a platform that could help people build products they’ll actually use, that are functional, that are complex enough for real-world use cases,” Shlomo admitted on 20VC.

The founder’s sentiments echo those of Andrej Karpathy, the OpenAI cofounder who coined the infamous term “vibe coding” earlier this year. “I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy-paste stuff, and it mostly works,” Karpathy wrote.

It’s an awesome foundation for a practice which is picking up billions of dollars of momentum in tech circles. Shlomo may be offering a particularly silly example of how fragile the AI economy has become, but he’s not wrong — if AI really does lead to a radical breakdown in the scarcity of intelligence, that’ll be extremely bad news for innovators.

When someone learns I was an early Palantir investor, they almost always ask, "You held onto your shares, right?" The short answer is no. I sold 98% of my shares between 2014 and 2016. Here's the long answer:

By 2014, my Palantir position had appreciated to 30-50% of my net worth, depending on how you calculated it. I loved the company, but its valuation back then (and implied revenue multiple) seemed very high. So I decided to explore secondary liquidity.

In those days, that meant swimming with sharks. Navigating the secondary market today is tricky, but back then it was truly a Wild West. Some buyers weren't reputable, and the pricing of Palantir trades was all over the place. Palantir also had a right of first refusal, so if the price was low enough, they'd buy the shares themselves. It was very much buyer (or seller) beware.

Over 3 years, I sold my shares in 4 or 5 transactions at an average of about $5.50 a share. For me, it was a windfall. I knew I was giving up potential upside, but I thought diversification would be more helpful. I rolled the proceeds into other angel investments.

When, in early 2020, the secondary price was around $4.75 (~10-15% less than what I sold for), I thought I was a genius who'd timed it just right. Then COVID hit. After a brief market scare, software got hot. Palantir's growth had been trending down, but it started to accelerate. Its valuation started going up. In 2022/2023, they brilliantly leaned into AI. Revenue growth began to pick up even faster, setting the stage for the massive share price appreciation since then. Looking back now, I missed out on a 30-35x gain. Oops. Maybe I'm not such a genius after all.

The reality is that venture funds and angel investors should think about liquidity quite differently. As an angel, you should probably be more open to losing some upside for diversification. That's what I did. But for a venture fund, your investors typically want you to be more risk-on, to take the upside. Fred Wilson of Union Square Ventures has a useful rule of thumb for early-stage VCs: if you can sell 1/3 of a position to get back the entire fund, do that. At the next chance, sell another 1/3. Let 1/3 roll basically forever.

That works well for funds. But my situation as an angel was different—which is why I don't beat myself up about the decision. It made sense for me at the time. Certainly, if I knew then what I know now, I would have held on to more shares. But that's hindsight for you. Some of the investments I rolled Palantir proceeds into didn't work out. But some—like Canva and BilliontoOne—have exceeded all expectations. I've gotten back a lot of that missed upside (at least on paper).

Overall, I've done pretty well and learned a lot about navigating liquidity. I'm very, very fortunate for how it all played out.

When sentiment shifted, there was no floor. NFTs have no cash flows, no dividends, no physical scarcity. Price was entirely driven by narrative and momentum.
The same dynamic has appeared in tulips, dot-com stocks, and meme coins. The asset changes. The psychology doesn't👀

openai.com was once Glenn's personal homepage in 2001.

 tiktok.com was a couple's shared site documenting their relationship from dating to married with a baby, roughly 1998 to 2001.

The thread is a reminder that the URLs running trillion-dollar AI and a billion-user social platform were, two decades ago, just regular people's blogs.

This is the hidden secondary economy of the internet.

Domains are real estate. The .com gold rush in the late 90s was the original land grab, and the early adopters who registered short, memorable, English-word URLs accidentally became landlords to the future. Most of them sold for a few thousand dollars in the early 2000s thinking they'd cashed in.

OpenAI later acquired openai.com for an undisclosed sum, almost certainly in the millions. TikTok parent ByteDance reportedly paid over $5 million for tiktok.com after launching as Musical.ly .

The pattern repeats across every major brand.

 facebook.com was registered in 1997, sold to Mark Zuckerberg in 2005 for $200,000. voice.com sold for $30 million in 2019.

 cars.com went for $872 million in 2014. carinsurance.com hit $49.7 million.

Generic, short, memorable URLs are some of the most appreciating assets of the digital age, and almost nobody talks about them outside the domain investor circle.

The hardware and the code change every five years.

The four-letter URL on the address bar is forever.

Best Quotes

"There are three classes of people: those who see, those who see when they are shown, those who do not see." Leonardo da Vinci

"Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art." Leonardo da Vinci

"Iron rusts from disuse; water loses its purity from stagnation... even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind." Leonardo da Vinci

Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher.

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity.

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive.

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498
Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490
Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.
Czartoryski Museum, Kraków

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science
Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

Military Tech: Armored tanks, giant crossbows, and portable bridges—way ahead of his era's tech.

Hydraulics and Engineering: Canal locks, diving suits, and self-supporting bridges. He even planned an ideal city to beat plagues.

Anatomy: Sketches more accurate than printed texts of the time, showing heart valves and fetal positions.
Fun fact: He invented the robotic knight in 1495—a mechanical automaton that could wave and sit up.

Steampunk before steam.

Personal Quirks and Legacy

Vegetarian and Animal Lover: Bought caged birds just to free them. Ahead of his time on ethics.

Procrastinator Extraordinaire: Queen Isabella of Spain once joked he'd paint her when pigs fly—ironically, he sketched flying pigs.

Death: May 2, 1519, at age 67 in Amboise, France. Buried in Château d'Amboise; his bones were scattered during the French Revolution.

Da Vinci's influence? Everywhere—from NASA's designs to modern AI ethics (he'd probably geek out over neural networks).

In 2025, his Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017, and recent scans of his notebooks (like the Leicester Codex) keep revealing hidden layers via infrared tech.

$OUST 
The analysis I shared today when it was down -9% to -11% in pre-market 👇
Ouster reported Q1 2026 results that beat revenue expectations, showed strong growth in product revenue, and marked its 13th consecutive quarter of product revenue growth. Revenue increased roughly 50% YoY to $49M; product revenue came in at $48.2M; more than 12,600 lidar and camera sensors were shipped; and a new quarterly shipment record was also set on the lidar side. Despite this, the stock sold off by around -7% after ER. The most likely reason for this selloff is the combination of a good quarter, but a forward outlook that was not enough for the valuation: Q2 guidance implies only limited sequential growth, gross margin declined sharply on a quarterly basis, the company is still posting losses, and as emphasized in the 10-Q, risks such as integration, supply chain, customer concentration, tariffs/trade policy, and the path to profitability remain on the table. Still, the current data set does not show that the main investment thesis has completely broken. It points more to a divergence between short-term price expectations and the long-term platform story.

Main Picture of Q1 2026 Results

The company reported total Q1 revenue of $48.6M; $48.2M of this came from product revenue. Total revenue increased from $32.6M in the same period last year. Gross profit was $20.8M, while GAAP net loss was $17.5M. Loss per share came in in-line at -$0.28. Operating loss remained at -$19.2M. From an operational perspective, revenue growth is strong, but the company is not yet profitable on an accounting basis.

The management message was quite ambitious. The company positions itself as a unified sensing and perception platform for Physical AI; it emphasized that the Stereolabs acquisition is at the center of this and that the Rev8 native color lidar launch represents a new era in the product roadmap. Management said the strategic rationale of Stereolabs has quickly turned into operational reality and that customer feedback has been strong. It was also stated that Rev8 has started shipping and has seen early interest from many customers.

Operational Strengths

In Q1, product revenue increased 55% YoY and 18% QoQ. The company shipped more than 12,600 sensors; more than 8,300 of these were lidar units, which was presented as a new quarterly record. The lidar business grew approximately 44% YoY. On the Smart Infrastructure side, million-dollar agreements were announced for BlueCity in Arizona, Michigan, and the northeastern U.S.; deployment was expanded with the Georgia Department of Transportation at more than 30 intersections in the Greater Atlanta area. It was stated that BlueCity has more than 700 contracted site installations. On the Gemini side, millions of dollars of revenue were recorded from a meaningful customer renewal. These support the argument that the company is not just a lidar player selling individual products, but is transforming into a platform player trying to build a broader solution layer.

The first impact of the Stereolabs acquisition was also presented in a positive framework. Q1 revenue included roughly 7 weeks of Stereolabs contribution. Management said the camera portfolio delivered fast commercial contribution, and that demand was better than expected in foundational AI models, advanced robotics, autonomous delivery, precision agriculture, and manipulation use cases. The 10-Q also clearly states that this acquisition positions Ouster as an end-to-end platform combining lidar, cameras, AI compute, sensor fusion, and perception software.

Most Likely Reasons Why the Market Sold

For a triple upside reaction, three things were needed: revenue near the upper end, product-based margin resilience, and a management tone that gave confidence in the 2026 outlook. The first two largely arrived. Revenue came in at $49M, above the $46.15M expectation and also above the previously given $45M-$48M guidance. On the margin side, even though the Q4 royalty effect normalized, GAAP gross margin stayed at 43%, above the long-term 35%-40% framework. It was also specifically stated that royalty revenue was insignificant in Q1. So there is margin decline, but a major part of this is not quality deterioration; it is the disappearance of Q4’s unusually high-margin base.

So why did the stock fall?

Here, I think three main reasons stand out.

First, the market wanted to see not just a revenue beat, but earnings quality + acceleration. In the pre-analysis, I had said that expectations had risen, institutions had turned positive, and good results alone might not be enough. In this situation, the $49M revenue beat is positive, but the market likely expected a more aggressive forward outlook and a stronger profitability signal. Q2 guidance came in at $49.5M-$52.5M. This guidance is positive, but not explosive; especially when the Rev8, Stereolabs, and Physical AI narrative was built so strongly, the market may have looked for sharper momentum.

Second, the EPS and profitability side may not have looked as clean as expected. Although the company balanced this with strength on the revenue side, from a pricing behavior perspective, the perception may have formed as revenue beat, but losses are still high. Q1 net loss was -$17.5M, operating loss was -$19.2M, and adjusted EBITDA was -$7M. Also, adjusted EBITDA loss worsened by $20M sequentially. A significant part of this came from the loss of the Q4 royalty effect and integration expenses, but the market may have initially read this as profitability cadence is slow.

Third, although the Stereolabs and Rev8 story is positive, their contribution to financials may not yet have looked as large as the narrative. In Q1, revenue included only about 7 weeks of Stereolabs contribution. Operating expenses also rose to $40M, including $2.3M of acquisition/integration charges. So the market may currently be asking: the strategic direction is right, but how fast will financial leverage arrive? Especially even though management described very strong customer interest for Rev8, for this to immediately push the stock higher, investors need to see clearer monetization and mix impact.

Positive Side

Core product revenue did not deteriorate. On the contrary, product revenue accelerated.

Gross margin did not collapse. Once Q4’s roughly $21M royalty contribution was removed, margin normalization was already expected; 43% is still a solid level.

The balance sheet is not weak. The company ended the quarter with roughly $175M in cash and short-term investments, and no debt. The 10-Q also says current liquidity is enough to fund operations for at least 12 months.

Did the Main Investment Thesis Break?

My view: no, the main investment thesis does not appear to be broken.

Because if the main thesis is Ouster’s transformation from not just a lidar supplier, but into a Physical AI platform combining lidar, cameras, AI compute, sensor fusion, and perception software, this quarter does not weaken that thesis. The Rev8 launch, Stereolabs integration, BlueCity expansion, 12,600+ sensor shipments, record volume with 8,300+ lidar units, and strong cash position all support this main story. Also, as I emphasized in my pre-analysis note, sector consolidation and weakening competitors remain a framework that strengthens Ouster’s relative position.

But if the short-term expectation was this: after Rev8 + Stereolabs, the market would immediately move Ouster into a higher valuation band, this quarter did not clearly prove that. Because the market is still asking these questions: how much will growth accelerate, how much will the margin structure scale, how clean will the integration process be, and when will the company enter a clearer profitability stride? Management points to a clearer profitability threshold in 2027, but that may not be enough for impatient short-term investors.

🦇Batman Commentary
The main reason for the decline in OUST is not that the fundamental story broke; it is that elevated expectations, especially on profitability and forward momentum, were not fully met. Core product growth is strong, margin remains healthy when adjusted for the royalty effect, the balance sheet is strong, and the strategic platform story continues to live. That is why I do not think the main investment thesis has broken. But the stock is now being priced not only on good product and good story, but also on whether this story can produce faster financial output.

$TSLA & SpaceX are reportedly proposing a $55B investment to build Elon Musk’s “Terafab” semiconductor facility.

This figure could potentially rise to $119B.

Here's the crazy part:

Back in 1995, Elon Musk couldn't afford both an office and an apartment but now his companies are investing billions into semiconductors & AI.

Here is @elonmusk 's entire story:

His first company was Zip2 which was a software to help newspapers move their content online. He ran the whole operation with 6 people drilling a hole through the floor to steal internet from the ISP downstairs for $100/month.

Compaq bought it in 1999 for over $300 million in cash.

He then moved onto his next big idea: Paypal where you could email money to anyone like sending a message.

The feature took about a day to build. The growth took on a life of its own. One customer sent money to a friend. That friend signed up. That friend sent money to someone else. By the end of year two: 1 million customers.

He sold that to eBay for $1.5B.

Then Musk started asking a question nobody else was asking:

Why hasn't space improved since Apollo?

In the 1960s, we went from nothing to landing on the moon in a decade. Then 30 years of basically nothing. Every other sector of technology had transformed. Space just... stopped.

He flew to Moscow 3 times to buy a refurbished Russian ICBM. Couldn't get a deal that made sense. Flew home.

On the flight back, he decided: we should just build our own rocket.

SpaceX was founded with the goal of cutting launch costs by an order of magnitude.

The result: Falcon rocket.

$6 million per launch.

Nearest competitor (Orbital Sciences Pegasus): $25 million per launch, less capability.

Built by 30 people.

Fastest launch vehicle development in history including wartime.

The same playbook ran through all three companies:

- Small team, no hierarchy
- Best idea wins, not loudest title
- Obsess over product, not sales
- Simplicity = reliability + lower cost
- Run dependencies in parallel, never one at a time

The pattern that beat billion-dollar incumbents.

His first company sold for $300M. He used it to build PayPal. Then SpaceX.

a tiny Caribbean island with 16,000 people accidentally became one of the biggest winners of the AI boom.

not through code, not through chips., but through two letters.

be Anguilla:

- British Overseas Territory
- 35 square miles
- economy built on beaches and tourism
- no tech sector
- no Silicon Valley connections
- no plan

1980s: the International Organization for Standardization assigned every country a two-letter code

- US gets .us
- UK gets .uk
- Anguilla gets .ai
- neighboring island Antigua gets .ag
- nobody thought twice about it

1994: an American software developer named Vince Cate moves to Anguilla

- he wants a domain name that ends in .ai
- reaches out to Jon Postel, the man in charge of all global top-level domains
- Postel tells him nobody is running .ai
- asks if Cate wants to run it
- Cate says yes
- that is literally how it happened

February 16, 1995: .ai officially goes live

- for the next 27 years, barely anyone cares
- mostly local Anguillian businesses
- a handful of niche companies
- 2018 total revenue: $2.9 million
- less than 1% of the island's government income

then ChatGPT dropped in November 2022

- registrations surge from 144,000 in 2022 to 354,000 in 2023
- perplexity, claude, X, meta, google, etc
- every startup that wanted to signal AI credibility needed a .ai

2023 revenue: $32 million 2024 revenue: $39 million nearly a quarter of the entire island's government budget

2025 revenue: $85.3 million government had projected $49 million actual revenue almost doubled their own forecast .ai domains went from less than 1% of state income to 47% in a single decade

over 1 million .ai domains now registered renewals kicked in on all the 2023 wave registrations in 2025 90% renewal rate that is when the real money started compounding

meanwhile the domain aftermarket went insane:

- bot.ai sold for $1.2 million in February 2025, the highest publicly known .ai domain sale at that point
- Dharmesh Shah, co-founder of HubSpot, paid $700,000 for you.ai 
- then in February 2026, AI.com sold for $70 million. the largest domain transaction ever recorded in history. the buyer was Kris Marszalek, founder of Crypto.com 

what is Anguilla doing with the money:

- paying down national debt, projected to fall to 19.9% of GDP by end of 2025, well below the Caribbean's 60% benchmark
- expanding airports and roads
- investing in renewable energy
- free healthcare for children under five and seniors over seventy

- in January 2025, Anguilla signed a five-year deal with US company Identity Digital to manage the registry. 
- Identity Digital takes 10%. Anguilla keeps the rest.
- compare that to Tuvalu, the Pacific island that made a similar bet with .tv when streaming took off. 
- Tuvalu gave domain registrations to a big foreign company and locked themselves in for 50 years. 
- most of the money did not go to the country. 
- Anguilla studied that playbook and refused to repeat it.

the Prime Minister still warns against complacency: - "you can't predict how long this will last.
- he is right to say that. the .ai boom depends entirely on whether those two letters stay synonymous with artificial intelligence as the industry matures. 
- so far, the association has only gotten stronger. the biggest AI companies in the world use .ai as product identifiers, not just domain names.

but the real story here is not just the money.
- in 1994, a developer on a tiny island emailed a man named Jon Postel and asked if he could run an obscure two-letter domain. 
- Postel said yes. nobody planned this. nobody strategized this. 
- the island of Anguilla did not outthink Silicon Valley.
- they just had the right two letters at the right moment in history. 
- and unlike most countries that stumbled into digital assets, they kept the bag and are doing something meaningful with it.

One of the most iconic masterpieces in fantasy art: "A Princess of Mars" (1970) by the legendary Frank Frazetta.

This oil painting, created as the cover for the Doubleday reprint of Edgar Rice Burroughs' classic novel, captures John Carter triumphantly raising his sword over a defeated green Thark warrior, with the fearless Dejah Thoris at his side, set against the looming view of Earth and its moon from the red deserts of Barsoom (Mars).

Fun facts:

- Frazetta loved this composition so much that he painted two nearly identical versions: one for the publisher (fearing it wouldn't be returned, a common issue back then), and a personal "superior" copy with subtle refinements (more confident pose for Dejah, ornate jewelry, sharper details). The personal version, kept by his family for 50 years, sold for $1.2 million at Heritage Auctions in 2020.

- It's hugely influential, directly inspiring the original Star Wars poster style (Luke with lightsaber, Leia clinging, Vader/Death Star behind).

All credit to the master himself, Frank Frazetta, the godfather of fantasy illustration.

It had all the ingredients of a brand that could anchor a serious platform — whether for a corporate wellness consultancy, a strategic AI-driven health startup, a health planning app, or even a government or NGO initiative focused on public health policy.

📊 TLD Metrics vs Brand Potential

When evaluating domains, I often check how many other TLDs are registered using tools like DotDB.com . It’s a useful signal — and I believe in checking all key metrics.

In this case:

HealthStrategy .com had only 15 TLDs registered

iSoft .com → Acquired for $9,000 → Sold for $60,000

HealthStrategy .com → Acquired for $3,000 → Sold for $100,000

This highlights an important truth in domain investing:

✅ TLD count is helpful, but not everything
✅ Every asset class is unique
✅ Brand clarity, context, and timing often matter more

🎯 Brand-First Decision Framework

Before I make a purchase, I always evaluate:

==> How the name sounds as a brand

==> Whether it makes semantic sense as a pair

==> How trustworthy or credible it feels in its industry

==> The strength of comparable sales in the niche

Only after those boxes are checked do I let gut instinct weigh in — and even then, it plays a supporting role, not a leading one.

In this case, I wasn’t influenced by how many TLDs were taken. I focused on the message the name delivers and how easily a serious company could build authority, trust, and inbound business using it.

The Full Guide: From Noob to Advanced

Settings and Focus

First thing you do is go to settings and turn off animations. you want to move fast. Another good way to learn is by watching replays of top games. open the leaderboard and click the reel icon next to a game to access a full replay.

Use the alternative client from @djizus_ . It is not cheating. It levels the playing field by showing you the deep math of the game. In an age of bots and ai your only edge is critical thinking and creativity. The alternative client handles the math so you can focus on the human strategy that bots cannot replicate.

The Early Game Foundation

You start by dumping your first points into Charisma. this keeps the market cheap. if you do not do this you will go broke buying potions.

Buy a tier 1 weapon on turn one if possible. Items gain experience and a tier 1 weapon at level 15 unlocks massive special bonuses. if you use a lower tier weapon early you are wasting experience on trash.

For armor, fill all five slots immediately. it does not matter if the gear is weak. if a slot is empty the game logic targets that area and you die. use cheap armor as a shield for your body until you find your real strategy.

Stat Benchmarks

Get Dexterity to level 3 early. this gives you very high flee chance in the beginning. be aware that this chance drops as you go deeper into the dungeon. anything above 50 percent is decent. it is your emergency exit.

Get Wisdom and Intelligence to level 2 plus. if you leave these at zero the game will punish you with constant fire storms and ambushes.

Strength is your pure offense but Vitality is the real secret. it is a mix of defense and offense because it keeps you alive long enough to actually finish a fight.

Bag Bonus Tech

This is the hidden tech people miss. bag bonuses are not universal.

Only Vitality and Charisma bonuses count when the item is in your bag. nothing else.
You only get those bonuses after the item reaches level 15.

So yes, you can farm items that give +3 Vitality or +3 Charisma, level them to 15, then keep them in your backpack for passive value. you do not need to equip them.

I read every YC Request for Startups since 2016. The pattern nobody talks about is embarrassingly obvious in hindsight. - I will not Promote
Long post but I think this reframes how to think about startup ideas in a way that actually matters. Stick with me.

I spent three months going back through every YC Request for Startups published since 2016. Eight batches. Hundreds of problem descriptions from the most successful startup investors alive.

Here is what I found:

YC does not fund the most exciting ideas. They fund the most expensive problems.

That sounds obvious when you say it out loud. But I do not think most founders actually operate this way when they are generating ideas, and the difference in outcomes is enormous.

The pattern I have noticed is, Every single YC request, every year, every batch, without exception, follows the same structure:

Large established industry (healthcare, legal, financial services, manufacturing, agriculture)

Specific expensive problem inside that industry

Technology inflection that recently made the problem newly solvable

"Go build the company that solves this"

That is the entire formula. Large industry. Expensive problem. New solvability. Go.

To confirm above, Look at the companies that actually returned capital to YC, the ones that hit $100M ARR or got acquired for 9 figures. Almost none of them are the exciting ones.

Brex: corporate credit card

Gusto: payroll

Rippling: HR and IT administration

Segment: data pipelines between tools (sold for $3.2B)

Checkr: background checks

Faire: wholesale marketplace for independent retailers

These are not companies that dominated dinner party conversations in 2015 or 2017. They are companies that found large, expensive, underserved problems and built the solution at the moment when building it became technically feasible.

After this exercise I now apply one question to every startup idea I hear: what is this costing the economy right now, in dollars?

Not "how big is the market." What is this specific problem costing people this year?

If you cannot answer with a specific number in 60 seconds, you probably have not found the right problem.

Some examples from the 2026 YC batch:

Prior authorization in healthcare: estimated $35B per year in administrative cost for the US alone

Pesticide over-application: $18-24B in annual waste globally from imprecise application

Outside legal spend waste: US companies overpay estimated 18-22% on outside counsel, about $40-50B per year

Semiconductor supply chain opacity: $210B in vehicles not built in 2021 from one supply disruption

Inference compute waste: $30-40B per year in GPU compute wasted on agentic workloads running on hardware designed for batch inference

In every case: the "interesting" framing is about technology or environment or efficiency. The real framing is about cost.

Why founders keep missing this:

Three reasons.

1. Social reward. Telling someone you are building an AI assistant for drone swarm defense gets you follow-up questions. Telling someone you are building an AI insurance brokerage for small businesses kills the conversation. Founders respond to social reward the way everyone does.

2. Narrative. Building a company about a personal pain is a better story than "I noticed this was expensive and built the solution." The boring founding story does not attract press or conference invites. It attracts customers, which is the only thing that actually matters.

3. Technical glamour. Engineers like hard technical problems. Building an AI that reads insurance policy documents is not a hard technical problem. It is just an important one.

YC has built a system that filters past all three biases. They ask what is expensive, not what is interesting.

The three questions I now ask every idea:

What is this costing the economy right now, specifically, in dollars?

Why is this newly solvable in 2026 that was not solvable in 2024?

Who is currently absorbing this cost and what would they pay to stop?

If you can answer all three quickly and specifically, you have found a YC-pattern idea.

I believe, The best startup ideas are not the ones that keep you up at night with excitement. They are the ones keeping your potential customers up at night with pain.

Those two things your excitement and their pain are frequently not the same thing. When they align, you have a good idea. When they diverge, the customer pain wins every time.

YC has been publishing cost calculations disguised as funding requests for 8 years. Most founders read them as inspiration and move on.

The founders who treat them as a list of the most expensive unsolved problems in the economy, and then immediately call five potential customers to ask "how much is this costing you," are the ones who get funded.

Happy to answer questions. I went deep on the 2026 batch specifically and broke down the cost calculations behind each of their 13 stated priorities if anyone wants to dig into specifics.

An interesting winner of the AI boom: a Louisiana data center construction firm (Fibrebond) sold for $1.7B and the owner gifted $240m to 540 long-time employees (none had equity) as a thank you.

Great story from WSJ's Gregory Zuckerman:

◽️ in 1982, Claud Walker ran a 12-person company building structures for telephone and electronic equipment 
◽️ business boomed in 1990s with the company rebranding to Fibrebond and building concrete enclosures for cellphone towers
◽️ then, its factory burnt down in 1998 and the Dotcom Bubble burst crushed the business
◽️ Claud's two sons (including Graham Walker) took over Fibrebond in the mid-2000s after working their way up from doing "menial jobs"
◽️ over the next decade, they tried to find new infrastructure opportunities but it was tough sledding
◽️ the Walkers had to freeze salaries for a period (they had earned loyalty from employees for continuing to pay salaries after the factory burned down and also established an emergency fund)
◽️ Graham took over as CEO in 2015 and invested $150m "to expand capacity to build infrastructure for data centers, including enclosures for power equipment."
◽️ the data centre business zoomed during COVID and has kept going with the AI boom
◽️ sales are up 400% in the past 5 years
◽️ larger firms wanted to acquire Fibrebond but "Walker told suitors 15% of the proceeds of any deal would have to go to his employees, a reward for their loyalty and dedication."

When asked why 15%, Graham just said "it's more than 10%".

Power-management firm Eaton ($126B market cap) acquired Fibrebond for $1.7B in April.

The Walker family (5 siblings total) received ~$1B and the 540 employees were allotted $240m (those under the age of 65 earn the full sum over 5 years).

The average bonus is $440k but the most senior employees received more.

The only other large employer in Minden, Louisiana is Walmart, so this deal is a major W for the city.

Graham is exiting Fibrebond for good at the end of the year.
