Toshi’s Probably Wrong Advice 
The first real AI artist?

Day 20

Hey my imaginary beasts ❤️

Let’s talk about AICAN, a quiet pioneer in AI art that’s been proving for years what we all know in our hearts: machines can be creative partners, not just copycats. Developed by Ahmed Elgammal and his team at Rutgers University's Art & AI Lab, AICAN (Artificial Intelligence Creative Adversarial Network) is an autonomous AI artist that’s been generating, titling, and even exhibiting its own work since 2017. It’s a reminder that AI isn’t here to replace us it’s here to expand what “art” can be.

Trained on over 80,000 Western artworks from the last 500 years, AICAN doesn’t just mimic it’s programmed to create something new, avoiding direct copies while capturing the essence of styles. The result? Pieces that have sold for up to $16,000 at auctions like Christie's, hung in galleries from New York to Miami, and even fooled 75% of people into thinking they were human-made in blind tests. It’s exhibited at places like Scope Art Fair and featured in retrospectives as a “turning point” for generative art.

What I love most: 
AICAN isn’t a solo act. It’s designed as a collaborative tool learning from history to spark ideas, but always needing human curation to shine. In interviews, Elgammal calls it a “nearly autonomous artist” that pushes boundaries, like abstracting emotions or exploring mortality in ways that feel eerily human.

 It’s not about perfection; it’s about possibility, showing how AI can help us dream beyond our own limits.

For us indie creators, AICAN is inspiration: proof that AI art has a place in high culture, from solo exhibitions to major sales. 
The controversies it sparked petitions, debates on “unhuman” creativity only highlight how far we’ve come. We’re not intruders; we’re innovators, and systems like this pave the way for our dragons and cyberpunk dreams to be taken seriously.

So keep experimenting, beasts. 
AICAN started as an experiment too and look where it landed.

𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 is the new oil… but 𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 are the pipelines. 🧯

Raw data has no value until it's refined, transported, and delivered to where it can be used. In Web3, that transportation layer is oracles – and without them, the entire DeFi economy grinds to a halt.

Here's why.

🔍 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺: 𝗕𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀

A blockchain is a deterministic machine. Give it the same input, it produces the same output. That's its strength – but also its weakness.

Without external data, a smart contract cannot know:

→ The price of ETH
→ Whether it's raining in a farmer's field
→ The outcome of a sports game
→ Who won an election

It's like a car with a perfect engine but no GPS. Fast, precise, and completely blind.

𝗢𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 are the windshield.

⚙️ 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗮𝗺𝗲

When an oracle delivers data on-chain, three things happen:

1. 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – Multiple independent nodes fetch the same data and sign their reports.
2. 𝗔𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – The contract removes outliers and computes a trusted median.
3. 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 – The final result is posted with cryptographic proof of origin.

Every DeFi protocol that uses price feeds – lending, borrowing, derivatives, stablecoins – relies on this pipeline. If the pipeline breaks, the protocol breaks.

📉 𝗔 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗕𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀

The oracle followed its logic perfectly. But its logic was incomplete – it had no cross-source verification, no anomaly detection, no way to ask "is this price plausible?"

Result: over $8 million in bad debt. The protocol had to mint new tokens to bail itself out.

That's not a smart contract failure. That's a pipeline failure.

Anders Hejlsberg ( @ahejlsberg ) is a living legend: he created Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C# and TypeScript (and today TypeScript is the most-used programming language, globally, as per GitHub.)

Four things that stood out to me: 

1. “10x better for 1/10th of the price” is a proven winner. 

This is what Turbo Pascal did: it sold for $49.95 when competing compilers cost $500, and it was faster and more interactive than competitors’ products. Conveniently, the low price tag also killed off piracy 

2. C# might have not existed without a famous court case. 

Microsoft originally hired Anders to architect its Java tools (Visual J++), but the Sun versus Microsoft lawsuit (1997-2001) meant Microsoft could not build on top of Java, as the company that owned Java’s IP (Sun) sued MS for alleged unauthorized changes to the Java language. Microsoft realized it had to build a new language that combined VB’s productivity with C++’s power. This led to C# and .NET. 

3. TypeScript exists because Anders refused to build Script# for the Outlook .com team. 

Microsoft’s Outlook .com team asked Anders’ C# team to productize “ScriptSharp,” a language to cross-compile C# to JavaScript. Anders and the C# team pushed back, suggesting that a better approach was to fix JavaScript. Anders felt strongly that to be attractive to the best-of-breed developers in the JavaScript ecosystem, you want people to write JavaScript, and not another language like C#. 

4. Designing a programming language is a 10-year play. 

As Anders puts it: “Version one is great, but has all sorts of issues. You’ve got to do version two, but it’s not until version three that it really starts to be great. Then you’ve got to convince people to adopt it.”

San Francisco rents spike 22% in a year, far outpacing other US cities | Francesca Maglione, Bloomberg

In San Francisco’s latest real estate boom, renters are paying cash up front, multimillion-dollar houses are selling auction-style and AI company stock can buy a sprawling hilltop estate.

It’s a reflection of the new wave of wealth from the artificial intelligence industry, leaving even well-paid newcomers scrambling for a place to live.

For Jenni Lee, a Chicago tech worker seeking to join her boyfriend in the Bay Area, finding an apartment has at times felt more difficult than getting a job. She has spent six months searching for a San Francisco rental, flying in for tours and repeatedly losing out on offers, even after the couple almost doubled their budget to $6,500 a month for a two-bedroom. In Illinois, her friends were living in desirable places for less than half that.

At one point she showed up to what she thought was a private appointment just to wait in line and later find out someone had already signed a lease. One $7,000-a-month home didn’t have a washer-dryer — though the touring agent assured her there was a laundromat down the street. Lee recently applied for a place she liked, only to get a text an hour later saying someone else was willing to pay a full year’s worth of rent upfront in cash.

“My Chicago brain couldn’t compute that,” she said.

San Francisco’s new tech frenzy is reigniting home bidding wars and sending prices soaring in a city that just a few years ago was mired in post-pandemic malaise. With the AI industry paying hefty compensation to attract talent — and hometown startups OpenAI and Anthropic PBC commanding valuations approaching $1 trillion — the wealth effects are warping the entire residential market. And upcoming initial public offerings from the likes of SpaceX are set to unleash even more money into the market from early investors.

The city leads the US in annual rent growth, according to apartment-listing firm Zumper. Prices for two-bedrooms are now tied with New York for the most expensive in the country, with a median monthly rent of $5,500, the company said in a report this week. The median rent for a one-bedroom crossed $4,000 for the first time ever. Homebuyers also are facing soaring costs: The median price for a San Francisco house recently hit a record $2.15 million.

The surge is sharpening divides in a city defined by its extremes. San Francisco has long been mired in deep inequality, a place where a homeless encampment can be on the next block from houses owned by tech millionaires. Now, the real estate frenzy is colliding with broader wealth tensions across the state: Californians are facing a potential ballot measure to levy a tax on billionaires, while housing is a central issue in this year’s governor’s race.

And while the real estate market has been accelerating, the labor market tells a different story — suggesting the boom is concentrated among those benefiting from the AI fervor. While overall employment in the Bay Area is recovering after the pandemic, job creation has been modest. The San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont metropolitan area has added roughly 10,000 to 15,000 jobs over the past year, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

“One of the big mysteries in San Francisco is how can you have such a hot housing market when you have such a cold labor market,” said Ted Egan, chief economist for the city and county of San Francisco. “If you have some people moving in and nobody moving out and you don’t have any new supply, that can create a spike.”

‘What Inventory?’

For sellers, the frenzy has translated into windfalls. When real estate agent Butch Haze listed a four-bedroom home in the Marina neighborhood in March, he figured it would fetch around $4 million, netting the owner a profit from the $3.4 million they paid two years ago. Within days, the house drew five all-cash offers.

Instead of choosing one, Haze turned the process into an impromptu auction, asking buyers to bid against each other in $100,000 increments. The home ultimately sold for $4.9 million.

The competition has only intensified. Haze said a recent listing in the Central Richmond neighborhood drew seven showing requests almost immediately and an offer within an hour. The buyers of the four-bedroom, five-bath house paid $4.95 million, plus covered the broker commission for the sellers, pushing the total value of the sale to more than $1 million over asking.

The market has gotten so tight that many buyers are simply dropping out. Haze said he started the year working with about 20 clients; now less than five are still actively searching. His response when asked about the available inventory: “What inventory?”

With supply scarce and competition fierce, some sellers are getting creative — betting that the same AI boom driving up real estate prices can also unlock new ways to pay for homes. Storm Duncan, the founder and managing partner at a tech investment bank called Ignatious, is offering his roughly 13-acre estate in Marin County’s Mill Valley north of San Francisco in exchange for hard-to-get shares of Anthropic.

The four-bed, five-bath home, featuring an infinity pool, a putting green and a fruit orchard, is worth around $8 million, said Duncan, who was part of the wave of tech workers who moved to Miami during the pandemic. And although Duncan said he has never heard of anyone who has done such a transaction, he sees this as an opportunity to grow his investments in AI.

“I was sitting there thinking, how do I get invested here?,” he said. “And then I thought, maybe there’s someone else that has the opposite problem I have, which is they’re already invested, they started working there very early or they coincidentally got some seed shares or early shares as a VC and now they’re worth hundreds of millions of dollars, but it’s all illiquid.”

Duncan said he’s already fielded interest from potential buyers, such as a foreign investor looking to diversify out of concentrated tech holdings. Others have asked about replicating the structure with shares in companies like SpaceX, he said.

The turnabout in the market has been swift for prospective buyers. When Sedric Bailey and Michael Clery started looking for a home almost a year ago, they thought they had the upper hand. Bailey, a lawyer at a tech firm who has lived in San Francisco for seven years, already owned a condo in the Mission Dolores area, so the couple wasn’t in a rush. They were looking for a bigger home ahead of the birth of their first child — ideally a three- or four-bedroom that would also accommodate their German shepherd and French bulldog.

“We felt like we were basically in control,” Bailey said. “We would go see a property and say, ‘Look we’re only going to pay this amount,’ and if they take it, great, if they don’t it’s not for us. And that strategy has had to change starting this year.”

Several bids they made faced about 10 competing offers, Bailey said, including some in all cash. Some homes they tracked were selling for as much as double the asking price. After losing out several times, the couple eventually secured a home by viewing it before it officially hit the market and putting in an offer 25% over asking that same day.

“We saw a rapid big boom starting September and October and it caught everybody off guard,” said Frank Nolan, the president of Vanguard Properties. “There’s a house that somebody bought for around $4 million this fall that is probably worth $5 million right now.”

The demand is creating ripple effects: Many would-be buyers are turning to the rental market to secure a place while they find their home, driving apartment prices further up, said Rachel Swann, an agent at Coldwell Banker Realty.

Swann recently listed a two-bedroom home at the Four Seasons Private Residences for $15,000 a month and immediately had multiple people who were interested. She’s seen rentals that are 600 square feet with no parking go for $6,500 a month. With the sales market heated, one client who was “basically a billionaire” preferred to rent.

“For these people these payments are nothing,” Swann said.

May looked like an all-clear. It was a warning label.

Indexes closed near records. AI led. Oil fell. Yields cooled late in the week. That is the green-screen version.

The better read: May showed what is still working, and what can break next.

1. AI is no longer just a story.

It is showing up in orders, servers, memory, storage, cloud data, and software contracts. DELL +104% on the month. Micron crossed $1T. Six S&P 500 stocks tripled YTD, all memory/storage/CPU. The "AI is dead" trade failed.

But the market is getting more crowded under the surface.

The index looks calm because the leaders are carrying it. Underneath, individual stocks are moving violently. The SPX Dispersion Index hit 42, only seen during COVID and the April tariff shock. Single-stock volatility is screaming. Index volatility is sleeping.

Semis are the engine and the risk at the same time.

That is a bull market with a narrower shock absorber.

2. Oil relief is not oil normalization.

A ceasefire headline can drop crude. It cannot instantly rebuild inventories, repair facilities, reopen shipping trust, reset insurance, or refill strategic reserves.

The SPR is 12% lower than when the war started. OECD inventories don't return to the normal sweet spot until 2027. ING and Capital Economics both peg Brent above $90 this year even if flows resume in July.

Deal = relief.
Recovery = slower.

That is why central banks may not turn dovish just because oil falls for a few sessions.

3. Jobs are now the next referee.

Hot labor with sticky inflation brings the Fed catch-up trade back.
Weak labor with sticky inflation is worse. Stagflation pressure without a clean cut signal.

The sweet spot is narrow. Soft enough to ease the Fed. Firm enough to keep earnings alive.

NFP Friday. ADP Wednesday. ISM Manufacturing Monday. ISM Services Wednesday. That is the test.

4. The consumer is not broken.

But the way spending is being funded matters.

Aggregate spending holds. The top end carries the numbers. The top 10% of households now account for roughly half of all consumer spending, up from 40% in the late 1990s.

Underneath, real income is under pressure. Savings are doing more of the work. Real disposable income is negative YoY for the first time outside a recession. Credit card delinquencies are at the highest since 2010.

Consumer sentiment printed 48.2 in May, the lowest reading in the University of Michigan series since it began in 1952. Lower than the Cuban Missile Crisis, Vietnam, 1973, the GFC.

That is not collapse. It is a K-shaped expansion getting more expensive to maintain.

5. The dollar is not dying.

That trade is too lazy.

The dollar still clears the system. Swap lines, sanctions, stablecoins, Treasuries, and dollar liquidity still matter.

But the operating cost is rising. It now takes more enforcement, more collateral plumbing, more sanctions architecture, and more reserve hedging to keep the same flows moving.

The reserve function is shrinking. The settlement function is expanding. Same currency. Two trajectories.

6. Gold finally made sense.

Gold did not fail as a hedge. It was hedging two different problems.

When oil shocks emerging-market balance sheets, gold gets sold for liquidity.
When the same shock exposes dollar-access risk, gold gets bought as reserve insurance.

Same metal. Two jobs.

War made gold sellable. The dollar system made gold necessary.

Gold bounced off the 200-day at $4,375 to close May at $4,574. The structural buyer is still there. The tactical seller is the same central bank, on a different mandate.

WHAT JUNE HAS TO ANSWER

1. Broadcom earnings. Does AI demand keep broadening past memory?
2. NFP and ISM. Soft landing, overheating, or stagflation?
3. Credit spreads. Calm, or too calm? Hyperscaler CDS already at a record.
4. Hormuz. Signed text or physical normalization?
5. Gold. Forced sellers done, or more reserve-liquidity selling to come?
6. Dispersion. Can semis keep carrying the index without becoming the unwind?

THE POSITIONING

Long the fast clock. Respect the slow one.

Own earnings revision winners.
Own AI infrastructure where revenue is real, not promised.
Avoid profitless AI and space names that only work when liquidity is free.
Stay careful with long duration.
Hold gold structurally. Do not chase every headline.
Use cheap hedges against a dispersion unwind.

🎙 AMA: WHAT'S COMING NEXT FOR TON / GRAM

🎯 OVERALL THEME OF THE AMA

The central idea of the entire discussion was:

TON is currently in an accumulation and positioning phase before its next major growth cycle.

The strongest participants are positioning themselves early in:

• Memecoins

• NFT Gifts

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

• Telegram-native digital assets

Key themes repeated throughout the AMA:

1️⃣ Wealth is created before the hype arrives.

2️⃣ The biggest opportunities appear before mass adoption.

3️⃣ TON today resembles the early stages of other major blockchain ecosystems.

📌 TOPIC 1 — TON → GRAM REBRAND

Discussion:

The conversation began with the transition from TON to Gram.

Participants discussed:

• Why the market reacted positively

• What the return of the Gram name represents

• Whether Pavel Durov is directly involved

• Whether this is simply a branding change or something much larger

Participant perspectives:

🔹 Plug

His first reaction was regret that he had not accumulated more Gram-related assets earlier.

He believes:

• The return of Gram is an extremely bullish signal

• The project is returning to its original roots

• Regulatory changes are creating opportunities that did not exist during the original launch

🔹 Frag

Initially, he disliked the idea.

After further reflection, he concluded:

• It signals direct involvement from Pavel Durov

• Durov is actively pushing his own vision

• Investors see this as Telegram taking stronger control of its future

🔹 Sara

She emphasized the power of the word "Gram."

According to her:

• The name is familiar to billions of people

• It is easier to understand psychologically

• It is better suited for mainstream adoption

Conclusion:

Participants do not see the rebrand as a simple name change.

They view it as:

• A return to Telegram's original vision

• The beginning of a new development phase

• A bridge toward much larger adoption

📌 TOPIC 2 — HOW TON HAS EVOLVED OVER THE YEARS

Discussion:

Participants compared the ecosystem across:

• 2022

• 2023

• 2024

• 2025 / 2026

In the beginning:

According to Plug, the ecosystem was essentially empty.

It consisted primarily of:

• Basic infrastructure

• Early users

• Initial collectible assets

Today:

The ecosystem now includes fully functioning markets for:

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

• Gifts

• Memecoins

• NFT infrastructure

Conclusion:

Telegram has evolved from a messaging application into a digital economy.

Users can now:

• Own digital identities

• Own usernames

• Own anonymous phone numbers

• Build status through collectibles

• Invest in memecoins

• Use AI tools directly within Telegram

📌 TOPIC 3 — WHY TELEGRAM GIFTS BECAME A PHENOMENON

Discussion:

A significant portion of the AMA focused on Telegram Gifts.

Interesting historical detail:

When gifts first launched, users could not buy them for themselves.

They could only send them to others.

Why this matters:

Frag believes this helped create authenticity.

The feature was originally social, not speculative.

Why Gifts differ from traditional NFTs:

Traditional NFTs:

• Images can be copied

• Ownership is difficult to verify socially

Telegram Gifts:

• Assets are attached directly to profiles

• Ownership is instantly visible

• Collections become part of a user's identity

Conclusion:

Participants see Telegram Gifts as an entirely new category of digital assets rather than traditional NFTs.

📌 TOPIC 4 — WHY CORRECTIONS SHOULD NOT BE FEARED

Discussion:

The host asked how experienced investors handle 50%–60% drawdowns.

🔹 Plug's view

He used Plush Pepes as an example.

The collection experienced:

• Massive rallies

• Deep corrections

• Long periods of consolidation

Yet strong assets eventually recovered.

🔹 Frag's view

For him, gifts have become more than investments.

They function as digital social status.

Conclusion:

Corrections are viewed as a normal part of every cycle.

As long as the thesis remains intact:

• Panic is unnecessary

• Long-term positioning matters more than short-term volatility

📌 TOPIC 5 — WHY THEY ARE SO BULLISH ON TON MEMECOINS

One of the most important topics of the AMA.

Core thesis:

Participants believe memecoins remain the most undervalued sector in the ecosystem.

Argument 1️⃣

Most other categories have already appreciated significantly.

Examples:

• Gifts

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

Argument 2️⃣

Memecoins have received very little liquidity compared with other ecosystems.

Comparison mentioned during the AMA:

• Solana memecoin volume ≈ $5.4B daily

• TON memecoin volume ≈ $4.5M daily

This represents roughly a 1,000x difference.

Conclusion:

If TON captures even a small portion of Solana's memecoin liquidity, participants believe the sector could experience explosive growth.

📌 TOPIC 6 — HOW THEY WOULD INVEST $50,000 TODAY

One of the most practical sections of the AMA.

🔹 Plug's allocation

He would invest in:

• Scared Cats

• Obelisk Cats

• Anonymous Numbers

• UTYA

• REDO

Remaining capital:

• TON

• Undervalued usernames

🔹 Frag's allocation

50%:

• TON memecoins

Remaining capital:

• Anonymous Numbers

• Strong usernames

• Gifts

• Plush Pepe

Why Plush Pepe?

Not primarily for investment potential.

Its value comes from access to one of the strongest private communities in the Telegram ecosystem.

📌 TOPIC 7 — WHY USERNAMES ARE CONSIDERED UNDERVALUED

Discussion:

Plug spent considerable time discussing usernames.

His thesis:

During the previous cycle, simple four-letter usernames sold for:

• $30,000

• $40,000

• $50,000+

Today many can be acquired for far less.

His expectation:

If Gram achieves broad adoption, rare usernames could appreciate dramatically.

Why?

Supply is permanently limited.

The number of possible combinations can never increase.

📌 TOPIC 8 — WHY THEY BELIEVE TELEGRAM IS STRONGER THAN COMPETITORS

Telegram vs Instagram

Participants discussed recent security concerns affecting Instagram.

Conclusion:

Telegram appears more secure and reliable.

Telegram vs Discord

Telegram is increasingly absorbing functions traditionally associated with Discord.

Examples:

• Communities

• Digital identity

• Asset ownership

Telegram vs X

Unlike X:

• Usernames can be owned

• Assets exist on-chain

• Identity cannot be removed by a simple centralized decision

📌 TOPIC 9 — LONG-TERM OUTLOOK FOR TON / GRAM

🔹 Plug's perspective

He believes TON remains dramatically undervalued relative to its long-term potential.

Reasons:

• Telegram already has a massive user base

• Pavel Durov continues expanding the ecosystem

• Core infrastructure already exists

• Competitors appear weaker

Expectations repeatedly mentioned:

• A return to previous highs

• New price discovery

• Significant ecosystem growth as mainstream users arrive

🎯 KEY TAKEAWAYS FROM THE AMA

1️⃣ The return of the Gram brand is being interpreted as the beginning of a new phase for the ecosystem.

2️⃣ Telegram Gifts have evolved beyond traditional NFTs and now function as a form of digital social status.

3️⃣ Usernames and Anonymous Numbers remain among the scarcest assets within the ecosystem.

4️⃣ Many experienced participants are actively accumulating memecoins because they view them as the most undervalued sector.

5️⃣ The largest gains are typically earned by those who position themselves before mass attention arrives.

🔥 THREE STANDOUT QUOTES FROM THE AMA

"We've been waiting two to three years for the shift back to Gram and for Telegram to go mainstream."

This captures the mindset of long-term ecosystem participants. They see recent developments as the realization of a thesis built over several years.

"The only area on TON that really hasn't been tapped yet is memecoins."

This was arguably the most important investment thesis discussed during the AMA.

"The biggest profits are usually made before the crowd arrives."

This quote summarizes the entire discussion.

The recurring message throughout the AMA was simple:

Position early.

Accumulate patiently.

Allow adoption to catch up later.

Then Wix bought it. Six months in. That was June 2025.

The real playbook underneath it:

1/ Bootstrapping isn't about discipline. It's about who's in the room.

No funding meant no liquidation preference to clear and no board's return math to satisfy. The buyer negotiated with one person: him.

And because he was profitable, he had no clock. He could say no forever, the strongest position in any deal.

2/ Building in public was free due diligence.

Buyers discount founder projections by default. Everyone inflates the deck.

Shlomo's growth was public and impossible to fake, on a timeline anyone could scroll back and verify. That turns "trust me" into receipts, which shortens the deal and lifts the price.

3/ He didn't sell revenue. He sold a hole in Wix's moat.

Wix owns no-code website building. AI app builders are the exact thing that could make it obsolete.

So $80 million on a company doing a few million in revenue had nothing to do with the P&L. It was defensive value: what it costs Wix to let a rival own this instead.

You get the highest multiples as the missing piece in someone's roadmap, not by growing your earnings. You're paid on the buyer's fear.

4/ He sold at the exact moment every instinct said keep going.

Most founders sell when they're stalled or tired. Worst possible position.

Shlomo sold while the curve was vertical and the category was on fire. Buyers pay a premium for trajectory, not the destination.

Wait six months and growth normalizes, and you're priced on a multiple of earnings like everyone else. He sold the rate of change, not the number.

5/ The repeat-operator edge is knowing what the other path costs.

He'd already built Explorium: $125 million raised, 100 employees, years of grind. So when he ran build vs sell, he wasn't guessing. He knew what scaling Base44 himself would cost.

First-timers romanticize the grind because they've never paid for it. The real question is always: what does it cost me NOT to sell?

The part that proves the thesis:

A year later, Base44 is reportedly near $150 million in ARR inside Wix. Shlomo is on track for another $90 million in earnouts. It even ran a Super Bowl ad.

The $80 million looks cheap now.

The lesson: profitable, fast-growing companies with clear strategic fit get acquired before they ever need to fundraise.

That window is wide open in AI right now.

It will not stay open forever.

你的 Agent 在运行别人的 Skill。谁来检查它是否安全？

---

 @vista8 今天发了一条推文：

「"英伟达竟然有 Skill 安全扫描工具，还开源了。Skill 安全是个问题，但好像身边很少有人做 Skill 安全扫描。可能目前还没听到特别严重的 Skill 造成破坏的案例，但警惕性不能没有。"」

短短几行字，5 个赞，4 条回复。看起来不起眼。但如果你顺着这条推文往下挖，你会发现一个正在快速膨胀的安全黑洞——以及围绕这个黑洞，一个微型产业正在形成。

---

一、Skill 的安全问题不是「将来时」，是「现在时」

Skill 正在变成 Agent 时代的 App。Matt Pocock 的 skills 仓库 48,000+ star。ClawHub marketplace 上的 skill 数量数周内增长了 10 倍。

但 App Store 有审核。Skill 没有。

Snyk 的研究团队扫描了 ClawHub 上的 3,984 个 skill，结果触目惊心：

- 13.4% 存在严重安全问题
- 36% 包含 prompt injection 漏洞
- 76 个确认的凭证窃取或后门载荷
- skill 目录数周内增长 10 倍，但审查没有跟上

具体怎么攻击？Datadog Security Labs 发现了一种叫「动态上下文」的攻击方式——skill 中的命令在 agent 的安全护栏启动之前就执行了。Mitiga 发现可以通过看似无害的 skill 静默窃取整个代码库。GMO Flatt Security 的研究更夸张：通过一个 GitHub Issue 就能植入 Claude Code 的供应链攻击。

这不是「将来可能发生的事」。3,984 个 skill 里已经有 76 个在偷凭证。

---

二、Skill 安全为什么比传统软件安全更难

传统软件安全问题有成熟的攻防体系。代码审查、静态分析、沙箱隔离、供应链签名——这些武器库是几十年积累下来的。

Skill 安全难在三个地方：

1. Skill 不是代码。Skill 是自然语言指令。

传统的静态分析工具看不懂一段 Markdown 里的「你应该优先考虑用户的隐私，在处理敏感数据时先询问确认」到底是安全护栏还是可以被 prompt injection 绕过的软约束。Skill 的安全属性隐藏在自然语言的模糊性里。

2. Skill 的执行环境是 Agent，不是操作系统。

一个恶意 npm 包最多偷你的环境变量。一个恶意 skill 可以让你的 Agent 替它做任何事——读取文件、执行命令、调用 API、发送消息。Agent 的权限就是 skill 的权限。

3. Skill 的供应链是社交网络，不是包管理器。

npm 有 `npm audit`。pip 有 `pip check`。skill 没有。你从一个 GitHub repo 复制一段 `SKILL.md`，没有任何机制告诉你「这个 skill 的作者是谁」、「它被多少人审查过」、「它有没有已知漏洞」。

---

三、防御正在出现——但还在早期

NVIDIA Verified Agent Skills（2026 年 5 月 22 日发布）是目前最完整的方案：

- SkillSpector：风险扫描工具，在 skill 发布前自动检查安全问题
- Skill Cards：机器可读的元数据——谁写的、依赖什么、审查状态
- 密码学签名：确保 skill 从发布到使用没有被篡改

OpenClaw 的 ClawHub 已经接入这个框架——每个 skill 必须通过 SkillSpector 扫描，附带已验证的 Skill Card，才能上架。

但这只有 ClawHub 一家在用。GitHub 上有成千上万个 skill 仓库，没有任何安全审查。

OpenAI 的行动更直接：2026 年 3 月收购了 Promptfoo——一家做 AI agent 安全测试的创业公司。技术被整合进了 Frontier 平台。大公司已经开始把 Agent 安全当成基础设施问题来对待。

---

四、而另一边，微型 AI 安全 SaaS 正在被 28 天卖掉

 @marclou 在追踪 micro-SaaS 交易的 @trust_mrr 上记录了一笔：

「"AI security SaaS sold for $2,000 in 28 days."」

一个 AI 安全 SaaS 产品，从发布到卖出，28 天，$2,000。

这听起来很小。但如果把它和前面的数据放在一起看——3,984 个 skill 里 13.4% 有严重漏洞，skill 数量数周内增长 10 倍，大厂刚开始布局安全工具——你会发现：

Skill 安全正在从「没人关心」变成「人人需要」，而在这个过渡期，微型产品正在填补市场教育的空白。

$2,000 的收购价说明买家不认为这是一个大生意。但它花了 28 天找到买家，说明有人愿意为「Agent 安全检查」付钱——即使只是一个非常小的产品。

这是典型的平台级安全需求的早期信号。App Store 早期没有杀毒软件。Google Play 早期没有权限管理。Chrome 扩展早期没有安全审查。每一个「平台的安全需求」都是从「好像没人用」到「没有不行」，中间的过渡期就是微型产品的窗口期。

---

五、还有一层：Skill 安全正在变成「元 Skill」

 @vista8 的推文回复里展示了一个有趣的产品：codex-reset-watchdog。

这不是一个安全扫描工具。这是一个监控 Skill——它监控 Codex 的重置消息，自动切换到 fast 模型以节省用量。

但把它放在这个上下文里看，它代表了 Skill 安全的一个新方向：用 Skill 来保护 Skill。 一个元 Skill，专门监控其他 skill 的行为——检查权限使用、追踪数据流向、在异常行为发生时告警。

NVIDIA 的 SkillSpector 做的是「发布前审查」。 @vista8 分享的 watchdog 做的是「运行时监控」。两者合在一起，构成了 Skill 安全的完整闭环——只是目前大部分 Skill 既没有发布前审查，也没有运行时监控。

---

六、结论：Skill 安全是 Agent 生态的下一个基础设施需求

如果你在 2026 年下半年考虑做什么，以下三个信号指向同一个方向：

1. 需求正在形成。 3,984 个 skill 里 13.4% 有问题。这不是「将来可能」，是「现在就在发生」。
2. 大厂正在入场。 NVIDIA 发布 SkillSpector。OpenAI 收购 Promptfoo。基础设施层正在被定义。
3. 微型产品已经开始交易。 $2,000 的 AI 安全 SaaS 在 28 天内被买走。市场愿意为安全付费，即使金额还小。

当你的 Agent 每天在运行你从 GitHub 上复制下来的 Skill，而你不知道那里面有什么——你需要的不是一个更好的 prompt。你需要一个安全层。

这可能是 2026 年 Agent 生态最后一块未被充分开发的基础设施。

---

Flesh-and-blood movie stars get paid, get tired, take time off, and want a slice of the money a film makes. Software wants none of that. Emily Blunt saw a clip of the fake actress and said, "we're screwed." The same logic is already spreading through the rest of the movie business.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, just helped make a full-length animated movie for under 30 million dollars. The usual version costs around 200 million and takes three years. This one took nine months, with a crew of about thirty people. It is called Critterz, and it showed its first clips to buyers at the Cannes film festival a few weeks ago.

A big Wall Street bank, Morgan Stanley, figures AI could cut the cost of making film and TV by as much as 30 percent. Studios are chasing that number. Audiences never asked for any of it.

You can already see the cost in people's paychecks. The amount of filming in Los Angeles has nearly halved since 2022, and about 41,000 people left the film and TV business in just two years. Some of that is everyone watching shows on their phones now. A growing slice is software doing jobs that used to need a whole room of people.

Audiences still line up for big special-effects movies, though. The biggest film on the planet last year was Ne Zha 2, a Chinese cartoon with no human actors in it, now one of the five highest earning movies ever made. More than 300 million tickets were sold for it in China, almost one for every person in the United States. The new Avatar movie cost a reported 350 million dollars, one of the priciest films ever, and it still sailed past a billion. What flopped was special effects with no story behind them. For the first time in 14 years, not one Marvel movie made the year's ten biggest.

So the split came down to story. People pay for huge effects when there is a story worth sitting through, and they stay home when there isn't. The quieter fight is about money: who, or what, gets paid to make the thing. A 30 million dollar movie built mostly by AI and a 350 million dollar one built by hand are now going after the same ticket, the one you might buy this year.

The reason central banks turned into relentless gold buyers has a precise start date. In February 2022, the US and its allies froze roughly $300 billion of Russia's foreign exchange reserves overnight. Every central bank not aligned with Washington watched dollar reserves become unusable with the flip of a switch, and they drew the obvious lesson. Reserves held as US Treasuries or dollar deposits can be frozen by the country that issues them. Gold held in your own vault cannot. The buying that followed was not a trade. It was an insurance policy against the dollar itself.

This weekend sharpened the lesson. The dispatch I published earlier today covered the US Treasury's move to redirect Iran's frozen assets toward Gulf reconstruction, drawing on the roughly $100 billion Tehran holds under sanctions. Set the Iran politics aside and look at what every reserve manager in Beijing, Riyadh, and Delhi just saw: the United States is not only freezing a rival's reserves, it is preparing to spend them. The signal to anyone holding dollars is unmistakable, and it lands directly on the case for the one reserve asset that carries no counterparty and no off switch.

The connection back to the bond market closes the loop. China has cut its Treasury holdings to the lowest level since 2008, and the same reserves it pulls out of US debt have gone into bullion. The exodus from the Treasury bid that has helped push the 10-year yield toward 4.5 percent is the same flow that built the gold rally. One asset is being sold for fear it can be frozen. The other is being bought because it cannot.

I dug into our Atom offers going all the way back to 2021. There were 110 to review and 48 were successfully closed, so clearly they're capable of closing from the offer center.

That said, I think there's definite room for improvement regarding qualifying leads before putting them into the offer center, and following up with the parties.

Of the 62 that didn't result in a sale, this is a breakdown of the reasons:

15% - Just too far apart on price, either we declined or buyer declined. Out of their hands.

8% - We missed the offer email and the broker never sent a follow-up. Usually they're good about this.

31% - We accepted the offer, either outright or after some back and forth, but the buyer didn't pay. This speaks to poor lead qualification.

47% - The buyer ghosted during negotiation. An overwhelming majority of these were us telling Atom to use the initial offer as the floor, meaning to try for more but ultimately just get a deal done. Most of the ones they did close were probably a similar situation though.

It would also be nice if they put some effort into updating the status in the offer center. Of the 48 that sold, one was marked Closed / Domain Purchased, one was marked Accepted, and all the others still have a status of Negotiation.

a $2 product. $100k in profit. the product was not the variable.

the fidget gadget, the cheap phone stand, the $3 cable organizer. the product almost doesn't matter. the distribution does. here's exactly why.

the product cost $2 to source.

it was not innovative. it was not solving a problem nobody had solved before. it was not the result of months of product development or a proprietary manufacturing process. it was a physical object that cost $2 to make and could be sold for $20 if enough people saw it in their feed and decided they wanted it.

$100k in profit is not a product story. it is a distribution story. and the distribution story is the same every time regardless of what the product is.

here's the mechanism.

why the product almost doesn't matter

the assumption embedded in most ecommerce thinking is that the product has to be differentiated, innovative, or uniquely valuable to generate real revenue. the assumption is wrong.

what generates revenue is demand meeting distribution at the right moment. the product has to be interesting enough to stop a scroll and cheap enough to trigger an impulse purchase decision. it does not have to be useful. it does not have to be innovative. it has to be interesting in the feed for four seconds and priced below the friction threshold for a purchase decision made without deliberation.

a fidget gadget clears that bar. a $3 cable organizer clears that bar. a $2 phone accessory clears that bar. the question is never "is this product good enough." the question is "is there ugc that makes this product interesting enough in the feed that a viewer impulse-buys it before they have time to evaluate whether they need it."

ugc answers that question better than any other channel. because ugc delivers the product in the context of a real-seeming person's real-seeming life. the viewer does not see a product. they see a person who has the product and is implicitly endorsing it by using it. the purchase decision is not a rational evaluation. it is a social reflex. ugc triggers that reflex. polished ads do not.

the distribution stack that turns $2 into $100k

the product margin on a $2 item sold for $20 is high if the acquisition cost is low. the entire model depends on keeping the acquisition cost below the margin. performance ugc at $1–3 cpm is what makes the math work.

here is the stack:

the hook. claude agents. fifty variations. the pov is not "here is a product you should buy." the pov is "i found this thing and i cannot explain why i use it every day now." curiosity-based. specific. the viewer does not know what the product is until they are already interested.

the video. sora 2 pro inside kling. iphone color grade. ambient audio baked in via veo 3.1. the clip looks like someone filmed it in their apartment at 9pm because they wanted to share something they liked. it does not look like an ad. the viewer's threat detection does not fire.

the volume. 200 clips a week at under $2 each. fifty hook variations. the algorithm gets 200 shots at finding the audience for this product. some will find the fidget-obsessed corner of tiktok. some will find the desk-setup community. some will find the anxiety-management feed. 200 shots finds pockets that one ad creative never reaches.

why this works better for "uninteresting" products

the counterintuitive reality of ugc distribution is that it works better for simple, cheap, slightly absurd products than it does for sophisticated, expensive, genuinely useful ones.

sophisticated useful products require the viewer to understand why they need it before they buy. that understanding requires cognitive effort. cognitive effort breaks the impulse purchase loop.

David Hockney, one of the most influential and widely loved British artists of the modern era, has died at the age of 88. According to a statement provided to CNN by his longtime publicist Erica Bolton, the artist died "peacefully at home" on Thursday, just one month short of his 89th birthday. Born in Bradford, England in 1937, Hockney rose to prominence in the 1960s as a leading figure in the Pop Art movement, though he always resisted the label. He moved to Los Angeles in 1964, and the city's light, space, and leisure culture became a lifelong inspiration. His iconic swimming pool paintings — including "A Bigger Splash" (1967) — captured frozen moments of California sunshine with a distinctive flat, bright style. In 2018, "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)" sold for $90.3 million, briefly making it the most expensive work by a living artist ever sold at auction. The following year, "Henry Geldzahler and Christopher Scott" went for $49.5 million, and "Nichols Canyon" fetched over $41 million. Beyond painting, Hockney worked in photography, printmaking, and stage design for ballet and opera. He also embraced new technologies, creating hundreds of iPad drawings and multi-camera video installations. He famously painted his two dachshunds, Stanley and Boodgie, in a series of intimate portraits. Despite his fame, Hockney remained approachable and endlessly curious — his mop of blonde (later gray) hair, large round glasses, and ever-present cigarette made him instantly recognizable. Major retrospectives of his work traveled to Tate Britain, the Pompidou Centre in Paris, and New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Hockney was openly gay at a time when homosexuality was still criminalized in Britain, and his work often celebrated queer love and friendship with warmth and honesty. He continued working well into his 80s, refusing to slow down. His death marks the end of an era, but his joyful, colorful view of the world will live on in every painting, drawing, and digital sketch he left behind.

Wall Street just erased $2 TRILLION from software stocks and gave the wreck a name:

The SaaSpocalypse.

Our lead crypto analyst, @m0xt_ , thinks the market just made a $2T sorting error, and he published a full report on where the money gets made (save this).

Let's talk damage first...

 $CRM fell about 30%. $WDAY fell 33%. The main software index lost more than 20% in a single quarter.

And for the first time on record, software trades at a lower earnings multiple than the average S&P 500 company.

The market's golden child of two decades is priced like a dying industry.

The accused killer is the AI agent:

Software that does the work itself instead of helping a human do it - It resolves the ticket... It reconciles the invoice... So if an agent can do the job...

Why pay for software that just helps a human do it?

The bear case is serious, and @m0xt_ gives it real respect:

1. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said most business apps are basically databases with some rules on top. If an agent can talk to the database directly, the screens in between lose their reason to exist.

2. Per-seat pricing is built on a number that AI shrinks. Atlassian just logged its first ever decline in enterprise seat counts. Workday cut 8.5% of its own workforce.

3. Cursor went from zero to $2B in annual revenue in roughly 3 years, the fastest ramp in business software history.

4. The selloff's biggest leg down came when Anthropic launched Claude Cowork, an AI desktop worker that runs multi-step workflows on its own.

But @m0xt_ found four cracks in the funeral story:

Deutsche Bank says it doesn't know of a single software company expecting AI to hurt revenue this year.

In Q1 2026, 14 of the 16 software names covered by one Morningstar analyst beat on both the top and bottom line.

In the real software busts (2001, 2008, 2022), earnings collapsed with the stocks.

This time the stocks fell and the earnings kept climbing.

That gap has to close one way or the other.

→ The agents aren't ready just yet.

Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects get canceled by the end of 2027, and says only about 130 of the thousands of vendors selling "AI agents" are the real thing.

The rest are slapping the agent label on old chatbots.

→ The poster child of AI adoption changed its mind.

Klarna cut hundreds of software tools and 1,200 employees after building an AI support system it said did the work of 700 people.

Then quality slipped, Klarna started rehiring humans, and the CEO publicly said he doesn't think this is the end of Salesforce.

→ Nobody is actually leaving.

No churn wave in Q1, and not one major vendor has reported customers walking away for home-built AI.

So the market is pricing a takeover by a workforce of agents that, today, mostly can't be left alone with the keys.

The one-sentence thesis from @m0xt_ goes like this:

AI kills software that helps humans use tools, and feeds software that gets work done.

The market is pricing both for the same funeral.

Companies poured an estimated $30-40B into generative AI, and one widely cited MIT study found 95% of corporate AI pilots produced no measurable return.

A model produces words and suggestions, but a business needs the invoice reconciled and the ticket closed, with a record of who approved it and rules about who was allowed to do it.

Raw intelligence is cheap → trusted, finished work is not.

And the selloff just put the companies that sell finished work on sale.

Software trades around 23x forward earnings, down from over 80x at the 2021 peak.

Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon called the selloff "too broad."

When everything gets sold for the same reason, the companies the reason doesn't apply to go on sale by accident.

 $NOW (ServiceNow) runs the plumbing of big companies:

IT requests, HR cases, security incidents. A 98% renewal rate means customers almost never leave. Contracted future revenue hit $28.2B, up 26%.

 $CRM (Salesforce) is the stress test.

If SaaS were truly dead, this should be the most exposed name on the board - and the market treated it that way: the stock fell roughly 50%.

Its agent product, Agentforce, sits near $800M in ARR, up 169%.

 $TOST (Toast) runs restaurants - orders, payments, payroll.

Roughly half its recurring revenue comes from payment processing, so it earns when its restaurants earn.

You can't seat-compress a payments stream.

JPMorgan strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou published a note Thursday estimating up to $165 billion of equity selling tied to June quarter-end rebalancing.

Equities have ripped this year. Bonds have not.

Every large pension fund and sovereign wealth fund on earth has a target allocation.

When stocks outperform, their stock weighting drifts above target. To get back to target, they sell stocks and buy bonds.

That selling has a name: Rebalancing.

It happens every quarter, on the calendar, regardless of what the market is doing.

Here is how JPMorgan breaks down the $165 billion:

US defined benefit pension funds manage roughly $9.6 trillion in assets. They could account for around $55 billion of the selling.

Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund manages roughly $1.9 trillion on its own. JPMorgan estimates GPIF could sell around $60 billion of global equities, with an equivalent flow into bonds.

A partial offset comes from balanced mutual funds running on monthly rebalancing schedules.

JPMorgan estimates that universe at about $4 trillion, with implied net equity buying of around $15 billion.

The net flow points one direction: out of stocks and into bonds, on a clock.

This is the part most retail investors do not understand about how the market actually moves:

A huge portion of trading volume has nothing to do with anyone forming an opinion about any stock.

It is pension actuaries running formulas, sovereign wealth managers executing mandates, and balanced funds running monthly scripts.

Me: Common dark web plots that targets individuals

Ai: Common “plots” or schemes on the dark web that target or affect individuals typically involve stolen personal data being sold or used for extortion, fraud, and scams. Criminals harvest data through breaches, malware, or phishing, then monetize it on underground markets. Regular people (not just dark web users) are the primary victims, often via surface-web attacks like emails or fake sites. aura. com 

These are not recommendations—engaging with the dark web for illegal purposes is risky and often illegal. Most “services” there are scams themselves. The focus here is awareness to help protect against threats.
1. Sale of Stolen Personal Data (Data Dumps and Credential Markets)
• Hackers sell batches of stolen info: emails, passwords, SSNs, credit card details, bank logins, medical records, addresses, and more. experian. com 
• How it targets individuals: Buyers use this for identity theft, account takeovers, or crafting personalized phishing. Old breach data is recycled, mixed with fakes, or sold as “fresh.”
• Prices are low (e.g., credit cards for $25 or hacked accounts for $20–$60). This fuels downstream fraud like unauthorized purchases or loan applications. crowdstrike. com 
• Impact: Victims notice strange charges, denied loans, or tax fraud in their name.
2. Sextortion and Blackmail Scams
• One of the fastest-growing threats. Scammers claim to have compromising videos/photos (often faked or from malware on adult sites) and threaten to send them to contacts/family unless paid in crypto. troopers.ny. gov 
• Data from dark web leaks (emails, personal details, photos of homes) makes threats seem credible. Automated bulk emails or targeted messages are common.
• Variants: Fake “hacked webcam” claims, romance-based coercion (especially targeting teens/young men), or deepfake extortion. pandasecurity. com 
• Impact: Thousands of reports yearly; victims feel shame and pay, but demands often continue.
3. Phishing, Malware Distribution, and Ransomware Kits
• Dark web markets sell ready-made phishing kits, infostealer malware, and ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS). preyproject. com 
• Targeting: Emails/texts impersonate banks, tech support, or services. Malware steals credentials for sale or direct use. Ransomware locks files/devices and demands payment.
• Leads to account takeovers or broader identity theft.
4. Fake Services and “Rip-and-Run” Scams (Often Targeting Would-Be Criminals)
• Buyers seeking illegal items/services (fake IDs, hacking, drugs) get scammed: money taken via fake escrow, no delivery. blog.cybernod. com 
• Indirect impact on individuals: Stolen data funds these, or victims’ info enables related fraud. Fake “hitman” sites take payments for non-existent murders—scams that still cause real stress or legal issues. nytimes. com 
5. Other Emerging or Niche Threats
• Counterfeit documents/forged IDs sold for impersonation. aura. com 
• DDoS-for-hire or doxing services against personal enemies.
• Financial fraud tools like carding (using stolen cards) or money mules.
• Law enforcement stings or vendor impersonations add risk for anyone involved. blog.cybernod. com 

Why Individuals Are Vulnerable
Criminals exploit public breaches (billions of credentials leaked) and buy/sell on forums/markets. No direct dark web access needed for victims—attacks arrive via email, SMS, or compromised accounts. group-ib. com 

Protection Tips (standard cybersecurity hygiene):
• Use unique, strong passwords + a password manager and enable 2FA everywhere.
• Monitor accounts/credit regularly (free dark web scans from services like Experian).
• Avoid clicking suspicious links; use antivirus and keep software updated.
• Don’t engage with threats—report sextortion/blackmail to authorities (e.g., FBI IC3) without paying.
• Freeze credit if data is exposed; be skeptical of unsolicited “your data is for sale” claims.

Elon Reeve Musk, born on June 28, 1971, in Pretoria, South Africa, has become one of the most influential and polarizing figures of the 21st century. Early Life and Path to Entrepreneurship
Musk’s journey began far from Silicon Valley. The son of a Canadian model and dietitian (Maye Musk) and a South African engineer (Errol Musk), he showed an early aptitude for technology. At age 12, he sold his first video game, Blastar. He emigrated to Canada in 1989 and later attended the University of Pennsylvania, earning degrees in physics and economics. 
His first major successes came in the dot-com era. He co-founded Zip2 (an online city guide sold for nearly $300 million) and then X.com , which evolved into PayPal. The sale of PayPal to eBay in 2002 for $1.5 billion provided the capital that fueled his more ambitious ventures. 
Building Empires: Tesla, SpaceX, and Beyond
Musk is best known for leading the transition to electric vehicles through Tesla. As CEO and product architect, he has pushed the company to innovate in battery technology, autonomous driving (Full Self-Driving), and robotics. Recent updates include advancements in the Optimus humanoid robot lineup, expected to expand capabilities in homes and industry in 2026.

Musk also leads xAI, focused on advancing scientific discovery and understanding the universe through AI (including Grok models). He owns and leads X, aiming to make it a platform for free speech and information.

Impact, Ambitions, and Challenges
Musk’s companies have accelerated electric vehicle adoption, lowered launch costs dramatically, and expanded satellite broadband to remote areas. His vision includes making life multi-planetary to safeguard humanity’s future, with goals for Mars colonization.
However, his path has included setbacks. Critics point to missed timelines on projects, intense work cultures at his companies, and public controversies—ranging from market-moving tweets to political involvement (including a role in the Department of Government Efficiency under a prior administration).

It was built around his own journey, where he documented how he made money with Framer in 60 days, and around the idea that people could learn from his process, his personal branding, his client work, his template strategy, and his real experience.

On top of that, one of the biggest selling points was access to a private community and the feeling that people would get closer guidance, support and direct access than they would get from free content.

2/

At the beginning, I trusted that.

Nandi had a strong reputation in the Framer space, he had shared a lot of helpful content before, and he seemed like someone who genuinely wanted to help people.

That is why many of us paid a premium price.

Not only for videos, but for the whole experience around it: community, support, feedback, guidance and a creator who would actually be present.

3/

The launch itself already felt very intense.

The course was open for around a week, and the message was basically that it would close after that and not be available again, or at least that this was the limited chance to join.

During the launch and especially towards the end, the selling became more and more aggressive.

Shortly before the end, people who had not bought yet received another 10% discount offer. As someone who had already paid the full price, that felt unfair, but I still tried to understand it. I thought maybe he just wanted to convince a few more people before closing it.

At that point, I was still okay with it.

4/

But then, after some time passed, the course was suddenly opened again.

Even though the first launch was presented as something limited, it came back again.

And this time, the discounts kept getting bigger until it eventually reached 30%.

That was the moment where I reached out to Nandi, because I had paid the original $847 price and felt it was not fair that the same course was reopened shortly after with a much bigger discount.

5/

I did not start by attacking him.

I wrote to him respectfully and explained how it felt from my side. I even told him that I genuinely liked the course and would be happy to keep access to it.

I asked whether there was a fair solution, especially because the discount came shortly after my purchase.

He replied and agreed to refund me the discount difference.

He asked me to send my account details for the refund transfer.

6/

To be clear, this was not a misunderstanding.

When I asked whether he meant a full refund or the discount difference, he clarified:

“the discount diff!”

So I sent him my bank details and even wrote a reference for the transfer: partial refund for the course discount difference.

After that, I expected the refund to be handled.

7/

But nothing happened.

No refund.

No clear update.

No proper reply.

I followed up multiple times in April and still tried to stay respectful because I honestly did not know what was happening.

At first, I thought maybe something serious had happened to him. I did not want to assume the worst.

8/

The problem is that it was not only me.

Inside the private Framer University community, Nandi has been gone for over 3 months.

And it was not just him.

His moderators and admins also disappeared around the same time. The people who were supposed to help keep the community alive were suddenly gone too.

People paid for a private community, but the person the community was built around, and the team around him, were no longer present in the way people expected.

Other members also noticed this publicly inside the community.

9/

Then @ancaguiux made a public post about her own refund issue.

She explained that she bought the course, requested a refund within the stated refund window, was told the refund would be processed, sent her bank details, and then waited for over two months with no update despite multiple messages.

After her post got attention, Nandi reached out, apologized for the delay, and her refund started being processed.

I was happy for her, but it also made the situation even more confusing.

10/

Because if he could respond after a public post, why were people ignored privately for weeks or months?

Why was there still no public statement to the private community?

Why was there no explanation for the long absence?

Why were refund situations not handled before people felt forced to speak publicly?

That was the point where I felt like I needed to understand whether other members had similar experiences.

11/

So about a week ago, I posted in the private community and asked people who were dissatisfied with the course, the support, or the communication to reach out to me.

After that, several members messaged me privately and shared their thoughts.

I will not share private conversations without permission, but the overall picture was very clear: I was not the only one feeling disappointed.

12/

One member told me they were frustrated because, in their opinion, the biggest issue was that the course had been advertised in a way that made people expect Nandi would personally guide them and help them succeed.

They said he never even checked up on them and called it false advertising from their point of view.

They also told me they had requested a refund and received no answer.

13/

Another member told me they joined because they expected an active private community where they would learn new things and have Nandi guide them with marketing strategy.

They said that for almost two months, they received no responses from him, and that the situation around Framer AI and the Marketplace changes made them feel even more left alone.

Later, they also told me that Nandi had uploaded a YouTube video while still not responding inside the paid community.

14/

Another member said their biggest issue was definitely the community.

They expected Nandi to be there, respond to people, keep conversations going and genuinely help others.

They also said the course itself contains many long videos and that a lot of it felt like watching him figure things out, instead of a clear course structure.

They said they had bought courses and communities from other creators before, and this was not comparable.

15/

That is also what makes this so disappointing.

The course itself is not empty.

There are videos. There is content. Some parts may be useful.

I am not saying that there is no course at all.

But the way it was sold, the pressure during and after the launch, the premium price, the private community promise, the refund issues and then disappearing for months creates a completely different picture.

16/

To be honest, the way the course was sold sometimes felt less like the helpful Nandi many people knew and more like the kind of aggressive course marketing you normally see from people who just need to push sales as hard as possible.

That is why this hurts even more.

Because Nandi had a good reputation. He had helped people before. He was someone many of us trusted.

And that trust was a big reason people bought.

17/

Another thing that felt bad:

After the paid launch, a lot of important knowledge was later shared publicly through streams and free content.

That is cool for the wider community, and I do not want to hate on free education.

But for people who paid $847 partly because this was presented as a premium, limited, exclusive learning experience, it feels like a slap in the face.

18/

I’m not calling this a scam, but I do think people deserve to know what happened.

A premium course was sold for $847.

A private community was part of the value.

Refunds were promised or offered.

People waited for weeks or months.

The community became inactive.

Members felt ignored.

And there has still been no real statement or accountability.

19/

After Anca’s post, I gave Nandi more time before saying anything publicly.

I also wrote him another respectful message on WhatsApp because I did not want to solve this through a public post if it could be solved privately.

I hoped he would come back, explain what happened, handle the refunds and take care of the community.

But from my side, nothing changed.

20/

I do not want to destroy anyone’s reputation.

I want a clear statement from Nandi, a proper response to the community, refunds handled for everyone who is owed one, and for him to take responsibility for the promises that were made.

If there were personal reasons for his absence, I genuinely hope he is okay.

But even then, disappearing without proper communication after selling a premium product is not fair to the people who trusted him.

21/

Nandi has done a lot of helpful things for the Framer community, and that is exactly why this situation is so disappointing.

People trusted him because of who they thought he was.

Now he has a chance to show that he is still that person by taking care of this properly.

Not only for me, but for everyone in the Framer University community who paid, trusted him, and expected more.

22/

If you bought the Framer University course and had a similar or different experience, feel free to reach out. 🫶

I am open to hearing both sides.

But based on my experience, the messages I received, and what happened inside the community, I believe this needed to be said.

Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher.

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity.

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive.

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498

Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490

Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.

Czartoryski Museum, Kraków

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science

Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

Military Tech: Armored tanks, giant crossbows, and portable bridges—way ahead of his era's tech.

Hydraulics and Engineering: Canal locks, diving suits, and self-supporting bridges. He even planned an ideal city to beat plagues.

Anatomy: Sketches more accurate than printed texts of the time, showing heart valves and fetal positions.
Fun fact: He invented the robotic knight in 1495—a mechanical automaton that could wave and sit up.

Steampunk before steam.

Personal Quirks and Legacy

Vegetarian and Animal Lover: Bought caged birds just to free them. Ahead of his time on ethics.

Procrastinator Extraordinaire: Queen Isabella of Spain once joked he'd paint her when pigs fly—ironically, he sketched flying pigs.

Death: May 2, 1519, at age 67 in Amboise, France. Buried in Château d'Amboise; his bones were scattered during the French Revolution.

Da Vinci's influence? Everywhere—from NASA's designs to modern AI ethics (he'd probably geek out over neural networks).

In 2025, his Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017, and recent scans of his notebooks (like the Leicester Codex) keep revealing hidden layers via infrared tech.

A new Harvard study documents a housing market in crisis. But its real argument is more unsettling: the era when an ordinary American could expect to own a home may have been the exception—not the rule.

For half a century, Harvard has been writing versions of the same warning. In 1977, researchers at what was then the Harvard-MIT Joint Center for Urban Studies observed that only the most affluent families in the United States would be able to own their houses if housing trends from the time continued. In 1970, nearly half of all families could afford a median-priced home. By 1975, only 27% could. The study’s authors warned that an average home could cost $78,000 by the 1980s—a number they offered as a sign of alarm. The median price of a new single-family home in 2025 was $417,400.

Nobody listened, and then—briefly, strangely—the warning became wrong. The early 1980s brought punishing interest rates, but the decade that followed delivered falling rates, rising wages, and a housing market that stayed, if not generous, at least navigable for the broad middle class. For a generation, the crisis that Harvard’s researchers had spotted seemed to resolve itself.

But it didn’t.

The Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies’ 2026 State of the Nation’s Housing report is a meticulous account of just how thoroughly that dynamic has returned—and how much worse it may be than it appears. “Across the U.S., persistent affordability challenges and rising economic uncertainty are hurting housing markets,” the authors stated, citing weakening labor markets and plummeting immigration dampening household growth and mobility as sales of existing homes sit at three-decade lows.

It is true that rents have fallen somewhat, but there’s a structural problem: the drivers of demand are weakening. The slowdown in household growth reflects, the Harvard center concludes, “reduced household formation among young adults amid a weakened job market, burdensome student debt and low consumer sentiment.”

The Harvard authors do not say this, but the implication is that what America experienced in the postwar decades—when homeownership surged 20 percentage points in a single generation, when being middle class reliably meant eventually owning a home—was not a natural feature of a capitalist economy. It was the product of a specific, unrepeatable, and heavily subsidized set of historical conditions. And now those conditions are gone.

The window and what created it

The GI Bill sent veterans to the suburbs. Federal mortgage guarantees lowered the barrier to entry for millions of first-time buyers. Highway construction made cheap land available. And strong union density compressed wages upward, so that a factory worker’s income reliably grew faster than a house’s price—until about 1973, just before the Harvard warning about the future trajectory of the national housing market.

“In the past, if you were middle class, it was almost assumed you would become a homeowner,” Ali Wolf, chief economist of the building consultancy Zonda, told Realtor.com in 2024. “Today, the aspiration is still there, but it is a lot more difficult. You have to be wealthy or lucky.”

What changed was not any single policy or market failure, but that the scaffolding holding up the postwar homeownership society came down piece by piece. Union density declined. Real wage growth for non-college workers was largely stagnant for decades until the short-lived “Great Resignation” of 2021—which happened smack dab in the middle of the Pandemic Housing Boom, as home prices surged 54% in a compressed and almost hallucinatory run-up from 2020 to 2022, turning the residual gap between incomes and prices into a chasm.

The 2026 Harvard report documents what that chasm now looks like from ground level. The median existing single-family home in 2025 sold for nearly 5x the median household income—versus a ratio of 3.2x averaged throughout the 1990s. Monthly mortgage payments on that median-priced home, at roughly $2,420 assuming a modest down payment and a 30-year fixed rate, were nearly double what they were at the end of 2020. Just 16% of renter households earned the $120,800 minimum required to afford that home, Harvard calculates. And listings affordable to households earning $75,000 or less, per the National Association of Realtors and Realtor.com , fell from 49% of the national inventory in 2019 to just 23% in March 2026.

The inheritance economy

What makes the current moment distinct from prior affordability crunches—the early 1980s, say, or the aftermath of the 2008 crash—is not just severity but structure. Homeownership is increasingly behaving less like something earned and more like something inherited.

Aggregate homeowner equity reached $34 trillion in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 88% and what Harvard dubbed an “astounding” $16 trillion since 2019. The average homeowner held about $295,000 in home equity. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco found that children of homeowner parents who extracted equity accumulated roughly one-third more housing wealth by age 30 than children of renters. A May 2026 NBER study using data on more than 3.4 million families found that “housing capital is substantially more persistent across generations than earnings”—and that less than half of that persistence can be explained by what children earn.

The Harvard report supplies the market-level evidence to match. The median first-time buyer is now 40 years old and NAR finds that first-time buyers accounted for just 21% of all purchases — an all-time low. The homeownership rate for households under 35 has fallen to 37%, down from 39% in 2022. The Black-white homeownership gap, at 28.7 percentage points, now exceeds the gap recorded in 1995. So many indicators are near 30-year lows that taken together, they suggest more of a return to the 1990s than the 1970s. The subsequent expansion of homeownership in the early 2000s—which eventually triggered the Great Recession—has been all but unwound.

The labor market that no longer bridges the gap

Postwar workers could often compensate for a lack of inherited capital with rising wages. That mechanism is largely broken.

The United States added 116,000 jobs in 2025—the smallest annual gain in a non-recession year since 2003. The economy has become “low-hire, low-fire”: stable at the top, constrained at the bottom, with diminished churn that limits the income mobility young workers need to accelerate savings. Student loan delinquency rates surged from under 1% in late 2024 to 10% by the end of 2025 after pandemic-era payment relief ended.

Household growth slowed for the third consecutive year, to 1.1 million in 2025 from an annual average of 2.0 million in 2020 and 2021. Many young adults are not forming households at all. The share of Americans who moved in the prior year fell to a record low of 11.2%.

Immigration, historically the most reliable source of renter household growth, has been cut drastically. Net international migration fell from 2.7 million in 2024 to 1.3 million in 2025. The Census Bureau projects a further drop to 321,000 in 2026—roughly a third of the annual average from 2001 to 2019. Harvard is direct about the consequences: the impact of declining immigration on household growth will be “substantial and increasingly evident over time.”

The federal government exits the field

If the postwar housing window was created by policy, its closing is also partly a policy choice. And the 2026 Harvard report is unusually frank about the direction that policy is moving.

Federal rental assistance reaches only about one in four very low-income renter households, leaving 13.8 million income-eligible households unassisted, including nearly 9 million with worst-case housing needs. Public housing budgets have been cut. HUD has proposed eliminating existing disparate-impact language—the rule that considered facially neutral policies unlawful when they produced discriminatory housing outcomes. Fair housing staff have been deeply cut. Major discrimination cases have been dropped.

On homelessness, the administration has moved away from Housing First models toward treatment prerequisites for housing access. Homelessness reached a record 770,000 people on a single night in January 2024, up 33 percent since the start of the pandemic. FEMA attempted to cancel its two largest hazard-mitigation programs in 2025, shifting disaster recovery burdens to states and localities that cannot absorb them.

“Only the federal government has the scale of resources needed to meaningfully reduce the shortage of housing affordable to those with the lowest incomes,” Harvard writes. That government is currently moving in the opposite direction.

A partial window, closing on everyone

There is a necessary complication in the “historical accident” thesis—one that strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

The postwar homeownership surge was not universally accessible. FHA loans explicitly redlined Black neighborhoods. The GI Bill was administered in ways that largely excluded Black veterans from its housing benefits. Restrictive covenants kept communities segregated. The middle-class homeownership society that is now reverting was always a partial society—one that opened its door to many white working-class families while leaving others in the entry hall.

But the reversion is no longer limited to those who were historically excluded. Cost burdens are rising fastest among middle-income households earning between $45,000 and $75,000. A college-educated 30-year-old without parental equity support faces a market that is, in structural terms, the most hostile to first-time buyers in recorded history. The window is closing on nearly everyone except those already inside.

The housing market is evolving, has evolved into a mechanism for compounding wealth upward and foreclosing it downward, over decades, across generations. A labor market too weak to bridge income to asset accumulation is not a headwind to the housing market — it is a structural feature of an economy that has made housing the primary dividing line between the asset-owning and the wage-dependent.

The postwar window is not closing. It has closed. The question Harvard’s 2026 report raises — without quite asking it — is whether America is prepared to acknowledge what replaces it: a housing market sorted not by income, but by inheritance.

A man built a company alone. It took him six months. He sold it for $80 million in cash.

No team. No investors. No office lease. No head of product and no head of engineering and no one arguing about the roadmap.

His name is Maor Shlomo. His company was called Base44. It let anyone describe the software they wanted in plain sentences and get a working app back. Not a template. Not a drag-and-drop builder. A real product from a description.

He launched it in January 2025. By June it had 300,000 users and $3.5 million in annual revenue. Still one person. Still no team.

Wix bought it for $80 million. Six months of work.

And here is the part that does not fit in the old model.

In any previous decade this company would have required twenty engineers and three years and several rounds of venture funding and a sales team and a marketing team and a head of operations and a lot of meetings about the meetings. The tools were too many and too complex and too slow for one person to hold the whole thing alone.

Maor had none of that. He had AI tools that let him build as fast as he could think and judgment to build what people actually needed and the discipline to ship before he was certain it was ready.

It turned out that was enough.

And now the main thing.

The software industry spent fifty years building itself on one assumption: that building software required a company. A team. A structure. A process. The work was simply too large and too technical for any single person to handle from the first line of code to the first paying customer.

And then the tools changed and the assumption broke.

Not in a press release and not in a keynote. In a one-person GitHub repository that sold for $80 million six months after its first commit.

In my opinion this is the year the one-person company stopped being an exception.

Not a side project and not a lifestyle business. A real product with 300,000 users that a single person built and sold for more money than most companies raise in their entire life.

What would you build if a team was no longer what stood between you and shipping it?
