THIS SOLO DEV MADE $100K FROM A FEATURE OPENAI WAS ALWAYS GOING TO COPY

he built a tiny ChatGPT browser extension called Easy Folders.

the idea was simple: ChatGPT had messy chats, he wanted folders and subfolders like a real file system.

nothing revolutionary.

but it still made over $100,000 in revenue and later sold for five figures.

the playbook:

> built it while working a full-time software engineering job
> had zero browser extension experience
> launched fast instead of waiting for the perfect product
> promoted it on Reddit, Facebook groups, and OpenAI forums
> watched Stripe for the first paying customer
> used customer emails and bug reports as the roadmap

the real win was not the money.

it proved software was not just something he could build for an employer. it was something he could own, ship, sell, and turn into an asset.

then the platform risk hit.

OpenAI shipped Projects.

Easy Folders did not die instantly, but the extension became less essential overnight. Every ChatGPT update could break the product, and now OpenAI had a native feature overlapping with the core use case.

so he sold.

the exit lesson most builders miss:

> sell while growth is still trending up
> serious buyers move fast, so get on calls within days
> buyers care about revenue, traffic, support load, maintenance, growth, and transferability
> clean handover matters: codebase, domain, payment accounts, docs, and how the app actually works

he waited too long and thinks it cost him a few thousand dollars in the final sale price.

the bigger lesson for AI builders:

coding is getting cheaper every month.

the edge is knowing what to build, judging AI output, talking to users, shipping fast, and getting distribution before the platform copies your feature.

small products can still become real assets.

but only if you ship them before the obvious feature becomes native.

Every time an AI company buys a website ending in “.ai”, a tiny Caribbean island of 15,000 people gets paid.

Decades ago, long before anyone cared, an internet standards body handed out two-letter codes to countries and territories. The one Anguilla was assigned: “.ai”.

For years it meant nothing. Just a random suffix for a tiny island almost nobody could find on a map.

Then ChatGPT launched. And suddenly every AI company on earth wanted a website that ended in .ai.

OpenAI, Perplexity, Meta, xAI, Google, they all wanted it. Because “.ai” instantly signals what your company does. And to register one, you have to pay a fee. To Anguilla.

The scale of what happened next is staggering.

There are now over a million .ai domains registered. Each one costs around $140 every two years. And roughly 90% of them renew.

So this island of 15,000 people now collects a small tax every single time anyone, anywhere in the world, wants an AI web address.

In 2023 it made about $32 million from this. By 2025 it was pulling in nearly $90 million a year.

That’s close to HALF of the island’s entire government budget. From two letters.

And they’re using it well.

Anguilla has cut its national debt by 37% in under five years. It’s funding free healthcare for every kid under 5 and every senior over 70. It eliminated tax on essential food. It’s building a new international airport. And it’s setting up a sovereign wealth fund to protect the money for future generations.

During the actual gold rush, most miners went broke. The people who got rich were the ones selling picks and shovels.

Anguilla didn’t dig for AI gold. It didn’t train a model or chase funding or compete with anyone.

It just happened to own the two letters everyone else needed.

And it’s quietly getting rich off the entire world’s obsession, one domain at a time.

🟢 You'll Know When It Matters

Zoide now has verified email and browser notifications. Here's what that actually means — and why it was built this way.

Until this week, Zoide had exactly one way to tell you something: the bell in the header. It worked, but it had an obvious flaw. If you weren't on the site, you didn't know. An offer landed on your piece, someone outbid you forty seconds before an auction closed, a drop opened its mint window — and you found out whenever you happened to come back.

On a marketplace, that gap isn't a minor inconvenience. It's money.

An accepted offer reserves the piece for 24 hours. That clock starts whether or not you're looking at it. A mint window on a good drop closes in minutes. The difference between knowing now and knowing tomorrow is the difference between a sale and a missed one.

So the gap is closed. Zoide can now reach you three ways: the bell, your browser, and your inbox.

🟢 Three channels, and only two of them are yours to turn off

The bell is always on. It is not configurable, and that is deliberate — it's precisely what makes everything else safe to switch off. Silence your browser notifications and your email entirely, and a time-sensitive notice still waits for you in the bell. You can never lose an opportunity by turning something off. That guarantee is the foundation the rest is built on.

Browser notifications reach you on desktop and mobile, even with the tab closed. You grant the permission once, per device, and you can be selective about what comes through.

Email reaches you anywhere. But it comes with a condition, and that condition is the most important part of this release.

🟢 No email goes to an address you haven't proven is yours

Before this release, Zoide had email addresses on file that nobody had ever confirmed. Typos. Abandoned mailboxes. Addresses typed in a hurry years ago. Sending account information to any of them would have been, at best, useless — and at worst, sending your data to a stranger.

So verification was built, and made a precondition, not a suggestion.

When you change your email address, nothing is saved. You get a six-digit code at the new address, and only when you enter that code does the address become yours on the account. Abandon the process halfway and your previous address stays exactly as it was. There is no state in which Zoide holds an unconfirmed address and treats it as real.

The email channel doesn't open until that's done. Not to be difficult — because consent to receive mail at a mailbox you've proven you control is the only kind of consent that means anything.

And if you later change your address, verification is revoked automatically. The consent belonged to that mailbox, not to the field.

🟢 Not everything was switched on, deliberately

This is the decision most likely to be questioned, so here it is straight.

When you verify your email, Zoide does not start sending you all 22 notification types. Only two categories are on by default: sales and offers — the ones with money and a clock attached. Collections, airdrops, community activity: off, until you decide otherwise.

Opening the tap would have looked more generous. It would also have meant roughly forty-six emails a day flowing out of a domain that was registered days ago, and the fastest way to end up in everyone's spam folder is to behave like something worth filtering. That reputation, once lost, follows every message ever sent — including the one telling you your piece just sold.

Restraint here isn't caution. It's making sure the messages that matter actually arrive.

Everything else is one click away in your settings, grouped by category, switchable individually or all at once.

🟢 The exception: your own account

There is one category that cannot be switched off, and it's better explained than hidden.

Notices about your account itself — your subscription, an affiliate invitation, a courtesy grant — always reach you. They aren't broadcast; they're correspondence about your account, the same class of thing as the bell. You'll find them absent from the settings screen along with a line saying exactly that.

Hiding them and staying quiet about it would be the worse choice.

🟢 What this is really about

None of this is glamorous. Nobody mints a notification preference.

But a marketplace that can't reliably tell you that your piece sold isn't a marketplace yet — it's a gallery with a payment button. The infrastructure that lets a platform reach the right person, at the right moment, through a channel they consented to, is the difference between a project and a business.

This is the first step, and it's a load-bearing one. Verified addresses are what make it possible to send a receipt, a settlement notice, a security alert. Push is what makes a time-limited offer something you can actually act on. Preferences are what keep all of it from becoming noise you learn to ignore.

It was built in the order that made the guarantees possible, not the order that demoed best.

🟢 Turning it on

Open Settings.

Next to your email address there's a green check if it's verified, or an orange cross if it isn't. Press Edit to change it and confirm the code that arrives.

Under Notifications, flip the browser switch. Your browser will ask for permission — that request only happens when you ask for it, never on page load.

Then open any category and set it exactly how you want it.

On iPhone, one extra step: browser notifications only work if Zoide is added to the home screen. That's an Apple restriction, and the settings screen flags it when it applies.

🟢 If this was useful, pass it on

Half the people who'll benefit from this don't know it exists yet. If you found it useful — or if you know someone who has a piece listed and no idea when it sells — send it their way.

A marketplace works better when the people in it actually know what's happening. That's not a marketing line; it's the entire reason this was built. Every collector who turns notifications on is one more person who answers an offer in an hour instead of a week, and that's better for whoever made the offer too.

Share it with a collector, a creator, or anyone who's ever come back to Zoide and found out something had already happened without them.
